courseMetadata.title: Pixel to Production: Senior Frontend Engineering from Runtime to Craft
courseMetadata.description: A 13-section course for working engineers moving into **senior frontend** roles. It runs from the JavaScript runtime and the browser pipeline, through framework internals, algorithms, system design, performance, accessibility, testing and delivery, to CSS architecture, motion, design systems, visual judgment, and a capstone with interview readiness. Every section pairs explanation with **runnable JavaScript**, predict-then-run snippets, graded code challenges, and real-world transfer tasks.

prerequisites.description: About two or more years of professional JavaScript: you write `async`/`await`, array methods and modules without looking them up.
Has shipped at least one feature with a component framework (React is used in examples) and basic HTML and CSS.
Comfortable reading TypeScript type annotations; writing advanced types is taught in Section 1.
Can use browser DevTools (Elements, Network, Console) and run Node.js and npm scripts locally.
Take the **prior knowledge check** before Section 1. Its routing notes tell you which lectures you can skim.

interleavingGroups.rationaleNote: Async work from primitives to product: debounce and pools (s1) reappear as useFetch deduping and abort (s3), the typeahead lifecycle (s5), and its unit tests (s8).
The event loop (s1) is where the rendering pipeline (s2) runs; long tasks (s6) and per-frame springs (s10) are the same model under load.
Pipeline stages are the explanatory lens for jank (s2), virtualization (s5), LCP/CLS fixes (s6), layout choices (s9), and compositor-only motion (s10).
Graph traversal with a visited set recurs in deepClone (s1), DOM/JSON traversal (s4), topological sort (s4), the bundler (s8), and token resolution (s11).
Identity by key links keyed reconciliation (s3), keyed diffs and LRU keys (s4), id-based feed merges (s5), and convergent merges (s13).
Where state lives: render snapshots and re-render triggers (s3), state ownership in design (s5), normalized server cache vs UI state (s5), and headless component context (s11).
Validate what crosses a boundary: typed parsers (s1), storage and CORS (s2), money parsing and error masking (s8), and component prop contracts (s11).
Measure before claiming: profiling renders (s3), rendering-strategy numbers (s3), field p75 (s6), and post-ship observability (s8).
Accessibility across component work: the combobox (s5), widget contracts and announcements (s7), gesture alternatives (s10), headless Dialog/Select (s11), and form redesign (s12).
Prioritize and explain: audit triage (s7), motion audits (s10), and critique structure (s12) share the observation → principle → outcome → change shape.
The craft layer builds on itself: fluid scales and layers (s9) become tokens and themes (s11), then critique vocabulary and type specimens (s12).
Choosing where and when to render: rendering strategies (s3), code splitting and waterfalls (s6), view transitions and flushSync (s10), and capstone scoping (s13).
Release discipline: CI and previews (s8), flags and kill switches (s8), and design-system versioning and deprecation (s11).
Communication under pressure: the talk track (s4), pushback handling (s5), critique delivery (s12), and full loops (s13).
Decisions with evidence: design docs (s5), decision records (s11), fidelity choices (s12), and case studies and stories (s13).

options: then, sync, timer
sync, timer, then
timer, then, sync
sync, then, timer

optionFeedback.feedback: .then callbacks are always deferred, even on a resolved promise; only the executor is synchronous.
The timer is a task, and all queued microtasks run before the next task.
Synchronous code always finishes before any queued callback runs.
Right: synchronous code first, then the microtask checkpoint, then the timer task.

probeQuestions.prompt: A dashboard calls `Promise.all([loadA(), loadB(), loadC()])` and `loadB` rejects after 50 ms. What happens to the requests behind `loadA` and `loadC`?
options: They keep running; only the aggregate promise settles early
They are cancelled automatically
Promise.all waits for them, then rejects
They pause until loadB is retried

optionFeedback.feedback: Right: combinators never cancel work. Cancelling takes an AbortSignal.
Nothing cancels them. Settling the aggregate promise does not stop the underlying work.
That describes allSettled followed by a check. Promise.all rejects on the first rejection.
Promises have no pause or resume mechanism.

probeQuestions.prompt: `const order = (await res.json()) as Order;`. Which statement is correct?
options: TypeScript validates the JSON against Order at runtime
Typing it any instead would be equally safe
It fails to compile
It compiles, but nothing checks the shape at runtime

optionFeedback.feedback: Types are erased. An as-cast is an unchecked assertion.
any turns off checking everywhere the value flows; unknown would force a check.
res.json() returns Promise<any>, which is assignable to anything, so it compiles.
Right: types are erased, so validate at the trust boundary.

probeQuestions.reviewPromptOverride: const order = (await res.json()) as Order;. Which statement is correct?

optionFeedback.feedback: no-cache sets no freshness lifetime.
That is no-store.
That is closer to public vs private.

probeQuestions.prompt: A list of checkboxes uses `key={index}`. The user checks row 2, then deletes row 1. What do they most likely see?
options: The checkmark stays on the same item
All checkboxes reset
The checkmark appears on a different item
React throws an error

optionFeedback.feedback: Keys decide which node belongs to which item, so this only holds with stable keys.
Nodes are reused, not recreated, so their state survives on the wrong item.
Right: index keys reuse DOM nodes by position, so DOM-held state lands on the wrong item.
React silently reuses nodes.

probeQuestions.prompt: `useEffect(() => { subscribe(trackId) }, [])` reads `trackId`. The track changes. What happens?
options: The subscription stays on the first track (a stale closure), and nothing unsubscribes
The component unmounts and remounts
React warns and rewrites the dependencies
The effect reruns because trackId changed

optionFeedback.feedback: Right: an empty dependency array keeps the first render's values, and there is no cleanup.
Changing props does not remount a component unless its key or type changes.
A lint rule can warn, but React never rewrites your dependencies.
Effects rerun only when listed dependencies change, and trackId is not listed.

probeQuestions.prompt: A BFS over 50,000 nodes uses `queue.shift()` to dequeue. What is its time complexity?
options: O(1) per operation, so O(n) overall
O(n²) in the worst case
O(log n)
O(n)

optionFeedback.feedback: Only end operations (push/pop) are amortized O(1).
Right: each shift moves every remaining element. Use a head index instead.
BFS visits every node, so it cannot be sublinear.
Visiting each node once is O(n), but shift is O(n) itself.

competencies.title: JavaScript Execution Model
competencies.description: Covers the event loop, the call stack, microtask vs macrotask queues, closures, prototypes, and `this` binding. Learners use these to predict behavior and to debug async code from first principles.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict the exact output of snippets that mix synchronous code, promise reactions, `await`, and timers, and justify every line.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-js-execution-model (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Debug closure, prototype, and `this` bugs by reasoning about bindings and call sites, without running the code.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-js-execution-model (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A setTimeout with 0 ms runs before an already-resolved promise's .then callback.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The microtask queue drains completely before the next macrotask starts, so every queued promise reaction runs before any timer callback, whatever its delay.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run Runnable Example s01-r1 and Predict-the-Output s01-p1, tracing each with the two-list method (microtasks vs tasks) from Lecture 1.1. Then write your own snippet that races a resolved promise against setTimeout(0), predict the order on paper, and run it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: await pauses the whole program until the promise settles.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: await suspends only the enclosing async function and returns a pending promise to the caller, which keeps running synchronously; the rest of the function resumes later as a microtask.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s01-r2 (prepareDish) and narrate where control goes at each await. Then redo Exercise s01-e1 and explain why the mutant that awaits each input in a loop ignores an early rejection.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: this is fixed by where a function is defined.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: That is true only for arrow functions. For regular functions, this is set at call time by new, call/apply/bind, a method call, or a plain call (undefined in strict mode).
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Work through s01-r4 line by line, labelling which of the four call-site rules applies to each call. Then take a class method you use as an event handler at work and fix it three ways: bind, an arrow field, and a wrapper.

competencies.title: Async Control Flow and Concurrency
competencies.description: Covers composing, limiting, cancelling, and rate-limiting async work: promise combinators, pools, debounce/throttle, and AbortController.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement promise combinators, a concurrency-limited pool, and debounce/throttle that pass hidden test suites.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-async-control-flow (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Choose between debounce, throttle, cancellation, and latest-wins guards for a stated user need, and defend the choice.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-async-control-flow (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: The function passed to new Promise runs later, like a callback.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The executor runs synchronously during construction. Only .then/.catch/.finally reactions are deferred, which is why creating a promise starts the work immediately.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s01-p1 and point to the lines that log during construction. Then redo Exercise s01-e2 and explain why a pool must accept task functions rather than promises.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: When Promise.all rejects, it cancels the other promises.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Combinators only settle the aggregate promise early. The other operations keep running and their handlers still fire; only an explicit AbortSignal stops the work.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s01-p2 and s03-r3, then add AbortController-based cancellation to your s01-e2 pool and your s03-e3 query client. Verify in the Network panel that the aborted requests show as cancelled.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Debounce and throttle are interchangeable; they just have different defaults.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Debounce fires once after calls stop for the wait period, while throttle guarantees at most one call per wait period during continuous input. They make different promises to the user.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Compare the timelines in media s01-m4, then run debounceScenario (s01-e4) and the throttle suite (s01-t1) on the same input stream. For three real UI inputs (search box, drag preview, scroll analytics), write which one each needs and why.

competencies.title: Type-Driven Design in TypeScript
competencies.description: Covers generics, discriminated unions, utility types, and inference used to make invalid states unrepresentable. It also covers judging when strictness is worth its cost.

desiredOutcomes.description: Model a domain with discriminated unions and generics so invalid states fail to compile, and validate `unknown` data at trust boundaries.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-type-driven-design (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Argue where a codebase's strictness prevents real bugs and where it has become ceremony.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-type-driven-design (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: TypeScript types validate data at runtime, so a typed API response is safe.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Types are erased at compile time. An as-cast on network data checks nothing, so data crossing a trust boundary still needs a runtime parser.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s01-e5 (parseOrderEvent) and s02-t2 (prefs store). Then find one `as SomeType` on fetched or stored data in a codebase you know and replace it with a parser that returns a Result.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: unknown and any are equivalent escape hatches.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: unknown forces you to narrow or validate a value before using it; any switches type checking off for that value and everything it flows into.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Take a function that accepts any and change it to unknown, then fix each compile error with a narrowing check. List which of those errors were real bugs any had been hiding.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Maximum strictness is always better.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Types nobody can read or that need many casts stop proving anything and slow the team. Judge strictness by the bugs it prevents per unit of reading cost.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Write the Lecture 1.4 strictness memo for a codebase you know: two types that prevent real bugs, one that has become ceremony, and a proposed simplification.

competencies.title: Browser Rendering Pipeline
competencies.description: Covers the path from URL to pixels (parse → DOM/CSSOM → style → layout → paint → composite) and using that model to diagnose jank, layout thrashing, and slow first render.

desiredOutcomes.description: Name the first pipeline stage any DOM or style change invalidates, and diagnose forced layout and jank from a Performance recording.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-browser-rendering-pipeline (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: All style changes cost the same.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A change reruns the first pipeline stage it affects and everything after it: geometry changes trigger layout, color changes trigger paint, and transform/opacity on a layer can be composite-only.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s02-r1 and s10-r2, then record two versions of the same animation (top vs transform) in the Performance panel and label the Layout and Paint blocks in each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Reading offsetHeight is free.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A geometry read after a write forces a synchronous layout, because the browser cannot return a stale answer; in a loop this becomes layout thrashing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s02-r2 and predict s02-p1 before running it. Then redo Exercise s02-e1 (DOM batcher) and use it to remove a forced reflow from a real page, with before/after traces.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: requestAnimationFrame guarantees smooth animation.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: rAF schedules work just before the next frame; it cannot shrink the work. A 45 ms callback still misses the ~16.7 ms budget and drops frames.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s02-e1 and explain why the mutant that wraps each call in rAF still thrashes. Then do s06-e4 and compare deferring 240 ms of work with chunking it.

competencies.title: HTTP Caching, CORS, and Browser Storage
competencies.description: Covers designing a caching strategy with Cache-Control and validators, explaining how CORS is enforced, and choosing between cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design cache headers for hashed assets, HTML, and personal data, and predict what the browser does on the second visit.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-http-caching-and-storage (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Diagnose a CORS failure from its exact message and choose the right storage for a stated requirement, including where auth credentials belong.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-http-caching-and-storage (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Cache-Control: no-cache means the response is not cached.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: no-cache means store the response but revalidate before every use; no-store is the directive that prevents storage.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s02-r3 and redo Exercise s02-e2. Then serve one page with no-cache + ETag and show the 304 on the second visit in the Network panel.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: CORS protects my server from attackers.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The browser enforces CORS to protect users' credentialed requests. The server still receives simple requests, and curl or server-to-server calls ignore CORS entirely.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s02-e3 and explain why serverProcessed is true even when blocked. Then reproduce a CORS failure between two local origins and show the 200 in the server log alongside the browser error.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: localStorage is a safe place for auth tokens.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Any script on the origin, including an XSS payload, can read localStorage. It is also synchronous and string-only; session credentials belong in HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s02-p2, then redo s02-t2. Write the Lecture 2.4 storage memo that places a session credential, a theme preference, and an offline reading list, with the security reasoning.

competencies.title: React Rendering Model
competencies.description: Covers render and commit phases, reconciliation and keys, hook semantics, and effect timing. The goal is to predict re-renders and fix effect bugs deliberately.

desiredOutcomes.description: Predict which components render and which commit for a given state or context change.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-react-rendering-model (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Fix stale closures, missing cleanups, and index-key bugs deliberately, explaining each from how React actually works.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-react-rendering-model (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A re-render means the DOM updated.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Rendering produces a description; reconciliation compares it with the previous one and commits only the differences. Many renders commit nothing.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s03-r1 and redo Exercises s03-e1 (reconcileKeyed: zero operations for an unchanged list) and s03-e4 (rendered vs committed). Then use the React Profiler on a real app and find a component that renders without committing.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: useEffect is componentDidMount.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Effects synchronize with their dependencies: they run after every commit where a dependency changed, and their cleanup runs before each rerun and on unmount.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s03-e2 (implement useEffect) and fix s03-t2 (PlayerProgress). Then find an effect with an empty dependency array that reads props or state and make its dependencies honest.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Keys just silence a warning, so an index works fine.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Keys decide which DOM node, and the state it holds, belongs to which item. Index keys attach inputs, focus, and checkmarks to the wrong items when a list reorders or shrinks.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s03-p2, then redo Exercise s03-e1 comparing id keys with index keys. Build a small list with uncontrolled inputs, delete the first row, and watch the drafts move.

competencies.title: Rendering Strategy Selection
competencies.description: Covers choosing among client rendering, SSR, Server Components, streaming, static generation, and edge rendering for a given product constraint, and backing the choice with measurements.

desiredOutcomes.description: Recommend a rendering strategy for a stated product constraint and back it with measured TTFB, LCP, JS bytes, and interactivity.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-rendering-strategy-selection (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Server Components are just SSR.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: SSR renders HTML and then ships and hydrates every component. Server Components run only on the server, so their code is never shipped or hydrated.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-read the "What each ships" table in Lecture 3.5 and build the s03 album page with SSR and with RSC. Compare JS transferred and hydration time on a throttled profile.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: SSR is always faster than client rendering.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: SSR can improve first paint while increasing TTFB (server work) and delaying interactivity (hydration). Whether it wins depends on the page and must be measured.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Measure the CSR and SSR versions of the album page on a mid-range mobile profile (5 runs each). Report TTFB, LCP, and time until the play button responds, and explain where SSR lost.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Edge rendering always lowers latency.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Rendering close to the user but far from the data turns each sequential query into a long round trip, which can make TTFB worse.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Sketch the Lecture 3.5 edge timeline for a page that makes three sequential queries to a distant database. Calculate TTFB for region vs edge rendering with your own RTT numbers.

competencies.title: Algorithmic Pattern Recognition
competencies.description: Covers classifying a problem into a core pattern (two pointers, sliding window, hashing, stack/queue, BFS/DFS, binary search, backtracking, basic DP) quickly, then implementing it with correct complexity.

desiredOutcomes.description: Classify an unseen problem into its pattern within about a minute, state the invariant, and implement it with correct complexity.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-algorithmic-pattern-recognition (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Memorizing solutions builds pattern recognition.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Recognition comes from reading constraints and stating the invariant. A recalled template breaks on a small twist, like document order requiring DFS, or Kahn's algorithm needing its cycle check.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For five problems from your parallel-track log, write only the signals, pattern, and invariant before coding (Lecture 4.1). Redo Exercises s04-e2 and s04-e6 and explain which invariant each mutant skipped.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Built-in array methods like shift, includes, and find are O(1).
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: shift, unshift, includes, indexOf, find, and splice are O(n). Inside a loop over n items they make the whole algorithm quadratic.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s04-r1 and redo Exercises s04-e3 and s05-e4, whose tests count array reads. Then search a codebase you know for find/includes/shift inside loops and fix one with a Map, Set, or head pointer.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Recursion is always the clean choice.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: JavaScript engines allow roughly 10^4 to 10^5 stack frames. Recursing over deep or untrusted input overflows the stack, so an explicit stack or queue is sometimes required.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s04-r3 and redo Exercise s04-e1 (flattenObject) iteratively. Then convert one recursive traversal you own to an explicit stack.

competencies.title: Data Structures in UI Engineering
competencies.description: Covers recognizing trees, graphs, queues, caches, and linked structures hidden inside frontend problems (DOM traversal, dependency graphs, LRU caches, path-based access) and implementing them.

desiredOutcomes.description: Recognize the tree, graph, queue, or cache hiding in a frontend problem and implement it (LRU, topological sort, traversals, keyed diffs).
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-ui-data-structures (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Frontend work doesn't need data structures.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The DOM, component trees, module graphs, undo stacks, caches, and nested API data are all classic data structures, and treating them as flat records produces bugs.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercises s01-e3 (deepClone as graph traversal) and s04-e4 (getPath with a frontier). For one feature at work, name the tree, graph, queue, or cache hiding inside it.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A Map-based LRU is a hack.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Map's insertion-order iteration is specified by ECMAScript, so delete-then-set is a legitimate O(1) move-to-recent. A plain object is the risky substitute, because it lists integer-like keys first.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s04-r2, predict s04-p2, and redo Exercise s04-e5 with numeric-looking keys. Write both LRU versions and compare their complexity.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Topological sort is only for build tools.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Any ordering under dependencies is a topological sort: migrations, form-field validation, onboarding steps, spreadsheet recalculation, and loading a truck.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s04-e6, including the dockTasks graph, then list three dependency-ordering problems in your own product and sketch the graph for one of them.

competencies.title: Live Problem-Solving Communication
competencies.description: Covers thinking aloud, clarifying constraints, stating an approach before coding, and handling follow-ups and hints under time pressure.

desiredOutcomes.description: Run a timed round out loud (clarify, examples, approach and complexity, code, test, follow-ups) and score it with evidence from a recording.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-live-problem-solving-communication (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Silence while coding is efficient.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Interviewers can't grade or hint at reasoning they can't hear. Narrating intent lets them give credit and steer you away from dead ends early.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Record a 25-minute timed problem (for example s13-e5) and count the silences longer than 30 seconds. Redo it narrating intent with the Lecture 4.4 talk track and compare the two recordings.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Only the correct final answer is graded.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Rubrics score understanding, approach, code quality, testing, and communication separately. A clean process with a small bug often beats a silent perfect answer.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Score your last recorded mock round on the s4 rubric across all six dimensions, then pick the two lowest and plan one practice action for each.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A follow-up question means I got it wrong.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Follow-ups usually come after you have met the baseline; the interviewer is probing for depth and seniority.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Practice the Lecture 4.4 follow-up script: for three solved problems, write the most likely follow-up and a 60-second structured answer (acknowledge, reason from the operations, name the risk).

competencies.title: Frontend System Design
competencies.description: Covers leading an open-ended design of a client application: requirements, component boundaries, state ownership, data flow, API contracts, and performance and accessibility constraints, all defended under pushback.

desiredOutcomes.description: Lead a 45-minute frontend design session from requirements to deep dives, placing each piece of state at its correct owner.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-frontend-system-design (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Defend design trade-offs under pushback with constraint → cost → conditional alternative.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-frontend-system-design (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A design session should start with the component tree or the framework.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Requirements with numbers, the data model, and the API contract come first; component boundaries follow from data ownership.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo the first 12 minutes of "Design a trip feed" (Lecture 5.1) without drawing a component until the requirements, data model, and API are on the board. Then do it for a new prompt.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Put everything in a global store.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: State belongs at the lowest owner that needs it: component, nearby context, URL, or a server cache. A global store by default hides ownership and ties unrelated parts together.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Fill in the Lecture 5.1 state-ownership table for an app you know, labelling each piece of state as ephemeral UI, shared UI, navigational, server cache, or draft, and move one misplaced piece.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Virtualization is always better than pagination.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Virtualization breaks find-in-page, printing, and screen-reader navigation, and adds complexity; pagination fits shareable, searchable, printable views.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Apply the Lecture 5.3 decision table to three lists you use (a search results page, a feed, a data grid) and defend each choice against the opposite pushback.

competencies.title: Client Data Management
competencies.description: Covers normalized stores, selectors, cache invalidation, optimistic updates with rollback, request deduplication, and cursor pagination.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build normalized stores with memoized selectors, optimistic updates with rollback and reconciliation, and cursor-paginated feeds that merge without duplicates.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-client-data-management (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Server state and UI state are the same kind of state.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Server state is a cache of data owned elsewhere, with freshness and invalidation; UI state is local truth. Mixing them lets a refetch wipe out a user's draft.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s05-e2 and explain why the mutant loses the draft. Then check an app you know: does any refetch or cache reset overwrite UI state?

commonMisconceptions.misconception: An optimistic update just sets the new value.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: It also needs the last confirmed value for rollback, reconciliation with the server response, and a rule (such as sequence numbers or clocks) for which result wins.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s05-p1, redo Exercises s05-e3 (likes) and s13-e1 (convergent merge), and add rollback plus sequence numbers to one optimistic action in your own code.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Offset pagination works fine for live feeds.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: New items shift offsets, so the next page duplicates or skips items. Server-issued cursors and merging by id avoid this.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercises s02-e4 and s05-e5 and watch the offset mutants duplicate posts. Check whether a feed you use paginates by offset, and describe the fix.

competencies.title: Web Performance Optimization
competencies.description: Covers measuring and improving LCP, INP, and CLS with lab and field data, applying code splitting, image pipelines, and resource hints, and tying each fix to the rendering pipeline.

desiredOutcomes.description: Take a page from failing to passing Core Web Vitals, tying each fix to a metric, a sub-part, and a pipeline stage, with lab and field evidence.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-web-performance-optimization (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Explain lab vs field discrepancies and report p75 by metric, page, and device.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-web-performance-optimization (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A good Lighthouse score means users have a good experience.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Lighthouse is one synthetic page load on one simulated device with no interactions. Core Web Vitals are judged on field p75, and INP only exists in the field.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercises s06-e1 and s06-e5. Compare a real site's CrUX p75 values with five Lighthouse runs and write down two reasons they differ (Lecture 6.4).

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Preloading more resources speeds things up.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Preloads compete for bandwidth and priority, so preloading low-value resources delays the ones that matter, often the LCP image.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s06-p1 and redo Exercise s06-e2. Remove all but two preloads from a page, then compare waterfalls and LCP before and after.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Code splitting always makes pages faster.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Each chunk discovered only after its parent loads costs a round trip, and splitting code needed during an interaction delays that interaction.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s06-e3 and compare the chain, fan-out, and modulepreload cases. Find one dynamic-import chain in a real bundle and fix it with modulepreload or by merging.

competencies.title: Accessible Component Engineering
competencies.description: Covers building widgets that work with keyboards, screen readers, and reduced motion, using semantic HTML first and ARIA only where it's needed, with correct focus management and live regions.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build combobox, dialog, menu, and tabs widgets that pass keyboard and screen-reader scripts, with correct focus management and live regions.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-accessible-component-engineering (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Adding ARIA makes things more accessible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: ARIA only changes what the accessibility tree reports and adds no behavior. Wrong or redundant ARIA can override good native semantics and make things worse.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercises s07-e2 (aria-modal does not trap focus) and s07-e3 (errors in aria-label replace the name). Audit one component for ARIA that could be replaced with a native element.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: role="button" on a div is equivalent to a button.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The role changes only the announcement. The div still lacks focusability, Enter and Space activation, disabled semantics, and form behavior.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s07-p1, then redo Exercise s07-e1 including Space activation. Replace one clickable div in a real codebase with a button and test it with the keyboard.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A live region announces content that is inserted along with it.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Screen readers watch live regions that already exist. A region inserted together with its message is often treated as new content, not a change, and stays silent.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s07-p2 and redo Exercise s07-e4. Build a toast system whose regions render at app start, and verify it with VoiceOver or NVDA, including a repeated identical message.

competencies.title: Accessibility Auditing and Advocacy
competencies.description: Covers auditing an interface with automated and manual methods, prioritizing findings by severity and effort, and explaining fixes to both designers and engineers.

desiredOutcomes.description: Audit a real interface with automated and manual methods, prioritize by severity → effort → reach, and explain fixes to designers and engineers.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-accessibility-auditing (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Automated tools find most accessibility issues.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Automated checkers verify only the mechanically testable subset. Keyboard, screen-reader, zoom, and cognitive checks find most of the barriers that block tasks.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Run axe on a real flow, then do a keyboard-only pass and a screen-reader pass. List the findings the tool missed, following the Lecture 7.4 worked example.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Accessibility is a QA step at the end.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Most failures are baked in at the design-token and component-API level, where they are cheapest to fix and fixing them once fixes every page.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Trace three findings from an audit back to their root cause (a token, a component API, or a design pattern) and write the fix at that level.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: All accessibility violations are equally urgent.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A blocker such as a keyboard trap in checkout outranks hundreds of minor warnings. Prioritize by severity, then effort, then reach, grouped by root cause.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s07-e5 and explain why the effort-only mutant is wrong. Re-sort an existing audit report by severity → effort → reach.

competencies.title: Testing Strategy
competencies.description: Covers deciding what to test at the unit, integration, and end-to-end layers, writing behavior-focused tests, and justifying the split.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write a layered, behavior-focused test suite (unit, integration, one E2E journey) and justify the split in writing.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-testing-strategy (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: High coverage means high confidence.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Coverage measures which lines executed, not which behavior was asserted. The mutation question is: would a test fail if this line broke?
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s08-r1 and fix s08-t2 (validateTransfer). Run a mutation-testing tool (such as Stryker) on a well-covered module and kill three surviving mutants.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Unit tests should check a component's internals.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Tests coupled to implementation break on refactors without protecting behavior. Assert on what a user or caller can observe, and query the DOM by role and name.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s08-p1, then rewrite three tests in a real suite that assert on internal state or hook calls so they assert on observable behavior instead.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More E2E tests make the product safer.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: E2E tests are slow and flaky, and their failures are imprecise. A few critical journeys buy most of their value; logic and timing belong in unit tests.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Write the s08 layered plan for a feature you own: move each E2E-only case to the lowest layer that can catch it, and keep 1–3 critical journeys.

competencies.title: Build, Delivery, and Observability
competencies.description: Covers what a bundler does (module resolution, dependency graphs, tree-shaking), plus CI, preview deploys, feature flags, error tracking, and knowing a feature works after it ships.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build a minimal ESM bundler and a CI pipeline with preview deploys, and explain what each stage guarantees.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-build-and-delivery-pipeline (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Ship a feature dark behind a flag with a kill switch and trace a production error end to end.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-build-and-delivery-pipeline (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A bundler just concatenates files.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A bundler resolves a dependency graph, orders and scopes modules, evaluates each once, and can tree-shake only static ESM.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s08-e1 and run the concatenation mutant to see the ReferenceError. Then open a real bundle with an analyzer and find the module registry and one tree-shaken export.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A feature flag is just an if statement.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Flags are policy with a lifecycle: kill switch first, overrides, targeting, sticky rollout, and removal once the decision is made. Stale flags become debt.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s08-p2 and redo Exercise s08-e2, including staleFlags. Run a kill-switch drill on a flagged feature and time how long it takes to turn it off.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Shipped means done.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Without instrumentation (release-tagged errors, cohort metrics, a kill threshold) you cannot tell whether a feature works for real users.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s08-e3 and write the "what it works means" metrics for a feature you shipped recently, including the kill threshold.

competencies.title: Modern CSS Layout and Architecture
competencies.description: Covers grid, subgrid, flexbox, container queries, `:has`, logical properties, fluid scales, and cascade layers, along with structuring and choosing a styling approach for large codebases.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build layouts that adapt by container and viewport with grid, subgrid, container queries, and `:has`, with no media-query sprawl.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-css-layout-architecture (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Design a cascade-layers architecture and a styling-approach recommendation grounded in runtime cost and team scale.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-css-layout-architecture (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Specificity problems are solved with !important or more selectors.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Escalation invites more escalation. Cascade layers decide precedence before specificity, and :where() gives zero-specificity defaults, which solves conflicts structurally.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s09-p1 and s09-p2, redo Exercises s09-e1 and s09-e2, and move one legacy or vendor stylesheet into an early layer so you can delete its !important overrides.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Container queries replace media queries.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Components respond to their containers, but the app shell and user preferences (reduced motion, color scheme, pointer type) still respond to the viewport and media features.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s09-e3 and fill in the Lecture 9.2 container-vs-viewport table for your own app.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Tailwind vs CSS-in-JS is only a syntax preference.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Approaches differ in runtime style work, Server Component compatibility, token type-safety, and how they scale across teams.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s09-e4 and write the Lecture 9.5 recommendation for a real team, weighing runtime cost, RSC compatibility, token safety, and team size.

competencies.title: Motion Engineering
competencies.description: Covers implementing transitions, keyframes, springs, gestures, and view transitions with CSS, the Web Animations API, and libraries, while respecting reduced motion and judging when motion is functional.

desiredOutcomes.description: Implement compositor-only motion, springs with velocity handoff, and gesture-driven components that respect reduced motion.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-motion-engineering (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Audit a product's motion and classify each animation as functional or decorative, with proposed cuts.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-motion-engineering (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Any property is cheap to animate.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Width, height, top, and margin run layout (and paint) every frame; transform and opacity on a layer can stay on the compositor.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s10-r2, redo Exercises s10-e3 and s10-e4, and convert one height or top animation in a real product to a FLIP transform with trace evidence.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Reduced motion means no motion at all.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: The preference targets vestibular triggers (large movement, zoom, parallax). Fades and finger-driven dragging are generally fine and still carry information.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s10-p2, fix s10-t2, and turn on your OS reduce-motion setting to record which animations in two apps you use change and which stay.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A spring is just an easing curve.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Springs are physically parameterized: their duration emerges from stiffness, damping, and mass, and they can be interrupted or retargeted while preserving velocity.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s10-p1 and redo Exercises s10-e1 and s10-e2. Grab a sheet mid-animation in your own build and compare a restarted tween with a retargeted spring.

competencies.title: Design System Architecture
competencies.description: Covers tiered tokens and theming, composable component APIs, documentation, design-code sync, and versioning with deprecation paths.

desiredOutcomes.description: Build a three-tier token system with validated themes and headless compound components with small, closed APIs.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-design-system-architecture (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

desiredOutcomes.description: Evolve a design system safely: drift checks, semver, deprecation warnings, codemods, and migration guides.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 85% mastery threshold on mastery-design-system-architecture (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A design system is a component library.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Tokens, documentation, contribution rules, versioning, and deprecation paths are what make a set of components a system that people can adopt and upgrade safely.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s11-p2 and redo Exercise s11-e4. For a design system you use, write down its versioning and deprecation policy, or note that it has none.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More props make a component more flexible.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Every prop multiplies the states to design, test, and document, and free-form styling props bypass tokens and themes. Closed variants plus composition scale better.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s11-r2 and redo Exercise s11-e2. Write a props-vs-composition decision record for one component with more than eight props.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Design tokens are just color variables.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Tokens cover every design decision, and the semantic tier (purpose-named tokens that vary per theme) is what makes theming and dark mode possible without touching components.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s11-p1 and redo Exercises s11-e1 and s11-e3. Add a high-contrast theme to your token build by changing only the semantic tier.

competencies.title: Visual Design Judgment
competencies.description: Covers critiquing and improving typography, spacing, hierarchy, and color with specific, actionable language in design critiques and engineering reviews.

desiredOutcomes.description: Write critiques as observation → principle → outcome → change, and create hierarchy by removing emphasis rather than adding it.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-visual-design-judgment (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Taste is innate: you either have it or you don't.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Taste is trained pattern recognition backed by nameable principles (scale, measure, proximity, hierarchy) that anyone can learn to see.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s12-p2, then describe three real screens using only Lecture 12.1 vocabulary, naming the principle behind each observation.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Critique is just personal opinion.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Useful critique ties a visible observation to a principle and a user outcome, and proposes a concrete change. That makes it checkable and actionable.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s12-e1 and run your last five review comments through lintCritique, rewriting any that fail.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More color and emphasis create hierarchy.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Hierarchy is the contrast between levels. Emphasizing everything erases it, so removing emphasis from secondary elements usually works better.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s12-p1 and redo Exercise s12-e2. Take a busy screen, remove every accent except the primary action, and compare squint tests.

competencies.title: Prototyping and Fidelity Choice
competencies.description: Covers turning a rough brief into a clickable prototype at the right fidelity within a day, and using AI tools for exploration while keeping judgment over what ships.

desiredOutcomes.description: Ship a one-day prototype at the fidelity that answers a named question, and gate AI-assisted work before it ships.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-prototyping-and-fidelity (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Higher fidelity is always better.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Fidelity should match the question being tested. Extra polish costs time and attracts feedback on visuals when you wanted to learn about flow or wording.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s12-e3 and write the question and chosen fidelity for your next three prototypes before building any of them.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Prototype code should be production-ready.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Prototypes skip states, accessibility hardening, and tests on purpose so you can learn fast. Production means rebuilding properly, reusing decisions but not shortcuts.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: For your s12 one-day prototype, list every shortcut you took and what production would require for each, then label the prototype as disposable in its README.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: AI-generated code is ready to ship once it runs.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Running code can still fail accessibility, skip empty/error/loading states, hard-code styles, or mishandle private data. It must pass the same ship gate as any code.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s12-e4 and apply the gate to one piece of AI-assisted code you wrote, fixing every blocker it finds.

competencies.title: Senior Narrative and Portfolio
competencies.description: Covers communicating impact through case studies, a portfolio, and behavioral stories that show ownership, tradeoffs, and influence beyond one's own code.

desiredOutcomes.description: Publish a curated portfolio and decision-focused case study, and tell four STAR+L stories with a clear individual contribution.
desiredOutcomes.verificationCriteria: Reach the 80% mastery threshold on mastery-senior-narrative-and-portfolio (including an Excellent or Adequate self-rating on its written question, checked against the rubric), and succeed on at least one transfer exercise in a section that teaches this competency.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: More projects make a stronger portfolio.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Reviewer attention is fixed, so a few deep pieces with explained decisions beat a gallery where your best work may never be read.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Predict s13-p2 and redo Exercise s13-e4 on your own project list. Cut your portfolio to the capstone plus 3–4 pieces, each with a "why it matters" note.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: A case study describes features.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: A case study describes decisions: the choice, the alternatives, the reason, the cost accepted, the evidence, and what you would change.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Redo Exercise s13-e3 and rewrite one feature-tour paragraph from your case study as a decision record in the Lecture 13.2 format.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Saying 'we' in behavioral answers sounds collaborative.
commonMisconceptions.whyIncorrect: Interviewers need to hear your specific contribution. Use "I" for your actions and "we" for team context; collaboration shows through what you did with others.
commonMisconceptions.remediationStrategy: Re-run s13-r3, redo Exercise s13-e2, and run all four of your stories through checkStory until the Action section uses "I" for your own work.

options: sync, then, timer
then, sync, timer
timer, then, sync
sync, timer, then

`.then` callbacks are always deferred to the microtask queue, even on an already-resolved promise. Only the executor is synchronous.
Synchronous code always finishes before any queued callback runs, because of run-to-completion.
The timer is a task, and every queued microtask runs before the next task starts.

questions.prompt: `async function load() { await fetchMenu(); console.log('menu'); }`. After `load(); console.log('next');`, which statement is true?
options: next logs only after menu, because await pauses the program until the fetch completes.
next logs before menu, because load returns a pending promise at the await and the caller keeps running.
menu never logs unless the caller also uses await.
The order is random and depends on network speed.

optionFeedback.feedback: `await` suspends only `load`. The caller continues synchronously.
Reaching `await` hands control back to the caller, and the rest of `load` resumes later as a microtask.
The continuation runs whether or not the caller awaits the returned promise.
The network affects *when* `menu` logs, but `next` is synchronous and always logs first.

errorPatterns.description: Chose "next logs only after menu, because await pauses the program until the fetch completes.", which reflects the belief: await pauses the whole program until the promise settles.

questions.prompt: `const handler = order.markServed; button.addEventListener('click', handler);`. Inside `markServed` (a regular method in a class), `this.id` throws. Why?
options: The call site is no longer order.markServed(), so the method-call rule doesn't apply. The DOM calls it with this set to the element, or it's undefined in other plain calls.
this was fixed to order where markServed was defined, so the bug must be elsewhere.
addEventListener clones the function and drops its closure.
Class methods can't be used as event handlers.

optionFeedback.feedback: Detaching a method loses the method-call rule. Fix it with `bind`, an arrow field, or a wrapper.
Only arrow functions take `this` from where they're defined. Regular methods get it from the call site.
The function isn't cloned, and closures are preserved. Only `this` depends on the call.
They can. They just need their `this` bound.

questions.prompt: Explain in two or three sentences why `for (var i = 1; i <= 3; i++) fns.push(() => i)` produces functions that all return 4, and give one fix.
successCriteria: 1 point for "captures the binding or variable, not the value"
1 point for "`var` has one binding for the whole loop"
1 point for a valid fix (`let`, IIFE, or factory argument).

rubric.excellent: Earns full marks (3 points): 1 point for "captures the binding or variable, not the value"; 1 point for "`var` has one binding for the whole loop"; 1 point for a valid fix (`let`, IIFE, or factory argument). A model answer: The closures capture the `i` *binding*, not its value at push time, and `var` creates a single binding for the whole function. When the functions run, the loop has finished and `i` is 4. Using `let` creates a fresh binding per iteration, and passing `i` as an argument to a factory also works.
rubric.adequate: Gets the central idea right but misses one or two of the scored points ("`var` has one binding for the whole loop"; a valid fix (`let`, IIFE, or factory argument)), or states them without justification.
rubric.weak: Misses the central point ("captures the binding or variable, not the value") or restates the belief: this is fixed by where a function is defined.

questions.prompt: On the kitchen display, clicking **Fire order** runs `status.textContent = 'Sending…'` and then `calculateAllergenMatrix()`, which is synchronous and takes about 800 ms, and then sends the request. Users never see "Sending…". What's happening?
options: Microtasks always run after the browser renders, so the text is overwritten.

The browser can't render until the current task ends and microtasks drain. The text changed in the DOM, but no paint happens during the 800 ms of synchronous work, and by the time a paint happens the handler has moved on.
DOM writes are asynchronous like setTimeout, so the write is queued behind the calculation.
Adding await before calculateAllergenMatrix() would pause everything so the screen can paint.

optionFeedback.feedback: Microtasks drain before the loop reaches the render step.
Rendering happens between tasks, and run-to-completion blocks it. Fixes include yielding before the heavy work, moving it to a Worker, or chunking it.
The DOM update is synchronous. The *paint* is what waits.

`await` on a non-promise only defers the rest of the function to a microtask, and microtasks run *before* rendering. It doesn't help unless you yield to a task (for example `await new Promise(r => setTimeout(r))`).

questions.prompt: A ticket screen calls `Promise.all([loadOrders(), loadStations(), loadStaff()])`. `loadStations` rejects after 50 ms. What happens to the other two requests?
options: They keep running to completion. Their results are ignored by the aggregate promise, but any .then handlers attached directly to them still run.
Promise.all waits for them to finish and then rejects.
They pause until loadStations is retried.
They are cancelled automatically when Promise.all rejects.

optionFeedback.feedback: The aggregate promise settled early, and nothing else changed.
That's closer to `allSettled` followed by a check. `all` rejects as soon as the first input rejects.
Promises have no pause or resume mechanism.
Combinators never cancel work. Only an explicit `AbortSignal` does.

questions.prompt: While a staff member drags a ticket between columns, the screen must show a live drop preview. Which is right?
options: Either one. They're the same with different defaults.
A throttle of about 16–50 ms.
Neither. Run the preview on every pointermove event.
A trailing debounce of 250 ms.

optionFeedback.feedback: They make different promises to the user: quiet-then-once versus a steady maximum rate.
A throttle guarantees regular updates during continuous input, capped at a steady rate.
Unbounded handlers on high-frequency events can drop frames (see s2). Rate-limiting is the point.
A debounce shows nothing until the hand stops moving, so there's no live preview.

assessments.title: Section 1 Quiz: Type-Driven Design in TypeScript

questions.prompt: `const order = (await res.json()) as Order;`. Which statement is correct?
options: It fails to compile because res.json() returns Promise<any>.
It compiles, but nothing verifies the shape. Parse the unknown value at this trust boundary.
TypeScript checks at runtime that the JSON matches Order.
Typing it any instead would be equally safe, because both skip checks.

optionFeedback.feedback: `any` is assignable to anything, so it compiles, which is exactly the danger.
Validate at the boundary, then rely on the type everywhere after it.
Types are erased. `as` is an unchecked assertion.
`any` disables checking everywhere downstream. `unknown` would force a check.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: const order = (await res.json()) as Order;. Which statement is correct?

errorPatterns.description: Chose "TypeScript checks at runtime that the JSON matches Order.", which reflects the belief: TypeScript types validate data at runtime, so a typed API response is safe.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Redo Exercise s01-e5 (parseOrderEvent) and s02-t2 (prefs store). Then find one `as SomeType` on fetched or stored data in a codebase you know and replace it with a parser that returns a Result.

errorPatterns.description: Chose "Typing it any instead would be equally safe, because both skip checks.", which reflects the belief: unknown and any are equivalent escape hatches.

options: True
False

optionFeedback.feedback: That difference is why `unknown` is the right type for untrusted input.
They aren't equivalent escape hatches, because `unknown` stays safe.

questions.prompt: Give one sign that strict typing in a codebase has become ceremony, and the question you'd ask to decide whether to simplify it.
successCriteria: 1 point for a credible sign (unreadable type, many casts, slow builds for little benefit)
2 points for a cost/benefit question tied to real bugs prevented.

rubric.excellent: Earns full marks (3 points): 1 point for a credible sign (unreadable type, many casts, slow builds for little benefit); 2 points for a cost/benefit question tied to real bugs prevented. A model answer: One sign is a heavily nested conditional type guarding a rarely used helper that needs several `as` casts to satisfy, which means the type is expensive to read and no longer proves anything. The deciding question is: "What concrete bug does this type prevent, and how often would that bug happen?" If you can't name one, simplify.
rubric.adequate: Gets the central idea right but misses one or two of the scored points (a cost/benefit question tied to real bugs prevented), or states them without justification.
rubric.weak: Misses the central point (a credible sign (unreadable type, many casts, slow builds for little benefit)) or restates the belief: Maximum strictness is always better.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Give one sign that strict typing in a codebase has become ceremony, and the question you'd ask to decide whether to simplify it.

errorPatterns.description: Answer relies on the belief: Maximum strictness is always better.
errorPatterns.remediationAction: Write the Lecture 1.4 strictness memo for a codebase you know: two types that prevent real bugs, one that has become ceremony, and a proposed simplification.

questions.prompt: A delivery-integration team models an order as `{ id; isPaid: boolean; isRefunded: boolean; refundReason?: string; paidAt?: number }`. Bugs report "refunded but unpaid" orders. Propose a TypeScript model and explain how it removes this class of bug and where runtime validation is still needed.
successCriteria: 2 points for a union with state-specific fields
1 point for explaining why the bad state is unrepresentable
1 point for an exhaustiveness check
1 point for runtime parsing at the boundary.

rubric.excellent: Earns full marks (5 points): 2 points for a union with state-specific fields; 1 point for explaining why the bad state is unrepresentable; 1 point for an exhaustiveness check; 1 point for runtime parsing at the boundary. A model answer: Use a discriminated union on `status`: `'unpaid' | 'paid' (paidAt: number) | 'refunded' (paidAt: number; refundReason: string)`. "Refunded but unpaid" can't be represented because `refunded` requires `paidAt`. An exhaustive `switch` with a `never` default makes future statuses a compile-time checklist. Payloads from the payment provider still arrive as `unknown` and must be parsed at the trust boundary, because types are erased.
rubric.adequate: Gets the central idea right but misses one or two of the scored points (explaining why the bad state is unrepresentable; an exhaustiveness check; runtime parsing at the boundary), or states them without justification.
rubric.weak: Misses the central point (a union with state-specific fields) or restates the belief: TypeScript types validate data at runtime, so a typed API response is safe.

Animate transform: translateY(-100%) to translateY(0).
Animate height from 0 to 60px.
Animate top from -60px to 0.

On a promoted layer, `transform` is composite-only.
Height changes geometry, which forces layout of everything below it every frame.
`top` is geometry, so it triggers layout (and paint) on every frame.

questions.prompt: `items.forEach(el => { el.style.width = el.offsetWidth / 2 + 'px'; })` runs over 300 cards. What's the cost?

No layout, because offsetWidth is cached on the element.
One layout, because the browser batches style changes until the end of the task.
600 layouts, because both the read and the write cause one.

optionFeedback.feedback: Read-after-write in a loop is layout thrashing.
The value is recomputed whenever layout is dirty.
The browser can't defer when you *read* geometry after a write. Each read forces layout.
Writes only mark layout dirty. The reads pay the cost.

assessments.title: Section 2 Quiz: HTTP Caching, CORS, and Browser Storage

questions.prompt: Which header should the article HTML document have, given that it references content-hashed JS and CSS?
options: Cache-Control: no-cache with an ETag.
Cache-Control: no-store, so readers always get new HTML.
No header at all. The browser will do the right thing.
Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable.

optionFeedback.feedback: The browser keeps the HTML, revalidates each time, and gets a fast 304 when nothing changed.
This works, but it throws away cheap 304 revalidation. `no-cache` already guarantees freshness.
Browsers apply heuristic freshness when there's no header, which can serve stale HTML for hours.
The HTML would be frozen and would keep pointing at old asset hashes after a deploy.

questions.reviewPromptOverride: Which header should the article HTML document have, given that it references content-hashed JS and CSS?

errorPatterns.description: Chose "Cache-Control: no-store, so readers always get new HTML.", which reflects the belief: Cache-Control: no-cache means the response is not cached.

questions.prompt: Your API sends `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: https://news.example` only. An attacker runs `curl` against it. What does CORS do?
options: It encrypts the response so only the allowed origin can read it.
Nothing. CORS is a browser rule about which page scripts can read responses. Protect the API with authentication, authorization, and rate limits.
It makes the API return 403 to non-browser clients.
It blocks the curl request at the server.

optionFeedback.feedback: CORS has nothing to do with encryption.
CORS protects users' credentialed requests in browsers. It isn't server security.
Nothing in CORS changes server status codes.
CORS is enforced by browsers. curl ignores it, and the server processes the request.

questions.prompt: Why report p75 rather than the mean, and why segment by device?
successCriteria: 1 point for the outlier/tail reasoning
1 point for "it's the assessment percentile"
1 point for the segmentation reasoning.

rubric.excellent: Earns full marks (3 points): 1 point for the outlier/tail reasoning; 1 point for "it's the assessment percentile"; 1 point for the segmentation reasoning. A model answer: The mean is distorted by outliers and hides how many users have a poor experience. p75 says what the slower quarter of users gets, and it's the level Core Web Vitals are assessed at. Mobile and desktop have very different distributions, and combining them hides mobile problems behind fast desktop loads.

questions.prompt: After a deploy, the RUM dashboard shows mobile p75 CLS on product pages jumping from 0.04 to 0.18, while Lighthouse on the product page still reports CLS 0.01. Explain the likely discrepancy and how you'd find and fix the cause.
successCriteria: 2 points for explaining lab vs field (timing, scrolling, late content)

rubric.excellent: Earns full marks (6 points): 2 points for explaining lab vs field (timing, scrolling, late content); 2 points for the attribution-driven diagnosis; 1 point for a correct fix type; 1 point for confirming with field p75. A model answer: Lighthouse measures a single page load, often above the fold and without scrolling or late content. The field includes shifts that happen later: a delayed reviews widget, a cookie banner, a promo inserted after an A/B test loads, or images lower on the page without dimensions. Use RUM attribution (the largest shift's element and time) to identify the source, reproduce it in DevTools with the Layout Shift regions and a scroll, then reserve space (`min-height` or `aspect-ratio`), add dimensions, or insert the content below the viewport. Confirm by watching field p75 CLS return below 0.1 over the following weeks.

questions.prompt: Your audit of a vaccination-booking flow finds: (1) a CAPTCHA with no audio or alternative, (2) 60 images missing `alt` (all decorative icons in a repeated card), (3) error messages shown only in red text, (4) focus lost to `<body>` after closing the time-slot dialog. Prioritize them, give severity and effort, and write the one-line engineer fix for the top item.
successCriteria: 2 points for the correct order with a blocker first
2 points for sensible severity and effort
1 point for grouping (2) as one root cause
1 point for a concrete engineer fix for the top item.

rubric.excellent: Earns full marks (6 points): 2 points for the correct order with a blocker first; 2 points for sensible severity and effort; 1 point for grouping (2) as one root cause; 1 point for a concrete engineer fix for the top item. A model answer: (1) CAPTCHA without an alternative: **blocker** (blind and low-vision users can't finish booking), effort M–L. Engineer fix: replace it with a non-visual challenge or risk-based bot detection, or offer an accessible alternative path. (4) Focus lost after the dialog closes: **critical** (keyboard and screen-reader users are disoriented mid-task), effort S. Restore focus to the opener on close. (3) Errors in color only: **serious** (color-blind users may miss errors), effort S. Add an icon plus text and wire `aria-describedby`. (2) Missing alt on decorative icons: **moderate** (noise, but one root cause), effort S. Set `alt=""` in the card component once.
rubric.adequate: Gets the central idea right but misses one or two of the scored points (sensible severity and effort; grouping (2) as one root cause; a concrete engineer fix for the top item), or states them without justification.
rubric.weak: Misses the central point (the correct order with a blocker first) or restates the belief: All accessibility violations are equally urgent.
