learningExperiences.title: Lecture 1.3: Async Control Flow You Can Defend

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Implement `Promise.all`, `allSettled`, and `race` from scratch and explain their settle rules. (objective o3)
2. Implement a promise pool that limits concurrency and preserves result order. (objective o3)
3. Implement `debounce` and `throttle` with leading/trailing options and `cancel`, and choose between them for a stated need. (objective o3)
4. Make time-dependent code testable by injecting a scheduler. (objective o3)

terms.definition: For a promise to become fulfilled or rejected. It happens once and is final.
A function that builds one promise out of many (`all`, `allSettled`, `race`, `any`).
The maximum number of tasks *in flight* at once. Starting a task means calling the function that creates its promise.
Run a function only after calls have stopped for `wait` ms. **Leading** runs on the first call of a burst. **Trailing** runs after the quiet period.
Run a function at most once per `wait` ms during continuous calls, which gives a steady maximum rate.
Passing `now`, `setTimeout`, and `clearTimeout` in as parameters, so tests can drive a manual clock instead of waiting in real time.
The platform's cancellation signal. Section s3 uses it with `fetch`. Settling a combinator early does **not** abort anything by itself.

contentBlocks.content:
### Combinators: the settle rules

| Combinator | Fulfills when | Rejects when | Result shape |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Promise.all` | every input fulfills | **the first** input rejects | values in **input order** |
| `Promise.allSettled` | every input settles | never | `{status, value}` or `{status, reason}` per input |
| `Promise.race` | the first input settles, if it fulfilled | the first input settles, if it rejected | that first outcome |

Note what's missing: **no combinator stops the other work.** When `Promise.all` rejects, the other requests keep running and their results are ignored (misconception `async-control-flow.m2`). If you need real cancellation, pass an `AbortSignal` to each task and abort it yourself.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **combinators decide only how the aggregate promise settles.** Predict the output, run it, then swap `allSettled` for `all` and for `race` and predict again each time.

### Pools: limiting how much is in flight

A kitchen with four burners can't cook forty dishes at once. A **promise pool** takes an array of *task functions* (not promises) and keeps at most `limit` of them running. When one finishes, it starts the next. It writes each result to `results[index]`, so the output order matches the input order even when tasks finish out of order.

Why task *functions*? The work starts when a promise is created, because the executor runs immediately. An array of promises means everything has already started. That's misconception `async-control-flow.m1` showing up in API design.

### Debounce vs throttle: different promises to the user

- **Debounce** says "tell me once they've stopped." It fits a search box (query after typing pauses), autosave, and window-resize layout recalculation.
- **Throttle** says "keep me updated, but no more than N times per second." It fits scroll-position analytics, drag handlers, and live previews.

They are not interchangeable (misconception `async-control-flow.m3`). Debouncing a scroll listener means nothing happens while the user scrolls continuously, and throttling a search box sends queries in the middle of a word.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s01-m4): Debounce vs throttle timelines. A top row of input events (tick marks at irregular times from 0 to 600 ms). Beneath it, three rows show when the handler runs: "debounce, trailing, 100 ms" (one mark after the last event plus 100 ms), "debounce, leading" (a mark at the first event of each burst), and "throttle, 100 ms" (marks at 0, 100, 200, 300… during the burst). The regularity of the throttle row is highlighted.

contentBlocks.content:
### Testing time without fake timers

The engine has no fake timers, so the implementations here accept `{ scheduler }` with `now()`, `setTimeout`, and `clearTimeout`. Tests pass in a **manual scheduler** that advances time on command. This is a real production design choice, too: code that takes its clock as a parameter is deterministic under test.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: async control flow
contentBlocks.content:
- **`results.push(value)` in a combinator or pool.** It records completion order, not input order.
- **Passing promises to a pool.** They've already started, so the limit does nothing.
- **Forgetting the empty-array case.** Your `all` hangs forever.
- **Assuming `Promise.all` rejection aborts the other requests.** Abort them explicitly with `AbortController`.
- **Using `for (const p of promises) await p` as "all".** A later rejection is only observed once the loop reaches it, and it may surface as an unhandled rejection first.
- **Debounce with `leading: true` firing twice for a single call.** Clear the pending trailing call when the leading call has already consumed those arguments.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 1.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- `all` gives input-ordered values and rejects on the first failure. `allSettled` never rejects. `race` takes the first settle, whatever it is.
- Combinators don't cancel anything. Cancellation is a separate signal.
- Pools take task *functions*, cap how many run at once, and write results by index.
- Debounce waits for quiet, while throttle caps the rate. Pick by what the user must see during continuous input.
- Inject the clock and you can test time-based code without fake timers.

interactionSequence.prompt: A waiter tablet recalculates an expensive column layout when the screen size changes. During rotation, size events fire dozens of times, and only the final size matters. What fits?
options: A trailing debounce of about 150 ms
A throttle of about 16 ms
Either one; they are the same with different defaults
Neither; recalculate on every event

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Only the settled value matters, so wait for quiet and run once.
A throttle keeps recalculating during the rotation, which is exactly the wasted work.
They make different promises: quiet-then-once versus a steady maximum rate.
Unbounded expensive work on a high-frequency event drops frames.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Ask what must be visible **during** the burst. Nothing useful is, so debounce. Compare the drag preview in Worked Example 3, where the user must see updates during the burst, so throttle.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate calls `promisePool([fetchMenu(), fetchStaff(), fetchStock()], 1)`. What does the limit of 1 control?
options: Nothing: all three requests started when the array was built, and the pool also receives promises where it expects functions
It makes the three requests run one after another
It delays each request until the previous one resolves
It limits how many results are stored

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Calling `fetchMenu()` starts the work; a pool needs task functions so that it decides when to call them.
They were already running before the pool saw them.
Promises cannot be delayed after creation; the executor already ran.
The limit is about work in flight, not storage.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Pass `[() => fetchMenu(), () => fetchStaff(), () => fetchStock()]`. That API choice follows directly from the executor being synchronous.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Tasks take 20, 5, 5, and 30 ms, with limit 2. Drag the pool events into the order they happen.
options: t=20: task 0 finishes; nothing is left to start
t=0: start task 0 and task 1
t=40: task 3 finishes; resolve with results in input order
t=10: task 2 finishes; start task 3
t=5: task 1 finishes; start task 2

optionFeedback.feedback: Task 0 started at t=0 and takes 20 ms. By then task 3 has already been started, so there is nothing new to launch.
The pool starts `min(limit, tasks.length)` = 2 tasks immediately.
Task 3 started at t=10 and takes 30 ms, so it is the last to finish.
Task 2 started at t=5 and takes 5 ms. Its slot is reused for task 3.
Task 1 is the first to finish, and each finish frees exactly one slot.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Each finished task frees one slot and starts the next unstarted task. Results are written by index, so the output is in input order even though task 0 finished third.
hints: Write down each task's start time and end time.
A task can only start when another finishes.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: Explain why passing a scheduler (`now`, `setTimeout`, `clearTimeout`) into `debounce` makes its tests deterministic, and name one benefit of this design outside of tests.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Tests can pass a manual clock and move time explicitly (`advance(100)`), so the result never depends on real timing or machine speed. Outside tests, the same seam lets you run the logic in environments with different clocks (for example a Worker or server rendering) and makes time an explicit dependency instead of a hidden global.

workedExamples.title: promiseAll from the spec's rules
workedExamples.problem: promiseAll from the spec's rules
steps: **Wrap every input** with `Promise.resolve(value)`, so plain values count as already fulfilled.
**Store each result by index**, never with `push`. Completion order isn't input order.
**Count down** a `remaining` counter and resolve when it reaches 0.
**Handle empty input**: resolve `[]` immediately, or the counter never reaches zero from a callback.
**Reject on the first rejection** by passing the outer `reject` as each input's rejection handler. Later rejections are ignored because a promise settles only once.
workedExamples.conclusion: The whole combinator is about ten lines, and three of them (index storage, the empty case, first-rejection wins) are exactly where interview solutions fail.

fadedVariant.problem: Use the same rules to plan `promiseAllSettled(values)`.
givenSteps: 1. Wrap each input with `Promise.resolve`, and size `results` to the input length.
blankedStepPrompts: 2. What do you store for a fulfilled input, and where?
3. What do you store for a rejected input?
4. When does it resolve, including for empty input?
blankedStepAnswers: `{ status: 'fulfilled', value }` at `results[index]`.
`{ status: 'rejected', reason }` at `results[index]`. Never call an outer `reject`; `allSettled` does not reject.
Count down on every settle and resolve when `remaining` reaches 0. Resolve `[]` immediately for empty input.

workedExamples.title: A four-burner pool
workedExamples.problem: Tasks take 30, 10, 20, and 5 ms, with limit 2.
steps: t=0: start task 0 (30 ms) and task 1 (10 ms). In flight: 2.
t=10: task 1 finishes, so write `results[1]` and start task 2 (20 ms, ends at t=30).
t=30: task 0 finishes, so write `results[0]` and start task 3 (5 ms, ends at t=35). Task 2 also finishes at t=30, so write `results[2]`. There's nothing left to start.
t=35: task 3 finishes, so write `results[3]`. All four are done, so resolve.
workedExamples.conclusion: The in-flight count never went above 2, and the results come out in input order no matter the finishing order. Your tests should assert both properties.

fadedVariant.problem: Tasks take 10, 40, 10, and 10 ms, with limit 2. Trace the pool.
givenSteps: t=0: start task 0 (ends t=10) and task 1 (ends t=40). In flight: 2.
blankedStepPrompts: What happens at t=10?
What happens at t=20?
What happens at t=30 and t=40?
blankedStepAnswers: Task 0 finishes: write `results[0]`, start task 2 (ends t=20).
Task 2 finishes: write `results[2]`, start task 3 (ends t=30).
At t=30 task 3 finishes and nothing is left to start. At t=40 task 1 finishes, all four are done, and the pool resolves in input order. In flight never exceeded 2.

workedExamples.title: Choosing debounce or throttle for the kitchen display
workedExamples.problem: A kitchen display screen has two inputs. (1) Staff type in a "find ticket" box, and each lookup hits the server. (2) Staff drag a ticket across columns, and the screen must show a live drop preview.
steps: The search box should get a **trailing debounce** (about 250 ms). A request mid-word is wasted, and we only care about the settled query.
The drag preview should get a **throttle** (about 16–50 ms). A debounce would show no preview until the hand stops, which feels broken.
workedExamples.conclusion: Choose based on what the *user* needs to see during continuous input, not on which helper you remember.

fadedVariant.problem: Two more kitchen-display inputs: (1) analytics records how far staff scroll the ticket list; (2) a recipe-notes field autosaves.
givenSteps: **Scroll analytics:** throttle (about 250 ms). We want regular samples *during* continuous scrolling; a debounce would record only where scrolling stopped.
blankedStepPrompts: Autosave of recipe notes: debounce or throttle, and why?
What single question decides this choice in general?
blankedStepAnswers: A trailing debounce (about 1 s, often with a maximum wait): save once typing pauses. A throttle would save mid-word and send many partial saves.
What must the user see, or the system record, **during** continuous input?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 1.4: Types That Make Invalid States Unrepresentable

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Model a domain with **discriminated unions** so impossible combinations fail to compile, and use exhaustive checks with `never`. (objective o5)
2. Write generics that carry information through an API: a typed event emitter and an inferring `pipe`. (objective o5)
3. Explain why types are erased at runtime and write runtime validation at trust boundaries. (objective o5)
4. Judge when strictness pays off and when it has become ceremony. (objective o6)

terms.definition: A union of object types that share a literal-typed tag field (for example `status: 'placed' | 'cooking'`). Checking the tag narrows the value to one member.
TypeScript refining a value's type after a check (`typeof`, `in`, a tag comparison, a type guard).
Assigning the "leftover" case to a `never`-typed variable, so a new union member causes a compile error wherever it isn't handled.
A type parameter (`<T>`) that lets one function or type keep the relationship between its inputs and outputs.
Built-ins such as `Pick`, `Omit`, `Partial`, `Record`, and `ReturnType` that derive new types from existing ones.
TypeScript's types don't exist at runtime. The compiled JavaScript carries no checks.
Anywhere data enters from outside the type system: network responses, `localStorage`, `postMessage`, user input, query strings.
`unknown` means "could be anything, so prove it before use." `any` means "stop checking."

contentBlocks.content:
### From booleans to a state machine

A first attempt at an order often looks like this:

contentBlocks.title: About the TypeScript blocks
contentBlocks.content: The TypeScript examples in this lecture are type-checked with `tsc --strict` outside the course engine, and the `@ts-expect-error` lines are part of that check. They are shown read-only because the engine runs JavaScript only. The runtime half of this lecture (the parser in challenge s01-e5) does run here.
type OrderLoose = { id: string; isCooking: boolean; isServed: boolean; cancelReason?: string; servedAt?: number };
It allows nonsense: served *and* cancelled, cooking with a `servedAt` timestamp. The type describes the fields but not the **rules**. A discriminated union encodes the rules:
The `never` check turns "someone added a `refunded` status" into a list of compile errors pointing at every place that needs a decision.

### Generics that carry information

A **typed event emitter** ties each event name to its payload type, so `emit('orderServed', …)` can't be called with the wrong shape:

A **`pipe` with inference** passes each function's output type into the next function's input. Variadic generics can express this, but overloads stay the most readable option. Library code often stops at around 6–10 of them:

### Types are erased, so validate at the boundary

`const order = (await res.json()) as Order` compiles fine and checks nothing. If the server sends `{ status: 'served' }` without `servedAt`, you get `Invalid Date` three components later. Types describe what you *believe*. At a trust boundary you must *check* (misconception `type-driven-design.m1`). Type the raw input as `unknown`, which forces the check, and write a parser that returns either a valid value or an error. (Schema libraries like Zod or Valibot generate both the check and the type. The idea is the same.) `any` would silently skip all of this, which is why `unknown` and `any` are not equivalent (misconception `type-driven-design.m2`).

### Strictness has a price

Strict types pay off when they **catch real bugs at the edges people touch most**: public component props, API boundaries, state machines, event payloads. They become ceremony (misconception `type-driven-design.m3`) when:

- Nobody on the team can read the conditional-type puzzle guarding a helper used in two places.
- The types need so many `as` casts that they no longer prove anything.
- Compile times or IDE latency get worse for a guarantee that tests already cover more cheaply.

A useful test is **"what bug does this type prevent, and how often would it happen?"** If you can't name the bug, simplify the type.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s01-m5): Where types help vs. where they cost. A 2×2 grid. The x-axis is "how often this boundary changes / how many people touch it" and the y-axis is "cost to read and maintain the type." The bottom-right quadrant, "high traffic, cheap type," is labelled best value: props, API parsers, unions. The top-left, "low traffic, expensive type," is labelled ceremony: simplify. Example stickers are placed in each quadrant.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: TypeScript
contentBlocks.content:
- **`as SomeType` on network data.** This is an assertion, not a check. Parse `unknown` instead.
- **Reaching for `any` to silence an error.** Use `unknown` and narrow, or fix the type.
- **Optional-field soup (`a?: …; b?: …`) for mutually exclusive states.** Use a union.
- **No exhaustiveness check.** New union members then fall through silently.
- **Clever types nobody can maintain.** If the type is harder to read than the bug it prevents, simplify it.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 1.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Discriminated unions plus `never` checks turn domain rules into compile errors.
- Generics keep the relationship between inputs and outputs. Typed emitters and `pipe` are the classic examples.
- Types are erased, so validate `unknown` data at trust boundaries.
- Judge strictness by the bugs it prevents per unit of reading cost.

interactionSequence.prompt: A ticket shows "served" and "cancelled" at the same time. Which change makes that state impossible to construct?
options: A discriminated union on status, where only the served member has servedAt and only the cancelled member has reason
Keep the booleans and cast each order object with as Order
Type orders as any and catch the mistake in code review
Use status: string plus optional servedAt and reason fields

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Each member carries exactly the fields its state allows, so the bad combination does not type-check.
An `as` cast is an unchecked assertion; it makes nothing impossible.
`any` turns checking off, which is the opposite of the goal.
Optional fields still allow every combination, including the invalid one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Encode the **rules**, not just the fields. The union has 4 states instead of 8 flag combinations, and the compiler rejects the rest.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: What type does TypeScript infer for `pipe((items: string[]) => items.length, (count: number) => count > 2)` using the overloads from the lecture?
options: (a: string[]) => boolean
(a: unknown) => unknown
any
A compile error, because the steps have different types

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The overload `pipe<A, B, C>` carries `A = string[]` in and `C = boolean` out.
That is the implementation signature, which callers never see; the overloads are what they get.
Nothing here widens to `any`; that would defeat the point of the overloads.
Steps may have different types, as long as each output matches the next input: `number` feeds `number`.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Generics keep the **relationship** between inputs and outputs. Each step's output type becomes the next step's input type, and the whole pipe exposes only the first input and the last output.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your restaurant-ordering codebase has a helper type `DeepReadonlyExcept<T, K extends Paths<T>>`, 40 lines of conditional types. It is used in three files, those files contain eleven `as` casts to satisfy it, and nobody on the team can explain it. Should you keep it? Apply the lecture's test and state what you would do.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Ask: **what bug does this type prevent, and how often would it happen?** Eleven casts mean the type no longer proves anything at those sites, and nobody can maintain it, so the reading cost is high and the protection is low. A strong answer proposes replacing it with something simple (for example `Readonly<T>` at the boundary, or a plain type plus a test) and keeping strictness where it catches real bugs, such as the order union and the API parser.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: In two sentences, explain why a type annotation on API data is not enough, and what you write instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Types are erased at compile time, so `as Order` checks nothing when real data arrives. Type the raw input as `unknown` and run a parser that returns a valid value or an error; the type then describes data that has actually been checked.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Refactoring booleans into a union
workedExamples.problem: **Given** `{ isCooking, isServed, cancelReason? }` and a bug report: "Ticket shows 'served' and 'cancelled' at once."
steps: **List the real states:** placed, cooking, served, cancelled. That's 4, compared with 2×2×2 = 8 combinations from the booleans.
**List which fields are valid in each state:** `station` only while cooking, `servedAt` only when served, `reason` only when cancelled.
**Write one union member per state**, with the tag `status`.
**Replace the `if`-chains with a `switch` plus a `never` default.**
**Compile.** Every place that combined the flags inconsistently now errors, and each error is a bug you found without a test.
workedExamples.conclusion: The union made the reported bug impossible to represent, and the compiler found the other places with the same bug.

fadedVariant.problem: A table-booking model uses `{ isSeated: boolean; isPaid: boolean; noShowAt?: number }`, and a bug report says a booking is "paid but no-show".
givenSteps: 1. **List the real states:** booked, seated, paid, and no-show. That is 4 states, compared with 8 combinations of the two booleans and the optional field.
blankedStepPrompts: 2. Which fields belong to which state?
3. Write the union.
4. What makes the compiler list every place that must change when a `cancelled` state is added?
blankedStepAnswers: `table` when seated or paid; `paidAt` and `amount` only when paid; `markedAt` only for a no-show.

`type Booking = { status: 'booked'; id: string } | { status: 'seated'; id: string; table: number } | { status: 'paid'; id: string; table: number; paidAt: number; amount: number } | { status: 'noShow'; id: string; markedAt: number }`
A `switch` on `status` with a `never`-typed default in every place that handles bookings.

workedExamples.title: A runtime parser that matches the type
workedExamples.problem: For each `Order`-like event from the network: check that it's an object, check that `type` is one of the known tags, then check the fields that tag requires. Return `{ ok: true, value }` or `{ ok: false, error }`, and never throw on bad data from outside. The coding exercise `s01-e5` below implements it. In TypeScript its signature would be `parseOrderEvent(input: unknown): Result<OrderEvent>`.
steps: Type the input as `unknown`, so nothing can be read before it is checked.
Reject anything that is not a non-null, non-array object.
Check the field every event shares: `id` must be a non-empty string.
Switch on `type`. Each tag decides which other fields are required, mirroring the union.
Build and return a **new** object with only the known fields as `{ ok: true, value }`. Return `{ ok: false, error }` for any failure, and never throw on outside data.
workedExamples.conclusion: The type is the contract, and the parser is how you enforce it at runtime. You need both.

What turns "someone added a new status to the union" into compile errors at every place that needs a decision?
What question decides whether a strict type is worth keeping?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: The Kitchen Async Toolkit

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

The seven challenges go from **worked** to **independent**. Challenge 1 locks almost everything and leaves you a few lines. Challenges 2–4 give you the signature and helpers and leave the body to you. Challenge 5 has no scaffolding at all. Challenges 6 and 7 turn it around: first you write the tests for correct code, then you fix broken code against finished tests.

The locked lines are the same helpers the tests use, so your function keeps the contract the checker expects.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your throttle tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: A test suite that passes on correct code is only half the job. After challenge 6, paste your suite into each playground below. Both implementations are wrong in a specific way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "The Kitchen Async Toolkit."** Expected time is 8–10 hours, outside the guided minutes.

Deliver one repository containing:

1. `debounce` and `throttle` with `leading`, `trailing`, and `cancel`, plus test suites that use an injected scheduler. *(o3)*
2. `promisePool(tasks, limit)` that keeps results in input order, with a test proving the concurrency cap. *(o3)*
3. `promiseAll`, `promiseAllSettled`, and `promiseRace` from scratch, each with tests for the empty case, ordering, and first settle. *(o3)*
4. A `TypedEmitter<Events>` in TypeScript whose misuse fails to compile, proved by `@ts-expect-error` lines. *(o5)*
5. `deepClone` handling cycles, `Date`, `Map`, and `Set`. *(o4)*
6. `pipe`/`compose` with correct inference across at least four steps. *(o5)*
7. **Ten "what does this log?" snippets you wrote yourself**, each with the exact output and a paragraph of explanation. At least three must involve `await`, one must involve a promise executor, and one must involve `this`. *(o1, o2)*
8. **A one-page strictness memo** about a codebase you know. Name two places where types prevent real bugs and one place where they've become ceremony, and propose a change. *(o6)*

The emitter below has three bugs, one of them subtle. The test suite is finished and correct. Fix the code until every test passes. Don't edit the tests.

sections.title: The Browser as a Runtime
sections.description: Follow a page from URL to pixels: the **rendering pipeline** (style, layout, paint, composite), diagnosing **forced layout and jank**, designing **HTTP cache headers** that survive a deploy, and reading a **CORS failure** precisely while choosing the right browser storage. Examples come from an online newspaper: article pages, headline lists, a live blog, and subscriber accounts.

learningObjectives.description: Trace a navigation through parsing, CSSOM, style, layout, paint, and composite, and identify which stage a given change triggers
Diagnose forced synchronous layout and scroll jank in a Performance recording, fix them, and document before/after evidence
Build a read/write batching utility and an IntersectionObserver-driven infinite list
Design and demonstrate cache headers for immutable assets vs. revalidated HTML
Explain a CORS failure precisely and choose between cookies, localStorage, and IndexedDB for three stated requirements

motivationHooks.prompt: A page that animates `top` instead of `transform` re-lays-out the whole article on every frame. A homepage cached with the wrong header either serves stale HTML for a day or refetches on every single visit. This section is about telling the browser exactly what you mean, in both cases.

A loop over 100 story cards reads `card.offsetHeight` and writes `card.style.height` for each one, read-then-write, one card at a time. Before the lecture explains it, guess: how many forced layouts does that cost? Keep your number; Lecture 2.2 comes back to it.
A team's server logs show 200 OK for every request. Their browser console shows "Failed to fetch." Both are true at once. How?

This section is where Section 1's event loop meets pixels: rendering happens in the gap between tasks. Section 6 turns the pipeline into measured Core Web Vitals, Section 9 uses it to reason about CSS cost, and Section 10 builds motion entirely on the composite-only rule.

The answer is **100 forced layouts**, one per card, because every read follows the previous card's write and finds layout dirty. Reordering to "all reads, then all writes" drops that to **1**, with the exact same number of reads and writes. If you guessed 1 or 200, you've now met the forced-layout rule directly.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- Navigation runs DOM + CSSOM → style → layout → paint → composite. A change reruns the first stage it affects and everything after it: geometry means layout, color means paint, and `transform`/`opacity` on a layer mean composite only.
- Reading geometry after a write forces layout **right now**. Interleaved reads and writes thrash; batching all reads before all writes turns O(n) layouts into O(1).
- `requestAnimationFrame` schedules work at the right *moment*; it never makes the work itself cheaper.
- `no-cache` means store-and-revalidate, and `no-store` means never store. Hashed assets get a year-long `max-age`; HTML gets `no-cache` plus a validator; personal data gets `private, no-store`.
- CORS controls whether page JavaScript can *read* a cross-origin response. A simple request usually still reaches the server. Auth lives in an `HttpOnly` cookie, never in localStorage.
keyTakeaways: A change reruns the first pipeline stage it invalidates and every stage after it; only transform/opacity on a layer are composite-only.
A geometry read on dirty layout forces a synchronous layout right now; batch reads before writes.
rAF times your work; it does not shrink it. Heavy work still has to be split, moved off the main thread, or reduced.
Hashed assets: `public, max-age=31536000, immutable`. HTML: `no-cache` + a validator. Personal data: `private, no-store`.
`no-cache` stores and revalidates; `no-store` never stores.
A CORS failure usually means the server ran the request but the browser hid the response; CORS protects users, not servers.
Auth belongs in an HttpOnly cookie; small preferences in localStorage as JSON; large or structured offline data in IndexedDB.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 2.1: From URL to Pixels

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Describe the stages between typing a URL and seeing pixels, and what each stage produces. (objective o1)
2. Given a CSS or DOM change, name the first pipeline stage it invalidates and which stages follow. (objective o1)
3. Explain why render-blocking CSS and parser-blocking scripts delay first paint. (objective o1)

terms.definition: The browser's process of resolving a URL: DNS, connection (TCP/QUIC + TLS), request, response, then handing the bytes to the renderer.
Document Object Model: the tree of nodes built by parsing HTML.
The parsed form of all stylesheets. The browser needs it before it can style anything.
A resource that holds back first paint. Stylesheets in `<head>` are render-blocking by default.
A classic `<script>` without `defer`/`async`, which stops HTML parsing until it downloads and runs.
Matching CSS rules to elements to compute each element's final styles.
Computing each box's geometry: size and position.
Recording draw commands (text, colors, borders, shadows, images) for each layer.
Assembling painted layers, applying `transform` and `opacity`, and sending the frame to the screen, usually on the GPU and off the main thread.
A separately painted surface the compositor can move or fade without repainting.

contentBlocks.content:
### Start concrete: publishing one article page

A reader taps a headline. The browser resolves the domain, opens a connection, sends the request, and starts receiving HTML **while it's still downloading**. The parser builds the DOM incrementally. When it meets `<link rel="stylesheet">`, it fetches the CSS. Painting waits for that CSS so the reader doesn't see a flash of unstyled text. When it meets a plain `<script src>`, parsing stops until the script downloads and runs, because the script might call `document.write` or read the DOM.

When the DOM and CSSOM are ready enough, the browser runs the **rendering pipeline**:

```
DOM + CSSOM → Style → Layout → Paint → Composite → pixels
```

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s02-m1): The rendering pipeline. A horizontal flow: "HTML bytes → DOM", "CSS bytes → CSSOM", both merging into "Style (computed styles)" → "Layout (boxes with x, y, width, height)" → "Paint (draw lists per layer)" → "Composite (layers, transform, opacity → GPU)" → a screen icon. Under Style, Layout, and Paint sits a band labelled "main thread". Under Composite, a band labelled "compositor thread / GPU". A small inset shows a <script> tag pausing the "HTML → DOM" arrow with a stop sign.

contentBlocks.content:
### Which stage does a change trigger?

A change invalidates the **first** stage that depends on it, and every stage after that must run again:

| Change | First stage | Then |
|---|---|---|
| `width`, `height`, `top`, `margin`, `font-size`, adding or removing a node, changing text | **Layout** | paint, composite |
| `color`, `background-color`, `box-shadow`, `visibility` | **Paint** | composite |
| `transform`, `opacity` (on an element with its own compositor layer) | **Composite only** | none |

This is why "all style changes cost the same" is wrong (misconception `browser-rendering-pipeline.m1`). Moving a live-blog "new posts" pill with `top` re-lays out the whole page every frame, while moving it with `transform: translateY()` only recomposites. Section s10 builds all its motion on this rule.

> **Caveat you should say out loud in an interview:** `transform` and `opacity` are compositor-only **when the element has its own layer**. Browsers promote elements that are animating these properties, and `will-change: transform` requests promotion ahead of time. Every layer costs GPU memory, so don't promote hundreds of elements.

### What delays first paint

- **Render-blocking CSS.** A large stylesheet on a slow connection holds back the first paint. Fixes: inline critical CSS, keep the render-blocking CSS small, and load non-critical CSS without blocking.
- **Parser-blocking scripts.** A plain `<script>` in `<head>` stops DOM construction. `defer` downloads in parallel and runs after parsing, in order. `async` runs whenever the download finishes. `type="module"` scripts are deferred by default.
- **Web fonts.** Text may stay invisible until the font arrives. `font-display: swap` shows fallback text first.

Section s6 turns these into measured Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) improvements.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **`transform` and `opacity` skip layout and paint; almost everything else triggers layout.** Edit the map below to add two more CSS properties you use often, guess which stage each invalidates, then check yourself against the table above.

contentBlocks.caption: Every property from the table, printed as the stages it triggers. Predict each line before you run it.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: the pipeline
contentBlocks.content:
- **Animating `top`, `left`, `width`, or `height`** when `transform` would do. That's layout on every frame.
- **Saying "the DOM updated, so the screen updated."** Paint happens later, between tasks (s1).
- **Promoting everything with `will-change`.** Layers cost memory, and too many can be slower.
- **Putting classic scripts in `<head>` without `defer`.** That blocks parsing and delays everything.
- **Assuming a bigger page is always slower to first paint.** What matters is the render-blocking path.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 2.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Navigation → DOM + CSSOM → style → layout → paint → composite.
- A change reruns the first stage it affects and every stage after it. Geometry means layout, color means paint, and `transform`/`opacity` on a layer means composite only.
- CSS blocks rendering, and classic scripts block parsing. `defer`, `async`, and critical CSS shorten the path to first paint.

interactionSequence.prompt: A comment-count badge updates from `12` to `13` (text change), and separately its background flashes yellow with `background-color`. What is the first stage each triggers?
options: Text change: layout. Background-color: paint.
Both trigger only paint, since neither moves anything.
Text change: paint. Background-color: layout.
Both trigger composite only, since both are visual.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Changing text changes the content box, which is geometry; background-color only changes what gets drawn.
Text content changes geometry (the box may resize), so it invalidates layout, not just paint.
That has the two reversed: background-color never affects geometry.
Composite-only applies to transform/opacity on a layer, not to text or color changes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A change invalidates the **first** stage it depends on. Geometry (including text content, which can resize a box) means layout; color and shadows mean paint; transform/opacity on a layer mean composite only.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: An article page has a 220 KB stylesheet covering the whole site, most of it unused on this page, loaded from `<link>` in `<head>` with no other blocking resources. What is true about first paint?
options: First paint waits for the whole 220 KB to download and parse into CSSOM, even though most rules are unused
First paint is unaffected, because unused CSS rules are skipped during download
First paint only waits for the rules that match elements on the page
Paint happens immediately, and layout is what waits for CSS

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The browser cannot know which rules apply until it has the whole CSSOM, so render-blocking CSS blocks on the entire file.
The browser cannot skip parts of a stylesheet it has not finished downloading.
CSSOM construction is not selective by usage; matching happens after the full CSSOM exists.
Paint needs the computed styles, which need the full CSSOM, so paint is what waits.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is why "what delays first paint" calls out keeping the render-blocking CSS small: it is not enough for most rules to be irrelevant, the whole file still has to arrive and parse.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate says "the DOM updated, so the user sees it now." In two or three sentences, explain what actually has to happen between a DOM write and a pixel on screen, and when that can be delayed.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A DOM write only changes the tree in memory. The browser still has to run style, layout (if geometry changed), and paint, then composite, and none of that happens until the current task ends and the browser gets a chance to render — which is never mid-task. A long synchronous function after the DOM write, or a microtask chain that never lets the loop reach the render step, can delay the pixel far longer than the write itself suggests.
