learningExperiences.title: Lecture 4.1: Recognizing the Pattern in the First Minute

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Name the core patterns and the **signals** in a problem statement that point to each one. (objective o1)
2. State the **invariant** that makes each pattern correct. (objective o1)
3. Spot hidden O(n) costs in built-in array methods, and know when recursion depth is a risk. (objective o1)

terms.definition: A reusable problem shape with a known efficient strategy (for example the sliding window).
A phrase or constraint in the prompt that suggests a pattern ("contiguous", "sorted", "dependencies", "shortest").
A statement that stays true at every step of the loop and makes the algorithm correct ("the window's sum never exceeds the budget").
How work and memory grow with input size *n*, in Big-O notation.
The average cost per operation over a sequence, even if some single operations are expensive.
The number of nested function calls. JavaScript engines allow roughly 10⁴–10⁵ frames before throwing.

contentBlocks.content:
### The pattern map

| Pattern | Signals in the prompt | Invariant to state out loud | Typical cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Hash map / set lookup** | "find pair", "seen before", "dedupe", "group by", "match by id" | "The map holds everything to the left of *i*, keyed by what I'll need to look up." | O(n) time, O(n) space |
| **Two pointers** | sorted input, "pair that sums to", "merge", palindrome | "Everything outside [lo, hi] has been ruled out." | O(n) |
| **Sliding window** | "contiguous", "longest or shortest subarray/substring", "at most K" | "The window [left, right] always satisfies the constraint." | O(n) |
| **Stack** | "matching brackets", "undo", "next greater", nested structure | "The stack holds unresolved items, most recent on top." | O(n) |
| **Queue / BFS** | "shortest path", "level by level", "nearest" | "Everything in the queue is at distance *d* or *d+1*." | O(V+E) |
| **DFS** | "all paths", "connected components", tree traversal, document order | "Nodes marked visited are never re-entered." | O(V+E) |
| **Binary search** | sorted input, "minimum X such that…", monotonic yes/no | "The answer is always within [lo, hi]." | O(log n) |
| **Topological sort** | "dependencies", "must come before", build or schedule order | "A node is output only after all its dependencies." | O(V+E) |
| **Recursion / backtracking** | "all combinations", "permutations", "place N items" | "The path so far is valid, so extend it or undo it." | exponential |
| **Dynamic programming** | "number of ways", "minimum cost", overlapping subproblems | "dp[i] is the best answer for the prefix ending at i." | usually O(n) to O(n²) |
| **Heap / priority queue** | "top K", "next soonest", merging sorted streams | "The root is always the min (or max)." | O(n log k) |
| **Intervals** | "overlapping", "merge ranges", "meeting rooms" | "Sorted by start, each interval can only overlap the current merged one." | O(n log n) |

Recognition doesn't come from remembering the solution to "LeetCode #3" (misconception `algorithmic-pattern-recognition.m1`). It comes from reading the **constraints** and naming the **invariant**. If you can say the invariant, you can rebuild the code. If you only remember the code, a small twist breaks it.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s04-m1): Signal → pattern flowchart. A decision tree starting at "Read the constraints": "Input sorted?" → binary search / two pointers. "Contiguous range?" → sliding window. "Relationships / dependencies?" → graph (BFS if shortest, topological if order, DFS otherwise). "Need earlier values fast?" → hash map. "Nested/matching?" → stack. "Count ways / optimal choice with overlap?" → DP. Each leaf shows its invariant in a speech bubble.

contentBlocks.content:
### The hidden O(n) inside "simple" array methods

These look like constant time and aren't (misconception `algorithmic-pattern-recognition.m2`):

| Call | Actual cost | Why |
|---|---|---|
| `arr.shift()` / `arr.unshift(x)` | O(n) | Every remaining element moves one index. |
| `arr.includes(x)`, `indexOf`, `find` | O(n) | A linear scan. |
| `arr.splice(i, 1)` | O(n) | Elements after *i* move. |
| `[...arr]`, `arr.slice()`, `concat` | O(n) | A full copy. |
| `arr.push(x)` / `arr.pop()` | O(1) amortized | End operations. |
| `map.get`, `set.has` | O(1) average | Hashing. |

One of these inside a loop over *n* items makes the whole thing O(n²). A BFS written with `queue.shift()` is correct and quadratic. Use a head index instead (`queue[head++]`).

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **only `shift`/`unshift`/`includes`/`indexOf`/`splice` are secretly O(n); `push`/`pop` and Map/Set operations are O(1).** Add two more operations you use often to the map below, guess their cost, then check yourself against the table above.

### Recursion has a ceiling

Recursive DFS is elegant and fine for UI trees a few hundred levels deep. But a 100,000-level nested comment thread or a pathological JSON document overflows the call stack, and the engine throws (misconception `algorithmic-pattern-recognition.m3`). When the input can be deep and comes from outside, use an **explicit stack**. An explicit stack also makes it easy to stop early and to trace what's happening.

contentBlocks.caption: What `shift()` costs in a loop versus a head pointer, over 100 parcels. Predict both totals before running.
Recursion depth versus an explicit stack over a 100,000-deep comment chain. Predict which line throws before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: pattern recognition
contentBlocks.content:
- **Jumping to code before naming the pattern and invariant.**
- **`shift`/`includes`/`splice` inside loops.**
- **Recursing over untrusted, possibly deep input.**
- **Default `sort()` on numbers.** It compares as strings (see P1).
- **Assuming the input is sorted, or non-negative, or unique without asking.** These constraints decide the pattern.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 4.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Read the constraints, name the pattern, and state the invariant before coding.
- Know which built-ins are O(n), and keep them out of hot loops.
- Use explicit stacks when recursion depth depends on the input.

interactionSequence.prompt: "Given a sorted list of truck departure times, find two trucks whose departure times differ by exactly the required loading gap." Which approach and invariant fit best?
options: Two pointers from both ends, moving whichever side needs to shrink the gap. Invariant: every pair outside [lo, hi] has been ruled out.
Recall the "two sum" hash-map solution, since that solved a similar-sounding problem before.
Nested loops, since includes is constant time so checking every pair is still fast.
Recursion over every subset of departure times.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Sorted input plus a pair-difference target is the classic two-pointer signal, and it uses O(1) space instead of the hash map's O(n).
A hash map works, but it ignores the sorted constraint, which lets you do this in O(1) space instead. Recalling an answer without reading the constraints misses that.
Nested loops are O(n²); `includes` (and a linear scan in general) is O(n), not O(1).
That's exponential, and recursion isn't automatically the clean choice for a problem sorted input already solves in O(n).

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Sorted input is the signal for two pointers. State the invariant out loud before coding: "everything outside [lo, hi] has been ruled out."

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A dock scanner's BFS over a 50,000-bin location tree uses `const bin = queue.shift()`. What's its time complexity, and what's the fix?
options: O(n²) in the worst case, because each shift moves every remaining element. Use a head index instead.
O(n), because BFS visits every bin exactly once, and that's all that matters.
O(log n), since queues support binary search internally.
O(1) amortized, the same as push and pop.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The traversal itself is linear, but `shift()` on an array is O(n), so an O(n)-visit BFS written with `shift()` costs O(n²) overall.
Visiting each bin once is necessary but not sufficient — each visit's `shift()` call itself costs O(n), which is what makes the whole thing quadratic.
Queues (arrays) have no sublinear structure; nothing here does binary search.
Only end operations (`push`/`pop`) are amortized O(1). `shift()` operates on the front and has to move everything.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: One O(n) built-in inside a loop over n items makes the whole thing O(n²). A head index (or a real linked queue) keeps `shift`-style logic at O(1) per step.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A parser needs to compute the depth of a comment thread that can be arbitrarily deep and comes from an untrusted upload. What should you use, and why?
options: An explicit stack (or a simple loop with a pointer), because depth here depends on external, possibly adversarial input.
Plain recursion, because it is the cleanest and most idiomatic way to walk a tree.
Plain recursion wrapped in try/catch, retrying on a stack-overflow error.
JSON.stringify the thread and count characters as a proxy for depth.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Call-stack depth is bounded by the engine (roughly 10⁴–10⁵ frames); untrusted depth can exceed it, and an explicit stack is bounded only by heap memory.
Recursion is fine for UI trees a few hundred levels deep, but "clean" is not the same as "safe" once depth is attacker-controlled.
Retrying hits the exact same limit again immediately — the input didn't get any shallower.
That loses the tree structure entirely, and deep enough input can make stringifying itself throw.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Recursion is elegant, but it borrows a resource (the call stack) that a well-behaved UI tree respects and an untrusted upload might not. When depth depends on outside input, use an explicit stack.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Sorting dock numbers.** Write down the exact output, line by line, before you run it. Commit to an answer even if you're unsure — the gap between your prediction and the real output is what teaches you something.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
1,10,2,21,3
1,2,3,10,21
```

**Why intuition fails.** `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to **strings** and compares them in UTF-16 code-unit order, so `"10"` comes before `"2"`. Numbers need a comparator. `sort` also **mutates** the array in place, which is why both lines operate on the same `docks`. In an interview, saying "I'll pass a comparator because the default sort is lexicographic" costs one sentence and prevents a whole class of bugs.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: `Array.prototype.sort()` with no comparator converts elements to **strings** and compares them in UTF-16 code-unit order, so `"10"` comes before `"2"`. Numbers need a comparator. `sort` also **mutates** the array in place, which is why both lines operate on the same `docks`. In an interview, saying "I'll pass a comparator because the default sort is lexicographic" costs one sentence and prevents a whole class of bugs.
hints: What does `Array.prototype.sort()` compare elements as, when you don't pass a comparator?
The second `console.log` uses the same array `docks` after the first `sort()` already ran — does `sort` return a new array, or change the one it was given?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate says "I always reach for a hash map first — it's never wrong." In two or three sentences, explain what naming the invariant buys you that reaching for a familiar tool does not.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A hash map is often correct, but naming the invariant tells you *why* it's correct and *when* it stops being correct — for example, a hash-map lookup assumes you don't also need order or a bounded window. Stating the invariant ("the map holds everything to the left of i, keyed by what I'll need to look up") is what lets you notice when a twist in the problem — sorted input, a memory limit, a recency requirement — calls for two pointers, a sliding window, or an LRU cache instead. Recalling "hash map" without checking the invariant is exactly the pattern-recognition trap this lecture warns about.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Classifying in 60 seconds
workedExamples.problem: **Prompt:** "Given a conveyor log of parcel weights, find the longest run of consecutive parcels whose total weight fits the truck's budget."
steps: **Signals:** "longest," "consecutive," "fits a budget."
**Pattern:** sliding window, since it's contiguous and has a constraint that can be restored by shrinking from the left (weights are non-negative).
**Invariant:** "The sum of `weights[left..right]` is ≤ budget after the inner loop."
**Complexity:** each index enters and leaves the window at most once, so O(n) time and O(1) space.
**Say what would change the pattern:** negative weights would break the "shrink restores the constraint" property, so you'd need prefix sums plus a sorted structure.
workedExamples.conclusion: In under a minute you have the pattern, the invariant, the complexity, *and* the condition under which the approach fails. That last one is what signals seniority.

fadedVariant.problem: A supervisor asks: "Given the scan log for one shift (each entry marked fragile or not), find the length of the longest contiguous run of scans containing at most 3 fragile parcels."
givenSteps: **Signals:** "longest," "contiguous," "at most 3" — a hard cap on a count within the window.
blankedStepPrompts: **Pattern and invariant:** which pattern fits, and what invariant restores it when the cap is broken?
**Complexity, and what single change to the input would break this exact approach?**
blankedStepAnswers: Sliding window. Track a running count of fragile parcels in `[left, right]`; when it exceeds 3, shrink from the left (decrementing the count as fragile items leave) until it's back to ≤ 3. Invariant: "the window `[left, right]` never contains more than 3 fragile scans."

O(n) time, O(1) space — each index enters and leaves the window at most once, same as Worked Example 1. It breaks if a parcel's "fragile" mark could be un-set and re-set later for the *same* parcel already inside the window, because that non-monotonic change would mean shrinking no longer reliably restores the cap.

workedExamples.title: Spotting a quadratic loop in review
steps: The `shift` inside `while` over *n* items gives O(n²) element moves.
The `includes` on a growing `loaded` array gives another O(n²).
**Fix:** iterate with an index (or keep a head pointer), and replace `loaded` with a `Set` (O(1) `has`).
workedExamples.conclusion: The code reads as linear and runs in quadratic time. For 50,000 parcels that's about 2.5 billion operations instead of 100,000.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What are the signals that point to a sliding window instead of a two-pointer pair search?
What is the actual cost of `shift()`, `includes()`, and `splice()`, and what should replace `shift()` inside a hot loop?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 4.2: Frontend Problems That Are Secretly Trees and Maps

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Flatten nested objects into path keys, iteratively. (objective o2)
2. Search a DOM-like tree in **document order** (pre-order DFS) and by **level** (BFS). (objective o2)
3. Diff two arrays of records by key in O(n). (objective o2)
4. Implement a JSON-path `get` with wildcards by moving a **frontier** of nodes level by level. (objective o2)

terms.definition: Visit a node, then its children left to right. For DOM trees this *is* document order.
Visit all nodes at depth *d* before any at depth *d+1*, using a queue.
The set of nodes currently being expanded. A wildcard turns one node in the frontier into many.
A string like `parcel.dims.w` or `tags.0` that locates a value in nested data.
Comparing two lists by a stable id to find added, removed, and changed records.

contentBlocks.content:
### Why these show up in frontend interviews

Each of these is a real task in UI work: flattening form state for field-level errors (`address.zip`), finding the first focusable element in document order for a modal (s7), diffing server lists to animate insertions (s10), and reading nested API data (`orders[*].items[*].sku`). Interviewers use them because they reveal whether you see the **structure** behind the data (misconception `ui-data-structures.m1`).

### Document order is pre-order DFS, not BFS

"Find the first button" means the first one a screen reader or `querySelector` would find: pre-order DFS. BFS finds the *shallowest* match, which might come later in the document. Choosing BFS because "search means BFS" is recalling a solution instead of checking the invariant (misconception `algorithmic-pattern-recognition.m1`).

To get pre-order DFS iteratively, push children onto the stack **in reverse** so the leftmost child is popped first.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **"find the first X" means document order (pre-order DFS); BFS finds the shallowest match, which can be a different, later node.** Edit the tree below (move the button deeper on the left, or add a shallower one on the right) and predict whether DFS and BFS still agree.

### Wildcards: move a frontier, not a cursor

`getPath(inventory, 'warehouses.*.bins[*].sku')` can't be solved with one "current value" pointer, because `*` fans out. Keep an **array of current nodes**. For each path token, replace every node with its matches: one child for a key, all children for `*`. It's BFS over the path's levels.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s04-m2): A frontier expanding along a path. The inventory tree on the left. On the right, rows showing the frontier after each token: [root] → warehouses →  → [oakland, reno] → bins → [] → [binA1, binA2, binB1] → sku → ['A1', 'A2', 'B1']. Arrows fan out at each *.

contentBlocks.caption: BFS by level over a small warehouse zone tree. Predict each depth line before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: tree and map problems
contentBlocks.content:
- **BFS when the question means document order.**
- **`typeof x === 'object'` without checking for `null`.**
- **Recursive flatten or DFS on untrusted depth.**
- **Dropping falsy values** (`0`, `''`, `false`) with truthiness checks. Use `hasOwnProperty` or `in`.
- **Nested `find` for matching by id.** Build a `Map` first.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 4.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Document order = pre-order DFS. "Nearest or shallowest" = BFS.
- Wildcards need a frontier that expands level by level.
- Match records by key with a `Map` for O(n) diffs.

interactionSequence.prompt: A modal needs to focus the first focusable element in document order. Which traversal, and why?
options: Pre-order DFS: visit a node, then its children left to right — that is exactly what "document order" means.
BFS, because "find the first" always means the shallowest match.
Post-order DFS, so children are checked before their parent.
A sorted scan by pixel position on screen.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Document order is pre-order DFS; the DOM tree walked node-then-children-left-to-right is what a screen reader or `querySelector` returns.
BFS finds the *shallowest* match, which can appear later in the document than the true first match. "Search means BFS" is a recalled recipe, not the invariant this problem needs.
Post-order visits children first, which would find something *inside* a container before the container's earlier sibling — not document order.
Layout position is a rendering detail; document order is a property of the tree structure, independent of where things end up on screen.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: When "first" means document order, use pre-order DFS: push children in reverse so the leftmost child pops first.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A list screen currently finds each updated record with `after.find(a => a.id === b.id)` inside a loop over `before`. For 5,000 records, what should change?
options: Build a Map from id to record from one list first, then do single O(1) lookups while walking the other. That's O(n + m) total.
Nothing — find inside a loop is fine because find itself is O(1).
Sort both lists first and merge them, since sorting is always the fastest way to compare two lists.
Recurse over the records instead, since recursion avoids the cost of a loop.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A Map turns "is this id in the other list?" into O(1), so the whole diff is O(n + m) instead of O(n·m).
`find` is a linear scan, O(n), not O(1); calling it inside a loop over the other list makes the whole diff O(n·m).
Sorting costs O(n log n) on its own and solves a different problem than keyed matching; a Map is simpler and cheaper here.
Recursion doesn't change how many comparisons happen — it would still be doing the same O(n·m) work, just with call-stack overhead added.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is s3's keyed reconciliation with the DOM taken out: build a Map from one side, then a single pass over the other side, exactly like Worked Example 2's `diffByKey`.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Implementing `getPath(inventory, 'warehouses.*.bins[*].sku')`, a teammate keeps a single `current` variable and updates it token by token. What breaks, and what should replace `current`?
options: The first wildcard fans out into many possible values, and a single variable can only hold one of them. Replace it with a frontier: an array of every current match, rebuilt fully at each token.
Nothing breaks — a single variable is enough as long as you remember to loop over the final result.
It should be replaced with a Set, since sets are always the right structure for path-like problems.
The tokenizer is the problem, not the traversal.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A wildcard turns one node into many; you need the whole current frontier, and at each token you replace it with the union of every node's matches for that token.
A single "current value" pointer treats nested data as one thing to index into rather than a tree whose levels fan out; it will silently return only one match once a wildcard is hit.
A `Set` doesn't fix the fan-out problem by itself — what's needed is an array that gets rebuilt (potentially growing) at every wildcard token, in order.
The tokenizer (turning `"a.b[0].c[*]"` into tokens) is separate from — and already correct regardless of — how you walk the tokens.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Wildcards need BFS over the path's own levels: keep an array of current nodes (the frontier), and replace every node with its matches — one child for a key, all children for `*`.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A reviewer flags `typeof x === 'object' && x.keys.length === 0` as a bug in a flatten function. In one or two sentences, name the bug and the fix.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: `typeof null === 'object'` is true, so this throws on `null` (`null.keys` fails) before ever reaching the length check. Guard first with `x !== null && typeof x === 'object'`, and use `Object.keys(x).length` (or `hasOwnProperty`/`in`) rather than assuming a `.keys` property exists — the same `null` trap the lecture calls out for flattening and diffing.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Flattening a parcel record
workedExamples.problem: Input: `{ parcel: { id: 'P1', dims: { w: 2, h: 3 } }, tags: ['fragile', 'cold'] }`.
steps: Start the stack with `[root, '']`.
Pop root. Its keys are `parcel` and `tags`, so push them in reverse: `tags`, then `parcel`.
Pop `parcel` (path `parcel`). Push `dims` and `id` in reverse.
Pop `id`, a primitive, so write `parcel.id = 'P1'`.
Pop `dims` and push `h`, then `w`. Pop `w` and write `parcel.dims.w = 2`. Pop `h` and write `parcel.dims.h = 3`.
Pop `tags`, an array whose keys are `'0'` and `'1'`, so you get `tags.0` and `tags.1`.
workedExamples.conclusion: `{ 'parcel.id': 'P1', 'parcel.dims.w': 2, 'parcel.dims.h': 3, 'tags.0': 'fragile', 'tags.1': 'cold' }`. The explicit stack gives the same order as recursion, without the depth limit. Decide *out loud* how to represent empty objects and `null`. Keeping them as leaves is the usual choice, because it round-trips.

workedExamples.title: Keyed diff of dock assignments
workedExamples.problem: Before: `[{id:'P1', dock:4}, {id:'P2', dock:1}, {id:'P3', dock:2}]`. After: `[{id:'P2', dock:3}, {id:'P3', dock:2}, {id:'P4', dock:5}]`.
steps: Build `Map(id → record)` from *before*. That's O(n).
Walk *after*: P2 exists and its dock changed, so **changed**. P3 is equal, so nothing. P4 is missing from the map, so **added**.
Walk *before* for ids not seen in *after*: P1, so **removed**.
workedExamples.conclusion: `{ added: ['P4'], removed: ['P1'], changed: ['P2'] }` in O(n + m). The nested-`find` version gives the same answer in O(n·m). That's s3's keyed reconciliation, with the DOM taken out.

fadedVariant.problem: Before: `[{ sku: 'A1', qty: 12 }, { sku: 'A2', qty: 3 }, { sku: 'A3', qty: 7 }]`. After: `[{ sku: 'A2', qty: 5 }, { sku: 'A3', qty: 7 }, { sku: 'A4', qty: 2 }]`.
givenSteps: 1. Build `Map(sku → record)` from *before*. That's O(n).
blankedStepPrompts: 2. Walk *after*: what do you check for each SKU against the map, and what gets recorded for A2, A3, and A4?
3. Walk *before* for SKUs not seen in *after*: what's removed, and what's the total complexity?
blankedStepAnswers: For each SKU in *after*, look it up in the map. A2 exists with a different `qty` (3 → 5), so **changed**. A3 exists with the same `qty` (7 = 7), so nothing. A4 is missing from the map, so **added**.

A1 never turns up while walking *after*, so it's **removed**. Result: `{ added: ['A4'], removed: ['A1'], changed: ['A2'] }` in O(n + m), the same Map-based approach as Worked Example 2, applied to bin inventory instead of dock assignments.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What traversal is "document order," and how does it differ from what BFS finds?
How do you extend a "frontier" of nodes when a JSON-path token is a wildcard versus a plain key?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 4.3: Caches and Dependency Graphs

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Implement an LRU cache with a `Map`, and again with a doubly linked list plus a `Map`, and compare them. (objective o3)
2. Apply topological sort to module dependencies, with cycle detection that reports the cycle. (objective o4)
3. Recognize topological sort outside build tools. (objective o4)

terms.definition: A fixed-capacity cache that evicts the **least recently used** entry when full.
The order of last access. Both `get` and `set` count as "use."
Nodes with `prev` and `next`. You can remove a node in O(1) if you hold a reference to it.
Dummy head and tail nodes that remove edge cases from insert and remove.
A graph with directed edges and no cycles. It has at least one topological order.
The number of unmet dependencies of a node.
Repeatedly output a node with in-degree 0 and reduce its dependents' in-degrees.

contentBlocks.content:
### LRU with a Map is legitimate

JavaScript's `Map` **guarantees iteration in insertion order**. Deleting a key and setting it again moves it to the end. So:

- `get(k)`: if present, `delete` then `set` to mark it most recent. O(1).
- `set(k, v)`: `delete` if present, then `set`. If over capacity, delete `map.keys().next().value`, the oldest. O(1).

That isn't a hack (misconception `ui-data-structures.m2`). It relies on documented, specified behavior. A plain object is **not** a substitute, because its key order puts integer-like keys (`'7'`, `'101'`) first in numeric order, whatever order you inserted them in.

The **linked-list + Map** version is what you'd write in a language without an ordered map, and interviewers often ask for it as a follow-up. The Map points at list nodes. The list holds the recency order, with the head as least recent and the tail as most recent. Every operation is O(1): look up the node, unlink it, and append it at the tail.

| | Map-only | Linked list + Map |
|---|---|---|
| get / set / evict | O(1) | O(1) |
| Code size | ~10 lines | ~40 lines |
| Relies on | Map insertion order (specified) | pointer manipulation |
| When to prefer | JavaScript production code | languages without an ordered map, or when you need O(1) "move to any position" |

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **`Map`'s delete-then-set legitimately reorders recency, and a plain object's key order is not insertion order once a key looks like a number.** Edit the ids below (add a third numeric-looking id, or a non-numeric one) and predict each order before running.

### Topological sort, with cycles reported

Your s8 bundler has to emit modules so each one comes after its imports. Kahn's algorithm:

1. Count each module's unmet imports (its in-degree). Record who depends on whom.
2. Put every module with in-degree 0 into a queue.
3. Pop a module, output it, and decrement each dependent's in-degree. Enqueue any that reach 0.
4. **Invariant check:** if the output has fewer modules than the graph, the rest are in or behind a **cycle**. Walk remaining dependencies from any leftover node until a node repeats, and report that path (`a.js -> b.js -> c.js -> a.js`).

Topological sort isn't only for build tools (misconception `ui-data-structures.m3`). It orders database migrations, form fields whose validation depends on other fields, onboarding steps, spreadsheet recalculation, and in this domain, truck-loading tasks.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s04-m3): Kahn's algorithm, step by step. A five-module graph (app → router, store, router → utils, store → utils, api, api → utils) with in-degree badges on each node. Five frames show the ready queue and the output list growing: utils → router, api → store → app. A sixth frame shows a three-node cycle turning red, with the reported path.

contentBlocks.caption: Map's insertion order versus a plain object's key order, after touching one entry. Predict both lines before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: caches and graphs
contentBlocks.content:
- **Forgetting that `get` updates recency.** That turns LRU into FIFO.
- **Using a plain object as an ordered map.**
- **Losing `prev`/`next` pointers when unlinking a node.** Sentinel nodes help.
- **Kahn's algorithm without the "output count = node count" check.** Cycles then vanish silently.
- **Ignoring dependencies that aren't declared as keys** (external packages). They're still nodes.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 4.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Map-based LRU is O(1) and idiomatic. Linked list + Map is the portable O(1) version.
- Topological sort orders anything with dependencies. Always check for, and report, cycles.

interactionSequence.prompt: A colleague calls a Map-based LRU "a hack that relies on implementation details." What's the accurate response?
options: Map's insertion-order iteration is part of the ECMAScript spec, so delete then set is a legitimate, portable O(1) move-to-recent, and the first key from the iterator is the true least-recently-used key.
Agree, and switch to a plain object, which is simpler and just as ordered.
Agree, and always reach for the linked-list-plus-Map version instead, since only pointers are trustworthy.
Map order is only guaranteed in some engines, so it's risky in production.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. This is documented, specified behavior, not an implementation quirk — every conformant engine behaves this way.
Objects put integer-like keys first in ascending numeric order, regardless of insertion order, which breaks recency for ids like '7' and '101'.
The linked-list version is a legitimate portable alternative, but distrusting the Map version because it "feels like a hack" is the misconception, not a fact about correctness.
It's guaranteed by ECMAScript itself, in every engine, not just one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Map's insertion-order iteration is specified, documented behavior. That makes delete+set a correct, idiomatic O(1) LRU move — a plain object's key ordering rules make it the wrong tool, not the safer one.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team's migration runner uses Kahn's algorithm but occasionally "skips" a migration with no error, and the logs show three migrations referencing each other. What's the root cause, and what's missing?
options: The runner never checks that the number of output nodes equals the number of graph nodes, so cycle members never reach in-degree 0 and silently vanish instead of throwing.
Kahn's algorithm can't handle more than two dependencies per node.
The migrations should be ordered alphabetically instead of by dependency.
JavaScript Maps silently drop entries under heavy use.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The invariant check (`output.length === node count`) is exactly what turns a silent skip into a reported cycle with its path.
Kahn's algorithm handles any number of dependencies per node; that's not the constraint here.
Alphabetical order ignores the dependency relationships entirely — this is exactly a topological-sort problem, not a sorting problem.
Maps don't lose entries. The bug is the algorithm's missing invariant check, not the data structure.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Cycles don't announce themselves — Kahn's algorithm just quietly produces a shorter output. Always compare the output length to the node count, and when they differ, walk the leftover nodes to find and report the cycle.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Identity, hashing, and NaN.** Write down the exact output, line by line, before you run it. Commit to an answer even if you're unsure — the gap between your prediction and the real output is what teaches you something.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
3 2
undefined -1 true
7
```

**Why intuition fails.** `Set` and `Map` compare object keys by **identity**, not content. Three object literals are three different keys, and a freshly written `{ id: 'P1' }` never finds the stored one, so key by the id string. `indexOf` uses strict equality, where `NaN !== NaN`, while `includes` uses SameValueZero, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself. The last line is the LRU trap: after touching `'7'`, you'd expect `'101'` to be the oldest key, but objects list integer-like keys in ascending numeric order, so `'7'` still comes first. An eviction based on "first key" would evict the item you just used (misconception `ui-data-structures.m2`).

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: `Set` and `Map` compare object keys by **identity**, not content. Three object literals are three different keys, and a freshly written `{ id: 'P1' }` never finds the stored one, so key by the id string. `indexOf` uses strict equality, where `NaN !== NaN`, while `includes` uses SameValueZero, which treats `NaN` as equal to itself. The last line is the LRU trap: after touching `'7'`, you'd expect `'101'` to be the oldest key, but objects list integer-like keys in ascending numeric order, so `'7'` still comes first. An eviction based on "first key" would evict the item you just used (misconception `ui-data-structures.m2`).
hints: Do `Set` and `Map` compare object keys by their contents, or by reference identity?
`indexOf` uses strict equality (`===`); `includes` uses SameValueZero. What's different about how each one treats `NaN`?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: Explain, precisely, what Kahn's algorithm's invariant check is protecting against, and why a build system that skips it can ship a broken build without any error in the logs.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Kahn's algorithm only outputs a node once every dependency it needs has already been output. If some nodes form a cycle, none of them ever reaches in-degree 0, so they're never added to the queue and never appear in the output — the loop just ends early with a shorter list, no exception thrown. The invariant check (`output.length === total node count`) is the only thing that notices the output is short; without it, a bundler can silently ship a build missing exactly the modules involved in the cycle, and nothing in the logs says so.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: The LRU recency trap with numeric ids
workedExamples.problem: Capacity 2. Operations: `set('7')`, `set('101')`, `get('7')`, `set('55')`.
steps: After the two sets, the recency order (least → most) is `7, 101`.
`get('7')` makes the order `101, 7`.
`set('55')` pushes the size to 3, so evict the least recent: `101`. The keys are now `7, 55`.
**With a plain object** doing the same delete-and-reinsert, the key order is always numeric: `7, 55, 101`. Evicting "the first key" removes `7`, which is the most recently used item.
workedExamples.conclusion: Map's insertion order is the correct tool. Objects only look like they preserve order.

workedExamples.title: Loading the truck
workedExamples.problem: Tasks: `load truck` needs `print labels` and `pick items`. `print labels` needs `pick items`.
steps: In-degrees: load truck 2, print labels 1, pick items 0.
Ready: `pick items`. Output it, which drops print labels to 0 and load truck to 1.
Output `print labels`, which drops load truck to 0.
Output `load truck`.
workedExamples.conclusion: `pick items → print labels → load truck`. It's the same algorithm as module ordering, with a different domain.

fadedVariant.problem: Shift-open tasks: `unlock dock doors` needs nothing. `power on conveyor` needs `unlock dock doors`. `run safety check` needs `power on conveyor`. `open for pickups` needs `run safety check` and `unlock dock doors`.
givenSteps: 1. In-degrees: unlock dock doors 0, power on conveyor 1, run safety check 1, open for pickups 2.
blankedStepPrompts: 2. Which task is ready first, and what happens to the in-degrees of its dependents once it's output?
3. Continue Kahn's algorithm to the end: what's the final order?
blankedStepAnswers: `unlock dock doors` (in-degree 0) is ready first. Outputting it drops `power on conveyor` to 0 and `open for pickups` to 1 (it still needs `run safety check`).

Next ready: `power on conveyor` (in-degree 0), which drops `run safety check` to 0. Then `run safety check`, which drops `open for pickups` to 0. Final order: `unlock dock doors → power on conveyor → run safety check → open for pickups`.

retrievalPractice.prompt: How does a Map-based LRU mark a key as most recently used, in exactly two operations?
What check turns a silently-skipped cycle into a thrown, reported cycle in Kahn's algorithm?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 4.4: The Timed Round, Out Loud

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Run a structured talk track: clarify, give examples, state the approach and complexity, code, test, handle follow-ups. (objective o5)
2. Use hints and follow-ups as signals rather than alarms. (objective o5)
3. Review a recording of yourself against a rubric. (objective o5)

terms.definition: A predictable structure for narrating your reasoning so the interviewer can follow and grade it.
A question that settles an ambiguous constraint (sorted? duplicates? sizes? what to return on empty input?).
Stating the simplest correct approach and its cost before optimizing. It gives you a fallback and a baseline.
Tracing your code by hand on a small example, out loud, before claiming it works.
An extension question ("what if it doesn't fit in memory?"). It usually means you passed the baseline.

contentBlocks.content:
### The talk track (45 minutes)

| Minute | Step | What you say |
|---|---|---|
| 0–5 | **Clarify** | "Can weights be negative? How large is n? Return the length or the run itself? What about empty input?" |
| 5–8 | **Examples** | Work one normal and one edge example on the board *before* designing. |
| 8–12 | **Approach** | "Brute force checks every run, O(n²). The contiguous plus non-negative constraints mean a sliding window works. The invariant is… O(n) time, O(1) space." Get a nod before coding. |
| 12–30 | **Code** | Narrate *intent*, not syntax: "Now I restore the invariant by shrinking from the left." |
| 30–38 | **Test** | Dry-run the edge cases out loud. Fix bugs calmly and say what you're fixing. |
| 38–45 | **Follow-ups** | "If the data streamed in, I'd keep the same window state online…" |

Silence isn't efficient (misconception `live-problem-solving-communication.m1`). An interviewer can't give credit for reasoning they didn't hear, and can't hint you away from a dead end they can't see. The final answer isn't the whole grade either (misconception `live-problem-solving-communication.m2`). Most rubrics score problem understanding, approach, code quality, testing, and communication separately. A clean process with a small bug often beats a silent perfect answer.

### Hints and follow-ups

- **A hint** means the interviewer wants to see you move. Acknowledge it, restate it in your own words, and adjust: "Right, if it's sorted I don't need the map, so two pointers gives O(1) space."
- **A follow-up** usually means you've passed the baseline and they're probing for seniority (misconception `live-problem-solving-communication.m3`). Treat it as a design conversation: name the trade-offs, the new constraints, and what would change.

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Video (s04-m4): Two mock rounds, side by side. Production brief: A 6-minute video with split screen. Left: a candidate codes silently for 12 minutes, gets a correct answer, and can't explain the complexity. Right: a candidate follows the talk track, has one bug, finds it during the dry run, and handles a streaming follow-up. On-screen rubric scores are tallied for both, and the right candidate scores higher.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: live rounds
contentBlocks.content:
- **Coding within 60 seconds of hearing the problem.**
- **Narrating syntax ("now a for loop") instead of intent.**
- **Saying "it works" without a dry run.**
- **Treating a hint as failure and going quiet.**
- **Over-engineering before the baseline works.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 4.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Clarify, give examples, state the approach and complexity, code, test, then take follow-ups, all out loud.
- Process is graded alongside the result. Hints and follow-ups are part of the conversation.

---

### The Parallel Track: Algorithms Practice (weeks 4–13)

About **2 hours per week**, separate from the guided minutes. The point is spaced repetition, not volume.

**Weekly rhythm (three problems, each talked through out loud before coding):**
1. One problem from **this week's focus**.
2. One problem from **an earlier week's focus** (spaced review).
3. One **cold, timed** problem (25 minutes, recorded weekly from week 6).

| Weeks | Focus | Section running alongside |
|---|---|---|
| 4–5 | arrays, strings, hash maps, two pointers, sliding window | s4, s5 |
| 6–7 | stacks, queues, linked lists | s6, s7 |
| 8–9 | trees, recursion, BFS and DFS | s8, s9 |
| 10–11 | graphs, binary search, sorting | s10, s11 |
| 12–13 | light dynamic programming, then mixed review under time pressure | s12, s13 |

**Guardrail:** if this track starts taking most of your week, you've drifted toward mid-level prep. Frontend system design (s5) and your behavioral stories (s13) move the needle more at the senior level.

**Log template (one row per problem):** date · problem · pattern named in the first minute? (y/n) · invariant stated · time to working solution · bugs found in the dry run · follow-up handled · one thing to do differently.

interactionSequence.prompt: Put these moments of a structured talk track in the order they belong, from what you say first to what happens last in a 45-minute round.
options: State the approach and its complexity out loud, and get a nod before writing any code.
Ask clarifying questions that settle ambiguous constraints (sorted? duplicates? sizes? empty input?).
Work one normal example and one edge case by hand, before designing anything.
Narrate intent while writing the code ("now I restore the invariant by shrinking from the left"), not syntax.
Dry-run the edge cases out loud, and fix any bugs calmly while saying what you're fixing.
Treat a follow-up question as a design conversation about new constraints and trade-offs, not as a sign you got it wrong.

optionFeedback.feedback: Third: you need the clarified constraints and the examples in front of you before a brute-force-then-optimized approach makes sense to state.
First: an interviewer can't give credit for reasoning about the wrong problem, and this settles what the code even has to do.
Second: working an example by hand, before designing, is what turns a vague prompt into something you can name a pattern for.
Fourth: this is the coding phase — narrating the invariant as you restore it, not narrating "now a for loop."
Fifth: testing comes after the code exists, and a calm dry run is what catches a small bug before anyone else has to.
Last: follow-ups usually mean you've already passed the baseline, so they come at the end, as a design conversation.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the 45-minute talk track: clarify → examples → approach and complexity → code → test → follow-ups. Skipping straight to code is the single most common way candidates lose points they could have kept.
hints: Which step has to happen before you can even name a pattern with confidence?
Testing and follow-ups both come after working code exists — which of those two comes first?

interactionSequence.prompt: Twenty-five minutes into a round on an unfamiliar warehouse-routing problem, the interviewer asks, "What if the graph didn't fit in memory?" What does this most likely mean, and what should you do?
options: You've likely met the baseline, and they're probing how you reason about a new constraint. Discuss streaming or partitioning the graph and the trade-offs, out loud.
Your solution is wrong, so scrap it and start over.
They want you to stop explaining and just type faster.
It's irrelevant small talk, since only the final working code gets graded.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Follow-ups are where seniority gets shown — treat the new constraint as a design conversation, not an alarm.
Follow-ups usually come *after* you've passed the baseline, not as a signal you failed it.
The question is explicitly asking for reasoning out loud about a new constraint, which is the opposite of going quiet.
Most rubrics score problem understanding, approach, testing, and communication separately from the final code — the follow-up conversation is part of what's graded.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A follow-up is a signal, not an alarm. Acknowledge it, restate the new constraint in your own words, and reason about the trade-offs out loud.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: You're 30 minutes into a round and realize your approach to a bin-packing problem is O(n²) after the interviewer asks about input size. Write the script for what you say and do in the next two minutes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong answers: (1) acknowledge without panic — "good point, let me reconsider the size"; (2) quantify the problem concretely — "with n up to 10⁵, that's about 10¹⁰ operations, too slow"; (3) name the pattern and invariant of the fix, not just "I'll optimize it"; (4) state the new complexity; (5) say you'll re-test with a dry run after the change, then actually narrate the edit and do it. A response that jumps straight to rewriting code without saying any of this out loud loses most of the credit even if the final code ends up correct.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Watch (or imagine watching) your own recording against the mock-round rubric. Which single habit — long silences, narrating syntax instead of intent, treating a hint as failure, or skipping the dry run — would cost you the most points right now, and what's one concrete change you'll make before your next timed problem?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: There's no single correct habit to name — the value is in being specific. A strong answer names one habit precisely (not "I need to communicate better"), ties it to a rubric dimension it would cost points on, and commits to one testable change for the next attempt (for example: "I'll say the invariant out loud before I start typing, every time" is checkable; "I'll try to talk more" is not).

workedExamples.title: Handling a follow-up well
workedExamples.problem: **Baseline solved:** LRU cache with Map. **Follow-up:** "What if your language didn't have an ordered map?"
steps: **Acknowledge:** "Then I need to maintain recency order myself."
**Reason from the operations:** "I need O(1) lookup, which means a hash map, and O(1) move-to-end and remove-oldest, which means a doubly linked list. The map will point at the list nodes."
**Name the risk:** "Pointer bugs. I'll use sentinel head and tail nodes so there are no null checks."
**Code the unlink and append helpers first**, then `get` and `set` in terms of them.
workedExamples.conclusion: The follow-up became a chance to show structured reasoning, which is exactly what it was for.

learningExperiences.title: Lab: The Dispatch Toolkit

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. Some tests here check **complexity** without timing, by counting how many times your code reads the input array with a Proxy: an O(n²) solution fails even on a fast machine.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenges 1, 4, 5, and 6 give you fixtures or a class skeleton and leave the core algorithm to you. Challenge 2 gives you a small DOM-like tree and a predicate and leaves the traversal to you. Challenge 3 has no in-function scaffolding at all: the `before`/`after` fixtures are given, but `diffByKey` itself is entirely yours, checked case by case instead of by a written test suite. The two test-suite challenges turn the direction around: first you write tests against code that's already correct, then you fix broken code against tests that are already written.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your longestRunWithinBudget tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the sliding-window test-writing challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. Each wrong version is wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on all three.

## Practical activity

**Build: "The Dispatch Toolkit" + one recorded mock round.** Expected time is 8–10 hours, plus about 2 hours per week of parallel track from here on.

1. **Pattern cheat sheet in your own words** for two pointers, sliding window, hash map lookup, stack/queue, BFS/DFS, binary search, recursion/backtracking, and basic DP. For each: the signals, the invariant, one example from your own work, and the complexity. *(o1)*
2. **Frontend-flavored implementations** with tests: `flattenObject`, `findFirst` (DFS), `nodesAtDepth` (BFS), `diffByKey`, `memoizeWithLRU(fn, capacity)` built on your LRU, and `getPath` with wildcards. *(o2)*
3. **LRU cache two ways**, plus a written complexity analysis and a note on when you'd choose each. *(o3)*
4. **Topological sort on a real graph:** extract the import graph of a small real project (parse the `import` statements) and print a valid module order. Introduce a cycle deliberately and show the reported path. *(o4)*
5. **One timed mock round, recorded.** 45 minutes with a peer (or a mock-interview platform) on an unseen medium problem. Review the recording against the rubric below and write a one-page self-review. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Mock round rubric (used here and again in s13)
rows: Asked about size and edge cases
Settled every ambiguous constraint and confirmed with examples
Brute force → optimized, invariant named, trade-offs weighed
Dry-ran edge cases out loud and fixed bugs calmly
Narrated intent throughout and used hints well
Reasoned about new constraints and trade-offs

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 6: flatten a nested object with path keys

Implement `flattenObject(value)` that returns an object mapping dot-separated path keys to leaf values. Keep `null`, primitives, and **empty** objects or arrays as leaves, and handle arbitrarily deep input without recursion.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: A stack of `[value, path]` pairs replaces the call stack.
Pushing children in reverse key order makes pops come out in natural order.
`typeof null === 'object'`. Guard against it before calling `Object.keys`.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 6: first matching node in document order

Implement `findFirst(root, predicate)` that returns the first node, in **document order**, for which `predicate(node)` is true, or `null`. Nodes look like `{ tag, className, text, children }`.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: What order does `querySelector` use? Name the traversal.
With a stack, the last child pushed is visited first. Push in reverse.
Return from inside the loop the moment the predicate passes.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 6: diff two lists of records by key in O(n)

Implement `diffByKey(before, after, key = 'id')` that returns `{ added, removed, changed }` as id arrays (`added`/`changed` in *after* order, `removed` in *before* order), where "changed" means some own property differs by `Object.is`.

The `before`/`after` fixtures and the read-counting harness above are given. `diffByKey` itself has no in-function scaffolding — the whole body is yours, checked case by case.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Which structure answers "is this id in *before*?" in O(1)?
Two passes (or three) over the inputs is still O(n). A pass *inside* a pass isn't.
For "removed," you need the set of ids you saw in *after*.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 6: JSON-path `get` with wildcards

Implement `getPath(data, path)` that returns an **array** of all values matching a path like `warehouses.*.bins[*].sku`. It supports dot keys, `[n]` indexes, and `*` or `[*]` wildcards over arrays and objects, returns `[]` when nothing matches, and returns `[data]` for an empty path.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: A single "current value" can't represent `*`. What can?
For each token, build the *next* frontier from *every* value in the current one.
`hasOwnProperty` keeps `0` and `''`. A truthiness check drops them.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 5 of 6: LRU cache, two ways

Implement `MapLRU` (Map only) and `LinkedLRU` (doubly linked list plus Map), each with `get(key)`, `set(key, value)`, and `keys()` (least → most recent), with O(1) operations and eviction of the least recently used entry.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: What single Map operation pair moves a key to "most recent"?
For the linked version, write `_unlink` and `_append` first, and everything else is two calls.
Sentinel head and tail nodes mean you never check for `null` neighbours.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 6 of 6: topological sort with cycle reporting

Implement `topoSort(graph)` where `graph` maps each node to the array of nodes it depends on. Return an order in which every node comes after its dependencies (Kahn's algorithm: FIFO ready queue, initial ready nodes in first-seen order, dependents in declaration order), and throw `Error('Cycle detected: a -> b -> a')` naming one cycle when none exists.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: In-degree counts a node's unmet dependencies. Which nodes can go first?
Use a head pointer, not `shift()` (Lecture 4.1).
Every node left over after Kahn's has at least one leftover dependency, so following them must eventually repeat a node.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working sliding window, you write the tests

**Brief:** `longestRunWithinBudget(weights, budget)` returns the length of the longest contiguous run of parcels whose total weight is ≤ `budget` (weights are non-negative). It's correct. Write tests that would catch the three hidden wrong versions. Think about runs that need *shrinking* rather than restarting, single parcels over budget, zero weights, and empty input. Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **four** tests). Then confirm your suite catches all three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite pins down the sliding-window *invariant*, not just one happy-path answer: a run that needs the window to shrink from the left rather than restart (wrong version 1 restarts instead of shrinking, which undercounts a run like `[3,3,3,1]` at budget 7); the order of measuring the best-so-far length relative to restoring the invariant (wrong version 2 measures `best` before shrinking, so it briefly counts a window that's over budget); and the exact boundary where a sum equals the budget (wrong version 3 shrinks on `sum >= budget`, wrongly treating an exact match as over-budget). A suite that only checks one typical case catches none of these — you need a case that forces a mid-run shrink, a case where the sum lands exactly on the budget, and a case with a single over-budget parcel.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests here pin down the window's *invariant* (what stays true after every shrink), not just one typical input.
hints: Start from the brief's own categories: shrinking vs restarting, a single over-budget parcel, zero weights, and empty input — that's already four.
Write one input where the correct answer requires the window to shrink partway through, not just grow to the end.
Write one input where a parcel's weight lands exactly on the budget — off-by-one bugs love equality.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken `nodesAtDepth`, make the tests pass

**Brief:** `nodesAtDepth(root, depth)` should return the names of all nodes at `depth`, **left to right**. The version below has several bugs. Fix it without changing the tests. Don't use `shift()`.

codeExercise.solutionNote: a stack gives right-to-left DFS order, so level-order needs a queue. With a head pointer the queue stays O(n). Leaves may have no `children`. An empty tree is valid input. Stopping at the target depth is an easy efficiency win.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Every bug here comes from reusing a DFS-shaped template (a stack) for a problem that needs BFS order, plus two missing guards.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. A `stack` (pop from the end) gives DFS order — what does level order (BFS) actually need?
What happens when a node has no `children` property at all, like a leaf?
What should happen for an empty (null) tree, and does stopping once you reach the target depth save any work?

interactionSequence.prompt: After you finish the Dispatch Toolkit and your recorded mock round, answer: which of your six implementations took the most attempts to get right, and which specific test (not just "it failed") told you what was wrong? Then name one habit from your mock-round self-review you're committing to fix before next week's timed problem.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong answers name a specific failing test or case (not "the tests failed"), tie it to the exact wrong-answer pattern it caught (recursion depth, a quadratic scan, BFS instead of DFS, plain-object key ordering, a missing invariant check), and commit to one concrete, checkable habit for the next mock round — for example "I'll state the invariant out loud before I start typing" is checkable; "I'll communicate better" is not. Check your six implementations and your mock-round notes against the rubric table above before you submit.

learningExperiences.title: In the Wild: Find the Algorithm in Your Own Codebase

contentBlocks.content: This exercise happens in your own codebase (or a real open-source project) and on a live call with a peer, not inside the course engine. The 20 minutes here cover planning and reflection; finding and fixing the quadratic pattern, and running your first timed round, take a few hours more. Nothing here is graded or gates your progress. It builds evidence you will reuse in the Section 13 portfolio.

Start your parallel-track log this week, and schedule your recurring weekly mock slot with a peer. If you can, join or start a small study group at work or in a local meetup, so your talk-through practice has a live audience.

learningExperiences.title: Review: Retrieval, Transfer, and the Section 4 Quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Close the section in three moves

1. **Retrieve** without looking back: answer the four cues below from memory.
2. **Transfer** the pattern-and-invariant habit to two systems with nothing to do with warehouses: a university course planner and a festival wristband scanner.
3. **Prove it** in the Section 4 quiz and the two cumulative mastery checks for `algorithmic-pattern-recognition` and `ui-data-structures`, which live here because this is the section that teaches them.

contentBlocks.title: Your review schedule
contentBlocks.content: Every retrieval item here follows the expanding schedule **Day 1 → Day 3 → Day 7 → Day 16 → Day 35 → Day 75**. Two items below also bring back earlier sections — keyed reconciliation from Section 3, and cache directives from Section 2 — because interleaving keeps older material in rotation.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before the quiz: which of this section's five skills would you least want to be handed cold right now — naming a pattern in a minute, tree/map traversal, the LRU/topological-sort pair, or talking through a problem live? Name it and write one sentence on what feels shaky.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Naming the shaky part precisely is what makes the next review useful. Re-read that lecture's summary and worked examples, and if it's the live-round skill, re-watch the mock-round video before you open the quiz.

retrievalPractice.prompt: For "longest contiguous run under a limit," name the pattern, the invariant, and the complexity.
Why is `queue.shift()` a problem inside BFS, and what do you use instead?
How does a Map-based LRU mark an entry as most recent, and why can't a plain object do the same job?

transferExercises.scenario: Students pick courses that have prerequisites, and some prerequisites were accidentally made circular by an admin.
transferExercises.task: Design the feature that shows a valid semester-by-semester order and a helpful error naming the circular chain. Which pattern, which invariant, what complexity, and how would you group courses into semesters, meaning levels of the order?
successCriteria: Names topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) as the pattern and states the invariant: a course is scheduled only after every one of its prerequisites has been scheduled.
Detects a circular prerequisite chain by checking that the output count equals the course count, and reports the actual cycle (for example `CS201 -> CS310 -> CS201`), not just "invalid schedule."
Groups courses into semesters by BFS-by-level over the dependency graph (each wave of newly-ready, in-degree-0 courses is one semester), not by re-sorting alphabetically or by credit count.
States the complexity as O(V + E) in the number of courses and prerequisite links.

transferExercises.scenario: Gates scan wristbands and must reject a wristband seen at another gate in the last 10 minutes, on a device with limited memory.
transferExercises.task: Choose the data structures (hint: recency and bounded memory), state the invariant, and describe how you'd talk through this problem in a live round, including the clarifying questions you'd ask first.
successCriteria: Chooses a Map (or the linked-list-plus-Map version) keyed by wristband id, not a plain object, since eviction must be by true recency and ids can be numeric-looking.
States the invariant precisely: a wristband is rejected only if it's present AND its last-seen time is within the 10-minute window; anything scanned more than 10 minutes ago has already aged out.
Recognizes this as bounded-memory recency tracking, not an unbounded log: old entries must be evicted, by time or by capacity, so memory doesn't grow with festival duration.

Talks through it out loud in the right order: states clarifying questions first (how many gates, is 10 minutes a hard cutoff or sliding, what's the actual memory limit) before naming the data structure.

sections.title: Frontend System Design
sections.description: Lead a whiteboard design round the way it actually goes: **requirements with numbers**, a **data model** and **API contract**, then component boundaries. Build the systems that make those rounds hard — a **typeahead** with debounce, cancellation, and a latest-wins guard; a **variable-height virtualized list** with prefix sums and scroll anchoring; a **normalized store** with memoized selectors; and an **optimistic-update feed** with rollback, reconciliation, and cursor-based merging — then defend the trade-offs under pushback. Examples come from a travel booking and trip-sharing product: destination search, a trip feed, shared itineraries, and a bookings table.

learningObjectives.description: Lead a 45-minute design session: clarify requirements, define the data model and API contract, then derive component boundaries
Build a typeahead with debounced queries, request cancellation, result caching, and keyboard navigation, and justify each decision in a design doc
Build a variable-height virtualized list that preserves scroll position when data updates
Build a cursor-paginated feed with optimistic likes and rollback, plus invalidation on new posts
Build a library-free normalized store with selectors
Produce four two-page walkthroughs (feed, editor, typeahead, table) and defend their tradeoffs under pushback

motivationHooks.prompt: A design round is graded on the order you reveal ideas in as much as the ideas themselves, and a shipped typeahead with no latest-wins guard will show a traveler results for a city they stopped typing minutes ago. This section is about doing both under a clock: correctly, and in the right order.

A typeahead debounces every keystroke at 200 ms and aborts the previous request on every new one. Before the lecture explains it, guess: can a user still see results for a query they've already changed? Keep your answer; Lecture 5.2 comes back to it.

A "like" button shows a red heart instantly, the save request fails, and a toast says "Couldn't save your like" — but the heart stays red and the count stays one too high, forever, until the next refetch quietly fixes it. What did the toast actually do?

This section pulls together almost everything so far: Section 1's debounce and cancellation, Section 2's cursor pagination, Section 3's query cache and keys, and Section 4's binary search and talk track, all inside one whiteboard round and one shipped system.

Yes. Debounce reduces how many requests go out, and abort saves bandwidth, but a response can already be in flight before the abort fires. Only a **latest-wins guard** — ignoring any response whose query isn't the current one — actually prevents a stale response from updating the screen. If you guessed "no, debounce plus abort is enough," you've now met the gap Lecture 5.2 is built to close.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- A design session runs requirements (with numbers) → data model → API contract → component architecture → deep dives → trade-offs. Frameworks and component trees are consequences, not starting points.
- Put each piece of state at its lowest owner: component, shared UI, URL, or server cache. Server state and UI state have different lifecycles even when they live in the same store.
- Debounce, cancellation, and caching each solve a different problem; only a **latest-wins guard** actually prevents a stale response from winning a race.
- Virtualization isn't free: it costs find-in-page, screen-reader navigation, SEO, and complexity. Choose pagination, infinite scroll, or virtualization from what users need to do with the list, and use prefix sums plus binary search — not a linear scan — to find the visible range.
- An optimistic update needs three paths: apply immediately, reconcile to the server's response on success, and roll back to the last **confirmed** value on failure, with sequence numbers guarding rapid repeated actions, and refreshed feed heads get merged by id, never by position.
- Handle pushback with constraint → cost → conditional alternative — it's usually a probe of your reasoning, not a verdict.
keyTakeaways: Requirements with numbers → data model → API contract → architecture → deep dives → trade-offs; frameworks are a consequence, never a starting point.
Put each piece of state at its lowest owner, and keep server state (cached, stale, invalidated) separate from UI state (local truth).
Debounce reduces requests, abort saves bandwidth, and only a latest-wins guard prevents a stale response from winning a race.

Virtualization costs find-in-page, screen-reader navigation, SEO, and complexity — choose it, pagination, or infinite scroll from the users' tasks, and use prefix sums plus binary search (not a linear scan) to find the visible range.
Optimistic = apply + reconcile on success + roll back to the last confirmed value on failure, with sequence numbers for rapid repeated actions; merge refreshed feed heads by id, not position.
Answer pushback with constraint → cost → conditional alternative.
