learningExperiences.title: Lecture 5.1: Leading a Frontend Design Session

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Run a design session in a fixed order: requirements → data model → API contract → component architecture → deep dives → trade-offs. (objective o1)
2. Separate functional from non-functional requirements and turn them into numbers. (objective o1)
3. Decide where each piece of state lives. (objective o1, o5)

terms.definition: What the product does ("travelers can like a trip post").
How well it does it: latency, scale, offline support, accessibility, device range, internationalization.
The client-side entities and their relationships (Trip, User, Post, Booking).
The request/response shapes, pagination scheme, errors, and real-time channel between client and server.
Where one component's responsibility ends. Good boundaries follow data ownership.
Which layer owns a piece of state: local component, shared UI store, URL, or server cache.
A client-side cache of data the server owns. It can be stale, and it needs fetching, invalidation, and deduping.
State owned entirely by the client: an open menu, a draft, a selected tab.

contentBlocks.content:
### Start with requirements, not React

The most common failure in a frontend design round is opening with "I'd use Next.js with Redux…" (misconception `frontend-system-design.m1`). Framework choices are *consequences* of requirements. A useful structure for 45 minutes:

| Minutes | Step | Output on the whiteboard |
|---|---|---|
| 0–7 | **Requirements** | 4–6 functional bullets. NFRs with numbers: "feed p75 LCP < 2.5 s on mid-range Android", "10 k bookings in the table", "WCAG 2.2 AA". Out of scope, stated explicitly. |
| 7–12 | **Data model** | Entities, ids, and relationships. Note what is server state and what is UI state. |
| 12–18 | **API contract** | Endpoints, pagination (cursor), error shape, optimistic mutation responses, and the real-time channel (SSE or WebSocket) if needed. |
| 18–25 | **Architecture** | Component tree derived *from* the data model, with the owner of each state labelled. |
| 25–40 | **Deep dives** | The 2–3 hardest parts: virtualization, optimistic updates, caching, accessibility, performance. |
| 40–45 | **Trade-offs and extensions** | What you'd do with more time, and what you consciously didn't do. |

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s05-m1): A whiteboard laid out for a design round. Six labelled regions filled in for "Trip Feed": Requirements (with NFR numbers highlighted), Data Model (Trip, Post, User boxes with ids and arrows), API (GET /feed?cursor=, POST /posts/:id/like), Component tree (FeedPage → FeedList (virtualized) → PostCard → LikeButton), Deep dives (optimistic like, image loading/CLS), and Trade-offs. Arrows show that the component tree was derived from the data model.

contentBlocks.content:
### Where state lives

Put state at the **lowest owner that needs it**. A global store isn't a default (misconception `frontend-system-design.m2`):

| Kind of state | Owner | Examples in a travel app |
|---|---|---|
| Ephemeral UI | the component | a dropdown being open, a hover preview |
| Shared UI | a context or small store near the users of it | the selected trip in a split view |
| Navigational | the URL | search query, filters, sort, page, selected tab |
| Server cache | a query cache (s3) or a normalized store (Lecture 5.4) | trips, posts, bookings |
| Form drafts | the form, and persisted if losing it would hurt | a booking form in progress |

Server state and UI state are different kinds of things (misconception `client-data-management.m1`). Server state has an owner elsewhere, a freshness, and invalidation rules. UI state is local truth. When you mix them in one blob, a refetch wipes out the user's draft.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **state belongs at its lowest owner, and mixing server state with UI state is what breaks first.** Edit the map below to classify two more pieces of state from a trip-sharing app (your own choice) into the right bucket, then compare with the state-ownership table above.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: running the session
contentBlocks.content:
- **Opening with frameworks or a component tree.**
- **NFRs without numbers.** "Fast" isn't a requirement.
- **Everything in a global store.**
- **Offset pagination for a live feed.**
- **Never saying what's out of scope.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 5.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Requirements (with numbers) → data model → API → components → deep dives → trade-offs.
- Put each piece of state at its lowest owner. Keep server cache separate from UI state, and put navigational state in the URL.

interactionSequence.prompt: Drag these into the order a 45-minute design session should follow, first to last.
options: Architecture: a component tree derived from the data model
Requirements: functional bullets and numbered NFRs, plus what's out of scope
Deep dives: the 2–3 hardest parts
API contract: endpoints, pagination, errors, real-time channel
Trade-offs and extensions
Data model: entities, ids, relationships, and which are server vs. UI state

optionFeedback.feedback: The component tree comes fourth: it is derived FROM the data model and API, not decided first.
Requirements come first. Every later decision is a consequence of them.
Deep dives come after the architecture is sketched, once you know which 2–3 parts are actually hard.
The API contract comes third, once the data model tells you what needs to move between client and server.
Trade-offs and extensions close the session, once the hard parts have been worked through.
The data model comes second: entities and relationships, informed by the requirements just gathered.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Requirements → data model → API → architecture → deep dives → trade-offs. Each step's output becomes the next step's input, which is why opening with a component tree or a framework skips the reasoning that should have produced it.
hints: The component tree and the API contract are both consequences of something decided earlier — what?
Numbers belong on the board before any code or diagram does.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: In a whiteboard round for "Design a collaborative itinerary editor," what should come out of the first five minutes?
options: Functional and non-functional requirements with numbers (concurrent editors, offline needs, latency), plus what's explicitly out of scope
A decision between OT and CRDT for merging concurrent edits
The React component tree for the editor toolbar and document pane
A decision on which state-management library will hold presence and cursors

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Requirements, with numbers, come first and shape every later decision.
That's a deep dive, and a good one — but it's premature before you know the concurrency numbers that would justify it.
A component tree is a consequence of the data model and architecture, not a starting point.
That's a tool choice made before knowing what state exists or who owns it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Numbers first: how many concurrent editors, what offline behavior is required, what latency is acceptable. Everything else, including the OT-vs-CRDT deep dive, follows from those numbers.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A bookings table has a search filter, a selected row for a side panel, and the fetched booking rows themselves. Where should each live?
options: Filter in the URL; selected row in local or shared UI state near the table; booking rows in a server cache
All three in one global store, since they're all "table state"
All three in the server cache, since they all come from or affect what's displayed from the server
All three as local component state inside the table component

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Navigational state goes in the URL, ephemeral UI stays local or shared nearby, and server-owned data lives in a cache.
A global store isn't a default. Each of the three has a different lifecycle and a different natural owner.
The filter and the selected row are not server-owned data; folding them into the server cache mixes freshness/invalidation rules with local UI truth.
Local-only state can't be shared by URL or survive a reload, which the filter specifically needs to do.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Put each piece of state at its lowest owner: the filter is navigational (URL), the selection is shared UI, and the rows are server state with their own freshness and invalidation rules.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 3 taught that a component's render snapshot and its re-render triggers determine what that component "sees" at any instant, and that state has a clear owner. How does that same idea of clear ownership show up in Lecture 5.1's rule to put state at its lowest owner?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Both are about making it unambiguous who is responsible for a piece of state and when it changes. In Section 3, a component only ever sees the props and state captured in its own render snapshot, so ownership has to be explicit or reads go stale. In Lecture 5.1, putting each state at its lowest owner (component, shared UI, URL, or server cache) is the design-time version of the same discipline: if ownership is fuzzy — for example a draft comment living inside the same blob as fetched trips — a refetch can silently wipe out state nobody meant to touch, the design-level equivalent of reading a stale snapshot.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: The first 12 minutes of "Design a trip feed"
workedExamples.problem: The first 12 minutes of "Design a trip feed"
steps: **Clarify:** "Is the feed personalized? Chronological or ranked? Do we need real-time new-post notices? Images per post? Which devices? Any offline need?" The answers: ranked but paginated by the server, a "new posts" pill (not auto-insert), up to 4 images per post, mid-range Android, no offline.
**NFRs with numbers:** p75 LCP < 2.5 s, INP < 200 ms while scrolling and liking, no layout shift from images (CLS < 0.1), keyboard- and screen-reader-accessible.

**Data model:** `Post {id, authorId, tripId, text, images[{url, w, h}], likeCount, likedByMe, createdAt}`, `User {id, name, avatarUrl}`, `Trip {id, title}`. Images carry **dimensions**, which is what prevents CLS (s6).
**API:** `GET /feed?cursor=…&limit=20 → {items, nextCursor}`; `POST /posts/:id/like {liked} → {liked, likeCount}`; `GET /feed/head?since=cursor → {newCount}` polled or pushed.
workedExamples.conclusion: You haven't drawn a single component, and the hardest decisions (cursor pagination, image dimensions, the like response shape) have already been made from the requirements.

fadedVariant.problem: The first 10 minutes of "Design a shared packing checklist for a trip."
givenSteps: **Step 1, Clarify:** Ask about real-time sync across travelers, item categories, and whether items can be assigned to a specific person. Answers: yes, real-time (a few travelers, low volume), categories are free-text tags, assignment is optional per item.
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2: Write two NFRs with numbers for a packing checklist used by 2–6 travelers on flights with unreliable Wi-Fi.
Step 3: Sketch the data model: what are the entities and their relationships, and what's UI state vs. server state?
blankedStepAnswers: For example: sync latency under 2 s once connectivity returns (or explicit eventual consistency with an offline queue), and support at least 6 concurrent editors without lost writes. Numbers make an NFR testable, not just "fast" or "reliable."

Entities: `Trip {id, title}`, `ChecklistItem {id, tripId, text, category, assignedToId, checked}`, `User {id, name}`. The item fields (text, checked, assignedToId) are server state; which item is mid-edit right now, or a not-yet-saved new-item draft, is UI state kept separate so a background sync can't erase it.

retrievalPractice.prompt: List the six steps of a frontend design session in order, and what's on the board after the first step.
Where does navigational state (filters, page) live?
Section 3 talked about render snapshots and re-render triggers deciding what a component "sees." How does that connect to Lecture 5.1's rule about state ownership?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 5.2: The Typeahead, End to End

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Design a typeahead's request lifecycle: minimum length, debounce, cancellation, stale-response protection, and caching. (objective o2)
2. Design its keyboard and screen-reader behavior using the combobox pattern. (objective o2)
3. Write a design doc that justifies each decision. (objective o2)

terms.definition: An input with an associated popup listbox of suggestions (the WAI-ARIA pattern).
Tells assistive technology which option is "active" while DOM focus **stays in the input**.
A response for a query the user has already typed past.
Only the response for the most recent query may update the UI.
A map from normalized query to results. Repeated queries return instantly.

contentBlocks.content:
### The request lifecycle

For "Where to?" destination search:

1. **Normalize** the input: trim and lowercase.
2. **Minimum length** (2 characters): single letters match too much to be useful, and they cost server time.
3. **Cache hit?** Show it immediately. There's no need to debounce a free answer.
4. **Debounce** (about 200 ms, trailing): don't query mid-word (s1, debounce vs throttle).
5. **Cancel** the previous in-flight request with `AbortController`. That saves bandwidth and server work.
6. **Latest-wins guard:** even with aborts, a response can already be in flight. Ignore any response whose query isn't the latest input.
7. **Cache** successful results by normalized query. Consider a small LRU (s4) to bound memory.
8. **Errors:** show an inline message. Never show `AbortError` as an error.

Debounce doesn't prevent races. It reduces how many requests you send, but two requests can still be in flight with different latencies. Cancellation plus a latest-wins guard does prevent them.

### Keyboard and screen readers (full treatment in s7)

- Focus **stays in the input**. Arrow keys move a *virtual* active option through `aria-activedescendant`.
- `ArrowDown`/`ArrowUp` move and wrap. `Enter` selects the active option. `Escape` closes the list (and clears the input only on a second press). `Home`/`End` stay in the text field.
- The input has `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, and `aria-controls` pointing to the `role="listbox"`. Options have `role="option"` and `aria-selected` on the active one.
- A polite live region announces "5 results" after results settle. It isn't updated on every keystroke.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s05-m2): Typeahead timeline with a race. The top row shows keystrokes p, pa, par, pari at 0, 90, 180, and 260 ms. The debounce collapses them into requests for "par" (at 380 ms) and "pari" (at 460 ms, which aborts "par"). A second lane shows "par"'s response arriving late at 700 ms, crossed out by the latest-wins guard. "pari"'s response at 650 ms is rendered. Beneath the timeline, the listbox state changes and the live-region announcement "4 results" appears once.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **debounce alone still races.** The slower "par" response would win the naive race without a latest-wins guard. Add a third, even faster keystroke below and predict both `shown.naive` and `shown.guarded` before running.

contentBlocks.caption: The same race as the playground above, run as-is. Predict both lines before running, then compare with your edited version.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: typeaheads
contentBlocks.content:
- **Debounce without cancellation or a latest-wins guard.**
- **Showing "Something went wrong" for aborted requests.**
- **Moving focus into the list.**
- **Announcing on every keystroke** (live-region spam).
- **Unbounded caches.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 5.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Normalize → minimum length → cache → debounce → cancel → latest-wins → cache results.
- Combobox: focus stays in the input, arrows move `aria-activedescendant`, and a polite announcement fires once results settle.

interactionSequence.prompt: A typeahead aborts the previous request on every keystroke. A teammate says that's enough to prevent stale results from ever appearing. What's still missing?
options: A response can already be in flight before the abort fires; you still need a latest-wins guard that ignores any response whose query isn't the current one
Nothing more is needed; aborting guarantees the older response can never be shown
Switch to throttle instead of debounce, which sends requests more predictably
Raise the debounce delay so fewer requests race

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Abort reduces wasted work, but it can't retroactively stop a response that was already on its way.
Aborting a request doesn't retroactively cancel a response that had already started returning; a guard on the response itself is still needed.
Throttle sends requests mid-word and still races; it doesn't add the missing protection.
A longer debounce reduces how often requests overlap, but it can't make overlap impossible.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Debounce reduces requests, abort saves bandwidth, and the latest-wins guard is what actually prevents a stale response from updating the UI — none of the first two alone is sufficient.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate adds `role="combobox"`, `role="listbox"`, and `aria-selected` to the typeahead markup and says "now it's accessible." What's still missing?
options: Keyboard behavior: arrow keys must move a virtual active option via aria-activedescendant while focus stays in the input, and a live region must announce once results settle
Nothing; the correct ARIA roles are sufficient on their own
Moving DOM focus into each option as the user presses arrow keys
An aria-live="assertive" region that announces every keystroke's partial match

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Roles alone don't give you keyboard behavior or an announcement; both have to be built.
Adding ARIA roles alone doesn't make something accessible; the keyboard and announcement behavior still have to be implemented and tested.
Moving focus into the list breaks typing, which is exactly the error this lecture calls out.
Announcing on every keystroke is live-region spam, called out explicitly as a common error, and it doesn't wait for results to settle.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The combobox pattern needs the roles AND the behavior: focus stays in the input, arrows move `aria-activedescendant`, and a single polite announcement fires once results settle.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Why cache typeahead results with a bounded LRU (about 100 entries) instead of an unbounded Map or no cache at all?
options: It bounds memory over a long session while keeping repeated or backspaced queries instant, unlike an unbounded Map (which grows forever) or no cache (which re-queries on every backspace)
An LRU is unnecessary complexity; a plain unbounded Map is simpler and just as correct
No caching at all is best, since the debounce already limits how many requests go out
Cache only the single most recent query, since users rarely repeat searches

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. This is the same LRU idea from Section 4, applied to bound a cache that would otherwise grow for the life of the session.
An unbounded Map is a memory leak waiting to happen over a long session; the LRU isn't extra complexity, it's the fix.
Debounce limits requests while the user is actively typing; it does nothing for a query the user returns to later in the session.
A single-entry cache loses the instant hit for backspacing ("pari" → "par"), which is exactly the case the design doc calls out.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Section 4's Map-based LRU wasn't a one-off trick; here it's the structure that keeps a growing session's cache bounded while still serving instant repeats.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 1 built debounce and `AbortController`-based cancellation from primitives. Section 3's `useFetch` added deduping and abort-on-unmount for data fetching. What NEW problem does the typeahead in this lecture add that neither of those alone solves, and what's the fix?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Neither raw debounce-plus-abort nor a fetch hook's dedupe and abort-on-unmount guarantees that a still-in-flight older response won't resolve and overwrite newer results — a response can already be on its way before you call abort. The fix layered on top here is a latest-wins guard: compare the response against the latest query (or a sequence number) and ignore anything that isn't for it, on top of debouncing and aborting.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: The design doc paragraph for each decision
workedExamples.problem: Justify each decision in the destination-search design doc, pairing it with evidence and a rejected alternative:
steps: **200 ms trailing debounce.** The median gap between keystrokes for our users is about 120 ms, so 200 ms waits out a word. Alternative rejected: throttle, which queries mid-word (misconception `async-control-flow.m3`).
**Abort + latest-wins.** Aborting saves bandwidth, and the guard handles responses already in flight. Alternative rejected: debounce alone, which still races.
**Cache by normalized query (LRU 100).** Backspacing ("pari" → "par") is instant, and memory is bounded. Alternative rejected: an unbounded Map, which grows during long sessions.
**`aria-activedescendant`.** Screen readers track the option without focus leaving the input. Alternative rejected: moving DOM focus into options, which breaks typing.
**Minimum 2 characters.** 1-character queries return about 40% of all destinations. Alternative rejected: 0 characters, which shows popular destinations instead (possible v2).
workedExamples.conclusion: Each row pairs a decision with evidence and a rejected alternative. That's what "justify each decision" means in a design doc.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What four things protect a typeahead from races and wasted work?
Which ARIA attribute keeps focus in a combobox input while arrow keys move the active option?
Section 1 built debounce and cancellation from scratch; Section 3's useFetch added deduping and abort-on-unmount. What does a typeahead need beyond both of those, and why?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 5.3: Lists at Scale: Virtualization vs Pagination

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Choose between pagination, "load more," infinite scroll, and virtualization from the requirements. (objective o3, o6)
2. Compute the visible range for variable-height rows with prefix sums and binary search. (objective o3)
3. Preserve the scroll position when row heights or data change (scroll anchoring). (objective o3)

terms.definition: Rendering only the rows in or near the viewport, with spacer elements standing in for the rest.
Extra rows rendered just outside the viewport to avoid blank flashes during fast scrolls.
`offsets[i]` = the total height of rows before *i*. Row *i* spans `[offsets[i], offsets[i+1])`.
A placeholder height for rows that haven't been measured yet, corrected after measurement.
Adjusting `scrollTop` so the content the user is looking at stays put when things above it change size.
A CSS property that lets the browser skip rendering off-screen content. It's a lighter alternative for some long pages.

contentBlocks.content:
### Virtualization isn't free

Virtualization makes 10,000 rows cheap to render, but it costs you:

- **Find-in-page** (Ctrl+F) can't find rows that aren't in the DOM.
- **Screen readers** can't navigate the full list, and `aria-setsize`/`aria-posinset` have to be managed by hand.
- **SEO and printing** only see what's rendered.
- **Complexity:** measuring, estimating, anchoring, and restoring scroll on back navigation.

So "virtualization is always better than pagination" is wrong (misconception `frontend-system-design.m3`). Rules of thumb:

| Situation | Choose |
|---|---|
| Users need to find, compare, share, or print specific items; SEO matters | **Pagination** (URL-addressable pages) |
| Casual browsing with an unbounded feed | **Infinite scroll with cursor pages**, virtualized once the DOM grows past a few hundred heavy rows |
| A data grid with thousands of rows and fixed-ish heights | **Virtualization** (plus server-side sort and filter) |
| A long article or document | `content-visibility: auto`, not virtualization |

### Variable heights: offsets and binary search

Keep an array of measured (or estimated) heights and its prefix sums. For a given `scrollTop` and viewport height:

- **start** is the first row whose bottom edge is below `scrollTop`: `offsets[i+1] > scrollTop`.
- **end** (exclusive) is the first row whose top edge is at or below the viewport's bottom: `offsets[i] >= scrollTop + viewport`.

Both are **binary searches** over a monotonic array (s4): O(log n) per scroll event, instead of scanning every row.

### Anchoring: keep what the user is reading still

A photo in a post above the viewport finishes loading and grows by 240 px. Without anchoring, everything the user is reading jumps down 240 px. With anchoring, you find the first visible row *before* the change, remember how far into it the user was, and after recomputing offsets you set `scrollTop = newOffsets[anchorRow] + delta`. (Browsers do some of this natively with CSS `overflow-anchor`, but virtualized lists usually have to do it themselves because they manage the spacers.)

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Animation (s05-m3): Virtualized list with anchoring. Production brief: The left pane shows the full list conceptually, with a viewport window. The right pane shows only the rendered rows plus top and bottom spacers. A row above the viewport grows when its image loads. Version A (no anchoring) shows the content jumping. Version B shows scrollTop adjusted by the same 240 px, so the reading position stays still.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **binary search over offsets costs about the same handful of reads whether the list has 10 rows or 100,000.** Run this with 10 rows, then change the length to 100000 and compare the printed read count.

contentBlocks.caption: The same five rows as the Worked Example below, computed in code. Predict the offsets and the visible rows before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: large lists
contentBlocks.content:
- **Virtualizing by default** and breaking find-in-page and screen-reader navigation for small lists.
- **Linear scans over offsets on every scroll event.**
- **Assuming fixed heights for content that wraps.**
- **No anchoring when images or late data change heights.**
- **Losing the scroll position on back navigation.** Store it with the cursor.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 5.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Pick pagination, infinite scroll, or virtualization from the users' tasks, not from habit.
- Prefix sums + binary search give the visible range in O(log n). Anchoring keeps the reading position stable.

interactionSequence.prompt: For a bookings table where travel agents need to find, filter, and share links to specific results, rank these approaches from best fit to worst.
options: Virtualize all 10,000 rows and keep everything client-side
Server-side filter, sort, and paginate, with page and filter state in the URL
Infinite scroll with cursor-paginated pages, virtualized once the list grows long
Load all 10,000 rows unpaginated with no virtualization at all

optionFeedback.feedback: Better than nothing, but Ctrl+F, screen-reader table navigation, and shareable links to a specific row still break.
Best fit: pages are URL-addressable and shareable, and each page's payload stays small.
A reasonable middle ground for casual browsing, but an agent can't easily return to or share "page 4 of filtered results."
The worst of both worlds: a huge payload, and still no shareable, addressable view of a specific slice.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Match the strategy to what users need to DO with the list — find, filter, compare, share, print — before reaching for virtualization by default. That default reach is exactly the "virtualization is always better than pagination" misconception the lecture names.
hints: Ask what the travel agent needs to do with the list: just browse, or find, filter, and share specific results?
Shareability and printability point toward pagination; casual endless browsing points toward virtualization.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: Heights `[80, 40, 160]`, so offsets `[0, 80, 120, 280]`. `scrollTop = 100`, viewport `= 150`, no overscan. What is `{ start, end }`?
options: { start: 1, end: 3 }
{ start: 0, end: 2 }
{ start: 1, end: 2 }
{ start: 0, end: 3 }

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. `offsets[2] = 120` is the first offset greater than 100, so start = 1; `offsets[3] = 280` is the first at or past 250, so end = 3.
This ignores the bottom edge of row 0: `offsets[1] = 80` is not greater than `scrollTop = 100`, so row 0 is not visible.
This stops one row short: row 2 is still visible, since its top (`120`) is before `scrollTop + viewport = 250`.
This is the whole list; it ignores `scrollTop` entirely.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: start is the first row whose bottom edge is below `scrollTop`; end (exclusive) is the first row whose top edge is at or past `scrollTop + viewport`. Both are binary searches over the sorted offsets array.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A design uses virtualization by default for a 40-row settings list, because "virtualization is always better." What's wrong with that reasoning?
options: At 40 rows there's no rendering-cost problem to solve, and virtualization still costs find-in-page, screen-reader navigation, and complexity for no benefit
Nothing; virtualization is strictly better for any list, regardless of size
Virtualization only works with fixed-height rows, so it's technically impossible here
Virtualization is fine here, but it should be replaced by pagination purely for SEO reasons

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Virtualization is a cost paid to solve a rendering problem that a 40-row list doesn't have.
That's the exact belief this lecture calls a misconception: virtualization trades real costs (find-in-page, accessibility, complexity) for a rendering benefit that isn't always needed.
Variable-height virtualization is exactly what Lecture 5.3 covers with prefix sums; fixed heights aren't a requirement.
SEO isn't usually the deciding factor for an authenticated settings page, and this framing dodges the real question of whether virtualization is needed at all.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Rules of thumb, not habit: virtualize when the rendering cost is real (thousands of rows), and remember every virtualized list pays for it in find-in-page, screen-reader navigation, and complexity.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 2 used the rendering pipeline (style → layout → paint → composite) as the lens for explaining jank from forced layout. In Lecture 5.3, prefix sums plus binary search replace a linear scan for finding the visible range. Which expensive per-scroll-event work does this save, and how does that connect to the pipeline lens from Section 2?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A linear scan over offsets costs O(n) reads per scroll event, and — just like the forced-layout pattern from Section 2 — doing that much synchronous work inside a scroll handler risks piling up main-thread work on every scroll or frame. Binary search cuts it to O(log n), keeping the visible-range computation cheap enough that it doesn't become the next forced-synchronous-layout-style bottleneck: the same lesson about respecting the frame budget, just applied to plain JS work instead of layout reads.

workedExamples.title: Visible range by hand
steps: **start:** the first *i* with `offsets[i+1] > 120`. `offsets[1] = 100` is not greater and `offsets[2] = 150` is, so start = 1.
**end:** the first *i* with `offsets[i] >= 300`. `offsets[3] = 350`, so end = 3, meaning rows 1 and 2 are visible.
**Overscan 1:** render rows 0–3.
**Anchor:** the user is 20 px into row 1 (`120 − 100`). If row 0 grows to 340 px, the new `offsets[1]` is 340, so set `scrollTop` = 360.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two binary searches and one subtraction give the range and a stable reading position.

givenSteps: **Step 1, start:** the first *i* with `offsets[i+1] > 100`. `offsets[1] = 60` is not greater and `offsets[2] = 150` is, so start = 1.
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2, end: apply the same rule (first *i* with `offsets[i] >= scrollTop + viewport`) to find end. What is it, and which rows are visible?
Step 3, overscan 1: which rows actually get rendered?
blankedStepAnswers: `offsets[3] = 190` is not ≥ 250, `offsets[4] = 340` is, so end = 4. Rows 1, 2, and 3 are visible (indices in `[1, 4)`).
Widen by 1 on each side and clamp to `[0, count]`: `start = max(0, 1-1) = 0`, `end = min(6, max(4, 2)+1) = 5`, so rows 0 through 4 (five rows) actually render.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 5.4: Client Data: Normalization, Optimistic Updates, and Feeds

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Normalize nested API data into entities by id plus ordered id lists, and derive views with memoized selectors. (objective o5)
2. Implement optimistic updates with rollback and reconciliation, including rapid repeated actions. (objective o4)
3. Merge a refreshed feed head into an existing cursor-paginated list without duplicates, and detect gaps. (objective o4)

terms.definition: Storing each entity once, by id (`users.u1`), with references by id elsewhere (`trip.ownerId`).
A pure function from store state to the data a view needs. **Memoized** selectors return the *same* object when their inputs haven't changed.
Showing the expected result of a mutation before the server confirms it.
Restoring the last confirmed state when the mutation fails.
Replacing the optimistic value with the server's authoritative response (for example the real like count).
Marking cached data stale after something changed, such as the user posting, so it's refetched.
Missing items between a refreshed head and the existing list, shown as a "load newer" divider.

contentBlocks.content:
### Why normalize

The same traveler, Ben, appears as the owner of one trip, a member of another, and the author of twelve posts. Nested API data stores him fourteen times. When he renames himself, you'd have to find all fourteen copies. After normalization:

contentBlocks.caption: Illustrative data shape (a plain object literal, not a statement) — shown for the pattern, not runnable in this engine.

contentBlocks.content: A rename is one write. **Selectors** join the entities back into view models, and **memoization** (s3 `memoizeOne`) keeps their output referentially stable. When only `ui` changes, `selectTripCards` returns the *same* array, so memoized list components skip re-rendering.

### Optimistic updates need three paths

An optimistic update isn't just "set the new value" (misconception `client-data-management.m2`):

1. **Apply** the expected value immediately and remember the **last confirmed** value.
2. **On success**, **reconcile**: replace the optimistic value with the server's response (the like count may have changed because others liked it too), and record it as confirmed.
3. **On failure**, **roll back** to the last confirmed value and tell the user ("Couldn't save your like").

For rapid repeated actions (like, unlike, like), tag each mutation with a **sequence number**. Only the latest mutation's outcome is allowed to change what's shown. Older responses only update the "confirmed" record.

### Feeds: cursors, invalidation, and gaps

Cursor pagination avoids the duplicates and gaps that offsets cause when new items arrive (misconception `client-data-management.m3`, first seen in s2). When the user **posts**, invalidate the feed head: refetch page 1 and **merge** it. Fresh items come first, then the existing items not already present. If the fresh page doesn't overlap the existing list at all, there may be items in between, so flag a **gap** and render a "Load newer posts" divider rather than silently skipping them.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s05-m4): Optimistic like: three paths. A state diagram: confirmed {liked:false, 10} → user taps → optimistic {liked:true, 11}. The success arrow goes to server {liked:true, 12} ("reconcile"). The failure arrow returns to confirmed {liked:false, 10} with a toast. A side lane shows two rapid taps with sequence numbers 1 and 2, where the response to #1 arrives after #2 and is ignored for display.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **only the latest tap's outcome may change what's shown, no matter which response lands first.** Predict both `console.log(shown)` lines before running.

contentBlocks.caption: Normalization in code: predict both lines before running, then compare with the fourteen-copies problem in the prose above.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: client data
contentBlocks.content:
- **Storing nested copies of entities.**
- **Selectors that build new arrays on every call**, which causes re-renders everywhere.
- **Optimistic updates without rollback, or without reconciling to the server's value.**
- **Letting stale responses from earlier taps overwrite newer intent.**
- **Refetching the head and appending it**, which creates duplicates.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 5.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Normalize server data into entities by id plus ordered lists. Keep UI state separate. Derive views with memoized selectors.
- Optimistic = apply + reconcile on success + roll back on failure, with sequence numbers for rapid actions.
- Merge refreshed heads by id and surface gaps instead of hiding them.

interactionSequence.prompt: **An optimistic like with no rollback.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
toast: could not like
{"liked":true,"count":11}
```

**Why intuition fails.** The toast feels like the failure was handled, but nothing restored the post. The heart stays filled and the count is permanently one too high, until the next refetch "mysteriously" changes it back. The UI now disagrees with the server, and the user thinks the like went through. This is misconception `client-data-management.m2`: an optimistic update needs a remembered confirmed value and a rollback path, and on success a reconciliation with the server's number.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The toast feels like the failure was handled, but nothing restored the post. The heart stays filled and the count is permanently one too high, until the next refetch "mysteriously" changes it back. The UI now disagrees with the server, and the user thinks the like went through. This is misconception `client-data-management.m2`: an optimistic update needs a remembered confirmed value and a rollback path, and on success a reconciliation with the server's number.
hints: Trace what `likeNaive` actually changes on the `post` object, and what it never touches.
The `.catch` runs and logs a toast — does that toast actually undo anything on `post`?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Selector identity.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
false
true
true
```

**Why intuition fails.** The two un-memoized results *contain* the same trips, as the third line shows, so it seems they should be "equal." `filter` always returns a **new array**, and React's `memo`, `useMemo` dependencies, and `useSyncExternalStore` all compare by reference. Every UI-only change would re-render every list that uses the un-memoized selector. Memoizing on the input reference (`s.trips`) returns the same array until the trips themselves change.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The two un-memoized results *contain* the same trips, as the third line shows, so it seems they should be "equal." `filter` always returns a **new array**, and React's `memo`, `useMemo` dependencies, and `useSyncExternalStore` all compare by reference. Every UI-only change would re-render every list that uses the un-memoized selector. Memoizing on the input reference (`s.trips`) returns the same array until the trips themselves change.
hints: `filter` always allocates a brand-new array, even when its contents are unchanged — check what each selector compares.
React and friends compare with `===`; "same contents" and "same reference" are different questions.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: A booking-save button optimistically shows "Saved" immediately, and on failure just leaves it as "Saved" with no other change. What's broken, and what should happen instead?
options: On failure, roll back to the last confirmed state and show an error; on success, reconcile to the server's actual response rather than assuming the optimistic value was exactly right
Nothing; showing success immediately is the whole point of an optimistic update
Never show the optimistic state at all; wait for the server before updating anything
Retry the save silently forever until it succeeds, without telling the user

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Optimistic needs all three paths: apply, reconcile on success, and roll back on failure.
Optimistic updates aren't just "set the new value" — without a rollback, the UI disagrees with the server the moment the save actually fails.
That removes the whole benefit of an optimistic update, which is showing the expected result immediately.
Silent infinite retries hide the failure from the user and from the roll-back path entirely.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Apply immediately, reconcile to the server's response on success, and roll back to the last confirmed value (with an error) on failure — "just set the value" only covers the first of the three paths.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: After a user posts, the feed head is refetched and returns some posts that already exist in the list. How should the new page be merged in?
options: Merge by post id: fresh items first, then existing items not already present, flagging a gap when there's no overlap at all
Prepend the fresh page and slice off however many items were fetched from the end of the existing list
Discard the existing list and only show the fresh page until the user scrolls, restarting pagination from scratch
Append the fresh page to the end of the existing list, since new items are just added like any other page

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Matching by id survives new posts shifting everything else down, which position never does.
That's offset-style thinking: it assumes positions are stable, so it drops or duplicates posts the moment new ones have been published.
That throws away data the user already loaded, and it isn't necessary once you can merge by id.
New posts go first, not last — appending breaks the "newest first" ordering the feed depends on.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the same "identity, not position" idea as Section 3's keyed list reconciliation and Section 4's Map-based LRU keys — matching by id survives things shifting around, the way position never does.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Explain why a memoized selector needs to compare `state.entities` and `state.tripOrder` by reference rather than deep-comparing their contents, and what would break if you deep-compared instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Deep comparison would be correct but expensive — it would have to walk every entity and every array on every call, which defeats the point of avoiding extra renders and recomputation. Reference comparison is cheap because immutable updates guarantee a reference only changes when the underlying data actually changed, so `===` is a safe, fast proxy for "did anything relevant change," as long as every write goes through an immutable update instead of a mutation.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Rapid like, unlike, with out-of-order responses
workedExamples.problem: Start: confirmed `{liked: false, count: 10}`.
steps: Tap (seq 1) → show `{true, 11}`. The request `setLike(true)` is in flight.
Tap (seq 2) → show `{false, 10}`. The request `setLike(false)` is in flight.
Response 2 arrives first: `{false, 10}`. seq 2 is the latest, so show and confirm `{false, 10}`.
Response 1 arrives: `{true, 11}`. seq 1 isn't the latest, so update nothing on screen.
workedExamples.conclusion: The screen matches the user's last intent and the server's last answer to that intent. Without sequence numbers, step 4 would flip the heart back on.

fadedVariant.problem: Rapid follow/unfollow on a fellow traveler's profile, starting from confirmed `{ following: false, followerCount: 40 }`.
givenSteps: 1. Tap "Follow" (seq 1) → show `{ following: true, followerCount: 41 }`. `setFollow(true)` is in flight.
blankedStepPrompts: 2. Tap "Unfollow" immediately (seq 2) → what does the UI show, and what request is in flight?
3. If the response to seq 2 (`{ false, 40 }`) arrives first, then the response to seq 1 (`{ true, 41 }`) arrives late — what does the UI show after each, and why?
blankedStepAnswers: Show `{ following: false, followerCount: 40 }`. `setFollow(false)` is now in flight, alongside the still-pending seq 1 request.

After seq 2's response: seq 2 is the latest tap, so the UI shows and confirms `{ false, 40 }`. After seq 1's late response: seq 1 isn't the latest, so nothing on screen changes — the button correctly stays "unfollowed," matching the user's last action rather than flickering back.

workedExamples.title: Merging a refreshed head
workedExamples.problem: Existing: `[p5, p4, p3]`. The user posts, and the head is refetched: `[p7, p6, p5]`.
steps: The fresh items come first: `p7, p6, p5`.
Then the existing items not in the fresh set: `p4, p3`.
There's an overlap (`p5`), so there's no gap. If the fresh page had been `[p9, p8]` (no overlap), the result would be `[p9, p8, p3?…]` with a **gap** flag, because `p7`–`p4` might be missing.
workedExamples.conclusion: Merge by id, not by position. An offset-style "skip as many as we fetched" would drop or duplicate posts.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What are the three paths of an optimistic update?
Why normalize server data into entities by id?

Section 3 used keys to match old and new elements by identity, and Section 4 used a Map-based LRU keyed by request. What plays the same "identity, not position" role when merging a refreshed feed head?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 5.5: Four Walkthroughs, and Defending Them

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Deliver feed, collaborative editor, typeahead, and data-table designs in a two-page, whiteboard-ready shape. (objective o6)
2. Respond to pushback by restating the constraint, naming the trade-off, and offering a conditional alternative. (objective o6, o1)

terms.definition: A spoken, structured design, around 2 pages when written.
An interviewer's challenge ("Why not virtualize?"). It tests reasoning, not stubbornness.
"If X were true, I'd choose Y instead." It shows you understand the trade-off space.
Operational Transformation and Conflict-free Replicated Data Types: two families of algorithms for merging concurrent edits in collaborative editors.
Showing who else is viewing or editing, and where their cursors are.

contentBlocks.content:
### The two-page shape

Each walkthrough uses the same six headings from Lecture 5.1, with **numbers** in the requirements and **one diagram** for the architecture. Keep deep dives to the two or three things that make *this* system hard:

| System | The hard parts to deep-dive |
|---|---|
| **Trip feed** | cursor pagination + head invalidation, optimistic likes, image CLS, when to virtualize |
| **Collaborative itinerary editor** | document model, concurrent edits (OT vs CRDT, and why a library like Yjs), presence, undo per user, offline and reconnect |
| **Destination typeahead** | request lifecycle (Lecture 5.2), combobox accessibility, caching, highlighting matches safely (no `innerHTML` with user input) |
| **Bookings data table** | server vs client sort/filter/paginate, URL state, virtualization vs pagination, column resizing, keyboard grid navigation, CSV export |

### Handling pushback

A three-part response:

1. **Restate the constraint** you designed for: "I chose pagination because agents need to share a link to page 4 of filtered results."
2. **Name the cost you accepted:** "The cost is an extra click to go further."
3. **Offer the conditional alternative:** "If agents mostly scanned rather than shared, I'd use a virtualized infinite list and keep the filters in the URL."

This works because the interviewer is usually testing whether you **understand the trade-off space**, not whether you'll cave or dig in.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s05-m5): Four walkthroughs on one wall. A photo-style mockup of four A4 pages pinned side by side (trip feed, itinerary editor, typeahead, bookings table), each following the same six headings, with its hard-part deep dives highlighted in yellow. Sticky notes on each page hold one anticipated pushback question and its constraint → cost → conditional answer.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: walkthroughs
contentBlocks.content:
- **Deep-diving the easy parts** (component names, styling) instead of the hard ones.
- **No numbers.**
- **Treating pushback as "you're wrong."** Handle it as a trade-off conversation.
- **Choosing CRDT or OT without saying why**, or building one from scratch in the design instead of naming a proven library.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 5.5 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Same six-part shape, two pages, one diagram, deep dives on what's hard.
- Answer pushback with constraint → cost → conditional alternative.

interactionSequence.prompt: During a walkthrough of the destination typeahead, the interviewer asks: "why not just search on every keystroke instead of debouncing?" You're confident debouncing is right. What's the best response?
options: Restate the constraint (query cost and mid-word noise), name the cost of searching on every keystroke, and offer the conditional under which you'd change it (for example a tiny local dataset with no query cost)
Immediately agree and switch to search-on-every-keystroke, since being asked about it must mean the current design is wrong
Restate the design's benefits at length without naming any cost or trade-off
Move on without addressing the question, since the design is already correct

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Constraint → cost → conditional shows you understand the trade-off space, which is usually what pushback is testing.
A follow-up question is not proof the design is wrong; caving without weighing the trade-off wastes the chance to show your reasoning.
Naming zero costs reads as either not understanding the trade-off or refusing to engage with it.
Silence, or ignoring the question, reads as not engaging with the interviewer's reasoning at all.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Pushback is usually a probe of your reasoning, not a verdict. Restate what you designed for, name what it costs, and say what would change your mind.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: During your itinerary-editor walkthrough, the interviewer pushes back: "Why use a CRDT library instead of just locking the document while one person edits?" Using the constraint → cost → conditional structure, write your response.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Constraint: multiple travelers often edit different days of the same itinerary at once, including briefly offline on a flight. Cost of locking: it blocks concurrent edits entirely and handles reconnection badly — whoever reconnects last either overwrites the other or is blocked outright, with no real offline support. A CRDT, via a proven library like Yjs rather than one built from scratch, merges concurrent edits automatically and tolerates offline and reconnect. Conditional: if edits were rare and effectively sequential — say, only one editor per itinerary, ever — locking would be simpler, and I'd use it instead.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 4 described a "talk track" for live coding: narrate your approach, call out checkpoints, and handle interviewer nudges without treating them as failure. How does the constraint → cost → conditional structure for pushback serve the same underlying goal as that talk track?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Both are about making your reasoning legible in real time under evaluation pressure. The talk track narrates a plan so the interviewer can follow it and intervene before you go far down a bad path; constraint → cost → conditional narrates a trade-off so pushback reads as a probe of your reasoning rather than a verdict on your competence. In both cases, staying silent or treating any question as proof you're wrong works against you — the same two failure modes this section's misconceptions m1 and m3 name.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your two-page bookings-table walkthrough spends most of its space on component names and button styling, with one line on server vs. client sort, filter, and paginate. What's wrong?
options: The deep dives should cover the 2–3 hardest parts of THIS system (here: server vs. client sort/filter/paginate, URL state, virtualization vs. pagination), not the easy, low-risk parts
Nothing; thorough naming shows attention to detail
A walkthrough should never mention component names at all
The fix is to add a fifth page covering more surface details

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Deep dives are for the parts that are actually hard to get right, not the parts that are easy to fill space with.
This is exactly the "deep-diving the easy parts instead of the hard ones" error the lecture names — it reads as avoiding the harder decisions.
Naming components briefly is fine; the problem is spending your limited two pages on them instead of the hard parts.
More pages isn't the fix; the same two pages need to be reallocated toward the hard parts.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Two pages is a forcing function: spend it on the 2–3 things that make this system hard, and say so explicitly, rather than on the parts that would look the same in any design.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

workedExamples.title: Pushback on the bookings table
workedExamples.problem:
**Interviewer:** "10,000 bookings. Why not just load them all and virtualize?"

**Response:**
steps: *Restate:* "Requirements: filters and sorts over 10 k rows, results shareable by URL, and it must work on a travel agent's older laptop."

*Trade-off:* "Loading everything means a 3–4 MB payload plus client-side sorting on every change. Virtualization breaks find-in-page and makes screen-reader table navigation harder. Server-side filter, sort, and paginate, with the state in the URL, keeps the payload around 20 KB and makes views shareable."

*Conditional:* "If the dataset were under about 2,000 rows and agents needed instant client-side filtering offline, I'd load it once into IndexedDB (s2) and virtualize with proper `aria-rowcount` and `aria-rowindex`."
workedExamples.conclusion: You didn't abandon the design or refuse the idea. You showed where the boundary between the two options lies.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What is the pushback answer structure?
Section 4's talk track was: narrate approach, checkpoints, and handling of a nudge. What's the equivalent three-part structure for handling design-session pushback?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: Trips at Scale

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. The exercises here are the **logic cores** of each system (controllers, stores, and range math); you wire them to real UI in the Practical Activity.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenge 1 (the typeahead controller) gives you the full scaffold — a fake scheduler, a fake search, and the scenario runner — and leaves the debounce, cancel, latest-wins, and cache logic to you. Challenges 2 and 3 give you the store or likes-map skeleton and leave the normalization, rollback, and reconciliation logic to you. Challenge 4 locks the function signatures for the virtualization math and leaves the prefix-sum, binary-search, and anchoring logic to you. Challenge 5 has no scaffolding at all: the whole `mergeHead` program is yours.

The two test-suite challenges turn it around: the undo-stack challenge gives you correct code and asks you to write the tests that prove it; the bookings-table challenge gives you a correct test suite and asks you to fix broken code until it passes.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your undo-stack tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the undo-stack challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "Trips at Scale."** Expected time is 12–14 hours.

1. **Destination typeahead** (React or your framework) on your s05-e1 controller: debounced queries, abort, latest-wins, an LRU result cache (s4), and full combobox keyboard support with `aria-activedescendant`. **Design doc (≤2 pages)** justifying each decision in the table format from Lecture 5.2. *(o2)*
2. **Variable-height virtualized list** of 5,000 trip posts with images of known dimensions. It must preserve the scroll position when images load and when new data is prepended. Record a video showing it stays still. *(o3)*
3. **Infinite feed** with cursor pagination (s2 loader), optimistic likes with rollback (s05-e3), and head invalidation plus a gap divider after the user posts (s05-e5). Use a mock server with injectable latency and failure rate. *(o4)*
4. **Normalized store** with selectors, library-free, typed in TypeScript (`EntityState<T> = { byId: Record<string, T>; allIds: string[] }`). *(o5)*
5. **Four written walkthroughs, each ≤2 pages:** trip feed, collaborative itinerary editor, destination typeahead, bookings table. Each has requirements with numbers, a data model, an API, an architecture diagram, 2–3 deep dives, and trade-offs, plus **three anticipated pushback questions with your constraint → cost → conditional answers**. *(o6)*
6. **Mock design round:** run one 45-minute session with a peer as the interviewer, using one of your walkthrough prompts. Record it if both of you agree. *(o1)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for Trips at Scale (100 points)
rows: No races, cache, accessible keyboard behavior, every decision justified with a rejected alternative.
O(log n) range, stable anchoring, a documented choice of virtualization over pagination.
Rollback, reconciliation, sequence handling, no duplicates, visible gaps.
One write per entity update, stable selectors, UI state separated.
Consistent shape, numbers, deep dives on the hard parts, credible pushback answers.
Followed the session structure, and the self-review names two improvements.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 5 (most scaffolded): a typeahead controller (debounce, cancel, latest-wins, cache)

Implement `createTypeahead({ search, scheduler, debounceMs, minChars, onChange })` with `input(query)` and `getState()`. It normalizes queries, ignores those shorter than `minChars`, serves cache hits instantly, debounces misses, aborts the previous request, ignores stale responses, and never treats aborts as errors.

Each case runs a scripted list of `['type', text] | ['wait', ms] | ['respond', query, results] | ['fail', query, message]` steps through your `createTypeahead` using a manual clock and a fake search, then reports which requests were made, which were aborted, and the final state.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

cases.name: typical: a burst of typing sends one query
boundary: slow older response can't win
cache hit is instant, no new request

Implement `mergeHead(existing, freshHead)`, where both are arrays of post ids, newest first. It returns `{ items, gap }`: fresh ids first, then existing ids not already present, with `gap` set to `true` when the fresh page shares no id with a non-empty existing list.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working undo stack for the itinerary editor, you write the tests

The collaborative itinerary editor keeps a per-user undo stack. Before each edit, the editor calls `push(currentDoc)`. `undo(current)` returns the previous document, and `redo(current)` returns the next one. The implementation below is correct. Write tests proving that (1) undo and redo round-trip, (2) a new edit clears redo, (3) capacity drops the **oldest** history, and (4) undo or redo with no history returns the current document unchanged. Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **four** tests). Then confirm your suite catches each of the three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks the undo/redo round trip, that a new `push` clears redo, that capacity drops the **oldest** entry, and that undo/redo with no history returns the current document unchanged. Wrong version 1 forgets to clear `future` on `push` (stale redo history survives a new edit); wrong version 2 drops the **newest** entry once capacity is hit instead of the oldest; wrong version 3 returns `undefined` instead of the current document when there is nothing to undo or redo. A suite that only checks "undo returns something" catches none of the three.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests pin down behavior at the edges: what happens at capacity, what happens after a new edit clears redo, and what happens when there is nothing left to undo or redo — not just "it returns the previous value."
hints: Start with the simplest behavior: push once, undo, redo, and check you're back where you started.
Push after an undo. What should `canRedo()` report, and what should `redo()` return?
Push more entries than `capacity`. Which end of the history gets dropped?

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken bookings-table query, make the tests pass

`queryTable(rows, options)` powers the bookings table: filter by traveler name, sort, and 1-based pages. It has several bugs, including one that corrupts the caller's data. Fix it until every test passes.

codeExercise.solutionNote: `sort` mutates, and with no filter `out` *was* the caller's array. A comparator that never returns 0 plus `reverse()` scrambles ties, while flipping the comparator's sign keeps a stable sort stable. Pages are 1-based in the URL (`?page=1`). This is the same data-table deep dive from Lecture 5.5, in code.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All the bugs here come from treating the input as disposable: sorting the caller's own array in place, a comparator plus `reverse()` that scrambles ties, and an off-by-one on 1-based pages.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. Does `queryTable` ever call `.sort()` directly on `rows`, or on a copy?
A comparator that flips its sign for `direction === "desc"` behaves differently from one that sorts ascending and then calls `.reverse()`. Why does that matter for ties?
What should `page: 1` mean for `start`?

sections.title: Performance as a Practice
sections.description: Take a page from a failing Lighthouse score to real users having a good experience, and prove it with field data. Define **LCP, INP, and CLS** at p75, and learn why lab tools and field data disagree. Fix **LCP and CLS** with a real image pipeline (`srcset`/`sizes`, modern formats, explicit dimensions) and a deliberate, scarce **resource-hint budget**. Fix **INP** by breaking long tasks into yielding chunks and splitting code at real boundaries instead of creating request waterfalls. Then ship a **RUM script and a p75 dashboard** that catches what a single Lighthouse run never can. Examples come from a grocery delivery storefront: a hero promo, category grids of product photos, a cart drawer, and checkout.

learningObjectives.description: Take an app from failing to passing Core Web Vitals, with a changelog tying each fix to a metric and a pipeline stage
Implement route- and component-level code splitting and report the measured bundle and load impact
Build a responsive image pipeline (srcset/sizes, modern formats, explicit dimensions) that eliminates image-driven CLS
Design a resource-hint strategy and demonstrate its effect on the request waterfall
Ship a RUM script and a p75 dashboard, and explain lab vs field discrepancies

motivationHooks.prompt: On a fast office laptop, the storefront scores 96 on Lighthouse. Real shoppers at 6 pm, on mid-range phones over congested networks, get a field p75 LCP of 3.8 s and INP of 420 ms. Both numbers are true. This section is about knowing which one to trust, and how to move it.

A team preloads four resources at once — the hero image plus three fonts and scripts — on a slow mobile connection, "to make everything load faster." Before Lecture 6.2 explains it, guess: does the hero image arrive faster, slower, or about the same?

Lighthouse reports a low Total Blocking Time for the checkout page. Real users on older Android phones say the "Add to cart" button feels frozen for almost half a second. What did Lighthouse's lab run structurally never have a chance to see?

This section pulls together Section 2's pipeline stages and cache headers, Section 3's hydration cost and rendering-strategy numbers, and Section 5's habit of carrying image width and height in the data model, all in service of numbers real users actually feel.

Slower for the hero. On a constrained connection, all four preloaded resources start downloading at once and share the same bandwidth, so the hero image — the one that actually determines LCP — arrives roughly four times later than if it had the connection to itself. If you guessed "faster, because preload means priority," you've now met the gap Lecture 6.2 is built to close: hints are a scarce budget, not a blanket speed-up.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, and CLS ≤ 0.1 are all assessed at **p75 of real page loads**, segmented by device. A good Lighthouse score is one synthetic run and does not mean users are having a good experience.
- LCP splits into TTFB, load delay, load duration, and render delay. Find the biggest sub-part in a real trace before changing anything, and give every image explicit dimensions plus `srcset`/`sizes` so its space is reserved and the right file size ships.
- Resource hints are a scarce, shared budget. `fetchpriority="high"` belongs on exactly one image, and preloading more resources doesn't automatically speed anything up — it can slow the one resource that matters.
- INP = input delay + processing + presentation. Deferring a long task with `setTimeout` or `requestAnimationFrame` changes when it runs, not how long it blocks; only chunking the work and yielding between chunks protects the next interaction.
- Code splitting isn't automatically faster: a chain of dynamic imports each discovered only after its parent adds a round trip. Split at real boundaries, and preload dependencies you already know you'll need.
- A RUM pipeline collects with `web-vitals`, keeps the latest value per metric id, and flushes on `visibilitychange` → `hidden` with `sendBeacon` — sending at `load` misses INP entirely. Aggregate p75 per metric × page × device, never as one combined number.
keyTakeaways: LCP, INP, and CLS are assessed at p75 of real field loads, per device — a high lab score is not proof of a good real user experience.
LCP is four numbers (TTFB, load delay, load duration, render delay); fix the biggest one in the actual trace, and give every image explicit dimensions plus srcset/sizes.
Resource hints are a scarce budget: one fetchpriority="high" image, 1–2 preconnects, and preload only what's discovered late but needed early.
INP is input delay + processing + presentation; chunk long work and yield between chunks, because deferring alone only changes when the block happens.
Code splitting can create a request waterfall — split at real boundaries and preload chunks you know you need.
A RUM pipeline keeps the latest value per metric id and flushes on visibilitychange → hidden, then aggregates p75 per metric × page × device.
