learningExperiences.title: Lecture 6.1: Core Web Vitals, and Why Field Data Wins

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Define LCP, INP, and CLS, their "good" thresholds, and how they're assessed (p75 of real page loads). (objective o1, o5)
2. Explain why lab tools (Lighthouse) and field data (RUM, CrUX) disagree, and which to trust for which question. (objective o5)
3. Compute a p75 and a CLS value from raw samples. (objective o5)

terms.definition: The time until the largest image or text block in the viewport is rendered. Good ≤ 2.5 s, poor > 4.0 s.

Over the page's lifetime, roughly the worst latency from a user interaction (click, tap, key) to the next frame painted. Good ≤ 200 ms, poor > 500 ms. It replaced FID as a Core Web Vital in March 2024.
The largest burst ("session window") of unexpected layout-shift scores. Good ≤ 0.1, poor > 0.25.
The 75th percentile: 75% of page loads are at or better than this value. Core Web Vitals are assessed at p75, separately for mobile and desktop.
A synthetic, controlled run (Lighthouse, WebPageTest) on one simulated device and network.
Real User Monitoring: metrics collected from real visits (your own script, or Chrome's CrUX dataset).
A lab metric: the sum of each long task's time beyond 50 ms. It's a proxy for interactivity, because lab runs have no real interactions.
A group of layout shifts less than 1 s apart, lasting at most 5 s in total. CLS is the largest window's sum. Shifts within 500 ms of user input are excluded.

contentBlocks.content:
### Start concrete: the Tuesday-night grocery rush

On a fast laptop in the office, the storefront's Lighthouse score is 96. Real shoppers at 6 pm are on mid-range Android phones over congested mobile networks, with a cart drawer they open and close dozens of times. Lighthouse measured one synthetic page load with no interactions. The field data shows p75 LCP of 3.8 s and INP of 420 ms.

Both numbers are "true." They answer different questions:

| Question | Use |
|---|---|
| "Did my change make this page faster, all else equal?" | **Lab.** It's repeatable, so it's good for before/after and for CI budgets. |
| "Are real users having a good experience?" | **Field** p75, segmented by device and page type. |
| "Why is it slow?" | **Lab traces** (DevTools Performance) reproducing what the field data points at. |

A good Lighthouse score doesn't mean users have a good experience (misconception `web-performance-optimization.m1`). It's one run on one simulated device. INP can't be measured in a lab page load at all, because INP needs real interactions (the lab uses TBT as a rough proxy). Field distributions have long tails caused by devices, networks, cache state, and geography.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s06-m1): Lab vs field. Left: a single Lighthouse gauge at 96 labelled "1 run · simulated Moto G · no interactions". Right: a histogram of 40,000 real LCP samples with a long right tail, the p75 line at 3.8 s in the "needs improvement" band, and a device split showing desktop p75 at 1.6 s and mobile p75 at 3.8 s. Caption: "Both are true. Only one is your users."

contentBlocks.content:
### Why p75, not the average

A few very slow sessions drag the mean up, while very fast repeat visits pull it down. The p75 answers "what do most users get, including the slower ones?" without being dominated by the extreme tail. Compute it per metric, **per device class**, and ideally per page template.

### CLS is about bursts

CLS doesn't add up every shift over a long session, which would punish long sessions. It takes the worst **session window**. Shifts caused by the user's own input (within 500 ms) don't count, because they were expected.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **a single very slow session inflates the mean far more than it moves the p75.** Add one more very slow sample (for example `lcp.push(9500)`) to the array below and compare how much each number moves.

contentBlocks.caption: The same eight samples as Worked Example 1, computed in code. Predict the printed line before running.
The five layout shifts from Worked Example 2, folded into session windows. Predict the CLS value before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: measurement
contentBlocks.content:
- **Treating a Lighthouse score as the user experience.**
- **Reporting means or medians** instead of p75.
- **Mixing mobile and desktop** into one number.
- **Looking for INP in a lab page-load run.**
- **One lab run as "before" and one as "after."** Take the median of at least 5 runs.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 6.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms, CLS ≤ 0.1, all at **p75 of real loads**, per device class.
- Lab data is for controlled comparison and diagnosis. Field data is for truth.
- CLS = the worst session window of unexpected shifts.

interactionSequence.prompt: A product page is slow for real shoppers. Put these steps in the order you'd actually do them.
options: Reproduce the slow paint or interaction in a lab trace (DevTools Performance) to see why it's slow
Confirm the fix worked by watching field p75 over the following days
Segment field p75 by metric and device to find out where users are actually hurting
Ship the fix and take the median of at least 5 lab runs as your controlled before/after

optionFeedback.feedback: Second: once field data tells you where to look, a lab trace tells you why.
Last: only field p75, collected after the fix has been live, tells you whether real users actually got faster.
First: field p75, segmented by device, is where you find out there's a problem and who has it.
Third: the lab median-of-5 is your controlled before/after once you know what you're fixing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Field tells you where to look and whether you actually fixed it; lab tells you why it's slow and gives you a controlled comparison. Skipping straight to a lab run, or shipping a change with no field confirmation, is how a Lighthouse-driven fix misses what users actually experience.
hints: Which kind of data answers "are users having a good experience," and which answers "why is it slow"?
The lab median-of-5 needs to happen around the fix itself — you can't take a "before" median without already knowing what to change.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: Lighthouse reports 96 on a fast office laptop. A teammate says "we're good, ship it." What's missing from that conclusion?
options: Lighthouse is one synthetic run on one simulated device with no real interactions; only field p75, segmented by device, says what real users experience
Nothing; a 96 is a strong score and field data would only confirm it
The score should be re-run once more on the same laptop to be sure
Lighthouse should be run on a simulated desktop instead of the default mobile profile

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A lab score answers "did this change help, all else equal," not "are real users okay."
A good Lighthouse score does not mean users have a good experience — that's exactly the gap this lecture opens with.
Re-running the same lab profile again still only tells you about one simulated device with no interactions; it doesn't add field truth.
Switching which single device Lighthouse simulates doesn't fix the underlying problem: it's still one run, with no real interactions, on one device.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Both numbers can be "true" — Lighthouse for controlled before/after and diagnosis, field p75 for what real shoppers on real phones and networks actually get. A high lab score alone never confirms the second.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Shifts (time ms, score): `(500, 0.03) (900, 0.02) (5200, 0.06)` — none from user input. What is the CLS?
options: 0.06, because 500 and 900 form one window (sum 0.05) less than 1 s apart, and 5200 is more than 1 s past 900 so it starts a new, larger window on its own
0.11, the sum of all three shifts
0.03, only the largest single shift counts
0.05, only the first window counts because it came first

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Window A is `{500, 900}` (sum 0.05); the gap to 5200 exceeds 1 s, so window B is `{5200}` alone (sum 0.06). CLS is the larger of the two.
CLS is not a running total over the whole session — that would punish long sessions, which is exactly why session windows exist.
CLS takes the sum of the largest window, not the single largest shift.
CLS is the LARGER of the windows, not whichever came first.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Group shifts less than 1 s apart (and under 5 s total) into windows, sum each window, and CLS is the largest window's sum — here that's window B at 0.06.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 3 taught that profiling a render and choosing a rendering strategy both mean measuring real numbers before claiming a win. How does Lecture 6.1's insistence on field p75 over a single Lighthouse score apply that same "measure before claiming" discipline?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Both are about refusing to accept a plausible-sounding claim without evidence that actually generalizes. Section 3 profiled real re-renders and rendering-strategy numbers instead of trusting instinct about what "should" be faster. Lecture 6.1 does the same thing for the whole page: a single Lighthouse run on one simulated device is exactly the kind of unmeasured, single-sample claim that discipline warns against, and field p75 — a real distribution, segmented by device — is the equivalent of actually profiling before you claim the page is fast.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Computing p75 by hand
steps: Sort (already sorted).
Nearest-rank: rank = ceil(0.75 × 8) = 6, so p75 = the 6th value = **2600 ms**. That's "needs improvement" (> 2500).
The mean is 2825 ms, which is inflated by the single 8.2 s outlier. The median is 1900 ms, which looks "good" and hides the slower quarter.
workedExamples.conclusion: p75 says a quarter of these users waited 2.6 s or longer. That's the number Core Web Vitals use, and the one to move.

workedExamples.title: CLS session windows
steps: Drop the shift at 4000 ms because it came from user input.
Window A: 1000 and 1300 are less than 1 s apart, giving a sum of 0.09.
The gap to 6000 is more than 1 s, so start window B: 6000 and 6500 give a sum of 0.11.
CLS = max(0.09, 0.11) = **0.11**, which is "needs improvement."
workedExamples.conclusion: The fix target is window B, the late promo banner that shifts the grid at 6 s. Runnable Example R1 computes this.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 6.2: Fixing LCP and CLS: Images, Fonts, and the Critical Path

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Break LCP into its sub-parts and fix the largest one. (objective o1)
2. Build image markup with `srcset`/`sizes`, modern formats, explicit dimensions, and the right loading priority. (objective o3)
3. Design a resource-hint strategy (`preconnect`, `preload`, `modulepreload`, `fetchpriority`) and avoid over-preloading. (objective o4)

terms.definition: TTFB → resource load **delay** (time until the LCP resource starts downloading) → resource load **duration** → element render **delay**.
Candidate image files with their widths (`apples-640.webp 640w`) and the image's layout width per breakpoint (`(min-width: 768px) 33vw, 100vw`). The browser picks the best candidate for the device.
Serves AVIF or WebP with a JPEG fallback.
`width` and `height` attributes (or CSS `aspect-ratio`) so space is reserved before the image loads, which prevents CLS.
Defers off-screen images. **Never** use it on the LCP image.
Raises one resource's priority, typically the LCP hero image.
Opens the DNS, TCP, and TLS connection to an origin early.
Fetches a specific resource early at high priority (a font, or a CSS background hero).
Fetches and parses a JS module and its static dependencies early.

contentBlocks.content: ### LCP is four numbers, not one For the storefront's hero promo image: | Sub-part | Typical cause when large | Typical fix | |---|---|---| | TTFB | slow server render, no CDN caching of HTML | cache HTML at the CDN with revalidation (s2), or stream (s3) | | Load **delay** | the image is discovered late (CSS background, JS-inserted, lazy-loaded) | put the image in the HTML as ``, add `fetchpriority="high"`, or preload it if it's a CSS background | | Load **duration** | a huge file, the wrong format, no `srcset` | resize, use AVIF/WebP, serve `srcset` so phones get small files | | Render **delay** | render-blocking CSS/JS, a web font hiding text, hydration | trim critical CSS, `defer` scripts, `font-display: swap` | Find the biggest sub-part in a trace before changing anything.
### Images: the pipeline

- The **`width`/`height`** attributes give the browser the aspect ratio, so it reserves the box before any bytes arrive. No shift.
- **Only the LCP candidate** gets `fetchpriority="high"`, and it is never lazy-loaded.
- **Below-the-fold** grid images get `loading="lazy"`.

### Resource hints: fewer and more deliberate

Hints compete for the same bandwidth and connection slots. Preloading six fonts, three scripts, and two images makes all eleven arrive later, including the one that matters (misconception `web-performance-optimization.m2`). A useful budget:

- `preconnect` to **1–2** critical third-party origins (the image CDN, say), not every origin on the page.
- `preload` only for resources the parser discovers late but needs early: the LCP image when it's a CSS background, and one or two critical fonts.
- `modulepreload` for the next route's entry chunk when navigation is likely (on hover or when the link enters the viewport).
- `fetchpriority="high"` on the single LCP image, and `low` for below-the-fold carousels.

contentBlocks.altText: Screenshot (s06-m2): Waterfall before and after hints. Before: the hero image request starts at 1.9 s, after CSS and JS, because it's a CSS background. After adding <link rel="preload" as="image" fetchpriority="high"> and preconnect to the image CDN, the hero starts at 0.4 s. A third panel shows an over-hinted version with 11 preloads, where the hero starts at 0.4 s but finishes later because it shares bandwidth with fonts and scripts.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 6.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Split LCP into TTFB, load delay, load duration, and render delay, and fix the biggest part first.
- Every image gets explicit dimensions and `srcset`/`sizes`. Only the LCP image gets high priority, and below-the-fold images are lazy.
- Hints are a scarce budget. Preload only what's discovered late and needed early.

interactionSequence.prompt: Budget these resource hints from most to least deserving of a scarce preload/preconnect slot on the storefront's home page.
options: A below-the-fold carousel image
The LCP hero image, when it must stay a CSS background
The image CDN origin, via preconnect
The next route's JS chunk, only when navigation is likely (hover/viewport)

optionFeedback.feedback: Last, if at all: it's below the fold and should be lazy-loaded, not hinted early.
First: this is the one resource whose late discovery directly delays LCP.
Second: one or two critical origins via preconnect is cheap and helps everything that follows.
Third: only when navigation is actually likely — a speculative modulepreload for every link would be over-hinting.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Hints are a scarce budget: 1–2 preconnects, preload only what's discovered late but needed early, modulepreload only when navigation is likely, and fetchpriority="high" on exactly one image. A below-the-fold carousel image competing for that budget is the over-hinting mistake the lecture calls out.

What does the lecture say happens to LCP when you preload six fonts, three scripts, and two images all at once?

The load duration: resize and convert to AVIF, since file size is always the biggest lever
The render delay: trim critical CSS and defer scripts
TTFB: cache the HTML at the CDN

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. At 900 ms, load delay is by far the largest sub-part here, so it's the one worth fixing first.
Duration is only 300 ms here — smaller than delay. Fixing the biggest sub-part first means finding it in the trace, not assuming it's always the file size.
Render delay is the smallest number in this trace; it's not where the time is going.
TTFB is already fairly small here (200 ms); the delay is where nearly three-quarters of the time is going.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: LCP splits into four numbers. Find the biggest one in the actual trace before changing anything — here that's load delay, caused by late discovery.

interactionSequence.prompt: A developer preloads six fonts, three scripts, and two images "to make everything load faster," and LCP gets worse. Why?

Preload only works for images, so the fonts and scripts were ignored and had no effect
The order the preload tags appear in the HTML was wrong

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Hints are a scarce budget — more of them means everything, including the LCP image, shares bandwidth and arrives later.
Preload works for fonts and scripts too, which is exactly the problem: all eleven now compete for the connection.
Reordering the tags doesn't remove the contention; the resources still compete for bandwidth however they're listed.
Preloading more resources speeding things up is precisely the belief this lecture names as a misconception.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Preloading isn't free: every hinted resource competes for the same connection and bandwidth. A budget of 1–2 preconnects and a small, deliberate preload list protects the resource that actually gates LCP.

options: Explicit width and height (or CSS aspect-ratio) on every image, so its box is reserved before any bytes arrive
Lazy loading on every image, so the browser handles it automatically
Preload every product image so they all arrive faster
Animate the button's position so the movement looks intentional

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Reserving the box before the image arrives means there's no space for it to shift into later.
Lazy loading defers a request; it does nothing to reserve the image's box, so the shift still happens once it does load.
This adds network contention without reserving any space — the shift would still happen, just after a race for bandwidth.
That's still a layout shift (now on a timer), plus extra layout work every frame.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: CLS from images is fixed by reserving space up front with explicit dimensions or `aspect-ratio` — not by loading strategy, preloading, or disguising the shift.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 2 used style → layout → paint → composite as the lens for explaining jank, and Section 5's virtualization lecture used that same lens to justify binary search over a linear scan during scroll. How does Lecture 6.2's "find the biggest LCP sub-part in a trace before changing anything" apply that same pipeline lens?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three are the same discipline: name which pipeline stage (or, here, which LCP sub-part) is actually expensive before changing code to fix it. Section 2 traced jank to forced layout inside the style→layout→paint→composite pipeline rather than guessing; Section 5's virtualization lecture used the pipeline lens to justify replacing an O(n) scan with O(log n) binary search so per-scroll work stayed cheap. Lecture 6.2 does the same for LCP: TTFB, load delay, load duration, and render delay are four different stages with four different fixes, and picking the wrong one (say, compressing an image when the real cost is late discovery) wastes effort the way optimizing the wrong pipeline stage always does.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 6.3: Fixing INP: Long Tasks and Code Splitting

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Break INP into input delay, processing time, and presentation delay, and diagnose which one dominates. (objective o1)
2. Break long tasks into chunks that yield to the main thread. (objective o1)
3. Split code by route and component, and recognize when splitting creates request waterfalls. (objective o2)

terms.definition: The time from the interaction until its handler starts, spent waiting for whatever task was already running.
The time spent running the event handlers.
The time from the end of the handlers until the next frame is painted (style, layout, paint, s2).
A task over 50 ms.
Ending the current task so the browser can handle input and paint, then continuing in a new task (`scheduler.yield()` where supported, otherwise `setTimeout(0)` or a `MessageChannel`).
One chunk per route, loaded on navigation.
Lazy-loading heavy components (the checkout map, the recipe video player) when they're needed.
A chain of requests where each can only start after the previous one finishes.

contentBlocks.content:
### INP: three parts

When a shopper taps "Add to cart":

1. **Input delay:** the tap waits because a 180 ms analytics task is already running.
2. **Processing:** the handler recalculates promotions for the whole cart synchronously (120 ms).
3. **Presentation:** the cart drawer's re-render triggers layout on a 400-item DOM (60 ms).

The fixes differ for each part: move or split the analytics task, make the promotions calculation incremental or yield partway through, and shrink the DOM or virtualize it (s5). Yielding right after the visible update ("item added" feedback) lets the next frame paint before the remaining work continues.

### Yield, don't just defer

Wrapping a 240 ms job in `setTimeout` or `requestAnimationFrame` moves it but doesn't make it smaller. It's still one long task, it still blocks the next interaction, and the frame budget from s2 still applies (misconception `browser-rendering-pipeline.m3`). **Chunk** the work: process items until about 50 ms have elapsed, yield, and continue.

### Code splitting: less JS up front, but watch the waterfall

Route-level splitting keeps checkout code out of the home page bundle, and component-level splitting keeps the delivery-map library out of the cart. But code splitting doesn't always make pages faster (misconception `web-performance-optimization.m3`):

- Every chunk that's only discovered after its parent executes adds **a round trip**. On a 150 ms RTT connection, a chain of five small chunks can cost more than one medium bundle.
- Over-splitting tiny shared modules adds request overhead and hurts compression.
- Splitting code that's needed **during an interaction** (the "Add to cart" handler) makes that interaction wait for the network, which hurts INP.

Fixes: split at real boundaries (routes, rarely used heavy components), use `modulepreload` for chunks you know will be needed, and prefetch the next route's chunk on hover or visibility.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s06-m3): Three ways to ship checkout. A waterfall chart. (A) Monolith: one 300 KB request. (B) Over-split chain: main → checkout → payment → address-autocomplete, each starting after the previous finishes, which is visibly longer. (C) Route split + modulepreload of checkout's dependencies: parallel requests finishing earliest. Annotation: "RTT × depth of the chain."

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: INP and splitting
contentBlocks.content:
- **Deferring a long task instead of chunking it.**
- **Lazy-loading code that an interaction needs immediately.**
- **Chains of dynamic imports with no `modulepreload`.**
- **Measuring bundle size but not load time on a real RTT.**
- **Blaming "React" without a trace.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 6.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- INP = input delay + processing + presentation. Find the biggest part.
- Chunk long work and yield between chunks. Deferring alone doesn't help.
- Split at real boundaries, and preload known dependencies to avoid waterfalls.

interactionSequence.prompt: Order the steps of diagnosing and fixing the 420 ms "Add to cart" INP from Worked Example 3.
options: Reproduce it with a throttled CPU trace to see which parts are actually slow
Target each part with its own fix: move the widget off the main thread, make promotions incremental, yield before the rest
Confirm the fix with field p75 INP after enough real sessions
Get INP attribution from field data: which interaction, and how much of it is delay, processing, and presentation

optionFeedback.feedback: Second: once attribution names the interaction, a throttled trace shows what's actually running during each part.
Third: each part of INP gets its own targeted fix, not one generic "make it faster."
Last: field p75 INP after real sessions is what actually confirms the fix worked.
First: field attribution tells you which interaction and which of the three parts (delay, processing, presentation) to chase.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Attribution names the interaction and the dominant part; a lab trace reproduces why; the fix targets that specific part; and field p75 confirms it actually moved. Each fix in the worked example (moving the widget, incremental promotions, yielding before shipping estimates) maps to one specific part of INP.
hints: Which data tells you WHICH interaction and WHICH of the three parts is the problem, before you open DevTools?
What confirms a fix actually helped real users, as opposed to just the one trace you reproduced it in?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: INP attribution for a tap shows input delay 190 ms, processing 40 ms, presentation 30 ms. What should you investigate first?
options: Other tasks already running when the tap happened (third-party scripts, timers, hydration) — the main thread was busy before the handler even started
The click handler's own code, since that's what runs when you tap
The cart drawer's CSS, since that's what paints afterward
Nothing; 260 ms total is close enough to good

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Input delay dominates here, which points at whatever was already running on the main thread, not the handler itself.
Processing is only 40 ms — the handler is not where most of this interaction's time is going.
That would show up as presentation delay, which is only 30 ms here.
260 ms crosses the 200 ms "good" threshold; this isn't a case to leave alone.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: INP is input delay + processing + presentation, and the fix depends on which one dominates. Input delay means something else was already hogging the main thread before your handler got a turn.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A 240 ms recalculation is wrapped in `setTimeout(fn, 0)` so it runs "later." Does this fix its effect on INP?
options: No — it's still one 240 ms task; the next tap, scroll, or keypress that lands during it still waits up to 240 ms, and the next paint waits too
Yes, because moving work off the current call stack always keeps the page responsive
Yes, because setTimeout runs on a separate thread
No, but only because setTimeout has a minimum 4 ms floor

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Deferring changes when the work runs, not how big the task is — chunking with yields in between is what actually protects the next interaction.
`requestAnimationFrame` guarantees smooth animation is the exact misconception this echoes: moving work later doesn't shrink it.
`setTimeout` callbacks still run on the main thread, not a separate one; that's why the long task still blocks input and paint.
The 4 ms floor is real but not the reason this fails — a 240 ms task blocks regardless of exactly when it starts.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Wrapping a long computation in `setTimeout` or `requestAnimationFrame` changes when it runs, not how long it blocks. Only breaking it into chunks with yields between them keeps every slice under the long-task threshold.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Checkout is split `main → checkout → payment → address-autocomplete`, each chunk a dynamic import of the previous. On a 150 ms RTT connection, checkout got slower after the split. Why?
options: Each chunk is only discovered after its parent finishes loading, so the chain adds a round trip per level — a waterfall that can cost more than the bytes saved
Code splitting always makes pages faster, so this must be unrelated to the split
Smaller files compress worse, and that alone explains the regression
Dynamic imports block the main thread while downloading

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. RTT × chain depth can outweigh whatever bytes the split saved, especially over a slow connection.
Code splitting always making pages faster is exactly the belief this lecture calls a misconception — a chain of dynamic imports is the counterexample.
Compression matters a little, but it's not what turns a fast checkout into a slow one here — the waterfall is.
Downloading a chunk doesn't block the main thread; the cost is the extra round trip before the next chunk is even discovered.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Splitting isn't free. A chain where each chunk is discovered only after the previous one finishes adds one RTT per level — split at real boundaries and preload known dependencies instead.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 1 modeled the event loop step by step, and Section 2 used the rendering pipeline to explain the frame budget behind jank. How does Lecture 6.3's "chunk the work, yield between chunks" rule for INP apply that same event-loop-and-frame-budget model?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three rely on the same mechanics: the main thread runs one task to completion before it can handle the next input or paint a frame, and a task over about 50 ms risks missing that budget. Section 1's event loop explains why a long synchronous task delays everything queued behind it; Section 2's pipeline explains what has to happen (style, layout, paint, composite) before a frame can show. Lecture 6.3's fix — yield after each roughly-50-ms slice instead of running 240 ms straight through — is a direct application of both: yielding gives the event loop a chance to run a pending input handler and the pipeline a chance to paint, which deferring the whole task into one later callback never does.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.problem: Diagnosing a 420 ms INP on "Add to cart"
steps: **Field:** RUM attribution shows the slowest interaction is `click` on `button.add-to-cart`, with input delay 190 ms, processing 150 ms, and presentation 80 ms.

**Lab reproduction:** a Performance trace with 4× CPU throttling shows a third-party recommendation widget running a 200 ms task every few seconds (the input delay), and the handler recalculating promotions for all 60 cart lines (the processing).

**Fixes:** load the widget after first interaction and move its scoring to a Worker; make promotions incremental (only the changed line); update the cart badge first, then yield before recalculating shipping estimates.
**Evidence:** lab INP proxy (a trace of that interaction) goes from 410 ms to 120 ms. Field p75 INP goes from 420 ms to 170 ms after 28 days.
workedExamples.conclusion: Each fix targeted a specific part of INP, and field data confirmed it.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 6.4: Real-User Monitoring and the p75 Dashboard

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Collect Web Vitals from real users and send them reliably. (objective o5)
2. Aggregate samples into p75 by metric, page template, and device class. (objective o5)
3. Explain common reasons lab and field disagree. (objective o5)

terms.definition: Google's small library that reports LCP, INP, CLS, FCP, and TTFB with correct definitions and attribution.
A unique id per metric per page load. INP and CLS can be reported **several times** as they grow, and the latest value for an id wins.
Queues a small POST that survives page unload.
The most reliable moment to flush metrics (tab switched, app backgrounded, or page closing). `unload` isn't reliable on mobile.
Recording a fraction of sessions to control cost. It must be consistent per session.
Extra detail about *why* a metric was slow (which element was LCP, which interaction was slow).

contentBlocks.content:
### What a RUM pipeline does

1. **Collect:** `onLCP`, `onINP`, and `onCLS` from `web-vitals`, with attribution builds so you know the element or interaction.
2. **Batch and dedupe:** keep the latest value per metric id in memory.
3. **Flush** on `visibilitychange` to `hidden` via `sendBeacon`. INP is only final when the user leaves the page, which is why a script that reports "on load" never sees it.
4. **Aggregate:** group by metric × page template × device class, then compute p75.
5. **Dashboard:** p75 over time with the good/poor thresholds drawn in, plus deploy markers.

### Why lab and field disagree

- **Devices:** the lab emulates one phone, while the field includes older and slower ones.
- **Networks and geography:** real RTTs and packet loss.
- **Cache state:** labs often test cold loads, while the field mixes cold and warm.
- **Interactions:** only the field has them, so only the field has INP.
- **Content:** personalization, A/B tests, ads, cookie banners.
- **Page mix:** your lab tests the home page, while most field traffic lands on product pages.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s06-m4): RUM pipeline and dashboard. Left: a browser tab with web-vitals callbacks feeding a small in-memory map (latest value per metric id), flushed with sendBeacon on visibilitychange → hidden. Middle: an ingestion endpoint and a table with columns metric, value, page, device, release, and timestamp. Right: a dashboard with three p75 line charts (LCP, INP, CLS) split by mobile and desktop, dashed good/poor threshold lines, and vertical deploy markers, one of them followed by an INP drop.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: RUM
contentBlocks.content:
- **Sending on `load`**, which misses INP and late CLS.
- **Sending every INP update** instead of the latest per id.
- **Using `unload`/`beforeunload`** (unreliable, and it breaks the back/forward cache).
- **Aggregating strings, or with an off-by-one percentile.**
- **Not segmenting** by device and page template.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 6.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Collect with `web-vitals`, keep the latest value per metric id, and flush with `sendBeacon` on `hidden`.
- Compute p75 per metric × page × device, and chart it against the thresholds with deploy markers.

interactionSequence.prompt: Put the five stages of a RUM pipeline in order.
options: Aggregate: group by metric × page template × device class, then compute p75
Flush on visibilitychange to hidden, via sendBeacon
Collect metrics from the web-vitals library, with attribution
Dashboard: p75 over time against thresholds, with deploy markers
Batch and dedupe: keep only the latest value per metric id in memory

optionFeedback.feedback: Fourth: aggregation happens once samples have arrived on the server, after collection and flushing.
Third: flushing sends what's been batched so far, once the page becomes hidden.
First: you can't batch or flush a metric you haven't collected yet.
Last: the dashboard is built from already-aggregated p75s, not raw samples.
Second: keep the latest value per id in memory before you ever try to send anything.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Collect → batch/dedupe → flush on hidden → aggregate → dashboard. Skipping the dedupe step means sending every intermediate INP update instead of the final one; skipping the hidden-flush step means missing INP and late CLS entirely.
hints: Which step has to happen before you can keep "the latest value per id" in memory?
What's the one browser event this lecture says is the reliable moment to send data?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: A RUM script calls `sendBeacon` inside a `load` event listener, once, for every metric. What does it miss?
options: INP, which only reaches its final value after the user interacts and the page becomes hidden — sending at load means there's been no interaction yet
LCP, because LCP can only be measured after load
Nothing; sending once at load captures every Core Web Vital correctly
CLS, because layout shifts only happen before load

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. INP builds up over the page's lifetime; a script that reports "on load" runs before most interactions have even happened.
LCP is typically already known well before or around load — it's INP that a load-time send structurally can't capture.
Sending at load is a page-load snapshot, exactly the misconception this lecture warns about — it misses INP and any late CLS.
Layout shifts can and do keep happening after load — a late-inserted promo or ad is a classic example — so CLS isn't fixed at load either.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: INP is only final when the user leaves the page. The reliable moment to flush is `visibilitychange` → `hidden`, using `sendBeacon`, with the latest value kept per metric id.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Mobile LCP samples (ms): 1800, 2000, 2200, 2400, 2600, 2900, 3100, 4200 (sorted). Desktop: 900, 1000, 1100, 1300 (sorted). What does a single combined p75 across both devices hide?
options: A mobile-specific problem: mobile p75 alone is 2900 ms ("needs improvement"), while desktop is 1100 ms ("good"), and combining them lands near the boundary and masks which device actually needs the fix
Nothing; combining more samples always gives a more accurate p75
It hides a desktop problem instead, since desktop has fewer samples
It would only matter if the sample counts were equal

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Segmenting by device is what reveals that mobile — not desktop — is where the real problem is.
More samples isn't automatically better if it mixes two populations with very different experiences.
Desktop is the fast one here (1100 ms, "good"); it's mobile's slower distribution that a combined number would hide.
Unequal sample counts make the masking worse, but even equal counts from two different distributions would still hide the slower one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Segment by device before computing p75. A combined number can land in a deceptively "okay" middle while one whole segment is actually failing its threshold.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 3 taught you to choose a rendering strategy (SSR, CSR, static, streaming) using real measured numbers rather than a blanket rule like "SSR is always faster." How does Lecture 6.4's RUM/p75 pipeline connect to that choice?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The RUM pipeline you build here is exactly the source of the numbers that rendering-strategy decision needs. learningExperiences.title: Lab: Fresh and Fast

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. In the engine you build the decision and measurement logic: percentiles, CLS windows, image attributes, waterfall models, chunked work, and beacon batching. The real before/after evidence comes from DevTools, Lighthouse, and your RUM dashboard in the Practical Activity.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenge 1 (p75 by metric and device) gives you the thresholds table and sample data, and leaves `percentile` and `summarizeVitals` to you. Challenges 2 and 3 give you the fixed shapes (image widths, an import graph) and leave the attribute logic or the waterfall timing to you. Challenge 4 gives you the scenario runner and a fake clock, and leaves the chunk-and-yield logic in `processInChunks` to you. Challenge 5 has no scaffolding beyond the scenario runner: the whole `createVitalsReporter` is yours.

The two test-suite challenges turn it around: the `rateMetric` challenge gives you correct code and asks you to write the tests that prove it; the aggregation challenge gives you a correct test suite and asks you to fix broken code until it passes.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your rateMetric tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the rateMetric challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "Fresh and Fast."** Expected time is 10–12 hours.

1. **From failing to passing Core Web Vitals.** Take an existing app (yours or an open-source storefront) that fails at least one vital in the lab on a mobile profile. Keep a **changelog** in the format of Lecture 6.2's worked example: change → metric → sub-part or pipeline stage → lab median-of-5 before/after → field p75 before/after if you have traffic. *(o1)*
2. **Code splitting:** route-level and at least one component-level split. Report the bundle sizes (with a bundle analyzer screenshot) and the **load time** on a 150 ms-RTT throttled profile, and show one case where you *didn't* split because it would create a waterfall or hurt INP. *(o2)*
3. **Image pipeline:** a build step (for example with `sharp`) that emits AVIF/WebP at the Exercise s06-e2 widths plus a component that renders `<picture>` with `srcset`/`sizes`/`width`/`height`. Show CLS before/after on the product grid. *(o3)*
4. **Resource-hint strategy:** a written plan (which origins to preconnect, what to preload, what to modulepreload, and what you deliberately *didn't* hint) with before/after **waterfall screenshots**. *(o4)*
5. **RUM + dashboard:** `web-vitals` (attribution build) → your s06-e5 reporter → an endpoint you control (a serverless function is fine) → storage → a dashboard showing p75 LCP, INP, and CLS per page template and device, with threshold lines and deploy markers. Write one paragraph explaining a lab vs field discrepancy you actually observed. *(o5)*

Measured sizes *and* load times, with at least one justified decision not to split.
Correct `srcset`/`sizes`, modern formats, zero image CLS, and the hero never lazy.
A deliberate small set, waterfall evidence, and hints you rejected.
Latest-per-id batching, a flush on hidden, p75 per segment, and a real discrepancy explained.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working `rateMetric`, you write the tests

`rateMetric(name, value)` rates a p75 value as `'good'`, `'needs-improvement'`, or `'poor'` using the current thresholds (LCP 2500/4000 ms, INP 200/500 ms, CLS 0.1/0.25, where "good" is ≤ the first threshold and "poor" is > the second). It throws for unknown metrics. It's correct. Write tests that catch the three hidden wrong versions. **Boundary values matter.** Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **four** tests). Then confirm your suite catches each of the three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks: values exactly at the good threshold rate as `good`, values exactly at the poor threshold rate as `needs-improvement` (not `poor`), values past the poor threshold rate as `poor`, INP uses its own 200/500 thresholds rather than FID's retired 100/300, and an unknown metric throws. Wrong version 1 uses strict `<` instead of `<=`, so every boundary value is rated one grade worse than it should be. Wrong version 2 copies FID's old thresholds (100/300) onto INP. Wrong version 3 silently rates an unknown metric 'good' instead of throwing. A suite that only checks one comfortably-mid-range value per metric catches none of the three.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests pin down behavior at the edges: exactly at each threshold, just past the poor threshold, and the unknown-metric error path — not just one typical value per metric.
hints: Start with the boundary: what should `rateMetric('LCP', 2500)` return, exactly at the good threshold?

sections.title: Accessibility by Default
sections.description: Build components and flows that work for everyone from the start: the **accessibility tree** (name, role, state) and when ARIA actually helps, keyboard contracts and focus management for a **combobox, modal, roving-tabindex menu, and tabs**, predictable **SPA focus movement and live-region announcements**, accessible **form validation**, and **auditing, prioritizing, and explaining** fixes to both designers and engineers. Examples come from a public-health clinic appointment portal: booking a vaccination, rescheduling, uploading insurance cards, and reading test results.

learningObjectives.description: Build a combobox, modal (focus trap and return), roving-tabindex menu, and tabs that pass keyboard and screen-reader test scripts
Implement SPA route-change announcements and predictable focus movement
Build a validated form with error summaries and correct aria-describedby wiring, plus a live-region toast system
Audit a real site with axe plus manual testing and deliver a severity/effort-prioritized report
Explain three fixes in language suited to a designer and to an engineer

motivationHooks.prompt: For someone booking a vaccination with a screen reader or without a mouse, a clinic portal that only mostly works isn't a minor inconvenience, it's a blocked appointment. Most of the fixes in this section are small and native; the cost of skipping them lands entirely on the person who can least afford it.

A `
Book
` gets `role="button"` added. A screen reader now announces "Book, button." Is the keyboard experience now equivalent to a native `

A `
Appointment saved
` gets appended to the page the instant a save succeeds. The role is right. The message is right. Screen-reader users hear nothing. What did the code get wrong?

This section is where Section 4's document-order DFS becomes "focus order is document order," Section 5's combobox pattern gets its keyboard contract, Section 3's effect-with-cleanup becomes how focus is restored, and Section 6's unexpected layout movement becomes an accessibility problem, not just a performance one. Section 10 reuses this section's reduced-motion respect, Section 11 reuses its keyboard contracts for headless components, and Section 12 reuses its severity-and-audience framing for critique.

The answer is **no**. `role="button"` changes only what the accessibility tree reports, nothing else. The div still can't receive keyboard focus at all, so Tab skips it entirely, and Enter and Space still do nothing, because none of that behavior was ever added. Matching a native `<button>` means adding `tabindex="0"`, key handlers for both Enter and Space, and disabled handling yourself, or, far more simply, writing `<button>`.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- Every control exposes name, role, and state to the accessibility tree. ARIA changes only what's reported there; it adds no focusability, no keyboard behavior, and no form semantics. Use native elements first, and ARIA only for real gaps (tabs, comboboxes, live regions).
- Each composite widget has a full keyboard contract, and partial implementations are the norm: roving tabindex so Tab treats the widget as one stop, arrow keys that wrap and skip disabled items, Home/End, and activation on both Enter and Space. A modal adds trapping Tab, making the background inert, closing on Escape, and returning focus to the opener, none of which `aria-modal` provides by itself.
- Client-side route changes are invisible to assistive technology unless the app provides the signal: update the title, move focus to the new content (or announce, when moving focus would be disruptive), and never for in-page-only updates.
- A field's accessible name should stay its visible label; hints and errors belong in `aria-describedby`, additive and space-separated, never in `aria-label`. A live region has to exist before its content changes, so render toast regions empty at app start and clear-then-set their text to announce, including repeats.
- Automated scanning finds only the mechanically detectable minority of issues and is not a finish line; most failures trace back to design tokens and component APIs, where fixing them once fixes every page. Prioritize findings by severity, then effort, then reach, grouped by root cause, never by raw tool-reported volume.
- The same finding needs two explanations: a designer needs the user outcome and an alternative that preserves intent, an engineer needs the mechanism and exactly where it lives.
keyTakeaways: Every control exposes name, role, and state. ARIA changes only what is reported, never behavior, so use native elements first.
A widget's keyboard contract is not optional in parts: roving tabindex, wrapping, skipping disabled items, Home/End, and both Enter and Space to activate.
A modal traps Tab, makes the background inert, closes on Escape, and returns focus to the opener; aria-modal alone does none of this.
SPA route changes need a deliberate title update, a predictable focus move (or announcement), and none of that for in-page-only updates.
aria-describedby is additive for hints and errors; aria-label replaces the name outright. Live regions must exist before their content changes, and clear-then-set is what makes repeats announce.

Automated scanning finds a minority of what matters and is not a QA-gate finish line. Prioritize findings by severity, then effort, then reach, and explain the same fix differently to designers and engineers.

learningExperiences.title: Predict First: role="button" Under the Keyboard

contentBlocks.content: Before Lecture 7.1 explains the accessibility tree, commit to a prediction about three controls that all look and read the same, but are wired up differently underneath. You are not expected to get every cell right yet.

interactionSequence.prompt: **role="button" vs <button> under the keyboard.** Write down the exact output before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
<button>: activated by "Enter" | <button>: activated by " "
div[role=button]: (never focused) | div[role=button]: (never focused)
div[role=button][tabindex=0] + Enter handler: activated by "Enter" | div[role=button][tabindex=0] + Enter handler: nothing on " "
```

**Why intuition fails.** `role="button"` makes a screen reader *say* "button," so it feels finished. Roles only change the accessibility tree. The div isn't focusable, so keyboard users can't reach it at all. Even after adding `tabindex="0"` and an Enter handler, Space (which every native button supports) still does nothing. This is misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m2`: the native element comes with focusability, both activation keys, disabled semantics, and form behavior for free.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: `role="button"` makes a screen reader *say* "button," so it feels finished. Roles only change the accessibility tree. The div isn't focusable, so keyboard users can't reach it at all. Even after adding `tabindex="0"` and an Enter handler, Space (which every native button supports) still does nothing. This is misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m2`: the native element comes with focusability, both activation keys, disabled semantics, and form behavior for free.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 7.1: Semantics First

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Explain the accessibility tree and the three things every control exposes: **name, role, state/value**. (objective o1)
2. Apply "native element first, ARIA only for gaps" and explain why wrong ARIA is worse than none. (objective o1)
3. List what a native `<button>` gives you that `<div role="button">` doesn't. (objective o1)

terms.definition: The browser's parallel tree of objects (built from the DOM) that assistive technologies read.
What a control is called ("Book appointment"), computed from `aria-labelledby`, `aria-label`, `<label>`, `alt`, or text content, in that priority.
What a control *is* (button, link, checkbox, dialog, tab…). Native elements have implicit roles.
Current condition (`aria-expanded`, `aria-checked`, `aria-selected`, `disabled`, the input's value).
Accessible Rich Internet Applications: attributes that change **only** what the accessibility tree reports. ARIA adds no behavior, focusability, or keyboard support.
Can receive focus (programmatically) / is also in the Tab order (`tabindex` ≥ 0 or natively focusable).
The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines conformance level most laws and policies reference.

contentBlocks.content:
### Start concrete: the "Book" button that wasn't The clinic's booking page has a styled `
Book
`. With a mouse it works. With a keyboard, Tab skips it (it isn't focusable). A screen reader announces "Book" as plain text, not a control. Adding `role="button"` fixes only the announcement. It's still not focusable, and Enter and Space still do nothing (misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m2`). To match a native button you'd need `tabindex="0"`, key handlers for Enter (on keydown) and Space (on keyup, with scroll prevented), disabled handling, and form submission behavior. Or you could write `

### ARIA changes what's reported, not what happens

The first rule of ARIA use: **if a native element or attribute has the semantics and behavior you need, use it.** ARIA is for gaps HTML doesn't cover (tabs, comboboxes, tree views, live regions). Incorrect ARIA *removes* accessibility (misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m1`):

- `aria-label="Button"` on a "Book appointment" button replaces a good name with a useless one.
- `role="menu"` on site navigation tells screen-reader users to expect application-menu keys that aren't implemented.
- `aria-hidden="true"` on a focusable element creates a "ghost" that receives focus but announces nothing.

### What WCAG 2.2 AA asks of components (a working subset)

| Area | Requirement (paraphrased) |
|---|---|
| Keyboard | Everything operable by keyboard, with no traps (except intentional modal traps that you can leave with Escape). |
| Focus | A visible focus indicator. Focus order follows meaning. Focused elements aren't hidden behind sticky headers. |
| Names | Every control has an accessible name that matches its visible label. |
| Contrast | Text 4.5:1 (large text 3:1). Component boundaries and focus indicators 3:1 against their surroundings. |
| Target size | Pointer targets at least 24×24 CSS px (or enough spacing). |
| Status | Status messages announced without moving focus (live regions). |
| Motion | Respect `prefers-reduced-motion` for non-essential animation (s10). |

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **`aria-label` and `aria-labelledby` do not add to the visible text, they REPLACE the computed accessible name entirely.** Predict each computed name below, then add a fourth control of your own where `ariaLabel` and the visible text disagree.

contentBlocks.caption: Accessible name priority (Runnable Example R1): aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then <label>, then alt, then text content.
Runnable Example R3: which elements actually land in the Tab order, given tag, role, tabindex, disabled, and hidden.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: semantics
contentBlocks.content:
- **Clickable `div`s and `span`s.**
- **`aria-label` that contradicts the visible label** (it breaks voice control: "click Book" fails when the name is "Reserve").
- **ARIA roles without the matching keyboard behavior.**
- **`outline: none` with no replacement focus style.**
- **Using `aria-hidden` on focusable content.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 7.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Every control exposes name, role, and state. Native HTML supplies all three plus behavior.
- ARIA only changes what's reported. Use it for real gaps, and use it correctly, or not at all.

interactionSequence.prompt:
The clinic's booking page has `
Book
`. A developer adds `role="button"`. A screen reader now announces "Book, button." Is a keyboard user's experience now equivalent to a native `
options: Yes, the role makes it a real button in every respect
No: it still can't receive focus, and Enter and Space still do nothing, because ARIA changes only what's reported
Yes, as long as the div also has an onclick handler
No, because role="button" is only valid on <span>, not <div>

optionFeedback.feedback: A role changes the accessibility tree, not the element's focusability or key handling.
Right. Tab still skips it, and no key does anything, because none of that behavior was ever added. Only the announcement changed.
An onclick handler responds to pointer events. It still won't fire on Enter or Space, and the element still can't be reached by keyboard.
role="button" is valid on any element; the problem here has nothing to do with which tag carries it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the "Book button that wasn't" from the lecture: role="button" fixes only the announcement. Matching a native button also needs tabindex="0", Enter and Space handlers, and disabled handling, or you could just write <button>.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A "Book appointment" button gets `aria-label="Button"` added, "to be extra clear it's a button for screen readers." What happens?
options: Nothing changes; extra ARIA is always harmless
The button's accessible name becomes just "Button," replacing the useful name "Book appointment" that voice-control and screen-reader users relied on
The role becomes ambiguous and the element stops being focusable
It adds a second, louder announcement alongside the original name

optionFeedback.feedback: aria-label doesn't get ignored when it's redundant, it wins, and here it wins with a worse name than what was already there.

Right. aria-label always overrides the visible text as the accessible name, so "Book appointment" is gone and every user of that name (including voice control saying "click Book appointment") loses it.
Focusability is untouched by this; the name is what changes, and it changes for the worse.
There's no second announcement. The accessible name computation picks exactly one source, by priority, and aria-label sits above the button's own text.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Incorrect or redundant ARIA removes accessibility rather than adding to it. Here aria-label replaces a specific, useful name ("Book appointment") with a useless one ("Button").

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Put these four sources of a control's accessible name in the priority order the browser actually uses (highest priority first).
options: aria-label
aria-labelledby
A <label for> pointing at the control
The control's own visible text content

optionFeedback.feedback: aria-label wins over a native label and over text content, but it is still second: aria-labelledby is checked first.
aria-labelledby is checked first. When present, it wins even over aria-label on the same element.
A native `<label for>` is used only once neither ARIA attribute is present.
Visible text content is the fallback: it is used only when nothing more specific overrides it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: aria-labelledby, then aria-label, then a native label or alt, then text content. Each one that is present overrides everything below it, which is exactly why a stray aria-label can silently replace a perfectly good visible label.
hints: Runnable Example R1 checks these in exactly this order, top to bottom.
The two ARIA-based sources both outrank anything native; between them, which one names its own sub-tree of other elements?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain to a teammate why "ARIA only changes what's reported, not what happens" means that adding role="button" to a div is never, by itself, enough to make it work like a real button.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: ARIA attributes exist purely to change what the accessibility tree reports to assistive technology: the name, role, and state a screen reader announces. They add nothing to the element's actual behavior in the DOM, so a div with role="button" still cannot receive keyboard focus, still ignores Enter and Space, and still has no disabled or form-submission handling. Getting real button behavior means either implementing every one of those pieces by hand (tabindex, key handlers, disabled logic) or, far more simply, using a native <button> element, which supplies all of it for free.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Fixing the "Book" control, step by step
workedExamples.problem: Fixing the "Book" control, step by step
steps: **Replace** `<div class="btn" onclick>` with `<button type="button">`. Keep the class for styling.

**Name:** the visible text "Book" is ambiguous in a list of five slots, so write "Book 10:30 with Dr. Osei" as visible text, or add visually hidden context via `aria-describedby` pointing at the slot's heading. Don't use an `aria-label` that differs from the visible words.
**State:** when the slot is full, use the native `disabled` attribute and show why ("Full: join waitlist" as a separate button).
**Focus style:** `:focus-visible { outline: 3px solid var(--focus); outline-offset: 2px; }` with at least 3:1 contrast.
workedExamples.conclusion: Four small changes, all native, and no ARIA was required. That's the usual shape of a real fix.
