Which two keys activate a native button?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 7.2: Four Widgets and Their Keyboard Contracts

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Implement the keyboard contract for a combobox, a modal dialog, a menu button with roving tabindex, and tabs. (objective o1)
2. Implement a focus trap with focus return. (objective o1)
3. Test each widget with a keyboard-only script and a screen-reader script. (objective o1)

terms.definition: The keys a widget must support and what each one does (from the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices).
In a composite widget only the active item has `tabindex="0"` and the others have `-1`. Tab enters and leaves the widget as one stop, and arrow keys move inside it.
The alternative to roving tabindex: focus stays on the container or input, and this attribute points at the active item (used in comboboxes, s5).
While a modal is open, Tab and Shift+Tab cycle only through the modal's focusable elements.
When the modal closes, focus goes back to the element that opened it.
An attribute that makes a subtree non-focusable and hidden from assistive technology. It's used for background content behind a modal.
Arrow keys select the tab immediately, vs. arrows move focus and Enter or Space selects.

contentBlocks.content:
### The four contracts

| Widget | Keys | Focus model | Key attributes |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Combobox** (clinic search) | ↓/↑ move the active option, Enter selects, Esc closes/clears, typing filters | focus stays in the input, `aria-activedescendant` | `role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `role="listbox"`/`option`, `aria-selected` |
| **Modal dialog** (reschedule) | Tab/Shift+Tab cycle inside, Esc closes | trap inside, return on close, background `inert` | `<dialog>` + `showModal()`, or `role="dialog"` + `aria-modal="true"` + `aria-labelledby` |
| **Menu button** (appointment actions) | Enter/Space/↓ opens, ↓/↑ move (wrap, skip disabled), Home/End, Enter/Space activate, Esc closes and returns focus to the button, Tab closes | roving tabindex | `aria-haspopup="menu"`, `aria-expanded`, `role="menu"`/`menuitem`, `aria-disabled` |
| **Tabs** (Upcoming / Past / Results) | ←/→ move (wrap), Home/End, automatic or manual activation | roving tabindex on the tabs | `role="tablist"`/`tab`/`tabpanel`, `aria-selected`, `aria-controls`, `aria-labelledby` |

A note on menus: `role="menu"` is for application-style action menus. For site navigation, use a **disclosure** pattern (a button that toggles a list of links), which screen-reader users navigate as ordinary links.

### Modal dialogs: prefer the platform

The native `<dialog>` element opened with `showModal()` makes the rest of the page inert, puts focus inside the dialog, closes on Escape, and in current browsers returns focus to the previously focused element on close. Verify that last behavior in your target browsers. A custom dialog has to do all of this itself:

1. Remember `document.activeElement` (the opener).
2. Move focus to the first sensible element: the first field, or the heading with `tabindex="-1"` if the dialog is mostly text.
3. Trap Tab and Shift+Tab. Make the background `inert`.
4. Close on Escape. Restore focus to the opener.

`aria-modal="true"` **doesn't trap focus**. It only tells assistive technology that content outside is inactive (misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m1` again: the attribute adds no behavior).

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Video (s07-m2): Keyboard-only walkthrough. Production brief: A 4-minute screen recording with on-screen key captions. A user reschedules an appointment using only the keyboard: Tab to "Actions" (menu button), ↓ into the menu, ↓ skipping the disabled "Cancel", Enter on "Reschedule". The modal opens with focus on the date field. Tab cycles within the dialog, Esc closes it, and focus returns to "Actions". A VoiceOver caption track shows what's announced at each step.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **in a roving-tabindex widget, arrow keys skip disabled items and wrap at the ends, and only the active item ever has `tabindex="0"`.** Predict the sequence of focused ids for `['ArrowDown', 'ArrowDown', 'ArrowDown']` starting from index 0, then try starting from the last item and pressing ArrowDown once.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: widgets
contentBlocks.content:
- **Every menu item or tab in the Tab order.** Use roving tabindex.
- **Relying on `aria-modal` to trap focus.**
- **Not returning focus when a dialog or menu closes.**
- **Activating on Enter only.** Space is part of the contract.
- **Using `role="menu"` for navigation links.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 7.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Each widget has a keyboard contract. Implement all of it: wrap, skip disabled items, Home/End, Enter *and* Space, Esc.
- Modal = trap + inert background + Escape + return focus. Prefer `<dialog>` with `showModal()`.

interactionSequence.prompt: A menu's four items each have `tabindex="0"`, so all four sit in the page's Tab order. A keyboard user complains the menu "takes forever to tab past." What is the fix?
options: Remove tabindex from all four items so none of them are reachable
Roving tabindex: only the active item gets tabindex="0"; the rest get "-1", so Tab enters and leaves the menu as a single stop and arrow keys move inside it
Add role="menuitem" to each item, which handles the arrow-key movement automatically
Reduce the number of items so tabbing through them is faster

optionFeedback.feedback: That excludes keyboard users from the menu entirely, trading one problem for a worse one.
Right. This is the roving-tabindex pattern: Tab treats the whole composite widget as one stop, and arrow keys handle movement inside it, wrapping and skipping disabled items.
A role only changes what's reported to assistive technology; it implements no arrow-key handling by itself, exactly like role="button" implements no click handling.
The item count isn't the bug; the same four items with roving tabindex are just as fast to use, and this doesn't scale to a longer menu anyway.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Composite widgets (menus, tabs, roving-tabindex grids) should be one stop in the Tab order. Arrow keys, not Tab, move focus between the items inside.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A custom reschedule dialog sets `aria-modal="true"` and nothing else. Keyboard users report that Tab still reaches the page behind it. Why?
options: aria-modal is supposed to trap focus by itself; this must be a browser bug to work around
aria-modal only informs assistive technology that content outside is inactive; it traps no keys, so the dialog itself has to implement the Tab cycle (or use <dialog>.showModal() and inert)
The dialog needs role="alertdialog" instead
aria-modal requires a matching aria-hidden on the dialog itself

optionFeedback.feedback: It isn't a bug to work around: aria-modal was never a focus-trapping mechanism in any browser. Adding an ARIA attribute never adds behavior on its own.
Right. ARIA changes only what's reported. Trapping Tab, making the background inert, and returning focus are all behavior that has to be built, or taken from the platform via <dialog>.showModal().
role="alertdialog" changes semantics (it implies an urgent message), not focus trapping.
aria-hidden on the dialog itself would hide the dialog's own content from assistive technology, which is the opposite of what's needed.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the same lesson as Lecture 7.1, applied to a bigger widget: aria-modal is a report, not a mechanism. A real trap has to move focus in, cycle Tab and Shift+Tab, and restore focus on close.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A menu item's handler only listens for `keydown` on Enter. A tester using only the keyboard says they "can't pick anything with Space." What's missing?
options: Nothing; Enter is the only key a menu item needs to support
Space is part of the activation contract for a menu item, exactly like a native button, and needs its own handler (typically on keyup)
The tester should use Enter instead; Space is only for checkboxes
Space should close the menu without activating anything

optionFeedback.feedback: A native button answers to both Enter and Space; a custom menuitem promises the same contract and has to implement both.
Right. This is one of the three details the lecture calls out as easy to forget: activate on Enter AND Space, not just one of them.
Menu items follow the same two-key activation contract as buttons; nothing in the pattern reserves Space for checkboxes only.
Escape is the key that closes without activating; Space is expected to activate the focused item, the same as it does on a native button.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: role="menuitem" documents that an element behaves like a menu item; it doesn't wire up Space for you. Skipping disabled items, wrapping, and activating on both Enter and Space are the three details Worked Example 7.2 traces by hand.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: List the four things a correct modal dialog has to do (from opening to closing), and say which one native <dialog> with showModal() gives you automatically that a hand-rolled role="dialog" does not.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A correct modal: (1) remembers the previously focused element (the opener) when it opens, (2) moves focus to a sensible first element inside the dialog, (3) traps Tab and Shift+Tab so they cycle only within the dialog while making the background inert, and (4) closes on Escape and restores focus to the opener. Native <dialog> opened with showModal() gives you the inert background, the focus trap, and Escape-to-close for free, and in current browsers also restores focus on close; a hand-rolled role="dialog" + aria-modal has to implement all of that itself, since aria-modal supplies none of it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: A menu button's arrow logic, traced
workedExamples.problem: Items: Reschedule, Cancel *(disabled)*, Add to calendar, Print. Active: Reschedule (index 0).
steps: **↓:** the next item is Cancel, which is disabled, so skip to Add to calendar (index 2). Set `tabindex`: item 2 = 0, the others = -1. Focus item 2.
**↓:** Print (index 3).
**↓:** wrap to Reschedule (index 0).
**End:** the last enabled item is Print (index 3).
**Space:** activate Print, close the menu, return focus to the Actions button.
workedExamples.conclusion: Skipping disabled items, wrapping, and activating on *both* Enter and Space are the three details people forget. Exercise s07-e1 tests all three.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What is roving tabindex?
What are the four duties of a modal dialog?

learningExperiences.title: Predict First: A Live Region That Arrives With Its Message

contentBlocks.content: Before Lecture 7.3 explains live regions, predict what a screen reader actually announces when a `role="status"` toast is inserted into the page carrying its message, versus when an empty region has existed since page load and is updated afterward.

interactionSequence.prompt: **A live region that arrives with its message.** Write down the exact output before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
Reminder set | Appointment saved (again)
```

**Why intuition fails.** "It has `role="status"`, so it will be read" feels right, but the first "Appointment saved" is never announced. Screen readers track changes to live regions they already know about, and a region inserted together with its text is often just new content, not a *change*. Only the later update to that region was spoken, after it had existed for a moment. Real behavior varies by screen reader and browser, which is exactly why the reliable pattern is to render regions at app start and update them later (misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m3`).

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: "It has `role="status"`, so it will be read" feels right, but the first "Appointment saved" is never announced. Screen readers track changes to live regions they already know about, and a region inserted together with its text is often just new content, not a *change*. Only the later update to that region was spoken, after it had existed for a moment. Real behavior varies by screen reader and browser, which is exactly why the reliable pattern is to render regions at app start and update them later (misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m3`).
hints: Ask, for each region, whether the SCREEN READER already knew about it before the text changed.
A region and its first message arriving in the same instant often reads as "new content," not a "change."

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 7.3: Routes, Forms, and Announcements

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Handle SPA route changes: update the title, move focus predictably, and announce. (objective o2)
2. Build accessible validation: inline errors wired with `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, and an error summary. (objective o3)
3. Build a toast system on live regions that exist before their content changes. (objective o3)

terms.definition: Route changes without a page load. Screen readers get no "new page" signal unless you provide one.
An element whose content changes are announced (`aria-live="polite"`/`"assertive"`, or `role="status"`/`role="alert"`).
`polite` waits for the user to be idle. `assertive` interrupts, so reserve it for urgent errors.
A list at the top of the form linking to each invalid field, focused after a failed submit.
Points to one or more element ids whose text is read *after* the name, such as hints and errors.
Marks a field as currently invalid.

contentBlocks.content:
### Route changes

After the clinic app navigates from "Book" to "Confirm details" without a page load:

1. Set `document.title` ("Confirm details · Clinic").
2. Move focus to the new page's `<h1>` (with `tabindex="-1"`, so it's focusable but not in the Tab order), or to a skip-link target. Screen-reader users land at the start of the new content, and keyboard users don't have to tab through the header again.
3. Optionally announce "Navigated to Confirm details" in a polite live region, for pages where moving focus would be disruptive.
4. Don't move focus on in-page changes (a filter update). Announce a result count instead.

In React, this is an effect that runs when the route key changes (s3). Its dependencies are honest (`[pathname]`), and it doesn't run on every render.

### Forms that explain themselves

- Each field has a visible `<label>`, plus a hint (`id="phone-hint"`) when the format matters.
- On blur or submit, invalid fields get `aria-invalid="true"` and an inline error (`id="phone-error"`). `aria-describedby="phone-hint phone-error"` keeps **both** the hint and the error.
- **Don't** put the error in `aria-label`. That replaces the field's name ("Phone") with the error text, and voice-control users can no longer say "click Phone."
- After a failed submit, show an **error summary** at the top (`role="alert"`, or focus it with `tabindex="-1"`) with links to each field.

### Live regions must exist before they change Screen readers watch live regions that are **already in the accessibility tree**. If you insert `
Appointment saved
` in one step, many screen readers announce nothing, because the region and its content arrived together (misconception `accessible-component-engineering.m3`). The toast system should therefore: 1. Render empty `role="status"` (polite) and `role="alert"` (assertive) containers **at app start**. 2. To announce, clear the region's text, then set the new message on the next tick. That way, identical consecutive messages ("Saved", "Saved") are announced again. 3. Keep the visible toast separate from the announcement region if needed. Don't auto-dismiss critical messages quickly. Give toasts a pause-on-focus/hover and a dismiss button.

contentBlocks.altText:
Diagram (s07-m3): Live region timing. Two timelines. Top (fails): at t0 a new
Saved
is inserted, and the screen-reader lane shows silence. Bottom (works): at page load an empty
exists. At t1 its text is cleared, and at t2 it's set to "Saved", with the screen-reader lane showing "Saved". A third row shows the same message repeated and still announced because of the clear-then-set step.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **`aria-describedby` is additive, space-separated, and read in order after the name, so listing the hint id AND the error id keeps BOTH, but dropping the hint id when an error appears loses it.** Predict each line, then write a describedBy list of your own for a field with a hint, no error, and a second custom description.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: routes, forms, announcements
contentBlocks.content:
- **SPA navigation with no focus move or title change.**
- **Errors conveyed only by red color** (use icon plus text, too).
- **Replacing the hint id with the error id in `aria-describedby`.**
- **Errors in `aria-label` or placeholders.**
- **Creating a live region at the moment you need it.**
- **Using `assertive` for routine messages.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 7.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Route change: title, focus to `<h1>` (or announce), and only for real page changes.
- Fields: label + hint + error, with `aria-describedby` listing both hint and error, plus `aria-invalid` and a focusable error summary.
- Live regions exist from page load. Clear, then set, to announce.

interactionSequence.prompt: A single-page app navigates from "Book" to "Confirm details" with no full page load, no title change, and no focus movement. What does a screen-reader user experience?
options: An automatic "new page" announcement, the same as a hard navigation
No signal at all that anything changed, because screen readers get no built-in "new page" event for client-side route changes
The page announces the new URL automatically
Focus moves to the browser's address bar automatically

optionFeedback.feedback: There is no such automatic announcement; a full page load provides that signal, and an SPA route change specifically does not.
Right. Without deliberately updating the title, moving focus to the new content, or announcing, the route change is invisible to a screen-reader user, even though the visible content changed.
URLs aren't announced automatically; nothing about the address bar is read out on a client-side navigation.
Nothing moves focus to browser chrome on a route change; if anything, focus should move to the new page's own content.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Client-side navigation is invisible to assistive technology unless the app provides the signal itself: update the title, move focus predictably, and announce for pages where moving focus would be disruptive.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A form puts the error message directly in `aria-label` on the invalid field, so "screen readers are sure to read it." What breaks?
options: Nothing; aria-label is the correct place for error text
The field's accessible name is replaced by the error text, so users lose the field's name ("Phone") and voice-control users can no longer say "click Phone"
The field becomes unfocusable
The error is read twice, once as the name and once as the error

optionFeedback.feedback: aria-label doesn't add anything alongside the name here; it replaces the name outright, which is exactly the problem.
Right. Errors are descriptions, meant for aria-describedby, not names. Overwriting the name breaks voice control and disorients anyone re-focusing the field.
Focusability is unrelated to which attribute supplies the accessible name.
There's no double reading; the accessible name computation picks exactly one source, and here aria-label wins, silently discarding "Phone."

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: aria-describedby is for hints and errors, read after the name. aria-label replaces the name outright, so putting an error there costs the field its identity.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt:
A toast component renders `
Appointment saved
` fresh into the DOM only when a save succeeds. Screen-reader users report hearing nothing. Why, and what's the fix?
options: The wording is too short to be announced; make the message longer

Screen readers watch live regions that already exist; a region inserted together with its first message is often treated as new content, not a change. Render an empty region at app start and set its text afterward
Nothing needs to change: role="status" already guarantees that whatever content arrives with it gets announced
The div needs a fixed id before it will be announced

optionFeedback.feedback: Message length has nothing to do with it; even a one-word message in an already-existing region is announced.
Right. This is exactly the P2 predict-run result: the region has to exist first. Clearing and then setting its text is what triggers an announcement, including for repeated identical messages.
That's the exact assumption that fails here: the role is correct, but a live region inserted together with its content is often treated as new content, not a change, and stays silent.
An id isn't what live-region tracking depends on; whether the region existed in the tree before the text changed is what matters.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A live region has to exist before its content changes. Render both the polite and assertive regions at app start, empty, then clear and set their text later to announce (and re-announce identical messages).

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Using the three route-change steps from the lecture, explain what a "Confirm details" screen should do when the app navigates to it, and why an in-page filter update should NOT do the same thing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: On navigating to "Confirm details," the app should update document.title to something like "Confirm details · Clinic," move focus to that page's own <h1> (given tabindex="-1" so it's focusable without joining the Tab order), so both keyboard and screen-reader users land at the start of new content instead of the stale header, and optionally announce "Navigated to Confirm details" in a polite live region for cases where moving focus would be disruptive. An in-page filter update is not a real page change: moving focus there would yank a user's cursor away from what they were doing mid-task, so the right move is to announce a result count in a live region instead, without touching focus at all.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Wiring one field
workedExamples.problem: Field: mobile phone, with hint "We'll text your appointment reminder," required, format `+1` then 10 digits.
steps:
Markup: ``, `

We'll text your reminder

`, ``.

Submit with an empty value: set `aria-invalid="true"`, render `

Enter a mobile phone number

`, and set `aria-describedby="phone-hint phone-error"`.
The summary at the top: "There is a problem: Enter a mobile phone number" as a link to `#phone`. Move focus to the summary.
A screen reader on the field reads: "Mobile phone, edit text, invalid entry, We'll text your reminder, Enter a mobile phone number."

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 7.4: Auditing, Prioritizing, and Explaining

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Run an audit that combines automated scanning with keyboard, screen-reader, zoom, and contrast checks. (objective o4)
2. Prioritize findings by user impact (severity) and cost (effort), not by how many the tool reported. (objective o4)
3. Explain a fix in a designer's terms and an engineer's terms. (objective o5)

terms.definition: A rule engine that finds *detectable* failures (missing alt text, low contrast, missing labels).
Keyboard-only runs, screen-reader runs, 200–400% zoom and reflow, reduced motion, and cognitive review.
The impact on a user task. A *blocker* makes a core task impossible, such as a keyboard trap in booking.
The rough cost to fix: S (a CSS or attribute change), M (component changes), L (design or architecture changes).
Catching accessibility problems in design and component APIs, where they're cheapest to fix.

contentBlocks.content:
### What automation finds, and what it can't

Automated tools are excellent at what can be checked mechanically: a missing `alt`, a missing label, contrast below the threshold, invalid ARIA attributes. They can't judge whether the alt text is *meaningful*, whether the focus order makes sense, whether a custom widget works with the keyboard, whether errors are understandable, or whether content reflows at 400% zoom. Only a minority of WCAG success criteria can be fully verified automatically, so a clean axe report isn't a clean bill of health (misconception `accessibility-auditing.m1`).

Accessibility also isn't a QA step at the end (misconception `accessibility-auditing.m2`). Most failures come from design decisions (low-contrast brand colors, hover-only affordances, tiny targets) and component APIs (a `Button` that renders a `div`, an `Icon` without a label prop). Fixing the component or token fixes every page at once.

### Prioritize by impact on the task

Not all findings are equally urgent (misconception `accessibility-auditing.m3`):

| Severity | Definition | Example in the clinic portal |
|---|---|---|
| **Blocker** | A core task is impossible for some users | Keyboard trap in the date picker, so booking can't be finished |
| **Critical** | A core task is very hard or unreliable | Error messages not announced, so users can't tell why a submit failed |
| **Serious** | A significant barrier, with workarounds | Low-contrast placeholder used as the only label |
| **Moderate** | Friction | Headings skip levels |
| **Minor** | Polish | A redundant `title` attribute |

Order the report by severity first, then **effort** within each severity (quick wins first), then reach (how many pages or users are affected). A report sorted by "number of axe violations" puts 400 minor duplicate-id warnings above one blocker.

### Explaining fixes to two audiences

The same finding, told two ways:

| Finding | To a designer | To an engineer |
|---|---|---|
| Brand teal `#3fb8af` text on white (2.3:1) | "Body text needs 4.5:1 so people with low vision, or anyone outdoors on a phone, can read it. The darker teal `#0b6e4f` keeps the brand feel at 6.25:1. Let's make it the text token and keep the light teal for large display type and decoration." | "Swap `--color-text-accent` to `#0b6e4f` in the semantic token layer (s11). Every component picks it up. Add a contrast check to the token build." |
| Hover-only "Reschedule" affordance | "Touch and keyboard users never see it. Show the action at rest, or behind a visible '⋯' button." | "Render the action button always, and use `:focus-within` as well as `:hover` for any reveal." |
| Date picker traps focus | "Keyboard users get stuck and can't finish booking. The fix is invisible to mouse users." | "The grid handles Tab and prevents default with no escape. Use roving tabindex inside the grid, and let Tab leave it and Esc close it." |

**Conclusion:** Designers need the *user outcome* and a design alternative that preserves intent. Engineers need the *mechanism* and where the fix lives.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s07-m4): A prioritized audit report page. A mocked report layout: a summary bar (2 blockers, 3 critical, 7 serious, and so on), then a table with columns Finding, WCAG criterion, Severity, Effort, Pages, Owner (Design/Eng), and Recommended fix. The top two rows are highlighted blockers. A side note reads "sorted by severity → effort → reach".

contentBlocks.caption: WCAG contrast ratio (Runnable Example R2): the same sRGB-linearization formula an automated checker uses, run against four real clinic colors.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **findings sort by severity first, then effort, then reach — never by raw tool-reported volume.** Predict the order for the three findings below, then add a fourth, minor-severity finding with a huge page count and see where it lands.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: auditing
contentBlocks.content:
- **Treating "0 axe violations" as "accessible."**
- **Reporting raw counts instead of root causes.**
- **Sorting by tool volume or effort alone.**
- **Explaining fixes only in WCAG numbers.** Say what the user can't do.
- **Auditing only at the end** instead of fixing components and tokens.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 7.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Automation plus manual testing. Automation alone misses most of what matters.
- Group by root cause, then prioritize by severity → effort → reach.
- Explain the user outcome to designers and the mechanism and location to engineers.

interactionSequence.prompt: An automated scan of the clinic portal reports 0 violations. What can the team conclude?
options: The portal is fully WCAG AA conformant
The mechanically detectable issues are fixed; keyboard, screen-reader, zoom, and cognitive checks are still needed to know whether people can actually complete tasks
Only color contrast still needs manual checking
Accessibility work is done and the audit can be signed off

optionFeedback.feedback: Automated tools verify only a minority of WCAG success criteria; a clean report is not a clean bill of health.
Right. Automation is excellent at what's mechanically checkable and blind to whether focus order makes sense, whether a custom widget works with the keyboard, or whether errors are understandable.
Contrast is actually one of the things automation DOES check well; the gap is elsewhere, in what it can't judge at all.
Treating 0 violations as "done" is exactly the QA-gate misconception the lecture warns against.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Only a minority of WCAG success criteria can be fully verified automatically. Automated scanning plus manual keyboard, screen-reader, zoom, and cognitive checks together are what find most of what matters.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: An axe report shows 180 duplicate-id warnings (one root cause, moderate) and a keyboard trap in the date picker that blocks booking (blocker). Which goes first in the report, and why?
options: The 180 duplicate-id warnings, since that's the largest number of findings
The date-picker trap, because a single blocked core task outranks any number of lower-severity findings; volume is not severity
Whichever one is faster to fix
They should be reported together since both come from the automated scan

optionFeedback.feedback: Volume isn't severity. Ranking by raw tool count would put 180 minor duplicate-id warnings above the one finding that stops a user from booking at all.
Right. Order by severity first (blocker beats moderate, no matter the count), then by effort within a severity level, then by reach.
Effort only breaks ties WITHIN the same severity level; it never lets a low-severity quick win jump ahead of a blocker.
Grouping by which tool found something isn't a prioritization signal; severity and effort are, regardless of automated vs. manual origin.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Order findings by severity, then effort within each severity level (quick wins first), then reach. A report sorted by raw violation count buries the one blocker under hundreds of minor duplicates.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A brand teal `#3fb8af` is used as body text on white and measures 2.3:1 contrast. How should this finding be explained to a designer, versus an engineer?
options: Both should just get the WCAG success-criterion number (1.4.3) with no further explanation
The designer gets the user outcome and a design alternative that preserves brand intent; the engineer gets the mechanism (which token to change) and where the fix lives
Only the engineer needs an explanation; the designer's job ends once the ticket is filed
The same message, using WCAG terminology, works equally well for both audiences

optionFeedback.feedback: A bare success-criterion number tells neither audience what to actually do, and doesn't help a designer choose an alternative color.
Right. Designers need to know who's affected and what still looks like the brand; engineers need to know which token or component to change and where it propagates.
Most color and contrast decisions originate in design; leaving the designer out means the same mistake likely repeats in the next token or component.
WCAG numbers mean little to most designers; translating the finding into user impact and a design alternative is what makes it actionable for them.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The same finding, told two ways: the designer gets the user outcome ("people with low vision can't read this") plus an alternative that keeps the brand feel; the engineer gets the mechanism (swap --color-text-accent) and where it lives (the token layer).

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate says "we audit for accessibility right before each release, same as any other QA pass." Using the shift-left idea from the lecture, explain what's wrong with auditing only at the end.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Most accessibility failures originate in design decisions (low-contrast brand colors, hover-only affordances, tiny touch targets) and in component APIs (a Button that renders a div, an Icon with no label prop), not in individual pages. Auditing only right before release finds the same root cause repeated across every page that uses that color, button, or icon, forcing a scramble of one-off page-level fixes under release pressure. Catching the same problem earlier, in the design tokens and the shared components, fixes every page that uses them at once and is far cheaper than a pre-release sweep; that's the whole idea behind "shift left."

workedExamples.title: Turning 212 axe results into a plan
workedExamples.problem: Turning 212 axe results into a plan
steps: **Automated pass:** axe reports 212 issues. 180 are the same `duplicate-id` inside a repeated card component (one root cause). 20 are contrast on one token. 12 are missing labels on icon buttons.

**Manual pass:** a keyboard-only run finds the date-picker trap (**blocker**). A screen-reader run finds unannounced form errors (**critical**). A 400% zoom test finds the booking summary overflowing horizontally (**serious**).
**Group by root cause:** 212 results become 3 automated root causes plus 3 manual findings.

**Prioritize:** date-picker trap (blocker, M) → errors not announced (critical, S) → icon-button labels (critical, S) → contrast token (serious, S) → reflow (serious, M) → duplicate ids (moderate, S).
workedExamples.conclusion: The most urgent item didn't appear in the automated results at all, and the biggest automated number turned out to be one moderate fix.

learningExperiences.title: Lab: Care for Everyone

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content: Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. Screen-reader output can't be executed in the engine. The exercises give you a **fake document** (focus and tab order) and a **fake screen reader** (which announces only changes to live regions that already existed), so you can test keyboard contracts, focus management, and announcement logic. The Practical Activity checks everything with a real screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA, or TalkBack) and a keyboard.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenges 1 through 4 each give you a scaffold (a fake document with tab order, a fake screen reader, or fixture data) and leave the core logic to you: a menu's roving tabindex, a focus trap, form validation attributes, and a live-region announcer. Challenge 5 has no scaffolding beyond the fixture data: the whole sort is yours. The two test-suite challenges turn it around: first you write tests for correct contrast-checker code, then you fix a broken tabs keyboard handler against tests that are already written.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your contrast-checker tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the test-suite challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "Care for Everyone."** Expected time is 10–12 hours.

1. **Four widgets** (framework of your choice): clinic-search **combobox** (reuse s5), **reschedule modal** (`<dialog>` + `showModal()` *or* a custom dialog using your s07-e2 trap), appointment-actions **menu button** (s07-e1 reducer), and **tabs** (s07-t2). For each, run and record the **keyboard script** (every key in the contract) and a **screen-reader script** (VoiceOver + Safari, or NVDA + Firefox or Chrome), noting what's announced. *(o1)*
2. **SPA focus-management layer:** on route change, update the title, focus the `<h1>`, and announce politely (s07-e4). Show it working across three routes. *(o2)*
3. **Booking form** with validation (s07-e3), an error summary that receives focus after a failed submit, and a **toast system** on pre-rendered live regions (s07-e4) with pause-on-hover/focus and a dismiss button. *(o3)*
4. **Audit of a real site** (a public-sector site, a nonprofit's, or an open-source project's): axe plus a keyboard-only run, a screen-reader run, 400% zoom, and a reduced-motion check. Deliver a prioritized report (severity → effort → reach, grouped by root cause) in the Lecture 7.4 table format. *(o4)*
5. **Three fixes explained twice:** for three findings, write the designer version and the engineer version. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for "Care for Everyone" (100 points)
rows: Full keyboard contracts. Screen-reader scripts match the expected announcements. Focus return verified.
Title, focus, and announcement on real navigations only.
`describedby` keeps hints, the summary is focused, and live regions exist up front.
Manual findings present. Root causes grouped. Correct prioritization.
The designer version is outcome-focused with an alternative. The engineer version names the mechanism and location.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 5: menu button with roving tabindex

Implement `menuKeyDown(state, key)` for an open menu, where `state` is `{ items, activeIndex, open, focus, activated }`. ↓/↑ move to the next or previous **enabled** item and wrap. Home/End go to the first or last enabled item. Enter **and** Space activate the active item (closing the menu, setting `activated`, and returning focus to `'button'`). Escape closes and returns focus to `'button'`. Tab closes the menu and lets focus move on (`focus: 'next'`). `focus` is the active item's id otherwise. Also implement `tabIndexes(state)`.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Loop at most `items.length` steps with modulo arithmetic to wrap, skipping disabled items.
Home/End mean the first and last *enabled* items.
Which two keys activate a native button? A menu item promises the same.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 5: a focus trap that returns focus

Implement `createFocusTrap(doc, containerId)` with `activate()`, `handleKeyDown({ key, shiftKey })` (which returns `true` when it handled the key), and `deactivate()`. It focuses the first tabbable element inside the container on activation, cycles Tab and Shift+Tab within the container, and on deactivation returns focus to whatever was focused before `activate()`.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: The opener is simply whatever `doc.activeElement` was when you activated.
Returning `true` from `handleKeyDown` means "I prevented the browser's default Tab."
If focus has somehow ended up outside the dialog, Tab should bring it back to the first element (or the last, for Shift+Tab).

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 5: form validation with correct aria-describedby wiring

Implement `validateForm(fields, values)` that returns `{ summary, attrs }`. `summary` lists `{ fieldId, message }` in field order. `attrs[fieldId]` has `aria-describedby` (the hint id, then the error id when invalid, space-separated, omitted if neither) and `aria-invalid: 'true'` only when invalid. **Never** set `aria-label`.

Each field is `{ id, label, hintId?, required?, pattern?, patternMessage? }`. The required message is `` `Enter ${label.toLowerCase()}` ``. The error id is `` `${id}-error` ``. Values are trimmed before validation.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: `aria-describedby` accepts several ids separated by spaces, and it's read in that order.
An accessible name should match the visible label. Errors are *descriptions*, not names.
Trim before checking "required," so a field of spaces is still empty.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 5: an announcer for toasts and route changes

Implement `createAnnouncer(dom, schedule)` that creates a polite and an assertive live region **immediately**, and exposes `announce(message, { politeness })` and `announceRoute(title)` (polite, `` `Navigated to ${title}` ``). To announce, clear the region's text now, then set the message in a `schedule`d callback, so repeated identical messages are announced again.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: The screen reader only watches regions it saw *before* the change.
Setting the same text twice isn't a change. What could you do in between?
`schedule` gives you "later." Use it for the second half of the update.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 5 of 5: prioritize audit findings

Implement `prioritizeFindings(findings)` that returns finding ids ordered by severity (`blocker` > `critical` > `serious` > `moderate` > `minor`), then effort (`S` < `M` < `L`), then pages affected (more first), then id.

This one has no scaffolding beyond the fixture data: the whole sort is yours.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Turn the severity and effort words into ranks with lookup objects.
Chain comparisons with `||`: the next key only matters when the previous ones tie.
Sort a copy. The caller's report order shouldn't change.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working contrast checker, you write the tests

`contrastRatio(a, b)` and `meetsContrast(fg, bg, { largeText, level })` implement WCAG 2.x contrast (sRGB linearization, relative luminance, (L1 + 0.05)/(L2 + 0.05) with L1 the lighter, AA 4.5/3, AAA 7/4.5). They're correct. Write tests that catch the three hidden wrong versions. Use the known values from Runnable Example R2.

Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **4** tests). Then confirm your suite catches all three wrong versions in the three playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks four behaviors: matching known reference ratios (from Runnable Example R2, not re-derived with the same formula), symmetry regardless of argument order, the AA normal-text threshold at 4.5:1, and the large-text (3:1) and AAA (7:1) thresholds. Wrong version 1 forgets sRGB linearization entirely, so its ratios are wrong across the board. Wrong version 2 assumes the first argument is always the lighter color instead of sorting by luminance, so it fails whenever foreground and background are passed in the "wrong" order. Wrong version 3 collapses every threshold to a flat 3:1, so it wrongly passes normal text that fails AA. A suite that only checks "returns a number" catches none of the three.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests here pin down the contract against known reference values, not against a second copy of the same formula (which would just agree with itself, including its own bugs).
hints: Reuse the exact reference values from Runnable Example R2 rather than recomputing them with the same luminance formula.
Call contrastRatio with the two colors in both orders. Should the result differ?
Test meetsContrast at exactly its boundaries: 4.5:1 normal text, 3:1 large text, 7:1 AAA.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken tabs keyboard handler, make the tests pass

The results page has tabs Upcoming / Past / Results with **automatic activation** (arrow keys select). `tabsKeyDown(state, key)` has several bugs. Fix it until every test passes.

codeExercise.solutionNote: without wrapping, the arrows run off the end into `selected: 3` or `-1` (no tab, and focus lost). Home and End are part of the contract. The `((i % n) + n) % n` idiom handles negative indexes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The broken handler never wraps at either end and has no Home/End support at all. Fixing the wrap without adding Home/End (or vice versa) still leaves tests failing.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. What does ArrowRight return when selected is already the last tab?
The `((i % n) + n) % n` idiom wraps a possibly-negative index back into range in one line.
Check the "single tab" test: does your fix still return the same tab (and the same state reference, for the ignored-key case) when there's only one to wrap to?

interactionSequence.prompt: When "Care for Everyone" is done, paste a link or summary and answer: which screen-reader announcement surprised you most (in a bad way) before you fixed it, and which manual check (keyboard, screen reader, 400% zoom, or reduced motion) found something axe never would have?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong reports name a specific control and a specific announcement (or its absence), tie it to a specific fix (roving tabindex, a pre-rendered live region, restored focus), and name a manual check that caught something automation structurally cannot judge, such as whether an announcement makes sense or whether the focus order follows meaning. Check your work against the rubric table above before you submit.

learningExperiences.title: In the Wild: Spend an Hour as a Keyboard and Screen-Reader User

contentBlocks.content: This exercise happens with a real screen reader on a real site, not inside the course engine. The 20 minutes here cover planning and reflection; putting the mouse away and actually trying to book something takes longer, and filing a respectful issue can take longer still. Nothing here is graded or gates your progress. It builds evidence you will reuse in the Section 13 portfolio.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A real screen reader (VoiceOver, NVDA, or TalkBack), a real site with a booking, reservation, or appointment flow, and optionally a local or online accessibility meetup or usability session.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Experience a real task with the mouse put away and a screen reader on, log every place it broke down, and turn one specific failure into a respectful, actionable issue.
instructions: Turn on a screen reader (VoiceOver on macOS or iOS, NVDA on Windows, or TalkBack on Android). With the mouse or trackpad put away, try to book something real: a library room, a restaurant table, or a public-service appointment.
Keep a log of every place you got stuck, every unclear announcement, and every time focus went somewhere unexpected.
File one respectful, specific issue with the site's owner (many public bodies have an accessibility contact) or with an open-source project, including the steps to reproduce and a suggested fix.
**Stretch:** attend a local or online accessibility meetup, or watch a usability session with a disabled user if your company runs them. Write down one thing that changed how you build components.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A screen reader available on your OS (VoiceOver on macOS/iOS, NVDA on Windows, or TalkBack on Android).
A real task to attempt: a library room, a restaurant table, or a public-service appointment.
A place to file the issue: the site owner's accessibility contact, or an open-source project's issue tracker.
reflectionPrompts: Where did you get stuck, and was it a focus problem, a missing name, or a silent live region?
Which finding would you rank as a blocker, and why, using this section's severity definitions?
What did filing (or drafting) the issue teach you about writing a finding an engineer can act on without more back-and-forth?

selfAssessmentCriteria: I completed a real task using only a screen reader and logged every place I got stuck or heard something unclear.
I named the specific mechanism behind at least one failure (missing name, wrong role, lost focus, or a silent live region), not just its symptom.
I saved my anonymized log and the issue link for my Section 13 portfolio.

transferExercises.scenario: Passengers choose a seat from a grid of 180 seats, some unavailable, some premium. Reuse roving tabindex within a composite widget, correct accessible naming and state, and the rule that status messages are announced without moving focus.
transferExercises.task: Passengers choose a seat from a grid of 180 seats, some unavailable, some premium. Design the keyboard and screen-reader contract (which pattern? roving tabindex in a grid? what's announced for each seat?), how an unavailable seat is exposed, and how a price change is announced after selection without moving focus.
successCriteria: Chooses roving tabindex within a 2D grid role (or an activedescendant model) so Tab enters and leaves the seat map once, and arrow keys move between seats inside it.
Gives each seat an accessible name and state that includes its identity, availability, and price tier (for example "14C, window, premium, available"), not just a visual color or icon.
Exposes an unavailable seat via aria-disabled (or equivalent state), not by silently removing it from the grid, so its existence is still discoverable.
Announces a price change after selection in a polite live region without moving focus off the seat the user just selected.

transferExercises.scenario: A cooking app shows a running timer plus occasional urgent alerts, and one banner animates in a way that ignores reduced-motion preference.
transferExercises.task: A cooking app shows a timer and occasionally urgent alerts ("Oven door open", "Preheat complete"). Design the announcement strategy (polite vs assertive, what's visual-only, how to avoid a flood of timer ticks), and write the audit finding and dual explanation (designer and engineer) for a flashing "Preheat complete" banner that doesn't respect reduced motion.
successCriteria: Uses polite live regions for routine, expected updates and assertive only for genuinely urgent interruptions (an open oven door, not every timer tick).
Keeps per-second timer ticks visual-only, summarizing progress rather than announcing every change, to avoid flooding the user with noise.
Writes the audit finding for the flashing banner as serious-or-higher severity, since it can trigger real harm for vestibular or seizure-sensitive users, not just "polish."

Gives the designer version (an outcome and a static or reduced-motion alternative that keeps the banner's intent) and the engineer version (respect prefers-reduced-motion; replace the flash with a static state change or a single gentle transition).

sections.title: Testing, Tooling, and Shipping
sections.description: Build the discipline that separates code that runs from code you can trust in production. Choose the right test layer by asserting behavior through public interfaces instead of chasing coverage percentages, then write the frontend-flavored versions that actually show up on the job: a layered suite for a typeahead controller, a minimal ESM bundler with real dependency ordering and cycle detection, a CI pipeline that builds once and deploys a preview, a feature-flag evaluator with a kill switch and sticky rollout, and an error reporter with masked context. Examples come from a personal banking and payments app: balances, transfers, payees, and card controls, where a rounding bug or a silent flag failure is not a cosmetic problem.

learningObjectives.description: Write a layered test suite for the s5 typeahead (unit, Testing Library, one Playwright flow) and justify the split
Build a minimal bundler that resolves ESM imports, builds the dependency graph, and emits correctly ordered output
Configure CI that lints, type-checks, tests, builds, and deploys a preview on every pull request
Implement feature flags with a kill switch and demonstrate a dark launch
Trace a deliberately triggered production error end to end through error tracking and session context

motivationHooks.prompt: A validation module had 100% line coverage, and it still let a user send 28 cents instead of 29. In banking software, that's not a rounding footnote — it's money moving incorrectly, and every line that ran said nothing about whether the right thing was checked.

During a live incident, an engineer flips the kill switch for instant-transfers. A QA account with an `override: true` from testing keeps seeing the feature anyway. Is that a bug in the feature's code, or somewhere else entirely? Keep your guess; Lecture 8.4 comes back to it.

Two files each declare `const format = …`. Glue them together in a `<script>` tag and one silently overwrites the other; run them through a bundler and both work fine. Same two files, same browser — what is the bundler actually doing that concatenation isn't?

This section's dependency graph is s4's topological sort, now inside a bundler; its typeahead tests are s5's controller, now under test; its error tracking joins s6's RUM; and its accessible queries are s7's, reused to find elements the way assistive technology does.

It's an evaluation-order bug, not a code bug in the transfer feature. A flag isn't a boolean — it's a small rules engine, and if the override check runs before the kill-switch check, the override wins even during an incident. The kill switch must be evaluated first, beating every other rule, or it isn't actually a kill switch. If you guessed the feature's own code was broken, you've now met the trap Lecture 8.4's worked example is built around.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- Coverage measures what ran, not what was checked. Ask "would a test fail if I broke this line?" instead of chasing a percentage.
- Test behavior through public interfaces (what a caller or user observes), not implementation details like which hook or internal function ran — those tests break on safe refactors and can pass while a real bug ships.
- A bundler resolves a dependency graph, gives each module its own scope, and orders everything dependencies-first before it emits — concatenation breaks order, scope, and dead-code elimination all at once.
- A CI pipeline should fail fast and cheap first, build exactly once and pass that artifact to every later job, and treat every relevant check — including one E2E run against the real preview — as required.
- A feature flag is a small rules engine with an evaluation order that *is* the policy: kill switch, then overrides, then environment targeting, then sticky rollout — and flags get removed once the rollout is decided, or they become debt.
- "Shipped" and "it works" are different claims. Define the metrics that answer "does it work" — an error rate and a success rate by release and cohort — before the feature ships, not after someone notices it's broken.
keyTakeaways: Coverage shows what ran; it can't show what was checked. Ask what would make a test fail.
Assert on behavior through public interfaces, not on internal state or which function got called.
A bundler is graph plus order plus scope, not concatenation — and tree-shaking needs static, analyzable imports.
CI should fail fast and cheap first, build once, and make the checks that matter required.
A feature flag's evaluation order — kill switch, overrides, targeting, sticky rollout — is the policy itself.
"Shipped" is not "it works." Decide the success metrics before release, and watch them by release and cohort after.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 8.1: A Testing Philosophy You Can Defend

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Decide what belongs in unit, integration, and end-to-end tests, and justify the split for a real feature. (objective o1)
2. Write tests that assert **behavior** through public interfaces, not implementation details. (objective o1)
3. Explain why coverage isn't confidence, and use mutation-style thinking instead. (objective o1)

terms.definition: Tests one module's logic in isolation, through its public API. It's fast and precise.
Tests several units together, for example a component rendered with its hooks and a fake network, through what the user sees and does.
Drives the real app in a real browser against a deployed or local stack (Playwright). It's slow, and it's the most realistic.
A stand-in for a dependency: a *fake* (working lightweight implementation), a *stub* (canned answers), or a *spy/mock* (records calls).
Anything a user or caller can't observe: internal state names, private functions, which hook you used.
The percentage of lines *executed* by tests. It says nothing about what was *asserted*.
Deliberately introducing bugs ("mutants") and checking that the tests fail. A surviving mutant shows a missing assertion.
A test that passes and fails without any code change (timing, shared state, the network).

contentBlocks.content:
### Start concrete: the transfer that "had 100% coverage"

A bug shipped in the transfers screen: entering `0.29` sent 28 cents. The validation module had 100% line coverage. Every line ran in tests, but no test checked the amount for inputs like `0.29`, where floating-point multiplication goes wrong (`0.29 * 100 = 28.999999999999996`). High coverage doesn't mean high confidence (misconception `testing-strategy.m1`). Coverage tells you what code **never ran**, which is useful. It can't tell you what was **checked**. The question to ask is: "If I broke this line, would a test fail?" That's mutation thinking, and the mutants in this course's exercises are built on it.

### Test behavior through public interfaces

A test coupled to internals ("expect `setState` to have been called with `{loading: true}`") breaks when you refactor to `useReducer`, even though users see no difference. It still passes when the spinner never actually renders (misconception `testing-strategy.m2`). Test what a caller or user can observe:

- For a **controller** (the s5 typeahead): given inputs and time, what state and which requests result?
- For a **component**: find elements the way a user or assistive technology would (`getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Payee' })`), interact, and assert on what's rendered and announced.

Testing Library's accessible queries have a useful side effect. If a test can't find your control by role and name, a screen-reader user probably can't either (s7).

### Choosing the layer

| Layer | Put here | For the payee typeahead |
|---|---|---|
| **Unit** | pure logic, edge cases, timing, and races via an injected clock | debounce, abort, latest-wins, cache normalization, min length (s5-e1) |
| **Integration** (Testing Library) | component behavior, a11y wiring, rendering states | typing shows options, ↓/Enter selects, `aria-activedescendant` updates, error message appears |
| **E2E** (Playwright) | a few critical user journeys across real boundaries | "search a payee → select → send $10 → see confirmation" on the preview deploy |

More E2E tests don't make the product safer (misconception `testing-strategy.m3`). E2E tests are slow, and they're flaky under network and timing variance. A handful of critical-journey flows buys most of their value, and the rest belongs at lower layers where failures point straight at the cause.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s08-m1): Where each test lives. A three-band diagram: a wide base labelled "Unit: many, milliseconds, precise" containing typeahead controller cases; a middle band labelled "Integration: behavior through the DOM" showing a combobox with role queries; a thin top labelled "E2E: 1–3 critical journeys" showing a browser with the transfer flow. Arrows on the side show "cost per test ↑" and "failure precision ↓" going up.

contentBlocks.caption: A 'test' that runs every line of a buggy `toCents` and reports 100% coverage. Predict what it prints for `toCents('0.29')` before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: testing strategy
contentBlocks.content:
- **Chasing a coverage percentage** instead of asking "would a test fail if this broke?"
- **Asserting on internal state or hook calls.**
- **Mocking the thing under test**, or mocking so much that nothing real runs.
- **Many slow E2E tests for logic that unit tests cover precisely.**
- **Real timers in tests** (sleeping), which makes them slow and flaky. Inject the clock.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 8.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Unit tests cover logic and timing, integration tests cover behavior and a11y, and a few E2E tests cover critical journeys.
- Assert on observable behavior. Query the DOM like a user.
- Coverage shows what didn't run. Mutation thinking shows what isn't checked.

interactionSequence.prompt: The transfers module has 100% line coverage, yet shipped a rounding bug: `toCents('0.29')` returns 28, not 29. What does '100% coverage' actually tell you here?
options: That every line ran during tests — nothing about which behaviors were checked. Ask instead: "if I broke this line, would a test fail?"
That the module is well-tested, so the bug must be coming from somewhere else, like the backend.
That you should add E2E tests in a real browser until the number stays at 100% there too.
That the coverage tool under-counted, since a bug this real should have shown up as missing coverage.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Coverage tells you what never ran. It says nothing about what was asserted, which is exactly why `0.29` slipped through untested.
100% coverage is not the same as 100% confidence — every line of the buggy `toCents` ran, and it was still wrong.
More E2E tests are slow and flaky, and they wouldn't have been any more likely to happen to check `0.29` than the unit tests were.
The tool did its job correctly: every line really did execute. Coverage measuring execution, not correctness, is the whole point.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Coverage is a floor, not a ceiling: it can tell you code never ran, but it can't tell you an assertion was missing. Mutation thinking ("would a test fail if I broke this?") is what coverage can't answer.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A reviewer flags a test that does `expect(setState).toHaveBeenCalledWith({ loading: true })` inside a component test. After a refactor from `useState` to `useReducer`, the test fails, but the spinner still renders correctly on screen. What's the right response?
options: The test was coupled to an implementation detail (which hook is used), not to behavior a user can observe. Rewrite it to query the rendered spinner instead.
Update the mock to expect the new reducer's dispatch call instead, so the test still checks the same internal mechanism.
Delete the test — if a refactor breaks it, the test was never worth keeping.
Revert the refactor, since the test suite is what defines correct behavior.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A test coupled to internals breaks on a safe refactor and can pass even when nothing actually renders — assert on what a user or caller can observe instead.
That doubles down on the same coupling: the next internal change (a new state library, a different action shape) breaks the test again for the same reason.
Deleting it loses real coverage of the loading behavior — the fix is to test the behavior, not to stop testing it.
Reverting a refactor that doesn't change behavior, just because an internals-coupled test failed, protects the wrong thing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Test what a caller or user can observe — for a controller, given inputs and time, what state results; for a component, what's rendered and announced. `setState`/hook-call assertions are implementation details.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team proposes replacing the typeahead's unit tests for debounce, abort, and cache normalization with 15 new Playwright tests that exercise the same cases end to end. Is that a good trade?
options: No — those are timing and race cases that are deterministic and fast with an injected clock at the unit layer. E2E tests are slow and flaky for exactly this kind of case, and they don't point at the cause as precisely.
Yes — more E2E tests always make the product safer, since they run against the real thing.
Yes, as long as the 15 tests are marked optional so they never block a merge.
It doesn't matter which layer, since all three layers on the pyramid catch the same bugs.

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Debounce, abort, and caching are exactly the kind of deterministic, timing-sensitive logic that belongs at the unit layer with an injected clock — not spread across slow, flaky E2E runs.
More E2E tests don't make the product safer by default — they're slow and flaky under real network and timing variance, and they replace precise failures with vague ones.
Optional checks get ignored in practice, and the flakiness and slowness remain a tax on every CI run.
Each layer catches a different kind of bug at a different cost — that's the entire reason to split them instead of picking one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A handful of critical-journey E2E flows buys most of their value. Timing and races are unit-tested; keyboard and ARIA are integration-tested; E2E covers the few journeys that prove the pieces connect.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: **A test coupled to internals.** Write down the exact output, line by line, before you run it. Commit to an answer even if you're unsure — the gap between your prediction and the real output is what teaches you something.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
implementation test: fail
behaviour test: fail
```

**Why intuition fails.** Many people expect the implementation test to be the "strict" one that catches bugs. Look at *why* each one failed. The implementation test fails because the refactor stopped calling `pad`. It would fail even if the output were perfect, so it's noise that makes people distrust the suite. The behavior test fails because an overdrawn balance now displays as `$5.00`, a real bug users would see. If you fixed the minus sign, the behavior test would pass and the implementation test would still fail. That's misconception `testing-strategy.m2`: tests coupled to internals break on refactors and don't protect behavior.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Many people expect the implementation test to be the "strict" one that catches bugs. Look at *why* each one failed. The implementation test fails because the refactor stopped calling `pad`. It would fail even if the output were perfect, so it's noise that makes people distrust the suite. The behavior test fails because an overdrawn balance now displays as `$5.00`, a real bug users would see. If you fixed the minus sign, the behavior test would pass and the implementation test would still fail. That's misconception `testing-strategy.m2`: tests coupled to internals break on refactors and don't protect behavior.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: Testing Library's accessible queries (`getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Payee' })`) find elements the way a screen reader would. In two or three sentences, explain why a test that can't find your control by role and name is itself useful accessibility information, and how that connects to what s7 taught about accessible queries.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: If `getByRole` can't find a control, that's not just a test-authoring problem — it means the control has no accessible name or the wrong (or missing) role, which is exactly the information a screen reader needs and isn't getting. Writing tests through accessible queries, as s7 taught, forces the same query path a screen reader uses, so a failing query surfaces a real accessibility bug before a user ever hits it, at essentially no extra cost over writing the test at all.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: The payee typeahead's test plan, justified
workedExamples.problem: The payee typeahead's test plan, justified
steps: **Unit (12 tests):** everything with time and races uses the injected manual scheduler and fake search from s5, so there are no real timers and no flakiness. These are fast enough to run on every save.

**Integration (5 tests):** render `<PayeeSearch>` with a fake search function passed as a prop, which works without module mocking. ```jsx // for reading: runs with Testing Library in your project render(<PayeeSearch search={fakeSearch} scheduler={manual} />); await user.type(screen.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Payee' }), 'rent'); manual.advance(250); fakeSearch.respond('rent', [{ id: 'p1', name: 'Rent: Oak St' }]); expect(await screen.findByRole('option', { name: 'Rent: Oak St' })).toBeVisible(); await user.keyboard('{ArrowDown}{Enter}'); expect(screen.getByRole('combobox')).toHaveValue('Rent: Oak St'); ```

**E2E (1 flow):** Playwright against the preview URL: log in with a seeded test user, search a payee, send $10, and assert the confirmation and the new balance. ```js // for reading: runs with @playwright/test in CI test('send money to a saved payee', async ({ page }) => { await page.goto(process.env.PREVIEW_URL + '/transfer'); await page.getByRole('combobox', { name: 'Payee' }).fill('rent'); await page.getByRole('option', { name: 'Rent: Oak St' }).click(); await page.getByRole('textbox', { name: 'Amount' }).fill('10.00'); await page.getByRole('button', { name: 'Send' }).click(); await expect(page.getByRole('status')).toHaveText('Sent $10.00 to Rent: Oak St'); }); ```

**Justification (the paragraph you'd write):** "Races and timing are unit-tested with an injected clock because that's where they're deterministic. Keyboard and ARIA behavior is integration-tested through accessible queries. One E2E flow proves the pieces connect on real infrastructure. Adding more E2E tests would slow CI and add flakiness without catching different bugs."
workedExamples.conclusion: Each layer catches a *different kind* of bug, and none of them repeats another's work.
