learningExperiences.title: Lecture 9.2: Components That Respond to Their Container

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Use container queries so a component adapts to the space it's given. (objective o1)
2. Decide what should respond to the **container** and what to the **viewport**. (objective o1)
3. Use `:has()` to style a component based on its content or state. (objective o3)

terms.definition: An element with `container-type: inline-size` (and optionally `container-name`). Descendants can query its size.
A rule applied when the nearest (or named) container matches, for example `@container tile (min-width: 22rem)`.
`cqi`, `cqb` (1% of the container's inline or block size), used for sizing relative to the container.
A relational pseudo-class: `.tile:has(.alert)` matches tiles that *contain* an alert. It's sometimes called the parent selector.
A rule based on the viewport or device (`@media (min-width: …)`, `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-color-scheme`, `pointer: coarse`).

contentBlocks.content:
### The same tile, three homes

The soil-moisture tile appears in the main grid (wide), in the alerts rail (narrow), and in a modal (medium). Viewport media queries can't tell those apart, because the viewport is the same for all three. Container queries can:

### Container queries don't replace media queries

Container queries answer "how much room does *this component* have?" Media queries still answer page-level and user-level questions (misconception `css-layout-architecture.m2`):

| Decide by the **container** | Decide by the **viewport / user** |
|---|---|
| a tile's internal arrangement | whether the app shell shows a sidebar, a rail, or bottom navigation |
| how many columns a card list uses | `prefers-reduced-motion`, `prefers-color-scheme`, `prefers-contrast` |
| whether a table becomes stacked rows inside a narrow panel | `pointer: coarse` (bigger targets), `hover: none` |
| typography that scales with component size (`cqi`) | print styles |

The objective "no viewport media queries" in o1 applies to the **dashboard's components and grid**. The shell's navigation style and user preferences are page-level concerns and correctly stay as media queries.
### `:has()`: style by content

This removes many "add a modifier class from JavaScript" patterns. The markup describes the content, and the CSS reacts to it. Keep `:has()` selectors scoped (a component root, direct children). A page-wide `body:has(…)` makes the browser re-check far more elements whenever the DOM changes.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s09-m2): One component, three containers. A single soil-moisture tile rendered in a 300 px rail (stacked), a 480 px modal (sparkline beside the reading), and an 800 px main grid slot (with the mini table). Above it, the same viewport width (1280 px) is shown for all three, illustrating why viewport queries can't distinguish them. A side panel shows the shell switching from sidebar to rail to bottom-nav as the viewport changes.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: the app shell responds to the viewport, while a component's internal layout responds to its own container, even at the same viewport width. Edit the map below to classify two more decisions from a dashboard (your own choice) as container or viewport, then compare with the table above.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: container queries and `:has()`
contentBlocks.content:
- **Forgetting `container-type`.** `@container` then matches nothing.
- **Querying a container from inside itself** (the container can't style itself based on its own size, only its descendants).
- **Moving shell and user-preference logic into container queries.**
- **Page-wide `:has()` selectors** that are expensive to re-evaluate.
- **Using `:has()` to encode state that should be an accessible attribute** (put `aria-expanded` on the element, then style `[aria-expanded="true"]`).

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 9.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Components respond to their containers, and the page and user preferences respond to the viewport and media features.
- `:has()` lets components restyle by content. Keep it scoped.

interactionSequence.prompt: A soil-moisture tile needs a different internal arrangement depending on whether it sits in the wide main grid, the narrow alerts rail, or a medium-width modal, all at the very same 1280px browser viewport. What should decide the tile's arrangement?
options: The tile's own container width, via a container query
The viewport width, via a media query, since 1280px is a well-known breakpoint
Whichever query happens to run first in the stylesheet
JavaScript, since CSS alone cannot know which slot a component is in

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A container query answers exactly this question, because it knows how much room the tile itself has been given, not just the page.
The viewport is identical in all three cases here, so a media query cannot tell the three slots apart at all.
Source order doesn't decide this; the query condition does, and only a container query has access to the right measurement.
This is exactly what container queries were built to avoid needing JavaScript for.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Container queries answer "how much room does this component have," which is a different question from "how wide is the browser window." The viewport is identical for all three tile placements, so only a container query can tell them apart.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: What does the selector .tile:has(.alert--critical) match?
options: Tiles that contain a descendant with the class alert--critical
Elements with the class alert--critical that come after a tile
Alerts that are themselves tiles
Nothing valid, because CSS has no way to select a parent based on its children

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. :has() matches the subject of the selector, here the tile, based on what it contains.
That describes a sibling combinator, not :has(); the subject here is the tile, not the alert.
The selector's subject is the tile, and the alert class is the condition inside has(), not a second class on the same element.
This was true before :has() shipped; it is now a well-supported relational pseudo-class, sometimes called the parent selector.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: :has() is a relational pseudo-class: the element that matches is the one on the left (the tile), tested against whether it contains something matching the argument.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A component's container-width rule never seems to match, no matter how wide its slot is. What is the most likely cause?
options: No ancestor has a container-type set, so there is no query container for the rule to check against
22rem is larger than any real container can ever be
Container-width rules only work inside a media query
The rule needs !important to take effect

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Without a declared query container on an ancestor, there is nothing for the container query to measure.
22rem (352px) is a perfectly ordinary component width; the rule not matching points at a missing container, not an unreachable threshold.
Container queries stand on their own; they are not nested inside media queries.
!important changes precedence among declarations that already apply; it does nothing for a query that never matches in the first place.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Container queries need an explicit query container (container-type, and usually container-name) declared on an ancestor. Forgetting it is the single most common reason a container query silently matches nothing.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate wants the whole page shell to restyle whenever any tile anywhere on the page contains a critical alert, so they write a :has() selector rooted at the page body. Using this lecture's guidance on scoping :has(), explain what is expensive about that selector and how you would rewrite the intent more narrowly.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A selector rooted at the page body has to be re-checked against a huge, constantly changing subtree: essentially any DOM mutation anywhere on the page could flip whether the body matches, so the browser re-evaluates it far more often and over far more elements than a selector scoped to one component. The narrower fix is to scope :has() to the smallest useful root, for example a single tile testing for a critical-alert descendant, or, if the shell genuinely needs to react, set an explicit state (like a class or an aria attribute) from wherever the critical alert is decided and style off that attribute instead of re-deriving it with a page-wide :has().

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

steps: **Shell:** viewport 1024 px falls between 700 and 1100, so the navigation is a **rail** (a media query).
**Main tile area:** the container is 640 px wide, so 2 columns at 15rem minimum (intrinsic grid).
**A tile in the main area:** its container is about 312 px, below 22rem (352 px), so it's **compact** (stacked). This comes from a container query.
**The same tile in the rail:** 260 px, so also compact.
**User has `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`:** the sparkline animations are disabled (a media query, s10).

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 9.3: Fluid Type and Space with clamp()

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Derive a `clamp()` value that scales linearly between two sizes across two viewport widths. (objective o2)
2. Build a fluid type and spacing scale in custom properties. (objective o2)
3. Keep fluid type accessible: it respects user font settings and zoom. (objective o2)

terms.definition: A value that follows `preferred` but never goes below `min` or above `max`.
Font sizes that interpolate smoothly between a small and a large screen, instead of jumping at breakpoints.
Sizes generated by repeatedly multiplying by a ratio (such as 1.2 or 1.25).
Relative to the root font size, which follows the user's browser setting (often 16 px).
`--step-1: …;`, a variable that cascades and can be read by any component.

contentBlocks.content:
### The math

To go from **18 px at 320 px wide** to **24 px at 1280 px wide**:

1. Slope = (24 − 18) / (1280 − 320) = 0.00625 px per px of viewport, which is **0.625vw**.
2. Intercept = 18 − 0.00625 × 320 = 16 px, which is **1rem** at a 16 px root.
3. Result: `clamp(1.125rem, 1rem + 0.625vw, 1.5rem)`.

The `rem` part matters for accessibility. Pure `vw` values don't grow when the user increases their default font size, and they barely respond to browser zoom. That can fail WCAG "Resize text." A rem intercept keeps the user in control.
### A scale in custom properties

Components use `font-size: var(--step-1)` and `gap: var(--space-m)`. They never contain raw numbers. This connects directly to tokens in s11. Spacing that scales together with type keeps the visual rhythm consistent (s12).

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Animation (s09-m3): Fluid vs stepped type. Production brief: A 20-second screen recording of a browser window being resized from 320 px to 1600 px. The top half shows a heading with breakpoint-based sizes jumping at 768 and 1024 px. The bottom half shows the clamp() version growing smoothly and stopping at its maximum. A small overlay shows the computed font size in px as the window changes.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: the same clamp math produces 18px at a 320px viewport and 24px at a 1280px viewport, and flattens out exactly at those two anchors. Edit minSize/maxSize below to build your own type step, then predict the four sizes before running.

contentBlocks.caption: The clamp at four viewport widths from the worked example above. Predict each line before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: fluid scales
contentBlocks.content:
- **Pure `vw` font sizes**, which ignore the user's font settings and zoom.
- **Min and max swapped**, or a preferred value that never reaches the max within the intended range.
- **Raw pixel values in components** instead of scale tokens.
- **Fluid type with fixed spacing**, which breaks the rhythm at the extremes.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 9.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Slope = Δsize / Δviewport, expressed in `vw`. Intercept = the size at the minimum viewport minus the slope × that viewport, in `rem`.
- Put the scale in custom properties, and let components consume steps rather than numbers.

interactionSequence.prompt: Why write a clamp with a rem minimum, a rem-plus-vw preferred value, and a rem maximum, instead of the same visual sizes written entirely in px and vw?
options: The rem parts follow the reader's font-size setting and respond correctly to zoom, while a pure vw or px value ignores both
rem values render faster in the browser
px is not valid inside clamp()
A vw-only preferred value is invalid syntax

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A rem-based min, max, and intercept keep text responsive to the user's own font-size setting and to zoom; a pure vw or px value does not.
There is no rendering-speed difference between the two units here.
px is valid inside clamp(); it is just the wrong choice for text that needs to respect user settings.
A vw-only preferred value is valid CSS; it is simply the wrong choice here, and it still would not respond to font-size changes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Pure vw (or px) values don't grow when the reader increases their default font size and barely respond to browser zoom, which can fail the WCAG "resize text" requirement. A rem-based min, max, and intercept keeps the reader in control.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A fluid clamp is written with its min and max arguments swapped, so the smaller bound is listed where the maximum should be. What goes wrong?
options: The preferred value can never reach the intended maximum within the intended viewport range, since the smaller bound now clamps it down early
Nothing; clamp() automatically sorts its three arguments by size
The browser throws a CSS parse error and ignores the whole declaration
The value becomes fixed at exactly the swapped maximum on every viewport

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. clamp() takes its arguments positionally as minimum, preferred, maximum; swapping min and max changes which bound the preferred value gets clamped against, and here it clamps the growth down almost immediately.
clamp() does not reorder its arguments; whichever value is listed first is always treated as the minimum.
This isn't a syntax error, it's valid CSS that just produces the wrong visual result, which is what makes it a genuinely common mistake.
The preferred expression still varies with viewport width; it is the min and max bounds around it that are wrong.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: clamp() is positional: minimum, preferred, maximum. Swapping min and max is one of this lecture's named common errors, and unlike most CSS mistakes it produces no error at all, just a value that looks flat or backwards.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A dashboard uses a fluid clamp for every font size but keeps padding and gap as fixed pixel values. What breaks at the extremes of the viewport range?
options: The visual rhythm: spacing that no longer scales with the type around it looks cramped at large sizes and disproportionately loose at small ones
Nothing; spacing and type sizing are unrelated
The fixed spacing values become invalid CSS once type is fluid
The page stops being responsive at all

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. This is a named common error: fluid type paired with fixed spacing breaks the rhythm exactly at the smallest and largest ends of the range.
They are visually related: spacing that doesn't scale alongside type reads as inconsistent once type is fluid and spacing isn't.
Fixed pixel values stay perfectly valid CSS; the problem is visual, not syntactic.
The page is still responsive; only the relationship between type and spacing looks wrong at the extremes.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Put spacing in the same kind of scale as type, generated the same way and stored in custom properties, so the whole rhythm grows and shrinks together instead of just the words.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 7 required that a page reflow correctly at 400% browser zoom and covers the WCAG "resize text" requirement in depth. This lecture's clamp math uses a rem intercept specifically so fluid type keeps responding to the reader's font-size setting. Explain the connection: why would a fluid type scale built entirely from px and vw values risk failing Section 7's zoom requirement, even though it still looks fluid while resizing the browser window at 100%?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: vw units are a percentage of the viewport's width, and px is an absolute unit; neither one is defined relative to the reader's root font size, so increasing the browser's default font size or zooming, which effectively scales the root font size in most browsers, leaves a pure px or vw value completely unchanged. A page can look perfectly fluid while resizing the window and still fail Section 7's zoom requirement, because the text itself never grows when the reader asks it to. Anchoring the clamp's intercept in rem ties the minimum size to the root font size, so it grows exactly the way Section 7's "resize text" check expects.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Checking a clamp at four widths
workedExamples.problem:
`clamp(1.125rem, 1rem + 0.625vw, 1.5rem)`:

| Viewport | Preferred = 16 + 0.00625 × vw | Clamped result |
|---|---|---|
| 320 | 18.0 px | 18.0 px (the minimum) |
| 768 | 20.8 px | 20.8 px |
| 1280 | 24.0 px | 24.0 px (the maximum) |
| 1600 | 26.0 px | **24.0 px** (clamped) |
steps: **320 px:** preferred = 16 + 0.00625 × 320 = 18.0 px, already at the minimum, so the clamped result is **18.0 px**.
**768 px:** preferred = 16 + 0.00625 × 768 = 20.8 px, inside the range, so the clamped result is **20.8 px**.
**1280 px:** preferred = 16 + 0.00625 × 1280 = 24.0 px, exactly the maximum, so the clamped result is **24.0 px**.
**1600 px:** preferred = 16 + 0.00625 × 1600 = 26.0 px, past the maximum, so it clamps down to **24.0 px**.
workedExamples.conclusion: Linear between the two anchors and flat outside them. Runnable Example R2 reproduces this.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Derive the clamp() preferred value for a size that grows from 18px at a 320px viewport to 24px at a 1280px viewport.

Section 7 requires layouts to reflow correctly at 400% zoom and text to respect the reader's font-size setting. Why does a clamp built from rem and vw satisfy that, while one built from px and vw alone would not?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 9.4: The Cascade, on Purpose

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Compute specificity, including `:is()`, `:not()`, `:has()` (they take their most specific argument) and `:where()` (always zero). (objective o5)
2. Explain how cascade layers are ordered, and how `!important` reverses that order. (objective o5)
3. Design a layer architecture for a mid-sized app. (objective o5)

terms.definition: A triple (ids, classes/attributes/pseudo-classes, types/pseudo-elements) compared **left to right**, not as a number.
`@layer name { … }`. Declared layer order decides precedence *before* specificity is considered.
Set with `@layer reset, tokens, base, components, utilities;`. For normal declarations, later layers win, and **unlayered styles beat all layers**.
Reversed: important declarations in *earlier* layers win, and layered important beats unlayered important.
Wraps selectors with **zero** specificity, which makes it ideal for resets and defaults.

contentBlocks.content:
### How the cascade decides (for author styles)

1. **Importance:** `!important` declarations beat normal ones.
2. **Layers:** for normal declarations, unlayered > later layers > earlier layers. For important declarations, the order is reversed.
3. **Specificity:** compared as a triple.
4. **Order of appearance:** the last one wins.

Layers are decided **before** specificity. That's why they solve specificity wars structurally. Specificity problems aren't fixed by `!important` or by adding more selectors (misconception `css-layout-architecture.m1`). Each escalation invites the next, while a layer order states the intent once: "utilities always beat components."

### Specificity is a triple

`.a.b.c.d.e.f.g.h.i.j.k` (eleven classes) is `(0, 11, 0)`. `#status` is `(1, 0, 0)`. The id wins because the first column is compared first. There's no "carry," and specificity isn't a base-10 number.
### An architecture for the dashboard

Third-party CSS goes into its own early layer (`@import url(vendor.css) layer(vendor);`) so your components beat it without selector escalation. Resets and base styles use `:where()` so they have zero specificity.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s09-m4): The cascade funnel. A vertical funnel with stages: "Importance" → "Layers (reset < tokens < base < components < utilities < unlayered)" → "Specificity (a, b, c)" → "Order". Two example declarations fall through it: .card .title { color: slate } (components, 0-2-0) and .text-green { color: green } (utilities, 0-1-0). The utility wins at the Layers stage and never reaches Specificity. A mirrored side panel shows the reversed layer order for !important.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: layers are decided before specificity, so a later layer with lower specificity still wins. Edit the rows below (change a layer, a specificity, or add a third row) and predict the winner before running.

contentBlocks.caption: Specificity compared column by column, plus the wrong base-10 total it is sometimes mistaken for. Predict both lines before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: the cascade
contentBlocks.content:
- **Treating specificity as a number** (thinking eleven classes beat an id).
- **`!important` wars.**
- **Leaving legacy or third-party CSS unlayered**, where it silently beats everything.
- **Forgetting that `!important` reverses layer order.**
- **High-specificity resets.** Wrap them in `:where()`.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 9.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Importance → layers → specificity (a triple) → order.
- Declare the layer order once, and use `:where()` for zero-specificity defaults.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Eleven classes vs one id.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
blue (from :is(#alert-banner, .tile) span)
```

**Why intuition fails.** Two instincts pull the wrong way. The first is that eleven classes "add up" past one id, but specificity is compared column by column, so any id beats any number of classes. The second is that `:is()` averages or ignores its arguments. In fact it takes the **most specific** argument, `#alert-banner` (1,0,0), plus the `span` (0,0,1), which gives (1,0,1). That beats the plain id. Escalating selectors like this is how specificity wars start (misconception `css-layout-architecture.m1`). Cascade layers make these comparisons unnecessary.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Two instincts pull the wrong way. The first is that eleven classes "add up" past one id, but specificity is compared column by column, so any id beats any number of classes. The second is that `:is()` averages or ignores its arguments. In fact it takes the **most specific** argument, `#alert-banner` (1,0,0), plus the `span` (0,0,1), which gives (1,0,1). That beats the plain id. Escalating selectors like this is how specificity wars start (misconception `css-layout-architecture.m1`). Cascade layers make these comparisons unnecessary.
hints: Compare the specificity triples column by column, left to right, before you look at :is().
:is() takes the MOST specific of its comma-separated arguments, not an average and not the first one.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: **The unlayered legacy rule.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
blue
```

**Why intuition fails.** `a { color: blue }` has the lowest specificity in the list, so it "should" lose. Layer precedence is decided **before** specificity, and styles outside any layer beat every layer. A forgotten unlayered legacy stylesheet will override the whole design system. The fix is structural, not another selector: import the legacy CSS into an early layer, `@import url(legacy.css) layer(legacy);`.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: `a { color: blue }` has the lowest specificity in the list, so it "should" lose. Layer precedence is decided **before** specificity, and styles outside any layer beat every layer. A forgotten unlayered legacy stylesheet will override the whole design system. The fix is structural, not another selector: import the legacy CSS into an early layer, `@import url(legacy.css) layer(legacy);`.
hints: Layers are decided before specificity is even consulted.
An unlayered declaration ranks after every named layer, for normal declarations.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: A utility class in the utilities layer keeps losing to a more specific selector in the components layer. A teammate wants to add !important to the utility. What is the actual structural fix?
options: Make sure the layer order is declared with utilities after components, and that both rules are actually inside their layers, since layers decide before specificity is even considered
Add !important to the utility
Add another class to the utility selector
Give the utility an id selector instead of a class

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Declared layer order settles this before specificity is ever compared.
That starts an escalation, and inside layers !important also reverses the layer order, which can cause a new surprise later.
More selectors just moves the same war to a different rule.
That is escalation in its most extreme form, and it will itself eventually lose to some other id somewhere.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Cascade layers solve specificity wars structurally: declared layer order is checked before specificity, so the fix is the layer order, never another selector or !important.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Layer order is reset, tokens, base, components, utilities. A declaration in reset carries !important, and a declaration in utilities also carries !important, both matching the same element. Which one wins?
options: The one in reset, because !important reverses the normal layer order, so an earlier layer beats a later one
The one in utilities, because utilities is declared last, the same rule as for normal declarations
Neither; two !important declarations always tie and fall through to source order alone
The one in utilities, because !important simply beats layers entirely, regardless of which layer either side is in

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. For important declarations the layer order is reversed: earlier layers win.
That is the rule for normal declarations; !important flips it.
Layer order still applies to important declarations, it is just reversed; it is not a tie.
!important changes how layers are ranked against each other; it does not remove layers from the decision.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Importance is decided first, but among important declarations, layer order is reversed: earlier layers win. That is why a reset layer's !important can beat a utilities layer's !important.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank the four stages the cascade checks, in the order the browser actually applies them, first to last.
options: Specificity, compared as a triple
Layers (for normal declarations: unlayered, then later layers, then earlier layers)
Order of appearance: the last declaration wins
Importance: any !important declaration beats any normal one

optionFeedback.feedback: Specificity is checked third, only once importance and layers have already settled the question or left a tie.
Layers are checked second, right after importance and before specificity is even considered.
Source order is the final tiebreaker, used only when everything else ties exactly.
Importance is checked first: any !important declaration beats any normal one, before layers are even looked at.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Importance, then layers, then specificity as a triple, then source order. Each stage only gets consulted if the previous one left a tie, which is why checking the layer comes before counting any selector's classes or ids.
hints: Which stage would make every other stage irrelevant if it decided the question outright?
Layers are decided before specificity is even considered.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: After importing a third-party date-picker library's CSS, its buttons visually override your own component library's button styles, and a teammate proposes adding !important everywhere in your component layer. Recommend a structural fix, and explain why it belongs to the design system's layer architecture rather than to any individual component's CSS.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Import the library's CSS into its own early layer, declared before components in the layer order, so your component styles win by layer order alone, with no !important and no selector escalation anywhere. This belongs at the level of the design system's layer architecture, not inside any one component's stylesheet, because the decision, that vendor CSS always loses to your own components, is a rule about the whole system that should be stated once, in the shared layer order, rather than re-fought component by component every time a new third-party stylesheet gets imported.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Predicting the winner
workedExamples.problem:
Layer order: `reset, tokens, base, components, utilities`. Element: the title in a tile with `class="title text-green"`.

| # | Declaration | Layer | Specificity |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | `.tile .title { color: slate }` | components | (0,2,0) |
| 2 | `.text-green { color: green }` | utilities | (0,1,0) |
| 3 | `h2 { color: black }` | *unlayered* | (0,0,1) |
steps: No `!important` anywhere.
Layers: #3 is unlayered, so it beats both layered declarations. **Winner: black.**
Lesson: unlayered legacy CSS will override your whole layered system. Put it in a layer (`@layer legacy`) early in the order.
workedExamples.conclusion: Always check the layer before counting selectors. Exercise s09-e2 builds this resolver.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 9.5: Choosing a Styling Approach

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Compare utility-first CSS, CSS Modules, zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, and runtime CSS-in-JS on runtime cost, colocation, and team scaling. (objective o4)
2. Make a reasoned recommendation for a specific team and product. (objective o4)

terms.definition: Small single-purpose classes composed in markup (Tailwind). CSS is generated at build time from the classes you use.
`.css` files whose class names are locally scoped by the build step.
Styles written in JS or TS, extracted to static CSS at build time (vanilla-extract, Linaria, Panda).
Styles serialized and injected by a library while components render (for example styled-components, Emotion). React added `useInsertionEffect` specifically for these libraries.
Styles live next to the component that uses them.
Values that change at runtime, handled with CSS custom properties set on elements, or by generating styles at runtime.

contentBlocks.content:
### It isn't a syntax preference

The choice affects performance, tooling, and how a large team works (misconception `css-layout-architecture.m3`):

| | Utilities | CSS Modules | Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS | Runtime CSS-in-JS |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Runtime style work | none | none | none | serialize + hash + inject during render |
| Dynamic values | custom properties / conditional classes | custom properties | custom properties / variants | arbitrary JS (at a runtime cost) |
| Colocation | in markup | adjacent file | same file, typed | same file |
| Type safety for tokens | via config/plugins | limited | strong (TS) | varies |
| Team scaling risk | long class strings, and design drift if unconstrained | naming drift across modules | build tooling complexity | runtime cost, SSR setup, concurrent-rendering caveats |
| Server Components (s3) | works | works | works | often needs client components |

### How dynamic values work without runtime CSS-in-JS

A moisture tile's bar color depends on the reading. Instead of generating a new CSS rule for each value, set a **custom property** on the element and keep the CSS static:

.bar { background: linear-gradient(to right, var(--color-data) var(--level), var(--color-track) 0); }
.tile[data-state="dry"] .bar { --color-data: var(--color-danger); }

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s09-m5): Where style work happens. Four columns (utilities, CSS Modules, zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, runtime CSS-in-JS) on a build-time → runtime axis. For the first three, the arrow ends at "static .css file" before the browser. For runtime CSS-in-JS, an arrow continues into the browser's main thread labelled "serialize → hash → insert rule, per render." A shared lane shows dynamic values flowing through CSS custom properties for the static approaches.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: a runtime CSS-in-JS library serializes and inserts a rule on every render with a new prop combination, while a static approach never touches the browser at runtime. Edit the renders list below, then predict insertedRules before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: choosing an approach
contentBlocks.content:
- **Deciding by syntax taste alone.**
- **Runtime-generated rules for every dynamic value.** Use custom properties.
- **Mixing three approaches with no layer order**, so they fight in the cascade.
- **Utilities with unlimited arbitrary values**, which lets design drift in.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 9.5 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Compare approaches on runtime cost, colocation, type safety, rendering strategy, and team scale.
- Keep CSS static, and put dynamic values in custom properties.

interactionSequence.prompt: A colleague says choosing between a utility-first library and runtime CSS-in-JS is just a syntax preference, so the team should pick whichever they like. What is the strongest reply?
options: They differ in runtime cost during render, Server Component compatibility, token type safety, and how they scale across a team, so the decision should rest on those, not on syntax taste
Agree; both eventually produce CSS, so it really is just a matter of preference
The utility-first library is always the better choice
Runtime CSS-in-JS is always the better choice, since its styles are colocated with the component

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. These are engineering trade-offs with real runtime and tooling consequences, not a style preference.
Runtime CSS-in-JS does real work, serializing and inserting rules, while the component renders; that is not the same as a build-time approach.
It depends on the team, its constraints, and how strictly it needs typed tokens; there is no universal winner.
Colocation is available without a runtime cost too, through CSS Modules or zero-runtime CSS-in-JS.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The choice affects real things: runtime cost, Server Component compatibility, token type safety, and how a large team scales its CSS. None of that is a matter of taste.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A moisture tile's bar-fill color needs to change based on the current reading, without adding runtime CSS-in-JS. How should that dynamic value reach the CSS?
options: Set a custom property on the element from JavaScript, and reference it from static CSS that never changes
Generate a brand-new CSS rule for every possible reading value at runtime
Inline every property the bar needs directly in the style attribute, recomputing all of them on every render
Write one CSS class per possible reading value ahead of time, covering every percentage from 0 to 100

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A custom property carries the dynamic value into otherwise-static CSS, with no rule generation or serialization at runtime.
That is exactly the work runtime CSS-in-JS does, and exactly the runtime cost this pattern avoids.
Custom properties let you keep the CSS static and only touch the one value that actually changes, rather than recomputing everything inline.
A hand-written rule per percentage point does not scale and still cannot express an exact, arbitrary reading.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Custom properties set on an element are how static CSS approaches, utilities, CSS Modules, and zero-runtime CSS-in-JS, express a value that changes at runtime, without generating a new rule or paying a serialization cost.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team of five engineers building a TypeScript and React app that is moving to Server Components has strict token usage and INP problems on low-end tablets. Which conclusion follows from this lecture's reasoning?
options: Rule out runtime CSS-in-JS first, since it adds render-time work and complicates Server Components, then choose between the remaining approaches based on token safety and team habits
Runtime CSS-in-JS is still the right call, since its component-scoped styles reduce naming conflicts
The INP problems are unrelated to the styling approach and should be solved separately
Any of the four approaches works equally well here, since they all eventually produce CSS

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Given INP problems and a move to Server Components, runtime CSS-in-JS is the first thing to rule out; the remaining choice comes down to token safety and team scale.
Naming conflicts are solved by CSS Modules or utilities too, without paying a render-time serialization cost that a team already fighting INP cannot afford.
Runtime CSS-in-JS's serialize-and-insert work happens on the very main thread INP measures; the styling approach is directly relevant here.
The four approaches differ specifically on the axes, runtime cost, Server Component support, token safety, that this team's constraints are stressing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The recommendation follows from the team's actual constraints, in order: rule out what conflicts with Server Components and adds render-time cost, then decide between the remaining options using token safety and team scale.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 6 explained that work done on the main thread during rendering directly lengthens the time before the browser can respond to the next interaction, which is what INP measures. Explain, in those terms, why runtime CSS-in-JS's serialize-hash-insert cycle is specifically an INP risk on a low-end tablet, in a way that a zero-runtime CSS-in-JS library is not.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Runtime CSS-in-JS serializes a component's styles, hashes them, and inserts a new stylesheet rule while that component is rendering; all of that is JavaScript work happening on the same main thread that also has to handle the next tap or scroll, so on a low-end tablet it directly adds to the time before the page can respond, which is exactly what INP measures. A zero-runtime library does that same serialization once, at build time on a developer's machine, so by the time the component renders in the browser there is nothing left to compute: the CSS is already a static file, and the main thread only has to apply it, not generate it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: A recommendation for the dashboard team
workedExamples.problem: **Context:** five frontend engineers, one designer, a TypeScript + React app moving to Server Components, strict token usage, and INP problems on low-end tablets.
steps: **Rule out runtime CSS-in-JS:** it adds render-time work on the main thread (INP, s6) and complicates Server Components.

**Utilities vs zero-runtime:** the team wants typed tokens and component variants that mirror the design system (s11). Zero-runtime CSS-in-JS gives compile-time errors for unknown tokens. Utilities are faster to write, but need lint rules to prevent arbitrary values.

**Recommendation:** zero-runtime CSS-in-JS for components and variants (typed tokens), plus a small set of layered utility classes for layout and spacing, with dynamic values through custom properties. Revisit the decision if build times become a problem.
workedExamples.conclusion: The recommendation came from runtime cost, the rendering strategy, token safety, and team size, not from which syntax feels nicer.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Where should a value that changes at runtime live, if you want to avoid generating new CSS rules on every render?
Section 6 ties INP to work done on the main thread during rendering. Why does that make runtime CSS-in-JS a bigger INP risk than a zero-runtime approach?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: The Field Dashboard

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. The engine can't render CSS, so the layout work (grid, subgrid, container queries, :has()) is built and reviewed in the Practical Activity below, not checked automatically. The four graded challenges and the two test-suite challenges implement the rules the browser applies, specificity, the cascade with layers, fluid clamp() math, and layout decisions by container vs viewport, so you can predict what the browser will do before you open DevTools.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenges 1, 3, and 4 have no scaffolding: the whole program is yours. Challenge 2 gives you a small `d(...)` declaration helper and the layer order, and leaves the importance, layer, specificity, and order comparison to you. The two test-suite challenges turn it around: the fluidClamp challenge gives you correct code and asks you to write the tests that prove it; the media-query matcher challenge gives you a correct test suite and asks you to fix broken code until it passes.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your fluidClamp tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the fluidClamp challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "The Field Dashboard."** Expected time is 10–12 hours.

1. **Dashboard layout:** a shell with named grid areas; a tile grid with `auto-fit`/`minmax`; **subgrid** aligning title, sparkline, reading, and footer across tiles; **container queries** for the tile variants (compact, row, wide) and for a table that becomes stacked rows in narrow panels. **No viewport media queries** in components or the tile grid. The shell navigation and user preferences may use media queries, and you should document which ones and why (Lecture 9.2's table). *(o1)*
2. **Fluid scale:** at least 5 type steps and 5 space steps generated with your `fluidClamp`, in custom properties, and used everywhere. Include a screenshot at 320, 768, and 1440 px, and at 200% browser zoom. *(o2)*
3. **`:has()` card:** the tile restyles itself when it contains a critical alert, when it has a field photo, and when its form row has an invalid input, with no JS-added classes. *(o3)*
4. **Three styling approaches:** the tile, the button, and the alert styled with (a) utilities, (b) CSS Modules, and (c) a zero-runtime CSS-in-JS library. Write a two-page recommendation for the team in Lecture 9.5 (runtime cost, colocation, token safety, RSC compatibility, team scale), including a Performance-panel comparison with an equivalent runtime CSS-in-JS version if you can build one. *(o4)*
5. **Cascade-layers architecture:** `@layer reset, vendor, tokens, base, components, utilities;` with `:where()` resets, a vendor stylesheet imported into its layer, and a one-page architecture doc explaining the order, where new CSS goes, and the "no `!important` outside utilities" rule. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for the Field Dashboard (100 points)
rows: Aligned tiles, correct container/viewport split, documented media-query exceptions, DOM order = visual order.
Correct `rem` + `vw` clamps, used consistently, and it zooms properly.
Three content-driven variants with scoped selectors.
A fair comparison with evidence and a context-specific recommendation.
Clear order, vendor layered, zero-specificity resets, and rules for contributors.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 4 (independent): compute and compare specificity

Implement `specificity(selector)` that returns `[ids, classes, types]` for one complex selector, and `compareSpecificity(x, y)` (negative, 0, or positive).

Support: `#id`, `.class`, `[attr…]`, pseudo-classes (count as classes), `::pseudo-elements` (count as types), type selectors, `*` (zero), combinators, `:where(…)` (zero), `:is(…)`, `:not(…)`, and `:has(…)` (each takes the specificity of its most specific comma-separated argument). Other functional pseudo-classes like `:nth-child(2n)` count as one class.

This one has no scaffolding: both functions are yours.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: A single left-to-right scan with a cursor is enough. Each leading character tells you what kind of token comes next.
For functional pseudo-classes, find the matching `)` while counting nested parentheses.
`:is()`'s arguments are a selector list. Compute each argument recursively and keep the maximum.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 4 (scaffolded): a cascade resolver with layers and !important

Implement `resolveCascade(declarations, layerOrder)` that returns the winning `value`. Each declaration is `{ value, layer, important, specificity, order }`, where `layer` is `null` for unlayered. Precedence: importance → layers (normal: unlayered > later > earlier; important: reversed, so earlier > later > unlayered) → specificity (triple) → later `order`. Return `undefined` when there are no declarations.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
**The plausible wrong answer:**

```js
function resolveCascade(declarations, layerOrder) {
  const sorted = [...declarations].sort((x, y) =>
    (Number(y.important) - Number(x.important))
    || (y.specificity[0] - x.specificity[0]) || (y.specificity[1] - x.specificity[1]) || (y.specificity[2] - x.specificity[2])
    || (y.order - x.order)); // layers treated as mere grouping: "more selectors win"
  return sorted.length ? sorted[0].value : undefined;
}
```

The starter (specificity and order only) models the world where specificity is the only lever, which is why people reach for `!important` and longer selectors. It reveals **`css-layout-architecture.m1`**.

cases.name: typical: a later layer beats higher specificity

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Write the comparison as a chain of `||`, one level of the cascade per link.
Give unlayered declarations a rank *after* the last layer.
For important declarations, negating the rank reverses the order.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 4 (independent): decide by container or by viewport

Implement `planDashboard({ viewportWidth, panels })`, where `panels` maps panel ids to their container widths (px). Return `{ shell, panels }`. `shell` is decided by the **viewport** (< 700 → `'bottom-nav'`, < 1100 → `'rail'`, otherwise `'sidebar'`). Each panel's `variant` (< 320 → `'compact'`, < 560 → `'row'`, otherwise `'wide'`) and `columns` (auto-fit with a 240 px minimum and 16 px gap, at least 1) are decided by its **container** width.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

cases.name: typical: barn tablet with the alerts rail open

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Ask of each decision: "Who knows the answer, the page or the slot this component sits in?"
The column formula from Lecture 9.1: floor((width + gap) / (min + gap)), at least 1.
"< 320 is compact" means exactly 320 is already `row`.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 4 (independent): what each styling approach does at runtime

Implement `styleRuntimeWork(approach, renders)` that models the style work done **in the browser at runtime** for a component whose dynamic props across renders are given in `renders` (an array of plain objects). Return `{ serializations, insertedRules, dynamicVia }`.

Rules: for `'utilities'`, `'css-modules'`, and `'zero-runtime'`, both counts are 0 and `dynamicVia` is `'custom-properties'`. For `'runtime-css-in-js'`, every render serializes its style (one serialization per render), each **distinct** prop combination inserts one new rule (key by `JSON.stringify` with sorted keys), and `dynamicVia` is `'generated-rules'`. Unknown approaches throw `Error('Unknown approach: <name>')`.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

cases.name: typical: a moisture tile re-rendering 5 times at runtime
boundary: key order does not create new rules

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Which approaches produce all their CSS during the build?
A runtime library can't know the styles until the component renders with its props.
Normalize the key order before counting distinct combinations.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working fluidClamp, you write the tests

`fluidClamp({ minSize, maxSize, minViewport, maxViewport, root })` (all in px, `root` defaults to 16) returns a `clamp()` string whose preferred value is `<intercept>rem + <slope>vw`, with numbers rounded to 4 decimal places and trailing zeros removed. It's correct. Write tests that pin down the exact output and catch the three hidden wrong versions. Use Lecture 9.3's worked numbers. Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **four** tests). Then confirm your suite catches each of the three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks the exact worked-example string (18 to 24px across 320 to 1280), a second exact string with a non-round rounding case, that a custom root size is respected, and a general shape check with a regular expression. Wrong version 1 outputs px instead of rem, ignoring the user's font size; wrong version 2 anchors the intercept at the maximum viewport with the wrong sign; wrong version 3 skips the 4-decimal rounding entirely. A suite that only checks the function returns a string beginning with "clamp(" catches none of the three.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests here pin down the exact numeric contract from Lecture 9.3's worked example, not just "it returns a clamp string."
hints: Start with Lecture 9.3's own worked numbers: 18px to 24px across 320 to 1280px should produce exactly clamp(1.125rem, 1rem + 0.625vw, 1.5rem).
Write a second exact-string test with different numbers (16 to 20px across 375 to 1440px) to catch a rounding bug.
Pass a root other than 16 and check the output actually changes, to make sure your suite would catch a version that hardcodes the default root.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken media-query matcher, make the tests pass

The design-review tool previews the page shell at different widths. `matchesMedia(query, viewportPx)` supports `(min-width: X)` and `(max-width: X)` in `px`, `em`, or `rem` (in media queries, `em` and `rem` use the browser's initial font size, 16 px), joined with ` and `. It has three bugs. Fix it.

codeExercise.solutionNote: `min-width` and `max-width` are inclusive. Units matter (`40em` is 640 px in a media query). Every clause joined by `and` has to match, not just the first one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three bugs come from the same shortcut: checking only the first clause instead of every clause, and treating the boundary and the unit conversion as afterthoughts.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. Does the broken matcher check every clause joined by "and", or just the first one?
Is min-width: 700px matched at exactly 700, or does the current code require strictly greater?
How should em and rem units convert to px inside a media query?

interactionSequence.prompt: When your Field Dashboard build is done, paste a link or summary and answer: which layout, in your build, needed a container query and would have been impossible to get right with a media query alone?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong reports name a specific component (a tile, a table, a card) that sits in more than one slot on the page, name the exact width at which its variant changes, and explain why the page-level viewport width could not have told the two slots apart. Check your build against the rubric table above before you submit.

learningExperiences.title: In the Wild: Refactor a Real Stylesheet's Cascade

contentBlocks.content: This exercise happens on a real stylesheet, not inside the course engine. The 20 minutes here cover planning and the first pass; opening a PR and, optionally, giving a short talk take longer. Nothing here is graded or gates your progress. It builds evidence you will reuse in the Section 13 portfolio.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A stylesheet you maintain, or an open-source project's, that leans on !important or long selectors to win conflicts.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Count a real stylesheet's specificity escalation, migrate it to cascade layers in stages, and prove there is no visual regression.
instructions: Pick a stylesheet you maintain (or an open-source project's) that uses `!important` or long selectors to win conflicts. Count the `!important`s and the selectors with an id or three or more classes.

Introduce cascade layers: move resets into `:where()` inside a `reset` layer, put third-party CSS into a `vendor` layer, and components into `components`. Remove every `!important` that the layer order now makes unnecessary.
Open a PR (or share it internally) with the before/after counts and a screenshot diff showing no visual change.
**Stretch:** give a 10-minute talk at a CSS meetup or team demo called "Deleting !important with @layer."
materialsOrPrerequisites: A stylesheet you maintain, or a cloned open-source project, with its build tooling working locally.
A way to take a visual diff or before/after screenshots.
A place to open a PR or share the change internally.
reflectionPrompts: How many !important declarations and high-specificity selectors did you count before you started, and how many were left after?
Which layer did the hardest decision belong in, and why was it not obvious at first?
Did your before/after screenshot diff show any unintended visual change, and if so, what did that reveal about a selector you thought was safe to remove?

selfAssessmentCriteria: I counted the !important declarations and high-specificity selectors before and after, not just estimated them.
I put third-party CSS into its own early layer instead of leaving it unlayered.
I saved the PR link and the before/after counts for my Section 13 portfolio.

learningExperiences.title: Review: Retrieval, Transfer, and the Section 9 Quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Close the section in three moves

1. **Retrieve** without looking back: answer the cues below from memory.
2. **Transfer** the container/viewport and cascade-layer ideas to two systems with nothing to do with farms: an airport wayfinding kiosk and a newspaper's legacy templates.
3. **Prove it** in the Section 9 quiz and the cumulative mastery check for css-layout-architecture, which lives here because this is the section that teaches it.

contentBlocks.title: Everything this section reaches back to
contentBlocks.content: This section leans on Section 2's rendering pipeline (fixed heights to fake alignment cost a forced layout, so subgrid is the CSS-only fix), Section 6's reserved space and main-thread runtime cost (CLS and INP, which is exactly what a runtime CSS-in-JS library spends), and Section 7's zoom, reflow, and resize-text requirements (why a fluid clamp needs a rem intercept). One retrieval item below brings each of those back.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before the quiz: which idea from this section would you least want to explain live in an interview, specificity as a triple, container versus viewport, the clamp() derivation, cascade layers and !important, or the styling-approach comparison? Name it and write one sentence on what feels shaky.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Naming the shaky part precisely is what makes the next review useful. Re-read that lecture's summary and its worked examples before you open the quiz.

transferExercises.context: Airport wayfinding kiosks and a mobile companion app
transferExercises.scenario: The same "gate status" card appears on 55-inch portrait kiosks, a narrow sidebar in the airline's web app, and phones.
transferExercises.task: Plan which parts of the card respond to its container and which to the viewport, device, or user preferences (for example a contrast preference). Decide how the type scale should behave from phone to kiosk, and how you would layer the airline's brand CSS over a shared component library without a specificity war.

Assigns page-level chrome and user preferences, such as a high-contrast mode, to media queries rather than container queries.

Chooses a container-relative unit for type that scales with the card's own size on the kiosk, rather than a viewport-relative unit that cannot tell a 55-inch kiosk from a phone sidebar of the same code.
Puts the airline's brand CSS into its own layer, ordered relative to the shared component library's layers, instead of reaching for higher specificity or !important.

Write the one-paragraph explanation you would give the editors about why their embeds will now look consistent.
successCriteria: Sequences the migration so a reset and vendor layer land first (with embeds' CSS imported into an early, named layer), before any !important is removed from the site's own components.
Describes a concrete way to prove no visual regression at each stage, such as a before/after screenshot diff, rather than just asserting the migration is safe.

Explains to editors, in one paragraph and without jargon, that embeds now sit in their own early layer, so the site's own components always win without needing to fight each embed's specificity individually.

sections.title: Motion and Interaction
sections.description: Build motion that earns its cost and respects the person watching it: choosing **compositor-only properties**, writing a **spring integrator from scratch** (mass, stiffness, damping), **choreographing** staggered lists and shared-element **view transitions**, driving a **gesture-based bottom sheet** with velocity and snap points, and running a **motion audit** that classifies every animation as functional or decorative. Examples come from a fitness and workout tracker: exercise lists, a rest-timer bottom sheet, workout detail pages, progress rings, and a streak celebration.

learningObjectives.description: Implement a mass/stiffness/damping spring integrator that drives a draggable element with release momentum
Build a shared-element page transition with the View Transitions API
Build a staggered enter/exit list in pure CSS and in WAAPI, keeping animations on the compositor
Build a gesture-driven bottom sheet with snap points and velocity-based dismissal that respects reduced motion
Audit a product's motion, classify each animation as functional or decorative, and propose cuts

motivationHooks.prompt: A row-insert animation that runs layout on every frame turns janky the moment a workout list gets long, and a bottom sheet that goes rigid under "reduce motion" makes the app feel broken to exactly the users who asked for something gentler. This section is about choosing motion precisely: cheap enough to run every frame, and respectful of the one setting most teams get wrong.

Before Lecture 10.2 explains it, guess: a spring animates from 0 to 1 with stiffness 170 and damping 10 (no duration is set anywhere). About how long does it take to settle, and does it overshoot the target? Keep your guess; the lecture comes back to this exact spring.

A team disables every animation under prefers-reduced-motion, including the bottom sheet following the user's own finger while dragging. Users who turned the setting on say the sheet now feels broken and laggy, not calmer. How can removing motion make something feel worse for the person who asked for less of it?

This section is where several earlier ones meet: compositor-only properties and the frame budget (Section 2), a spring's state living in a closure advanced once per frame the same way a debounce's timer does (Section 1), the render/commit split that view transitions depend on (Section 3), and reduced motion and focus (Section 7). Motion is the section where "is this cheap enough, and does it respect the user" finally has to be answered in shipped code.

With stiffness 170 and damping 10, ζ ≈ 0.38 — under-damped — so it overshoots by about 26.3% before settling, and takes about 1,333ms, even though no duration was ever specified. A stiffer, better-damped spring (170/26, ζ ≈ 1) settles in about 775ms with no overshoot at all. If you guessed a fixed, easing-curve-style duration, you have now met motion-engineering.m3 directly.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- transform and opacity on a promoted layer are the only compositor-only properties; almost everything else (height, width, top, left, margin, box-shadow, stroke-dashoffset) costs layout or paint on every frame.
- A spring has no duration parameter. Its settle time emerges from stiffness, damping, mass, distance, and starting velocity, and it can be retargeted mid-flight without losing momentum — a tween restarted from the current position cannot.
- Stagger with transform and opacity, cap the total spread by compressing the step (not by capping each delay), and treat the View Transitions API as a progressive enhancement that needs a synchronous DOM update and unique names.
- A gesture's release decision comes from velocity (estimated over roughly the last 100ms) past a threshold, or otherwise the snap point nearest the projected position, and the release velocity hands off to a spring so the motion never restarts from rest.
- prefers-reduced-motion targets vestibular triggers (large movement, zoom, parallax), not motion itself: keep fades and the user's own dragging, and cut loops, bounce, and parallax.
- A motion audit classifies every animation as functional or decorative, checks its cost and frequency, and proposes a specific keep, speed up, gate, or cut, argued from what the user would lose, not taste.
keyTakeaways: Compositor-only means transform and opacity on a promoted layer; everything else costs layout or paint on every frame it changes.
A spring's duration is an output of stiffness, damping, mass, distance, and initial velocity, never an input.
Retargeting a running spring preserves position and velocity; restarting a tween from the current position resets velocity to zero and hitches.
Cap a stagger by compressing the step (maxTotal divided by count minus 1), not by clamping each delay, or late items clump together.
View transitions need a unique view-transition-name per snapshot and a synchronous DOM update, and are a progressive enhancement.
Estimate release velocity from roughly the last 100ms of samples; past a threshold it overrides the nearest-snap decision.
Reduced motion removes vestibular triggers (big movement, zoom, parallax) and keeps fades and user-driven dragging; it is not "no motion."
A motion audit decides keep, speed up, gate, or cut from purpose, cost, and frequency, not from personal taste.
