learningExperiences.title: Lecture 10.1: What to Animate, and Where It Runs

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Choose properties that animate on the compositor, and explain the cost of the ones that don't. (objective o3)
2. Choose duration and easing from the purpose of the motion. (objective o3, o5)
3. Distinguish functional motion from decorative motion. (objective o5)

terms.definition: An animation of `transform` or `opacity` on a promoted layer. The compositor thread produces frames without main-thread layout or paint (s2).
A curve mapping elapsed time to progress (`ease-out`, `cubic-bezier(…)`).
How long a time-based animation runs. For UI feedback, roughly 100–300 ms.
Motion that helps the user understand: feedback (a press), orientation (where something came from or went), continuity (the same object in a new place), or state change.
Motion for delight or brand that carries no information.
The Web Animations API: `element.animate(keyframes, options)`. It can be controlled from JS (pause, reverse, `finished`).

contentBlocks.content:
### Start concrete: the "Add set" button

When a user taps "Add set," a new row appears in the workout list and the rows below it move down. Two ways to animate it:

- **Animate `height`** of the new row from 0 to 56 px. Every frame changes geometry, so the whole list runs **layout, paint, and composite** on each frame. On a mid-range phone during a workout (with music playing and a timer running) that's jank.
- **Animate `transform: translateY()` and `opacity`** of the rows (the FLIP technique: First, Last, Invert, Play). Measure the old and new positions once, apply an inverted transform, and animate it back to zero. Each frame is **composite only**.

It isn't true that any property is cheap to animate (misconception `motion-engineering.m1`). Which properties you choose decides which pipeline stages run on every frame.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **transform and opacity are the only two properties that skip layout and paint entirely.** Edit the map below to add two more CSS properties you use often, guess which stage each invalidates, then check yourself against R2.

contentBlocks.altText: Screenshot (s10-m1): Height vs transform in the Performance panel. Two 300 ms recordings of the same "Add set" animation on a throttled CPU. Height version: every frame shows purple Layout and green Paint blocks on the main thread, and several frames exceed 16 ms (red). Transform version: the main thread is mostly idle, the compositor frames are steady, and there are no red frames.

contentBlocks.content:
### Durations and easing come from purpose

| Purpose | Typical duration | Easing |
|---|---|---|
| Press feedback (button scale) | 80–150 ms | ease-out |
| Small element entering (toast, row) | 150–250 ms | ease-out (fast start, gentle stop) |
| Element leaving | shorter than entering, 100–200 ms | ease-in |
| Large surface (sheet, page) | 250–400 ms, or a **spring** | ease-in-out or spring |
| Decorative celebration | as long as it's pleasant, but skippable | varies |

Motion that users trigger often (every set, every tap) must be fast, or it becomes friction.

### Functional or decorative?

Ask what the user would lose if the animation were removed. If they'd lose track of where something went, or not notice that something happened, it's **functional**. If nothing is lost, it's **decorative**. Decorative motion can still earn its place, for example a streak celebration once a week, but it's the first thing to cut or simplify, and it must respect reduced motion.

contentBlocks.caption: Every property from R2, printed as the pipeline-stage cost it adds over an 18-frame (300ms) animation. Predict each line before you run it.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: what to animate
contentBlocks.content:
- **Animating `top`, `left`, `width`, or `height`** for movement or size where `transform` works.
- **One long duration for everything.** Frequent actions need short, snappy motion.
- **`will-change` on everything.** Promote only what's about to animate.
- **Motion without a purpose on high-frequency interactions.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 10.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Transform and opacity by default. Everything else costs layout or paint on every frame.
- Duration and easing follow purpose and frequency.
- Functional motion explains something. Decorative motion is the first to cut.

interactionSequence.prompt: A "streak" badge animates from transform: scale(0.8) to scale(1), and an unread-count pill animates its width from 20px to 32px to fit a bigger number. Which one runs layout on every frame?
options: The badge, because scale transforms still trigger layout at large sizes
The pill, because width is geometry and forces layout every frame it changes
Both trigger layout, because any property is equally cheap to animate
Neither; both finish in under 300ms so the pipeline is skipped

optionFeedback.feedback: transform on a promoted layer is composite-only, regardless of the scale value.
Right. width is geometry, so every frame that changes it re-runs layout, and usually paint too.
Which pipeline stage a change invalidates depends on the property, not on cost being uniform.
Duration doesn't change which pipeline stage a property invalidates; a short animation on width still runs layout every one of its frames.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A change reruns the first pipeline stage it depends on, and every stage after it. Geometry means layout, color and shadows mean paint, and transform/opacity on a layer mean composite only.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Users tap "Add set" many times during a single workout. Which duration and easing fits best, and why?
options: 250-400ms with a spring, because large surfaces deserve a slow reveal
80-150ms ease-out, because a frequent action needs to feel immediate rather than becoming friction
1.8 seconds, matching the streak celebration, so it always feels special
Duration doesn't matter as long as the property is transform or opacity

optionFeedback.feedback: That duration fits a large surface like a sheet, not a small, frequent row insert.
Right. Motion the user triggers often has to be fast, or it becomes friction.
That duration is for a rare, decorative celebration, not a routine action performed every set.
Choosing a cheap property avoids pipeline cost, but duration still has to match how often and how urgently the user sees the motion.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Match duration and easing to purpose and frequency: frequent feedback (80-150ms), a small entering element (150-250ms), a large surface (250-400ms or a spring), decorative (as long as it's pleasant and skippable).

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In two or three sentences, explain why "any property is cheap to animate" is wrong, and describe what the FLIP technique does instead when a new row needs to visually grow into place.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Whether a property invalidates layout, paint, or only composite depends on the property itself: geometry properties like height, width, top, and margin force layout (and paint) on every frame, while transform and opacity on a promoted layer stay on the compositor. FLIP sidesteps the cost of animating real geometry by measuring the First and Last positions once, applying an Inverted transform so the element starts exactly where it used to be, then Playing an animation of transform and opacity back to zero, so growth reads as movement instead of a per-frame resize.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these implementations of the "Add set" row entrance from cheapest to most expensive per frame.
options: FLIP: transform and opacity only, on a promoted layer
stroke-dashoffset on one small SVG ring, alone
height animated on the new row alone
height animated on the new row, with every row below it repositioning each frame

optionFeedback.feedback: Composite-only: no main-thread layout or paint at all.
A paint property on one small element is cheap in isolation.
height is geometry: layout and paint run every frame for this one row.
The same layout cost as above, but it now cascades to every row below, multiplying the work each frame.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Cost scales with which pipeline stage a property invalidates, and then with how many elements and how much area are affected by that invalidation.
hints: Composite-only properties never touch layout or paint.
A layout change on one row can force layout on the rows that follow it too.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

workedExamples.title: Choosing properties for three animations
workedExamples.problem: Choosing properties for three animations
steps: **Rest timer ring filling:** `stroke-dashoffset` on an SVG circle is a paint property. It's acceptable for one small element (a small paint area), but don't animate it on 50 elements at once.

**Exercise card expanding to show notes:** animating `height: auto` causes layout on every frame. Use a FLIP transform on the card and its siblings, or accept a quick (150 ms) height change with `interpolate-size` where it's supported, if the list is short.
**"Personal best!" badge:** `transform: scale()` + `opacity` is compositor-only, and it's decorative, so it's skipped under reduced motion (the badge simply appears).
workedExamples.conclusion: The cost depends on the property, the number of elements, and the area. Choose transform and opacity by default, and accept a paint property only when the element is small and alone.

fadedVariant.problem: A "personal best" badge on a set uses `transform: scale()` + `opacity`, while a competing implementation grows the same badge with `font-size` and `padding`.
givenSteps: **Step 1, the transform version:** transform and opacity on a layer are composite-only. Nothing about the badge triggers layout or paint on the rest of the page.
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2, the font-size/padding version: which stage does that trigger, and what can it force on neighboring content?
Conclusion: which version is safer on a dense workout screen with many badges, and why?
blankedStepAnswers: font-size and padding are geometry, so they trigger layout. The badge's box grows, which can push neighboring rows and re-run their layout too.
The transform version, because it never triggers layout: one badge growing never risks moving the rows around it.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What are the two CSS properties that can animate on the compositor thread alone, and what does animating height cost on every frame instead?
What are the four purposes that make motion functional, and what turns it decorative instead?
What is the first pipeline stage invalidated by height, by box-shadow, and by transform on a promoted layer?

learningExperiences.title: Predict First: Interrupting a Tween vs a Spring

contentBlocks.content: Before Lecture 10.2 explains spring physics, commit to a prediction. You are not expected to get it right yet. The point is to find out which parts of your current model of motion are wrong, so the lecture has something specific to fix.

interactionSequence.prompt: **A tween and a spring, both interrupted at the same moment.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
positions: tween 262.5, spring 227.8
velocity at retarget: tween 0, spring 673.2 px/s
```

**Why intuition fails.** "A spring is just a fancy easing curve" suggests both will behave the same when interrupted. They don't. The sheet was moving at about 673 px/s. A restarted tween snaps that to 0 and begins a new curve, which the eye reads as a stall or a hitch. A retargeted spring keeps the 673 px/s and gradually reverses, the way a physical object would. This is misconception `motion-engineering.m3`: springs are parameterized by physics, their duration emerges, and they can be interrupted while preserving velocity.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: "A spring is just a fancy easing curve" suggests both will behave the same when interrupted. They don't. The sheet was moving at about 673 px/s. A restarted tween snaps that to 0 and begins a new curve, which the eye reads as a stall or a hitch. A retargeted spring keeps the 673 px/s and gradually reverses, the way a physical object would. This is misconception `motion-engineering.m3`: springs are parameterized by physics, their duration emerges, and they can be interrupted while preserving velocity.
hints: Simulate frame by frame: which force acts first, and which value updates first?
Track what the retarget/interruption does to the velocity, not just the position.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 10.2: Springs from Scratch

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Implement a spring with mass, stiffness, and damping using semi-implicit Euler integration. (objective o1)
2. Explain why a spring's duration comes from its physics, and how the damping ratio controls overshoot. (objective o1)
3. Retarget a spring mid-flight while preserving velocity, and hand off release velocity from a drag. (objective o1)

terms.definition: `−stiffness × (x − target)`: it pulls toward the target in proportion to the distance.
`−damping × velocity`: it resists motion and bleeds off energy.
Inertia. More mass means slower acceleration for the same force.
Advancing the simulation by `dt`: compute the acceleration, update the velocity, update the position.
Update the velocity first, then the position using the *new* velocity. It's stable for springs at frame-sized steps.
`damping / (2·√(stiffness·mass))`. ζ < 1 overshoots (bouncy), ζ = 1 is critically damped (fastest with no overshoot), ζ > 1 is sluggish.
The spring is "done" when both the distance to the target and the speed are below small thresholds.

contentBlocks.content: ### A spring is a tiny physics loop

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **a spring has no duration parameter.** Change stiffness and damping below and watch which frame the position settles near 100 — there is no duration input anywhere in the code.

contentBlocks.caption: Illustrative fragment (stiffness, x, target, damping, v, mass, and dt are not defined here) — shown for the shape of one integration step, not runnable on its own. See R1 for the runnable version.

contentBlocks.content: Run it once per frame (in `requestAnimationFrame`, using the real frame delta), write `x` to `transform`, and stop when the spring is at rest. The state lives in a closure (s1), just like the timer in your debounce.

### A spring isn't an easing curve

A cubic-bezier easing has a **fixed duration** and always starts from zero velocity. A spring has **no duration parameter**. How long it takes emerges from stiffness, damping, mass, the distance, and the starting velocity (misconception `motion-engineering.m3`). That's why springs feel natural in interactive UI:

- **Interruption:** if the user grabs the sheet halfway through, you keep the current position *and velocity* and retarget. A tween restarted from the current position begins at zero velocity, which causes a visible hitch.
- **Gesture handoff:** when the finger lifts at 1,500 px/s, the spring starts with that velocity and the motion continues seamlessly.

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Animation (s10-m2): Three springs, one target. Production brief: Three dots animate from 0 to 100 at the same time: ζ = 0.46 (stiffness 170, damping 12: overshoots and oscillates), ζ ≈ 1.0 (170/26: arrives quickly with no visible overshoot), and ζ = 2 (170/52: creeps in slowly). A graph beneath plots position over time, with the settle times marked. A second row shows the ζ ≈ 1 spring retargeted mid-flight, with its velocity arrow continuing smoothly, next to a restarted tween that visibly stalls.

contentBlocks.caption: A spring's path, frame by frame. Predict the six sampled positions before you run it, then check them against the overshoot the damping ratio predicts.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: springs
contentBlocks.content:
- **Using a fixed frame `dt` instead of the measured frame delta** (on 120 Hz displays the motion runs twice as fast). Clamp large deltas after a tab switch.
- **Updating the position before the velocity** (explicit Euler), which can explode at larger steps.
- **Resetting velocity to zero on retarget.**
- **No rest condition**, so the loop runs forever.
- **Animating `left`** instead of `transform` with the spring's output.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 10.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Spring = force from distance plus force from velocity. Integrate the velocity, then the position, once per frame.
- The duration emerges from the physics. ζ controls overshoot.
- Preserve velocity across interruptions and gesture releases.

interactionSequence.prompt: What determines how long a spring animation takes to settle?
options: A duration parameter you pass in, just like a tween
Its stiffness, damping, and mass, plus the distance and the starting velocity — the settle time emerges from the simulation
Only the frame rate the animation runs at
The easing curve attached to the spring

optionFeedback.feedback: A spring has no duration parameter to set.
Right. Nothing in the inputs says how long it takes; the settle time is an output of stepping the simulation.
With a measured dt, the same spring behaves the same at 60Hz and 120Hz; frame rate isn't what decides duration.
A spring isn't parameterized by a curve at all.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Tune a spring by feel: stiffness for speed, damping for bounce. The duration you see is a consequence of those choices, plus distance and starting velocity, never an input.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A sheet is mid-flight toward y=300 when the user grabs it and pushes it back toward y=0. Which implementation avoids a visible hitch at the moment of interruption?
options: Start a new 300ms ease-out tween from the sheet's current position
Retarget the running spring to 0, keeping its current position and velocity
Snap instantly to 0 and let a CSS transition pick up from there
Wait for the first animation to finish, then animate back

optionFeedback.feedback: A new tween starts at zero velocity, so the sheet appears to stall for an instant before the new curve takes over.
Right. Retargeting only changes where the force points; the object keeps the momentum it already had.
An instant snap throws away the sheet's momentum and reads as a jump, not a redirection.
Ignoring the user's input until the first animation finishes feels unresponsive, and isn't what direct manipulation promises.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is why springs suit interactive UI: interruption and gesture handoff both depend on carrying velocity across a change, which a fixed-duration curve cannot do.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A spring's state (x and v) lives in a closure that a requestAnimationFrame loop updates once per frame, the same shape as the timer inside debounce from Section 1. Explain in two or three sentences what that closure keeps alive between frames, and why recreating the spring object on every frame would break interruption.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The closure keeps the live position and velocity bindings alive across calls, the same way a debounce's closure keeps its pending timer id and latest arguments alive between calls. Recreating createSpring(...) on every frame would throw away v and reset it to the caller's default (usually 0), so every "step" would begin from rest — exactly the tween-restart mistake in motion-engineering.m3, just moved inside the loop instead of at the interruption point.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Settling times emerge from physics
workedExamples.problem:
Target distance 1 (normalized), mass 1, `dt = 1/120 s`, rest when the distance is < 0.001 and the speed is < 0.01:

| Stiffness | Damping | ζ | Settled after | Overshoot |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 170 | 26 | ≈ 1.00 | 775 ms | 0% |
| 170 | 10 | 0.38 | 1333 ms | 26.3% |
| 100 | 20 | 1.00 | 992 ms | 0% |
| 300 | 10 | 0.29 | 1325 ms | 38% |
steps: Nothing in the inputs said "775 ms." The duration came out of the simulation.
Lower damping means more overshoot *and* a longer settle, because it oscillates.
Lower stiffness at the same ζ gives the same shape, just slower.
Starting with velocity 8 toward the target (as after a flick), the 170/26 spring settles **sooner**: 725 ms.
workedExamples.conclusion: You tune a spring by feel (stiffness for speed, damping for bounce), and the duration follows. Exercise s10-e1 reproduces this table.

fadedVariant.problem: A different spring: stiffness 300, damping 10, mass 1, target distance 1, starting velocity 0.
givenSteps: **Step 1:** damping ratio ζ = damping / (2·√(stiffness·mass)) = 10 / (2·√300) ≈ 0.29. Since ζ < 1, this is under-damped: expect overshoot and oscillation.
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2: Compare this spring to the 170/10 spring (ζ ≈ 0.38, settles at 1333ms, 26.3% overshoot). Which one overshoots more, and roughly why?
Step 3: If you instead wanted the fastest arrival with zero overshoot, what damping would you choose for stiffness 300, mass 1?
blankedStepAnswers: This spring (ζ ≈ 0.29) overshoots more than the 170/10 spring (ζ ≈ 0.38), because a lower damping ratio means less energy is bled off before the object reaches the target, so it carries more speed past it.
Critically damped means ζ = 1, so damping = 2·√(stiffness·mass) = 2·√300 ≈ 34.6.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Write the two update lines of a semi-implicit Euler spring step, in order, in terms of force, mass, dt, v, and x.
What is the damping-ratio formula, and in one phrase each, what do zeta less than 1, zeta equal to 1, and zeta greater than 1 look like?
Why does an interactive UI element benefit from a spring instead of a fixed-duration tween, in terms of duration and interruption?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 10.3: Choreography: Staggers and View Transitions

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Build a staggered list entrance and exit in pure CSS and in WAAPI, compositor-only. (objective o3)
2. Cap stagger totals so long lists don't feel slow. (objective o3)
3. Build a shared-element transition with the View Transitions API as a progressive enhancement. (objective o2)

terms.definition: Offsetting each item's start by a small delay so a group reads as a sequence.
A maximum total spread (for example 240 ms), after which delays compress.
`document.startViewTransition(updateDOM)` snapshots the old state, runs your DOM update, and animates between them. Elements with the same `view-transition-name` morph into each other.
`@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` enables transitions between same-origin page loads in supporting browsers.
The feature improves the experience where it's supported and does nothing harmful where it isn't.

contentBlocks.content: ### Stagger in CSS

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **capping a stagger compresses the step; it doesn't just chop the tail off.** Try count 5, 12, and 40 below — does the LAST delay ever exceed 240?
Set `style="--i: 3"` from the template. For 30 exercises, 30 × 40 ms = 1.2 s before the last one appears, which is too slow. Cap the total spread (about 240 ms) and compress the step for long lists.

### Stagger in WAAPI

WAAPI gives you control: you can await `animation.finished`, reverse on exit, and cancel if the list changes mid-animation.

contentBlocks.caption: Illustrative WAAPI code (rows, delays, and row.animate are real DOM/browser APIs) — shown for the pattern, not runnable in this engine.

contentBlocks.content:
### Shared-element page transitions

From the workout list to the workout detail page, the exercise's thumbnail should *become* the detail hero image:

contentBlocks.caption: Illustrative shared-element transition code (uses real document.startViewTransition, matchMedia, and DOM helpers) — shown for the pattern, not runnable in this engine.

contentBlocks.content:
Things to get right: `view-transition-name` must be unique in each snapshot. The update callback has to change the DOM before it returns (or return a promise), which is why React code wraps state updates in `flushSync` (s3's render/commit). Move focus to the new page's heading after the transition (s7). And the whole thing is optional: without support, or under reduced motion, the page just changes.

For multi-page apps, cross-document transitions (`@view-transition { navigation: auto; }` on both pages, plus matching names) bring the same effect to server-rendered navigation (s3's rendering strategies). Check current browser support and treat it as an enhancement.

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Video (s10-m3): List to detail with a shared element. Production brief: A 10-second recording: a tap on the "Leg Day" card's thumbnail, which grows and moves into the detail page's hero while the rest of the page crossfades. A second pass with reduced motion enabled shows a plain crossfade. A third pass in a browser without support shows an instant page change, and it still works.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: choreography
contentBlocks.content:
- **Uncapped staggers on long lists.**
- **Animating `top` or `margin` for entrances.**
- **Duplicate `view-transition-name`s** (the transition is skipped).
- **Async DOM updates inside `startViewTransition`** without returning the promise.
- **No fallback when the API is missing, or no reduced-motion path.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 10.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Stagger with transform and opacity, and cap the total spread.
- View transitions morph shared elements. Use unique names, update the DOM synchronously, restore focus, and treat them as an enhancement.

interactionSequence.prompt: 18 new exercises enter the list, with a 40ms step and a 240ms cap. What step does the compressed stagger actually use, and when does the last row start?
options: Still 40ms; caps only apply to lists under 12 items
About 14ms, compressed so the last row starts at the 240ms cap instead of 680ms
0ms; every row appears at once once a list is 'too long'
40ms per row, but the animation's own duration shrinks instead of the delay

optionFeedback.feedback: The cap applies whenever the uncapped spread would exceed it, regardless of a fixed item count.
Right. Compressing the step to maxTotal / (count − 1) keeps the group readable as a sequence within a quarter second.
That would lose the sequential read entirely, not just cap its length.
The fix compresses the delay between items, not each item's own animation duration.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Uncapped, 18 rows at 40ms would spread over (18 − 1) × 40 = 680ms. Compressing the step to 240 / 17 ≈ 14.1ms keeps the last row inside the 240ms cap.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Two cards on the workout list both get style.viewTransitionName = 'workout-hero' set at the same time, right before startViewTransition. What happens to the transition?
options: It is skipped: view-transition-name must be unique within a snapshot, and duplicates break the match
Both thumbnails morph into the same hero image, in parallel
The browser picks whichever card was tapped, using pointer coordinates
Nothing changes; duplicate names are ignored and merged

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Assign the name only to the one card actually transitioning, and clear it again afterward.
A shared name can't resolve to two different elements at once, so the match fails instead.
View transitions match by name, not by which element was interacted with.
A duplicate name is not silently merged; it causes that transition to be skipped.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: view-transition-name must be unique in each snapshot. Set it only on the element that is actually transitioning, and clear it again once the transition has captured it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate's React code calls setDetailId(id) inside document.startViewTransition(() => { ... }) and the transition never animates the hero image, even though the DOM eventually updates correctly. Using this lecture's reasoning, explain what's wrong and how to fix it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: React state updates are normally batched and applied asynchronously, so by the time startViewTransition takes its "new" snapshot, the DOM hasn't actually changed yet — the callback has to update the DOM before it returns (or return a promise that resolves once it has). The fix is to wrap the state update in flushSync so React commits synchronously inside the callback: the same render/commit distinction from Section 3, where startViewTransition needs a commit, not just a scheduled render.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Capping a stagger
workedExamples.problem: Twelve new exercises, a 40 ms step, and a 240 ms cap:
steps: Uncapped spread: 11 × 40 = 440 ms before the last row starts.
Cap: the spread is at most 240 ms, so the step is min(40, 240 / 11) = 21.8 ms.
workedExamples.conclusion: The group still reads as a sequence, and the last row starts within a quarter second. Test-suite exercise s10-t1 is this function.

fadedVariant.problem: A results list refreshes with 24 new rows, a 40ms step, and a 200ms cap.
givenSteps: **Step 1:** uncapped spread would be (24 − 1) × 40 = 920ms, far past the 200ms cap, so the step must compress.
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2: what compressed step keeps the spread at exactly 200ms across 24 rows?
Step 3: why compress the step instead of capping each delay at 200ms directly?
blankedStepAnswers: Capping each delay at 200ms would make every row from the point it hits the cap onward start at the exact same moment, which reads as several rows appearing at once instead of a sequence; compressing the step keeps every row’s start distinct.

How do you cap a stagger's total spread without making the last several items appear at the exact same moment?
Why must the DOM update inside document.startViewTransition's callback happen synchronously (or as a returned promise), and what does React code do to guarantee that?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 10.4: Gestures: Drag, Velocity, Snap Points

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Implement dragging with pointer events and pointer capture. (objective o4)
2. Estimate release velocity from recent pointer samples. (objective o4)
3. Choose a snap point (or dismiss) from position plus projected momentum, and hand the velocity to a spring. (objective o4, o1)
4. Make the sheet accessible and reduced-motion-aware. (objective o4)

terms.definition: Unified mouse, touch, and pen events (`pointerdown`, `pointermove`, `pointerup`).
`el.setPointerCapture(e.pointerId)` keeps receiving moves even when the pointer leaves the element.
CSS telling the browser which gestures it may handle itself (`touch-action: none` on a drag handle).
Displacement over time across the last ~100 ms of samples, in px/s.
Where the element would end up if it kept moving: `position + velocity × k`.
Resting positions (open, half, closed).
A fast enough flick dismisses (or fully opens) regardless of position.

contentBlocks.content:
### The rest-timer bottom sheet

During a workout the rest timer lives in a bottom sheet with three snap points: **open** (y = 0), **half** (y = 400), and **closed** (y = 800).

1. `pointerdown` on the handle: capture the pointer, stop any running spring, and record `{ t, y }`.
2. `pointermove`: set `transform: translateY(y)` directly (following the finger), and keep the last ~100 ms of samples.
3. `pointerup`: estimate the velocity. If it's faster than 1000 px/s down, **dismiss**. If it's faster than 1000 px/s up, **open**. Otherwise **project** (`y + v × 0.2 s`) and snap to the nearest point.
4. Start the spring toward the chosen point **with the release velocity** (Lecture 10.2).

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **a fast flick overrides the nearest-snap position, but only past the dismiss threshold.** Change the last sample's y (or t) below and see when the estimate crosses 1000 px/s.

### Accessibility and reduced motion

- The sheet also needs **non-gesture controls**: a visible button to expand or collapse, focusable, and Escape to close (s7). A gesture can't be the only way to do something.
- With `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`, **keep the dragging** (the user is controlling it directly) but replace the springy release with a short crossfade or a quick, non-bouncy settle, and remove the parallax on the background. Reduced motion doesn't mean no motion (misconception `motion-engineering.m2`). The setting targets vestibular triggers (large movement, zooming, parallax, spinning). Opacity fades and small, user-controlled movement are generally fine and often still useful.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s10-m4): Release decision. A vertical axis from 0 (open) to 800 (closed) with snap points marked. Three release scenarios as arrows: (A) slow drag released at 380, projected to 420, snapping to half. (B) a fast downward flick at 1560 px/s from 400, dismissed to closed. (C) a fast upward flick at −1500 px/s from 380, opening fully. A reduced-motion inset shows the same decisions settling with a 150 ms fade-and-move and no bounce.

contentBlocks.caption: Release velocity computed from three different pointer-sample patterns. Predict the sign and rough magnitude of each before you run it.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: gestures
contentBlocks.content:
- **Estimating velocity from only the last two samples** (noisy), or from the whole drag (stale).
- **Snapping by position alone**, which ignores flicks.
- **Restarting motion from zero velocity after release.**
- **Gesture-only controls** with no button or keyboard path.
- **Disabling all motion under reduced motion**, including user-driven dragging and helpful fades.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 10.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Pointer capture, direct manipulation while dragging, and a velocity estimate on release.
- Flick beyond a threshold → dismiss or open. Otherwise → nearest snap to the projected position.
- Hand the velocity to a spring. Provide non-gesture controls. Under reduced motion, keep direct manipulation and fades and drop the bounce and parallax.

interactionSequence.prompt: At release, the sheet is at y=200 (snap points: open=0, half=400, closed=800), moving at 1400 px/s downward, with a dismiss threshold of 1000 px/s. Where does it go?
options: Half, because 200 is closer to 400 than to 0 or 800
Open, because 200 is closest to 0
Closed, because the downward flick exceeds the dismiss threshold, regardless of position
It stays at 200; a flick only matters if it starts past the halfway point

optionFeedback.feedback: Position-only reasoning is exactly what a flick threshold is meant to override.
200 is nearest to 0 by distance, but the fast downward flick overrides a nearest-snap decision.
Right. A flick past the threshold decides by direction and speed alone, whatever the release position was.
The threshold is checked against velocity, not against where the flick started.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Check the flick thresholds first. Only when the release velocity is under the threshold do you fall back to projecting the position and choosing the nearest snap.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, what should the rest-timer sheet do?
options: Disable pointer tracking during the drag, so the sheet no longer follows the finger
Keep following the finger during the drag, but replace the springy release with a quick, non-bouncy settle and drop the background parallax
Remove the sheet's motion entirely and just toggle its visibility
Slow every transition down to make it gentler

optionFeedback.feedback: Direct manipulation is motion the user is producing themselves; removing it breaks the control instead of protecting anyone.
Right. The preference targets vestibular triggers — bounce and parallax — not the user's own dragging.
That removes useful feedback along with the vestibular triggers; reduced motion isn't "no motion."
Slowing everything down doesn't address vestibular triggers and can make frequent interactions feel sluggish.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Reduced motion targets large movement, zoom, and parallax. Fades and finger-driven dragging are generally fine and still carry information.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The bottom sheet's handle gets role="slider" and full ARIA attributes so screen-reader users can hear its state. Is that enough to make it operable without a gesture?
options: Yes, ARIA alone describes the control well enough for any input method to use it
No; it also needs a real focusable, keyboard-operable control (a button, Escape to close) that doesn't depend on a drag gesture at all
No, because ARIA roles only work in Chromium browsers
Yes, as long as the aria-valuenow attribute updates during the drag

optionFeedback.feedback: ARIA describes a control; it doesn't give someone who can't perform the drag gesture a way to operate it.
Right. A gesture can't be the only way to do something — a keyboard-operable button and Escape are still required.
ARIA support varies by detail, but that isn't why a gesture-only control fails; it fails because there's no non-gesture path at all.
Updating the attribute helps announce state, but it still gives a keyboard or switch user no way to move the sheet.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Adding ARIA describes a control; it does not make it operable. A gesture-only interaction needs a real non-gesture path: a focusable button and a keyboard shortcut such as Escape.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

workedExamples.title: A flick from pointer samples
steps: That's more than 1000 px/s, so **dismiss** to closed (y = 800), whatever the position.
Hand off: the spring starts at y = 400 with v = 1562.5 px/s toward 800, so it keeps moving as though the finger threw it.
If instead the last samples were `(0, 340)`, `(100, 360)`, `(200, 380)`: the 100 ms window gives (380 − 360)/100 × 1000 = 200 px/s. The projection is 380 + 40 = 420, so it snaps to **half**.
workedExamples.conclusion: Velocity decides intent, projection decides the destination, and the spring keeps the motion continuous. Exercise s10-e2 implements the release logic.

fadedVariant.problem: Samples in the last 100ms: (0ms, 500), (30, 470), (60, 445), (90, 425). Snap points as in the lecture: open=0, half=400, closed=800. Dismiss threshold 1000 px/s.
givenSteps: **Step 1:** velocity = (425 − 500) / (90 − 0) × 1000 = −833.3 px/s (upward, since y is decreasing).
blankedStepPrompts: Step 2: is this past the dismiss threshold? What decision rule applies next if not?
Step 3: project the position with projectionS = 0.2s from y = 425, and pick the nearest snap.
blankedStepAnswers: No: |−833.3| < 1000, so it isn't a flick. Project instead: y + velocity × projectionS.
425 + (−833.3 × 0.2) = 425 − 166.7 = 258.3, which is nearer to half (400) than to open (0), so it snaps to half.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Over roughly how many milliseconds of recent pointer samples should you estimate release velocity, and why not just the last two samples?
Once the pointer is released, what two pieces of information decide which snap point the sheet goes to?
Under prefers-reduced-motion: reduce, what kinds of motion should you remove, and what should you keep?

learningExperiences.title: Predict First: What Reduced Motion Actually Keeps

contentBlocks.content: Before the motion audit lecture, predict what five different animations should do under prefers-reduced-motion. Most teams get at least one of these wrong by treating the setting as an on/off switch for all motion.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Five animations, one reduced-motion setting.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
set row enter: reduce to fade
sheet drag (finger-driven): keep
list-to-detail morph: replace with crossfade or remove
parallax header: replace with crossfade or remove
toast: keep
```

**Why intuition fails.** Many teams implement `prefers-reduced-motion` as "turn every animation off." The preference targets **vestibular triggers**: large movement, zoom, and parallax. Fades carry no such risk and still tell the user that something changed, and finger-driven dragging is the user's own motion. Removing everything also removes useful feedback. This is misconception `motion-engineering.m2`.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Many teams implement `prefers-reduced-motion` as "turn every animation off." The preference targets **vestibular triggers**: large movement, zoom, and parallax. Fades carry no such risk and still tell the user that something changed, and finger-driven dragging is the user's own motion. Removing everything also removes useful feedback. This is misconception `motion-engineering.m2`.
hints: Simulate frame by frame: which force acts first, and which value updates first?
Track what the retarget/interruption does to the velocity, not just the position.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 10.5: The Motion Audit

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Catalog every animation in a product, with its purpose, properties, duration, frequency, and reduced-motion behavior. (objective o5)
2. Classify each as functional or decorative, and flag cost and accessibility issues. (objective o5)
3. Propose cuts and changes with reasons a designer will accept. (objective o5)

terms.definition: A table of every animation: trigger, purpose, properties, duration, easing, frequency, and reduced-motion behavior.
How often a user sees it (every tap, per session, once a week).
Motion likely to cause dizziness or nausea: large-scale movement, parallax, zooming, spinning.

contentBlocks.content:
For each animation, ask:

1. **Purpose:** feedback, orientation, continuity, or state change (functional), or delight and attention-seeking (decorative)?
2. **Cost:** does it animate layout or paint properties? How many elements? Does it run during other work?
3. **Frequency × duration:** a 600 ms animation seen on every set logged is friction.
4. **Reduced motion:** what happens under `prefers-reduced-motion`? Is anything looping forever?
5. **Decision:** keep, speed up, simplify, gate behind reduced motion, or cut.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **the same five questions apply to any animation, not just the ones already flagged.** Add one more animation from an app you use to the list and classify it.

contentBlocks.altText: Screenshot (s10-m5): A motion inventory spreadsheet. A shared spreadsheet with columns Animation, Trigger, Purpose (functional/decorative), Properties, Duration, Frequency, Reduced-motion behavior, Issue, and Proposal, with about 12 rows for the workout tracker. Colored chips mark 'keep', 'speed up', 'gate', and 'cut'. A filter shows that only 2 of 12 animations account for most of the flagged issues.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: motion audits
contentBlocks.content:
- **Cataloging without frequency.** A cheap animation seen constantly still matters.
- **Cutting all motion.** Functional motion helps comprehension.
- **Ignoring infinite loops and parallax** under reduced motion.
- **Explaining cuts only as "performance."** Say what the user gains.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 10.5 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Inventory → classify → flag cost and accessibility → decide.
- Keep functional motion fast. Treat decorative motion as optional and rare. Never loop forever without a way to stop.

interactionSequence.prompt: A card flips 180 degrees to reveal a 'details' side when tapped, and separately, a confetti burst plays once a week after a streak. Which is functional, and which is decorative?
options: The flip is functional (state change); the confetti is decorative (delight)
Both are decorative, since neither is required to use the app
Both are functional, since both have a clear trigger
The confetti is functional (feedback); the flip is decorative (delight)

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The flip tells the user the content changed to a different state; the confetti carries no information the user would otherwise miss.
The flip's motion is exactly what tells the user the card's content changed — that's information, not decoration.
Having a trigger isn't what makes motion functional; ask what the user would lose if it were removed.
Confetti carries no information the user would lose without it, while the flip does — this has the two reversed.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Ask what the user would lose if the animation were removed. Losing track of a state change is a real loss; missing a confetti burst is not.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Your audit finds a "new personal record" ring that pulses box-shadow in an infinite loop, ignores reduced motion, and shows on every single set logged. What do you propose?
options: Keep it: box-shadow is a paint property, and paint properties are always cheap
Stop the loop (pulse once, only for an actual new record, and never under reduced motion), because infinite motion on every set is both costly and distracting
Switch the property to width instead, since geometry looks more "alive"
Remove all motion from the app so this kind of decision never comes up again

optionFeedback.feedback: A paint property is cheaper than layout, but it still isn't free, and cost isn't the only problem with an infinite, unstoppable loop.
Right. Frequency (every set) times an infinite loop is friction and a vestibular risk; cut the loop and gate it correctly.
That trades a paint property for a layout property — strictly more expensive, and still infinite.
Cutting all motion throws away functional motion along with the problem; the audit is about targeted cuts, not blanket removal.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Frequency multiplies cost: a cheap animation seen constantly still matters, and an infinite loop that ignores reduced motion is both a cost problem and an accessibility problem.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A designer pushes back on your motion-audit proposal to cut the pulsing button loop, saying "that's just your opinion." Using the lecture's framework, how do you respond?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Point to the concrete, checkable criteria instead of a taste claim: what the user would lose if the animation were removed (nothing — it is decorative, not feedback, orientation, continuity, or state change), its cost (an infinite loop that never lets the main thread rest and ignores prefers-reduced-motion, a vestibular trigger for some users), and its frequency (every visit). Critique grounded in what a user gains or loses is not personal opinion; treating it as unarguable taste is itself the misconception the framework is built to avoid.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Auditing the workout tracker
workedExamples.problem:
| Animation | Purpose | Properties | Duration | Frequency | Issue | Proposal |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Set row enters | feedback | height, opacity | 400 ms | every set | layout property, slow | FLIP with transform + opacity, 180 ms |
| Sheet release | continuity | transform (spring) | emergent | per rest | none | keep; reduced motion: no bounce |
| List→detail morph | orientation | view transition | 300 ms | per workout | none | keep; crossfade under reduced motion |
| Streak confetti | delight | transform, opacity | 1.8 s | weekly | none, if skippable | keep; show a static badge under reduced motion |
| Pulsing "Start" button | attention | transform (scale), infinite | loop | always | infinite loop, ignores reduced motion | cut the loop; one pulse on first visit only |
| Parallax header | decorative | transform on scroll | continuous | every scroll | vestibular trigger | cut under reduced motion, or cut entirely |
steps: Set row enters: functional (feedback), but animates height and opacity at 400ms on every set — a layout property, and too slow for something this frequent. Proposal: FLIP with transform + opacity, 180ms.
Sheet release and list-to-detail morph: functional (continuity and orientation), already compositor-only or view-transition based, with a sane reduced-motion fallback. Proposal: keep as-is.
Streak confetti: decorative but rare (weekly) and skippable under reduced motion. Proposal: keep, with a static badge shown under reduced motion.

Pulsing "Start" button and the parallax header: decorative, loop forever or run continuously, and ignore reduced motion — the parallax is a vestibular trigger. Proposal: cut the button's loop after the first visit; cut or gate the parallax under reduced motion.
workedExamples.conclusion: Two changes (the set row and the pulsing button) remove most of the cost and friction. The decorative streak celebration stays because it's rare and skippable.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What five questions does a motion-inventory row answer about a single animation?
Why does an animation's frequency matter as much as its duration when you're deciding whether it's a problem?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: The Workout Motion Kit

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. In this engine, "time" is a dt argument you pass to each simulation step, so every animation here is deterministic and testable.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

How this lab is sequenced

Challenges 2 and 4 give you a scaffold (the snap points and pointer samples, or the motion inventory) and leave the core logic to you. Challenges 1 and 3 have no separate scaffold marker, just TODO comments in place. The two test-suite challenges turn it around: first you write tests for correct code, then you fix broken code against tests that are already written.

The Practical Activity below is where the visual result (smoothness, choreography, feel) actually gets built and reviewed; the challenges here check the logic underneath it.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your staggerDelays tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the staggerDelays challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "The Workout Motion Kit."** Expected time is 10–12 hours.

1. **Spring-driven draggable:** your s10-e1 integrator in a `requestAnimationFrame` loop (measured `dt`, clamped), driving `transform` on a draggable card that keeps its momentum on release (velocity from s10-e2). Demonstrate interruption: grab it mid-flight and throw it back. *(o1)*
2. **Shared-element transition:** workout list → workout detail with `document.startViewTransition`, unique `view-transition-name`s, a synchronous DOM update (`flushSync` if React), focus moved to the detail heading afterwards, and fallbacks for no support and for reduced motion. **Stretch:** a cross-document version with `@view-transition`. *(o2)*
3. **Staggered list in two implementations:** pure CSS (custom property `--i`, capped) and WAAPI (your s10-t1 delays, cancel and reverse on exit), both compositor-only. Include a Performance-panel screenshot showing no layout during the animation. *(o3)*
4. **Rest-timer bottom sheet:** pointer capture, snap points (open, half, closed), velocity-based dismissal, a spring handoff, a visible toggle button and Escape to close, and reduced-motion behavior (direct drag kept, bounce removed, background parallax removed). Record a keyboard-only run as well. *(o4)*
5. **Motion audit** of a real product you use (or your capstone-to-be): a full inventory table, classification, issues, and a proposal list with keep, speed up, simplify, gate, or cut for each animation, written for a designer. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for the Workout Motion Kit (100 points)
rows: Stable integration, a measured `dt`, momentum on release, velocity-preserving interruption.
Shared element morphs, unique names, focus restored, graceful fallbacks.
Both implementations capped and compositor-only, with trace evidence.
Correct snap and dismiss decisions, spring handoff, keyboard path, reduced-motion behavior.
Complete inventory, correct classification, persuasive and specific proposals.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 4: A spring integrator with retargeting

Implement `createSpring({ mass, stiffness, damping, from, to, velocity, restDelta, restSpeed })` returning `{ step(dt), position, velocity, retarget(to), isAtRest() }` (semi-implicit Euler, velocity preserved on retarget), and `simulate(options, { dt, maxSteps })` returning `{ settledAtMs, overshootPct }` (the overshoot as a percentage of the distance travelled, rounded to 1 decimal place, with `settledAtMs` rounded to whole milliseconds).

Defaults: `mass = 1`, `stiffness = 170`, `damping = 26`, `from = 0`, `to = 1`, `velocity = 0`, `restDelta = 0.001`, `restSpeed = 0.01`, `dt = 1/120`, `maxSteps = 2000`.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Force from distance plus force from velocity, then *velocity first*, then position.
Retargeting changes where the force points, not how fast the object is moving.
Overshoot is how far past the target the position went, divided by the distance travelled.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 4: Release logic for the rest-timer sheet

Implement `estimateVelocity(samples, windowMs)` (px/s from the earliest sample within `windowMs` of the last one, or 0 with fewer than two usable samples) and `releaseTarget({ y, samples, snaps, dismissVelocity, projectionS })`. The latter returns `{ target, targetY, initialVelocity }`: a flick of at least `dismissVelocity` goes to the largest-y snap (down) or the smallest-y snap (up). Otherwise it goes to the snap nearest `y + velocity × projectionS`. `initialVelocity` hands the release velocity to the spring.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: `samples.find(...)` from the start gives the earliest sample inside the window.
Check the flick thresholds *before* projecting.
The spring that animates the sheet needs to know how fast it was already moving.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 4: A compositor-only, reduced-motion-aware list entrance

Implement `planListEnter(count, { reducedMotion, stepMs, maxStaggerMs, durationMs })` returning one `{ delay, duration, keyframes }` per item.

- **Normal:** keyframes `[{ opacity: 0, transform: 'translateY(8px)' }, { opacity: 1, transform: 'translateY(0)' }]`. Delay is `min(i × stepMs, maxStaggerMs)`. Duration is `durationMs`.
- **Reduced motion:** keep a short fade: `[{ opacity: 0 }, { opacity: 1 }]`, delay 0, duration 150.

Defaults: `stepMs = 40`, `maxStaggerMs = 240`, `durationMs = 220`.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Which two properties can run on the compositor?
`Math.min` caps a growing delay.
Reduced motion targets movement, not information. What's left once you remove the translate?

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 4: A motion audit, automated

Implement `auditMotion(animations)` returning `{ functional, decorative, issues }`.

- **Functional purposes:** `feedback`, `orientation`, `continuity`, `state`. Everything else (`delight`, `attention`) is decorative.
- **Issues** (in input order, several per animation allowed, as `` `${name}: ${message}` ``):
  - `animates layout property <prop>` for any of `width`, `height`, `top`, `left`, `right`, `bottom`, `margin`, `padding`
  - `too slow for feedback (<ms>ms)` when the purpose is `feedback` and the duration is over 300
  - `infinite loop ignores reduced motion` when `loops === Infinity` and `!respectsReducedMotion`

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Two lookup lists (functional purposes, layout properties) keep the logic readable.
One animation can have several issues. Check each rule independently.
The issue message format is part of the contract, because the audit report is generated from it.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working staggerDelays, you write the tests

`staggerDelays(count, { stepMs, maxTotalMs })` returns rounded delays in which the **total spread** (the last delay) never exceeds `maxTotalMs`. When `stepMs × (count − 1)` would exceed it, the step is compressed to `maxTotalMs / (count − 1)`. It's correct. Check runs your suite against the correct code, where it must pass, and needs at least **four** tests. Then use the three "wrong implementation" playgrounds in this lab to confirm your suite catches each one. Use Lecture 10.3's twelve-row example.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks the short-list step, the compressed and capped spread (using the twelve-row example), that delays stay strictly increasing with no clumping, and the zero and one-item edges. Wrong implementation 1 caps each delay directly instead of compressing the step, so late items clump together at 240ms; wrong implementation 2 divides by count instead of count minus 1, so the spread falls just short of the cap; wrong implementation 3 forgets to round. A suite that only checks the short-list case catches none of the three.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests pin down the exact numbers a caller depends on: the delays array itself, not just "it returns an array." Assert on the full sequence, and on the property that must always hold (never exceeding the cap, staying strictly increasing).
hints: Start with a short list where the step is never compressed, and check the exact delays array.
Use Lecture 10.3's twelve-row example: count=12 should compress the 40ms step so the last delay lands at 240.
What should a list of 0 items return? A list of exactly 1 item?

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken slide-in keyframes, make the tests pass

`slideIn(fromEdge, distancePx, { reducedMotion })` builds WAAPI keyframes for a panel entering from `'start'`, `'end'`, or `'bottom'`. It uses layout properties, ignores reduced motion, and doesn't handle right-to-left. Fix it. (For `'start'`/`'end'`, `rtl` flips the direction, because *start* is on the right in RTL layouts.)

codeExercise.solutionNote: `left`/`top` cost layout on every frame (`motion-engineering.m1`). Reduced motion keeps the information ("the panel arrived") as a fade (`motion-engineering.m2`). Logical edges (`start`/`end`) need the writing direction, just like the logical properties in s9.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All the bugs here treat keyframes as if only the shape mattered: layout properties instead of transform, a reduced-motion flag that is never read, and a direction flip that ignores rtl.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure: which properties does the broken version return, and are they the ones the pipeline-cost lecture recommends?
What should reducedMotion do to the returned keyframes, and does the broken version check it at all?
For start and end, which direction does rtl flip, and does the broken version look at rtl at all?

contentBlocks.content: This exercise happens on a real app with a screen recorder, not inside the course engine. Provides a motion-audit checklist covering purpose, cost and properties, frequency, and reduced-motion behavior for every animation, so the museum's designers can classify future motion themselves.

sections.title: Design Systems and Component APIs
sections.description: Build a three-tier **design token** system (primitive, semantic, component) with light, dark, and high-contrast themes; build **headless, compound, and slotted** components (Select, Dialog) that separate behavior from presentation; design a **Button** whose props resist explosion, with the rules encoded in types; keep **design and code in sync** with a normalized drift checker; and **evolve without breaking consumers** with semantic versioning, deprecation, codemods, and migration guides. Examples come from a platform shared by a group of museums and cultural institutions: collection browsing, exhibition pages, ticketing, and a members' area, each museum with its own brand.

learningObjectives.description: Build a three-tier token system (primitive → semantic → component) with light, dark, and high-contrast themes
Build headless Select and Dialog components with compound-component and slot patterns
Build a Button with variants, sizes, and states, and document the props-vs-composition decision
Write a script that syncs Figma variables with code tokens and flags drift
Cut a versioned release with a deprecation path and a migration guide for a breaking change

motivationHooks.prompt: Five museums share one Button component. One museum's marketing team asks for a gold gradient background "just for us." A color prop feels like the fastest way to say yes. This section is about the actual cost of that yes: what a single prop opens the door to, and what to build instead so every museum gets what it needs without every future request becoming a new prop.

A component token, button.primary.bg, points at a semantic token, color.accent, which points at a primitive. A team ships dark mode by writing a new object that swaps every primitive's value with the one below it in the palette, with no semantic tier at all. Before the lecture explains it, guess: does dark mode actually work? Keep your answer; Lecture 11.1's predict-run comes back to exactly this.

A Dialog component looks identical across two museum apps, down to the pixel, because one was built by copying the other's code. A year later, one has a serious keyboard bug and the other doesn't, even though nobody touched either file since. How is that possible?

This section reaches back to Section 9's cascade layers and fluid scales, which become the tokens layer here, Section 7's combobox and dialog contracts, which become the headless core's guarantees, Section 3's context and re-renders, Section 1's discriminated unions, and Section 8's CI and versioned releases. It reaches forward to Section 12's critique vocabulary, built on the tokens and type scale from this section.

It looks like it worked, since every value flipped. But look at what broke: the primitive named ink.900, the darkest ink in the palette, now holds the lightest color, so its own name lies, and there's no semantic tier to add a high-contrast theme or a second museum's brand without another blind global swap. If you guessed "yes, dark mode works," Lecture 11.1's predict-run is built to show you exactly what that swap actually costs.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- Three tiers, one job each: primitives are raw, semantics carry purpose and vary per theme, and components consume semantics and never change when the theme does.
- A headless core owns behavior and accessibility once; every brand's skin gets that contract for free instead of re-implementing it.
- More props don't make a component more flexible. A closed set of designed variants, plus composition and slots for everything else, is what actually scales.
- Comparing design and code tokens raw is noisy. Normalize first (hex case, short hex, px to rem), and check every token type, not just color.
- The most severe change decides the version bump, and a deprecation path, warn, codemod, guide, remove, lets you ship improvements now and break later, on purpose.
keyTakeaways: Primitive, semantic, component: only the semantic tier changes per theme, so theming never means editing a component.
Headless cores own behavior and accessibility; compound components share state through context (memoized, so options don't re-render on every keystroke); slots replace most configuration props.
Closed sets of designed variants beat prop explosion, and the rules (like icon-only needing a label) belong in the type system, not just in documentation.
A drift checker must normalize values and check every token type before its report is worth reading, and the team needs an agreed source of truth before automating failures.
Semver is decided by the most severe change; a deprecation path (warn, codemod, guide, remove) lets a system evolve without breaking the consumers depending on it.
