learningExperiences.title: Lecture 11.1: Tokens in Three Tiers, and Theming

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Organize tokens into primitive, semantic, and component tiers, and explain what each tier is for. (objective o1)
2. Implement light, dark, and high-contrast themes by swapping only the semantic tier. (objective o1)
3. Validate themes automatically (unresolved references, cycles, contrast). (objective o1)

terms.definition: A named design decision stored as data (a color, space, radius, type size, duration, shadow) and consumed by code and design tools.
A raw palette value with no meaning: `color.gold.600 = #8a6d1c`, `space.4 = 16px`.
A token named for its *purpose*: `color.text.default`, `color.surface.raised`, `color.accent`. It references primitives, and its values change per theme.
A token scoped to a component: `button.primary.bg`. It references semantic tokens.
A set of semantic values (light, dark, high-contrast, and per-brand).
`{color.gold.600}` means "the value of that token." The Design Tokens Community Group format writes tokens as objects with `$value`, `$type`, and `{…}` references.

contentBlocks.content:
### Why three tiers

Each museum on the platform has its own palette, and each needs light and dark modes plus a high-contrast mode for accessibility. If the `Button` used `#8a6d1c` directly, or even `color.gold.600`, then dark mode would mean editing every component. With tiers:

```
primitive:  color.gold.600 = #8a6d1c        color.gold.300 = #e0c46c
semantic:   color.accent (light) = {color.gold.600}   color.accent (dark) = {color.gold.300}
component:  button.primary.bg = {color.accent}
```

Switching the theme swaps only the **semantic** values. Components never change. Tokens aren't just color variables (misconception `design-system-architecture.m3`). The semantic tier is what makes theming, dark mode, high contrast, and per-brand variants possible without touching components. The same applies to spacing, radius, typography (s9's fluid steps), and motion durations (s10).
### Emitting CSS

The token build validates the tokens before emitting them: every reference resolves, there are no cycles, and the required text/background pairs meet contrast in **every** theme (s7's contrast function). High contrast must pass AAA (7:1) for text.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s11-m1): Token tiers and themes. Three columns: Primitives (swatches with raw names), Semantic (purpose names with arrows pointing to different primitives for each of light, dark, and high-contrast), and Component (button.primary.bg, card.bg) pointing only at semantic names. A theme switcher above the semantic column shows only its arrows re-routing. The component column doesn't move.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: switching a theme swaps only the semantic tier; component tokens never move. Add a fourth theme, "partner-dark", to the semantic map below (point it at existing primitives) and confirm button.primary.bg resolves without touching the component map.

contentBlocks.caption: One component token resolved across three themes. Predict all three lines before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: tokens
contentBlocks.content:
- **Components referencing primitives directly**, which means theming has to edit components.
- **Semantic names that describe appearance** (`color.gold`) instead of purpose (`color.accent`).
- **No validation**, so broken references and low-contrast themes ship.
- **Tokens only for color.** Spacing, type, radius, and motion drift too.
- **Per-component one-off values** that bypass tokens.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Primitives are raw, semantics carry purpose (per theme), and components consume semantics.
- Themes swap the semantic tier. Validate references, cycles, and contrast for every theme.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Theming by swapping primitives.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
light: card.bg=#f7f5f0 card.text=#1b1a17 badge.bg=#1b1a17 badge.text=#f7f5f0
dark:  card.bg=#1b1a17 card.text=#f7f5f0 badge.bg=#f7f5f0 badge.text=#1b1a17
"ink.900" now means #f7f5f0, which is the lightest colour in the palette
```

**Why intuition fails.** The output looks like it worked, since every pair inverted. Look at what it cost: the primitive named `ink.900` (the darkest ink) now holds the lightest color, so every name in the palette lies. The badge, which was meant to stay dark in both themes as an emphasis element, flipped too. There's also nowhere to add a high-contrast theme or a second brand without another global swap. This is misconception `design-system-architecture.m3`: tokens treated as color variables. A semantic tier (`color.surface.default`, `color.emphasis.bg`) would let each theme choose, per purpose, which primitive to use, and the names would stay honest.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The output looks like it worked, since every pair inverted. Look at what it cost: the primitive named `ink.900` (the darkest ink) now holds the lightest color, so every name in the palette lies. The badge, which was meant to stay dark in both themes as an emphasis element, flipped too. There's also nowhere to add a high-contrast theme or a second brand without another global swap. This is misconception `design-system-architecture.m3`: tokens treated as color variables. A semantic tier (`color.surface.default`, `color.emphasis.bg`) would let each theme choose, per purpose, which primitive to use, and the names would stay honest.
hints: Look at what the primitive named ink.900 holds after the swap, not just whether the pairs inverted.
There is no semantic tier here: every value is being read straight from a primitive.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: The Card component's stylesheet references color.gold.600 directly instead of a semantic token like color.surface.emphasis. What has to happen when the museum adds a dark theme?
options: Every component that references that primitive must be edited by hand, since there is no semantic layer between it and the raw palette
Nothing changes, because primitives already vary by theme
Only the custom property's name needs to be updated, not its value
The build script infers a dark equivalent for every primitive automatically

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Without a semantic tier to swap, theming means editing components one by one.
Primitives are raw and theme-independent by definition; they never carry per-theme values.
The value is exactly what is wrong; renaming the variable does not change what color it holds.
No such inference exists. A theme is an explicit semantic map, not a computed guess.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Components should consume semantic tokens, never primitives directly. The semantic tier is the only layer a theme switch is allowed to touch, which is what lets dark mode ship without editing a single component.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A semantic token is named color.warningRed. A rebrand changes the warning color to orange. What is wrong with the name itself, independent of the rebrand?
options: The name describes appearance, not purpose, so it starts lying the moment the color it points to changes
Nothing; semantic tokens should include the color name for clarity
The token should be a primitive instead
The token should be renamed every time the palette changes

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A purpose name like color.warning stays true no matter which primitive it points at; an appearance name does not.
Baking the color into the name is exactly the common error this lecture names: a semantic token should be named for what it means, not what it currently looks like.
Making it a primitive would remove the purpose meaning entirely and break theming.
Renaming on every palette change is the cost of the wrong name in the first place, not a fix for it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Semantic names carry purpose (color.warning, color.accent), never appearance. A name built from the current color is a name that lies as soon as that color changes.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A theme build emits CSS without checking contrast. High-contrast mode ships with a 3.2:1 text-on-background pair. What should have caught this before merge?
options: An automated contrast check in the token build, failing when a theme's required pairs do not meet its threshold (4.5:1, or 7:1 for high contrast)
A designer eyeballing the theme in Figma
Nothing; contrast is a components concern, not a token concern
Browser developer tools warn about this automatically at build time

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. The build should validate every required text and background pair, in every theme, against the threshold that theme is supposed to meet.
Eyeballing does not scale and misses exact ratios; an automated check is what this lecture's worked example runs.
Contrast is a token-and-theme concern precisely because the token build is what emits the paired colors in the first place.
Dev tools inspect a running page; they run nothing at build time and would not stop this from merging.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The token build validates references, cycles, and contrast together, before anything ships: unresolved references, cycles, and any text/background pair below its theme's threshold should all fail the build.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank the tiers resolveTokens walks through when resolving button.primary.bg for a theme, starting from what you asked for and ending at the raw value.
options: Semantic value: the theme-specific alias, for example {color.gold.600}
Component token: what you asked for, button.primary.bg
Primitive value: the final, raw value, for example #8a6d1c

optionFeedback.feedback: The semantic value comes second: it is what the component token points at, and it is the one thing that differs per theme.
The component token comes first: it is the name you actually asked resolveTokens to resolve.
The primitive value comes last: it is where every reference chain bottoms out, the same raw value regardless of theme.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Component asks, semantic answers per theme, primitive supplies the raw value. Each tier only ever points at the tier below it, never the other way around.
hints: Which tier is the one you call resolveTokens with?
Which tier is the only one that changes when the theme changes?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 4 built graph traversal (DOM and JSON traversal, topological sort) around a visited set that tracks the path so far, specifically to catch a cycle instead of recursing forever. resolveTokens in this lecture walks component to semantic to primitive references the same way. Using Section 4's idea, explain what resolveTokens must track while it resolves a name, and what an unguarded token cycle (a references b, b references a) would do without that check.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: resolveTokens has to carry the path of names already visited while walking one reference chain, exactly like a graph traversal's visited set, so that if the name it is about to resolve is already on that path, it can throw a token-cycle error instead of recursing forever. Without that check, a referencing b referencing a would recurse indefinitely, or blow the call stack, the same failure Section 4 taught for an unguarded graph walk. The difference here is that the check has to be per resolution chain, cleared between top-level component tokens, rather than global, since two unrelated component tokens can legitimately share a middle reference.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 9 derived a fluid spacing scale with clamp() and put every value in an early tokens cascade layer, as raw numbers with no theme dimension. This lecture puts spacing in the same three-tier system as color. Explain what changes once that scale becomes a token system: which tier do the clamp() values live in, and what does gaining a semantic tier actually buy a spacing token that a bare clamp() value did not have?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The clamp() values themselves become primitives, raw and meaningless names like space.4, the same role color.gold.600 plays for color. What a semantic tier adds is a purpose name, like space.compact or space.section, that a theme or a denser mode can point at a different primitive without touching any component, the same benefit theming gets for color. A bare clamp() value sitting in an early cascade layer with no semantic tier is exactly as stuck as a component referencing color.gold.600 directly: making one purpose use a different scale step means hunting down every place that number is used.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Resolving button.primary.bg in three themes
workedExamples.problem: Resolving button.primary.bg in three themes
steps: `button.primary.bg` → `{color.accent}` (component → semantic).
Light: `color.accent` → `{color.gold.600}` → `#8a6d1c`.
Dark: `color.accent` → `{color.gold.300}` → `#e0c46c`.
High contrast: `color.accent` → `{color.black}` → `#000000`.
Validation: the button's foreground `{color.surface.default}` on its background must reach 4.5:1 in light and dark, and 7:1 in high contrast. The build fails otherwise.
workedExamples.conclusion: One component token, three correct values, zero component changes. Exercise s11-e1 builds this resolver.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the three token tiers and what each one is for.
Which tier changes per theme, and why does that keep components untouched?
What three things should a token build validate before it emits CSS?
Section 4 tracked a visited path to catch graph cycles. Why does resolveTokens need the same idea, and what would a token cycle look like if it skipped that check?
Section 9 built a fluid spacing scale as raw clamp() values in an early cascade layer. Which token tier do those values become, and what does a semantic tier add that the raw values did not have?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 11.2: Headless, Compound, and Slotted Components

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Separate **behavior** (state, keyboard, ARIA) from **presentation** with headless components. (objective o2)
2. Build Select and Dialog as compound components that share state through context. (objective o2)
3. Use slots so consumers can customize structure without a prop for every case. (objective o2)

terms.definition: Provides behavior and accessibility (state, keyboard handling, ARIA props) with no styling, often through hooks or prop getters.
A set of components that work together through shared context: `<Select><Select.Trigger/><Select.Listbox><Select.Option/></Select.Listbox></Select>`.
A function returning the props an element needs (`getTriggerProps()`), merged with the consumer's props.
A named place in a component where consumers put their own content (`<Dialog.Title>`, `<Dialog.Footer>`), or the `asChild` pattern that renders the consumer's element with the component's behavior.
The value is owned by the parent (`value` + `onChange`), or internally (`defaultValue`).

contentBlocks.content:
### Why headless and compound

Every museum brand styles its "Choose a ticket type" select differently. The **behavior** (the listbox pattern from s7, typeahead, `aria-activedescendant`, keyboard contract) must be identical and correct everywhere. A headless core carries the behavior once, and each brand supplies the presentation.

A compound API keeps the pieces composable:

// for reading: React + TypeScript
<Select value={ticket} onValueChange={setTicket}>
  <Select.Label>Ticket type</Select.Label>
  <Select.Trigger className="museum-select" />
  <Select.Listbox>
    <Select.Option value="adult">Adult · $22</Select.Option>
    <Select.Option value="member" disabled>Member · Free (sign in)</Select.Option>
    <Select.Option value="student">Student · $12</Select.Option>
  </Select.Listbox>
</Select>

Internally, `Select` holds the state (open, active option, value) in context. `Select.Trigger` spreads `getTriggerProps()` (`role="combobox"`, `aria-expanded`, `aria-controls`, `aria-activedescendant`). Options register themselves in a list so keyboard navigation knows their order, and s3's keys and render behavior matter here: memoize the context value so options don't re-render on every keystroke.
### Dialog with slots

<Dialog.Root>
  <Dialog.Trigger asChild><Button variant="secondary">Plan your visit</Button></Dialog.Trigger>
  <Dialog.Content>
    <Dialog.Title>Plan your visit</Dialog.Title>
    <Dialog.Description>Choose a date and time slot.</Dialog.Description>
    {/* consumer content */}
    <Dialog.Close asChild><Button variant="ghost">Close</Button></Dialog.Close>
  </Dialog.Content>
</Dialog.Root>

The Dialog core wires `aria-labelledby` to the Title slot and `aria-describedby` to the Description slot, traps focus and returns it (s7), closes on Escape, and generates unique ids per instance. `asChild` lets the consumer's own `Button` become the trigger without wrapping a button in a button.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s11-m2): Headless core, many skins. Center: a "Select core" box listing state, keyboard contract, ARIA prop getters, and option registry. Three differently styled select skins (three museum brands) around it connect to the core through getTriggerProps/getOptionProps. A second panel shows the Dialog compound tree with Title and Description slots wired to aria-labelledby and aria-describedby.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: a memoized context value keeps the same reference across renders when its dependencies do not change, so consumers relying on reference equality (like React.memo on Option) do not re-render. Call makeContextValue twice with unchanged state and confirm the references are equal, then call it with a changed activeIndex and confirm they are not.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: component APIs
contentBlocks.content:
- **Behavior and styling fused**, so every brand re-implements keyboard handling.
- **Non-unique ids** when two dialogs are on the page.
- **Context values recreated every render**, so every option re-renders on each keystroke.
- **A prop for every visual tweak** instead of slots.
- **Wrapping interactive elements inside other interactive elements** (use `asChild`).

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Headless cores own behavior and accessibility. Brands own presentation.
- Compound components share state through context. Slots replace most configuration props.

interactionSequence.prompt: Museum Brand B copies Select's keyboard handling into its own component so it can restyle freely, instead of using the headless core. Six months later a keyboard bug is found in the typeahead logic. What does Brand B now have to do that a brand using the headless core would not?
options: Find and fix the same bug in its own copy, separately from every other brand's copy
Nothing; the bug only affects the headless core
Wait for the design tool to push a fix automatically
Report it to the core team, who fixes it for free in Brand B's copy too

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A copy has no connection back to the core, so every bug the core team fixes has to be independently rediscovered and fixed in every copy.
The copy runs its own code; nothing about the core protects a hand-rolled duplicate.
Design tools do not push behavior fixes into application code.
The core team cannot patch code it does not own or ship into.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is the cost of fusing behavior and styling: every brand that re-implements keyboard handling instead of using the headless core now owns that logic, and every future bug, independently, forever.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Two Dialog instances are on the exhibition page at once, both built with a hardcoded id="dialog-title" on their Title. What goes wrong for a screen reader user?
options: The second dialog's aria-labelledby may point at the wrong title element, or the duplicate id is simply invalid HTML
Nothing; the browser automatically disambiguates duplicate ids
The screen reader announces both titles at once, every time
The focus trap stops working entirely

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Two elements sharing an id makes an id-based reference like aria-labelledby ambiguous or wrong, which is exactly why the core must generate a unique id per instance.
HTML ids are not deduplicated by the browser; a duplicate id is simply invalid.
That is not how aria-labelledby resolves; it targets the id it names, not every element with a title role.
Focus trapping and unique ids are separate guarantees; one failing does not imply the other fails.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A headless Dialog core generates a unique id per instance specifically so aria-labelledby, aria-describedby, and aria-controls always point at the right element, even with several dialogs mounted at once.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A Select's Listbox re-renders every Option on every keystroke, even though only the active option's state changed. What is the most likely cause?
options: The context value passed to Select's Provider is a new object literal on every render, so every consumer sees a "changed" value even when nothing they care about changed
React re-renders all children of any component by default, and there is no way around it
Options should be class components instead of function components
The Listbox needs more props to control re-renders individually

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. An inline object literal is a new reference every render; context consumers compare by reference, so every Option re-renders regardless of whether its own data changed.
Re-renders are driven by what actually changed, including context identity; a re-render is not an unavoidable fact of nature.
Component style (class vs function) has nothing to do with this; the bug is the object literal's identity, not the component type.
More props do not fix an identity problem; memoizing the context value does.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Memoize the context value (for example with useMemo, recomputed only when open, activeIndex, or value actually change) so consumers keep the same reference across renders where nothing they depend on changed.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 3 explained that a context value re-created as a new object literal on every render makes every consumer re-render, even ones whose actual data did not change, because React compares that value by reference. Select's Trigger, Listbox, and every Option all read the same context. Explain what happens on every keystroke if Select's Provider passes value={{ open, activeIndex, value }} inline, and how memoizing that value fixes it.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: An inline object literal is a brand-new reference on every render of Select, so even though open, activeIndex, and value might be unchanged between two renders, the context value is "different" by reference, and every component reading that context, meaning every single Option, re-renders on every keystroke, including the ones nowhere near the active option. Memoizing the value, recomputed only when open, activeIndex, or value actually change, gives consumers the same reference across renders where nothing changed, so React can skip re-rendering options that do not depend on what changed, exactly the fix Section 3 taught for this pattern.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 7 specified the combobox and dialog keyboard and ARIA contracts down to which key does what and which ARIA attribute tracks which piece of state. This lecture's headless Select core is built to carry that exact contract. If Museum Brand C decides to skip the headless core and hand-roll its own keyboard handling to save time, what does it now own that it did not before, and why can't it just copy Section 7's contract once and be done?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Brand C now owns the entire keyboard and ARIA contract itself: every key handler, every aria-activedescendant update, every edge case Section 7 worked through (typeahead, wrap-around, disabled options), and it owns finding and fixing every bug in that logic forever, independently of every other brand. Copying Section 7's contract once is not the same as depending on the headless core, because the core is a single place that gets fixed once when a bug or a new requirement shows up, while a copy starts drifting the moment anyone touches either version, exactly the "behavior and styling fused" common error this lecture names.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Designing the Dialog's public API
workedExamples.problem: Designing the Dialog's public API
steps: **List what consumers need to control:** title, description, body content, footer actions, open state (controlled or uncontrolled), initial focus target.
**List what the system guarantees:** focus trap and return, Escape, `aria-modal`, ARIA wiring, portal and stacking, unique ids.
**Map needs to slots, not props:** `Title`, `Description`, `Close` as components. Body content as children. `initialFocus` as a ref prop (a real behavior option).
**Reject prop bloat:** no `titleColor`, `showCloseIcon`, `footerAlign`, `closeButtonText`. Consumers compose those with slots and tokens.
workedExamples.conclusion: A small API with slots covers more cases than a long prop list, and the guarantees stay inside the system.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What does a headless component own, and what does it deliberately not own?
Why do slots prevent prop explosion in a way that adding more props cannot?
Section 3 explained why a context value re-created every render forces every consumer to re-render. Why does Select's compound context need to be memoized for exactly that reason?
Section 7 specified the combobox and dialog ARIA and keyboard contracts in detail. What does a headless core carry over from that contract that a hand-rolled copy would have to re-earn on its own?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 11.3: Props vs Composition: the Button

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Design a Button with a small, closed set of variants and sizes and well-defined states (disabled, loading, icon). (objective o3)
2. Encode rules in types (icon-only requires a label) and at runtime (dev warnings). (objective o3)
3. Write the props-vs-composition decision record. (objective o3)

terms.definition: A named, designed style option (`primary`, `secondary`, `ghost`, `danger`), mapped to tokens.
A component accumulating props for every special case (`color`, `padding`, `rounded`, `iconRight`, `iconLeftSize`…).
A deliberately limited way to go off-system (`className`, or composing primitives), with its cost made visible.
A short document that records a design decision, the alternatives considered, and why.

contentBlocks.content:
### Few props, closed sets

More props don't make a component more flexible (misconception `design-system-architecture.m2`). Each prop multiplies the states you must design, test, and document: 4 variants × 3 sizes × loading × disabled × icon placement is already about 100 combinations. Props should be **closed sets of designed options**. Anything else goes through composition: put an `Icon` inside the button as a child, or build a new component from primitives.
### Encode the rules in types

### Loading and disabled

- **Disabled:** the native `disabled` attribute. It isn't focusable, and that's the correct choice when the action truly can't be taken. Consider explaining *why* nearby instead.
- **Loading:** keep the button **focusable** (focus mustn't jump away mid-submit), and set `aria-busy="true"` and `aria-disabled="true"`, ignoring clicks while it's loading. Show a spinner, and keep the label for screen readers.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s11-m5): The Button matrix. A documentation page showing the closed set: four variants (primary, secondary, ghost, danger) × three sizes, plus loading, disabled, icon-start, and icon-only states, all rendered in light, dark, and high-contrast themes. A struck-through panel titled "Not props" lists rejected requests (color, padding, rounded, iconEnd) with a link to the composition alternative for each.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: a closed API multiplies designed states manageably, but a handful of "small" extra props multiplies them far past what anyone designed, tested, or documented. Add one more prop of your own to exploded below and recompute.

contentBlocks.caption: Prop explosion, counted exactly. Predict both totals before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: Button APIs
contentBlocks.content:
- **Free-form color and spacing props.**
- **Icon-only buttons without an accessible name.**
- **Using `disabled` for loading**, which loses focus.
- **Boolean prop soup** (`primary`, `secondary`, and `danger` as separate booleans, all settable at once). Use one `variant`.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Closed sets of designed variants. Compose everything else.
- Encode the rules in types and dev-time checks. Record the decision.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team debates giving Button three separate boolean props, primary, secondary, and danger, all independently settable, versus one variant prop with a closed set of string values. What is wrong with the boolean version?
options: Boolean props can combine into invalid states, like primary and danger both true, that a closed variant set simply does not allow
Booleans are slower to check than strings at runtime
TypeScript cannot type boolean props
There is nothing wrong; more independent props give more flexibility

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A closed variant enum makes the invalid combination unrepresentable; boolean soup lets it exist and forces someone to remember never to set two.
There is no meaningful performance difference between checking a boolean and checking a string in this context.
TypeScript types booleans fine; the problem is the design, not the type system's capability.
More independent props is exactly the states nobody designed, tested, or documented.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Boolean prop soup lets a consumer set primary and danger at once, a state nobody designed for. A single closed variant set makes that combination impossible to express.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: An icon-only close button ships with icon="close" and no label prop. What does a screen reader announce for it, and what should the type system have prevented?
options: Nothing usable is announced, since there is no accessible name; ButtonProps should require label whenever iconOnly is true
It announces "close," because the icon name doubles as the label automatically
It announces "button," which is good enough
Screen readers skip icon-only buttons entirely, so no announcement is needed

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Without an accessible name the button is effectively unlabeled; the discriminated union in this lecture requires label whenever iconOnly is true, catching this at compile time.
An icon name is not exposed to assistive technology on its own; it has to be wired through an accessible name like aria-label.
A generic role announcement with no name tells a screen reader user nothing about what the button does.
Icon-only buttons are still interactive controls and are announced; the problem is what gets announced, not whether anything is.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: iconOnly: true still requires label in the ButtonProps union specifically so an icon-only button always has an accessible name, wired to aria-label, and the missing case fails to type-check instead of shipping silently broken.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A "Buy tickets" button sets disabled: true while the purchase request is in flight. A keyboard user who had just tabbed to the button and pressed Enter reports their focus "disappeared." What is the actual bug, and the fix?
options: disabled removes the element from the focus order immediately, losing focus mid-interaction; use aria-busy and aria-disabled instead and keep the element focusable
Add role="button" to a styled div instead of using a real button element
Add an aria-live region around the button so the loss of focus gets announced
Nothing is wrong; disabled is the correct way to prevent double submits

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A loading button must stay focusable. Communicate the state with aria-busy and aria-disabled, and ignore repeat clicks in the handler, instead of removing it from the focus order.
That trades a real, natively focusable and operable element for one that needs every behavior rebuilt by hand, and does not address the focus loss.
Announcing that focus vanished does not give it back; the fix is to never remove focus in the first place.
disabled is exactly what causes the bug: it is correct for actions that truly cannot be taken, not for a brief loading state.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Keep a loading button focusable. Set aria-busy="true" and aria-disabled="true", show a spinner, keep the label for screen readers, and ignore clicks in the handler while loading, instead of removing the element from the focus order.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 1 used a discriminated union so TypeScript could rule out an invalid combination of fields at compile time. This lecture's ButtonProps type unions two shapes: iconOnly?: false with a plain label, and iconOnly: true with both icon and label required. Explain what invalid state that union rules out, and what a single flat type with iconOnly?: boolean, icon?: IconName, label: string would have allowed instead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The union rules out an icon-only button with no accessible name: when iconOnly is true, the type requires both icon and label, so a call like describe({ iconOnly: true, icon: 'close' }) fails to type-check before the code ever runs, exactly like Section 1's discriminated unions catching an invalid combination at compile time instead of at runtime. A single flat type with iconOnly?: boolean would let iconOnly: true type-check fine with label or icon omitted, silently producing a button with no accessible name, the exact bug Section 1's pattern exists to prevent by construction rather than by remembering to add a runtime check.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 5 argued that a design decision needs a written record, not just a conversation, so the reasoning survives past the person who made it. This lecture's Button decision record lists a Decision, a Why, an Escape hatch, and Rejected alternatives. Explain what a Slack message saying "let's keep Button simple, no color prop" fails to give the next engineer that the decision record does.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A Slack message gives a conclusion with no reasoning attached: it tells the next engineer what was decided but not why, so when they hit a case that feels like it needs a color prop, they have no way to tell whether their case was already considered and rejected, or is genuinely new. The decision record's Why and Rejected sections are exactly what Section 5 argued a design doc needs: they let the next engineer check their proposal against the actual reasoning, that custom colors bypass tokens and break theming, and the alternatives already ruled out, instead of re-litigating the same conversation from zero or quietly reopening a decision made for a good reason.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: The decision record (excerpt)
workedExamples.problem:
> **Decision:** Button exposes `variant` (4), `size` (3), `loading`, `disabled`, `iconStart`, and `iconOnly` + `icon` + `label`. No `color`, `padding`, `radius`, or `iconEnd` props.
> **Why:** Every prop is a designed, tested state. Custom colors bypass tokens and break theming and contrast guarantees. Trailing icons appear in one place (external links), so that's handled with an `ExternalLink` component composed from `Button` + `Icon`.
> **Escape hatch:** `className` is allowed for layout (margins, grid placement) only. A lint rule flags color and spacing overrides.
> **Rejected:** a `color` prop (breaks themes), `as` polymorphism on Button (use `asChild` in the few cases that need a link that looks like a button).
steps: **Decision:** Button exposes variant (4 options), size (3 options), loading, disabled, iconStart, and iconOnly plus icon plus label. No color, padding, radius, or iconEnd props.

**Why:** Every prop is a designed, tested state. Custom colors bypass tokens and break theming and contrast guarantees. Trailing icons appear in one place (external links), so that is handled with an ExternalLink component composed from Button and Icon.
**Escape hatch:** className is allowed for layout (margins, grid placement) only. A lint rule flags color and spacing overrides.
**Rejected:** a color prop, because it breaks themes, and as polymorphism on Button, since asChild already covers the few cases that need a link that looks like a button.
workedExamples.conclusion: The record makes the trade-off explicit, so the next "can we just add a prop?" conversation starts from the reasoning, not from zero.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What ARIA attributes and focus behavior does a loading button need, and why not disabled?
Section 1 used a discriminated union to rule out an invalid field combination at compile time. What invalid Button state does the iconOnly union rule out the same way?

Section 5 argued a design decision needs a written record, not just a conversation. What does the Button decision record's Why and Rejected sections give the next engineer that a one-line Slack conclusion would not?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 11.4: Keeping Design and Code in Sync

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Export design-tool variables and compare them with code tokens. (objective o4)
2. Normalize values so only real differences are reported, across colors, dimensions, and aliases. (objective o4)
3. Decide the source of truth and the workflow for resolving drift. (objective o4)

terms.definition: Design-tool variables organized in collections with modes (for example light and dark). They can be exported through Figma's Variables REST API (availability depends on plan) or through plugins that write JSON.
A token that exists on only one side, or has different values on each side.
Converting equivalent representations to one form (`#FFF` → `#ffffff`, `16px` → `1rem` at a 16 px root) before comparing.
The side whose value wins when the two disagree. It's often the design tool for values and the code for names.

contentBlocks.content:
### A drift check in CI

1. **Export** design variables to JSON (in CI with an API token, or committed by the designer via a plugin).
2. **Flatten** both sides to `name → value`, resolving aliases.
3. **Normalize** values: lowercase hex, 3-digit to 6-digit hex, px to rem for dimensions (or everything to px), trimmed whitespace.
4. **Compare:** `onlyInDesign`, `onlyInCode`, `changed`.
5. **Report** as a PR comment. Fail the build only when you've agreed on the rules (for example, fail when a code-side value differs from design for semantic tokens).

Drift in spacing and type is as real as drift in color, so the checker must handle every token type, not just hex values (misconception `design-system-architecture.m3`).

contentBlocks.altText: Screenshot (s11-m3): A drift report as a PR comment. A bot comment titled "Token drift (design ↔ code)" with three sections: "Only in design (2): color.surface.sunken, space.3xl"; "Only in code (1): color.legacy.link"; "Changed (2): color.accent — design #8a6d1c, code #8b6d1c; space.m — design 1.25rem, code 1rem". A footer reads "Normalized: hex case, 3-digit hex, px→rem @16px."

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: normalizing (hex case, short hex, px to rem) before comparing removes noise so only real drift is reported. Add a pair of your own to `pairs` that looks different but should normalize to "same".

contentBlocks.caption: Normalizing four design/code pairs before comparing. Predict same or DRIFT for each line before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: design-code sync
contentBlocks.content:
- **Comparing raw strings** (case, short hex, unit differences) and drowning in false drift.
- **Checking only colors.**
- **No agreed source of truth**, so drift gets "fixed" in both directions.
- **Syncing names but not modes** (dark values drift separately).

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Export, flatten, normalize, compare, report, and do it for all token types and all modes.
- Agree on the source of truth and the resolution workflow before automating failures.

interactionSequence.prompt: A drift report lists 140 differences between design and code tokens. Almost all of them are #FFF versus #ffffff or 16px versus 1rem. What is the actual bug, and where does it live?
options: The comparison never normalizes values before checking equality, so equivalent representations are reported as drift
The design team and engineering team simply disagree on 140 tokens
Figma's export format is broken and needs a different plugin
The code tokens file is out of date and needs a full re-sync

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Case, short hex, and unit differences are equivalent representations, not disagreements; normalizing before comparing removes them from the report.
A raw string mismatch is not a real disagreement; it is exactly what normalization is built to filter out.
Nothing here points at a broken export; the bug is in how the two sides get compared, after export.
Re-syncing without normalizing would just reproduce the same noisy report.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Normalize both sides (lowercase hex, expand short hex, convert px to rem at a fixed root, or vice versa) before comparing, so the report only contains real drift, not equivalent spellings of the same value.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A drift checker only flattens and compares tokens whose name starts with color. A spacing token silently drifts from 20px in design to 1rem in code for three months. Why did the checker miss it?
options: It filtered by token type before comparing, so non-color drift, in spacing, radius, type, and motion, was never checked at all
Spacing tokens cannot drift because they are just numbers
The normalization function does not support px units
Spacing drift is invisible and no automated check could catch it

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Filtering to color.* tokens means every other token type is invisible to the checker, drift and all.
A number can drift exactly like a color can; nothing about being numeric makes a value immune to disagreement.
px-to-rem conversion is a normal part of normalizing dimension tokens; the missing piece here is checking those tokens at all.
The exact same normalize-flatten-compare approach used for color works for spacing; the checker just needs to run it there too.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Drift in spacing and type is as real as drift in color. A checker scoped to one token type misses every other kind of drift entirely, which is exactly the common error this lecture names.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Design changes a token's value, and independently, an engineer "fixes" the same token back to the old value in code, believing design made a mistake. What is missing from the workflow?
options: An agreed source of truth for each kind of token, and a resolution workflow, so a real disagreement gets decided once instead of silently reversed by whoever notices first
A faster CI pipeline
A rule that code always wins, no matter the token
Nothing; both sides will eventually converge on their own

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Without an agreed source of truth and a process for resolving real disagreements, the same token can get "fixed" back and forth indefinitely.
Speed has nothing to do with two sides disagreeing about which value is correct.
The lecture's key term notes the source of truth is often the design tool for values, not an unconditional rule either way.
Without a documented resolution, there is no reason the flip-flopping would ever stop on its own.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Agree on the source of truth (often the design tool for values, code for names) and a resolution workflow before automating failures, so a real disagreement gets decided once and stays decided.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A drift checker is set to fail the build whenever any difference appears between design and code tokens, including differences the team has not yet agreed are meaningful, like whether space.3xl should exist in code at all. What goes wrong with a zero-tolerance policy before the team has agreed on the rules, and what should the checker do instead in the meantime?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A zero-tolerance policy turns every open design conversation into a broken build, so engineers either stop trusting the check and start merging past it, or start silently "fixing" code to match design even when design was the one that was wrong, exactly the "no agreed source of truth" common error this lecture names. Until the team has actually agreed on the rules, for example which token types must match exactly and who wins when they do not, the checker should report drift as visible information, a PR comment listing onlyInDesign, onlyInCode, and changed, without failing the build, and only start failing once specific categories have an agreed answer.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Separating real drift from noise
workedExamples.problem:
| Token | Design | Code | After normalization | Drift? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| color.text.default | `#1B1A17` | `#1b1a17` | same | no (case) |
| color.surface.default | `#FFF` | `#ffffff` | same | no (short hex) |
| space.m | `20px` | `1rem` | 1.25rem vs 1rem | **yes** |
| color.accent | `#8a6d1c` | `#8b6d1c` | different | **yes** (a typo in code) |
| color.legacy.link | missing | `#0645ad` | only in code | **yes** (deprecate or add to design) |
steps: color.text.default: design #1B1A17, code #1b1a17. After normalizing case, both are the same. No drift.
color.surface.default: design #FFF, code #ffffff. After expanding the short hex, both are the same. No drift.
space.m: design 20px, code 1rem. After converting px to rem at a 16px root, that is 1.25rem versus 1rem. Drift.
color.accent: design #8a6d1c, code #8b6d1c. Still different after normalization. Drift, a typo in code.
color.legacy.link: missing in design, #0645ad in code. Only in code. Drift, deprecate it or add it to design.
workedExamples.conclusion: Without normalization you get noisy reports that everyone ignores. With it, the report is short and every item needs a decision.

retrievalPractice.prompt: List the normalizations a drift checker needs to run before comparing design and code tokens.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 11.5: Evolving Without Breaking Consumers

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Classify changes as major, minor, or patch under semantic versioning. (objective o5)
2. Run a deprecation path: warn, provide a codemod, document the migration, remove in the next major. (objective o5)
3. Explain why governance and release are part of the system. (objective o5)

terms.definition: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH. Breaking changes bump major, backward-compatible features bump minor, fixes bump patch.
Anything that can make existing consumer code fail or behave differently: a removed or renamed prop, a changed type, a removed token.
Marking something as "still works, will be removed," with a dev-time warning and a documented replacement.
A script that rewrites consumer code automatically (for example with jscodeshift).
Before/after examples, the reasons, and step-by-step instructions for upgrading.
How changes are proposed, reviewed, versioned, and communicated.

contentBlocks.content:
### A design system isn't just a component library

A library of components with no tokens, docs, contribution rules, versioning, and deprecation paths is a pile of code (misconception `design-system-architecture.m1`). Consumers at five museums can't upgrade safely if a rename ships in a minor release. Designers can't trust it if the tokens drift. Nobody adopts what isn't documented. The release process *is* part of the product.

### The deprecation path for `Button`'s `kind` → `variant`

1. **v2.8 (minor):** add `variant`. Keep `kind` working, but log a dev-only warning: "`kind` is deprecated, use `variant` (codemod: `npx museum-ds-codemod button-variant`)."
2. **Ship a codemod** that rewrites `kind="outline"` to `variant="secondary"`, `size="large"` to `size="lg"`, and `icon iconName="x"` to `iconStart="x"`, and reports what it couldn't migrate.
3. **Migration guide** with before/after snippets, why the change was made (closed variant set, theming), and a checklist.
4. **v3.0 (major):** remove `kind`. The changelog links the guide. Consumers upgrade when they're ready.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s11-m4): A deprecation timeline. A horizontal timeline: v2.7 → v2.8 ("variant added; kind deprecated; warning; codemod") → v2.9 ("usage telemetry: kind in 12% of call sites") → v3.0 ("kind removed; migration guide"). Beneath it, adoption bars for five museum apps show them moving from v2 to v3 at different times.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: the most severe change in a release decides the version bump, and version parts are independent integers, not decimals. Add a mix of changes of your own to a fresh call and predict the result before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: releases
contentBlocks.content:
- **Renames shipped in minor versions.**
- **Deprecations with no warning, no codemod, and no guide.**
- **Treating token value changes as invisible.** They change every consumer's UI, so document them.
- **No usage data before removing APIs.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 11.5 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- The most severe change decides the version bump.
- Deprecate → warn → codemod → guide → remove in the next major.
- Governance and release make a library into a system.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Which version number?.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
3.0.0
2.10.0
2.9.4
```

**Why intuition fails.** "Mostly small changes" feels like a minor release, but semver takes the **most severe** change. One rename among many additions still breaks callers, so the version is 3.0.0. The second line surprises people for a different reason: after 2.9 comes **2.10**, not 3.0, because version parts are independent integers, not decimals. The third shows that a lone bugfix is a patch. Treating releases casually is part of misconception `design-system-architecture.m1`: without a disciplined release process, consumers can't upgrade safely.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: "Mostly small changes" feels like a minor release, but semver takes the **most severe** change. One rename among many additions still breaks callers, so the version is 3.0.0. The second line surprises people for a different reason: after 2.9 comes **2.10**, not 3.0, because version parts are independent integers, not decimals. The third shows that a lone bugfix is a patch. Treating releases casually is part of misconception `design-system-architecture.m1`: without a disciplined release process, consumers can't upgrade safely.
hints: Find the single most severe change type among all the changes in each call, and let only that one decide.
After .9 comes .10, not a fresh major: version parts are independent integers, not decimal places.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: Version 2.10.0's changelog says "minor release: new Tag component, bug fixes, and Dialog's onDismiss renamed to onOpenChange." Five museum apps upgrade routinely, since it is "just a minor." What happens?
options: Every app that used onDismiss breaks immediately, because a rename is a breaking change regardless of what the release is labeled
Nothing; minor releases are always safe to adopt
Only apps that use the Tag component are affected
The rename is automatically aliased for one release

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A rename breaks existing callers no matter how the release is labeled; the version number should have reflected that.
A minor label does not make a breaking change safe; it just hides the fact that it is breaking.
Any consumer calling the Dialog with onDismiss breaks, whether or not they use Tag.
Nothing in this scenario provides an alias; the prop is simply renamed.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Semver is determined by the most severe change, and a rename is major, no matter how small the rest of the release is. Shipping it as a minor breaks every consumer on a routine upgrade.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A prop is removed in a major version with a one-line changelog entry and nothing else. What did the deprecation path skip, and what does that cost consumers?
options: It skipped the warning period, the codemod, and the migration guide, so every consumer has to rediscover the change by reading a diff or hitting a runtime error
Nothing was skipped; a changelog entry is sufficient documentation for any change
It skipped only the migration guide, since a codemod is not necessary for prop removals
The version number should have been a minor bump instead

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Warn, then codemod, then guide, then remove, is the path; skipping straight to removal with no notice leaves consumers to discover the break the hard way.
A changelog line names the change but gives consumers no warning before it happened and no automated way to migrate; treating "shipped" as "done" is exactly the gap this lecture calls out.
A codemod is exactly what turns a breaking rename or removal into a mechanical, low-effort upgrade instead of a manual hunt.
Removal is correctly major; the problem is the missing warning, codemod, and guide, not the version number.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A real deprecation path warns first (a dev-time message with the replacement), ships a codemod, documents the migration, and only removes the old API in the next major.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A patch release quietly changes color.accent's value across the whole system, treated as a bugfix since "it's just a token, not an API." What is wrong with calling this a patch?
options: A token value change repaints every consumer's UI; this lecture classifies it as at least a minor-level token-value-change, not a silent patch
Token changes never affect rendering, so patch is correct
Token changes should always be major, since they change what is on screen
Tokens should not be versioned at all

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. token-value-change is classified as a minor change in this lecture's scheme precisely because it is visible everywhere, and it should be documented, not shipped as an invisible patch.
A color value change repaints every component that consumes it; treating a token as too trivial to matter is exactly the belief this section's tokens lecture argues against.
This lecture's own classification puts token-value-change under minor, not major; treating every visual change as major would make ordinary theme tuning impossible to ship.
Tokens are part of the public contract of a design system and need the same version discipline as props and components.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The most severe change decides the version. A token value change is classified as minor here, visible and worth documenting in the changelog, but not breaking, and never something to slip through silently as a patch.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank the deprecation path for Button's kind to variant rename, from first to last.
options: Remove kind entirely in the next major version
Add variant in a minor release; kind still works but logs a dev warning
Ship a codemod that rewrites kind usage to variant automatically
Publish a migration guide with before and after examples and the reasoning

optionFeedback.feedback: Removal comes last, in the next major version, only after consumers have had a warning, a codemod, and a guide.
Adding the new prop with a warning on the old one comes first, in a minor release, so nothing breaks yet.
The codemod comes second: an automated way to migrate, shipped alongside or right after the warning.
The migration guide comes third: the human-readable explanation and checklist, ready before anyone is forced to move.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Warn, then codemod, then guide, then remove in the next major. Each stage exists to make the next one optional for as long as possible.
hints: Which stage has to happen before consumers can be asked to change anything?
Removal is the one irreversible stage; where does an irreversible stage belong?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 8 shipped risky code behind a feature flag, dark at first, then rolled out gradually, with a kill switch ready if something went wrong. Explain how the kind to variant deprecation path (add variant behind a warning, ship a codemod, then remove kind in the next major) is the same underlying idea applied to a public API instead of a runtime feature, and what plays the role of the kill switch here.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Both patterns let you ship a change without forcing everyone onto it at once: a feature flag lets code exist in production while only some traffic depends on it, and the deprecated-but-working kind prop lets the new variant API exist in production while only the consumers who have migrated depend on it, with the old path still there for everyone else. The kill switch here is the fact that v2.8 never removes kind, so if the new variant API turns out to need a change, nothing forces the team to remove the escape hatch before it is ready; the equivalent of flipping the flag back off is simply not shipping the major version yet, leaving consumers who have not migrated completely unaffected.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Choosing the next version
workedExamples.problem: Current `2.9.3`. Changes in this release: added `Tag` component, fixed focus ring on `Select`, deprecated `Card.Header` in favor of the `Card.Title` slot, **renamed `Dialog` prop `onDismiss` → `onOpenChange`**.
steps: The rename breaks existing callers, so this is **major**.
So the version is `3.0.0`, even though most of the changes are minor.
Better plan: ship the rename as an **added** `onOpenChange` with `onDismiss` deprecated in `2.10.0`, and remove it in `3.0.0` later, alongside other breaking changes.
workedExamples.conclusion: Semver is determined by the most severe change. Deprecation lets you ship improvements now and break later, on purpose.

retrievalPractice.prompt: A rename ships in a release. What version bump does it force, no matter how small the rest of the release is?
Walk the deprecation path from a first warning to removal, naming what happens at each stage.
Section 8 used a feature flag and a kill switch to ship risky code gradually. What plays the role of each in the kind to variant deprecation path?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: The Museum Design System

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. The engine exercises cover the design system's logic: token resolution, prop contracts, drift detection, and versioning. React compound components (headless Select and Dialog) are read as code above and built by hand in the Practical Activity below, not checked automatically, and the TypeScript union from Lecture 11.3 is type-checked with tsc --strict outside the engine.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenges 1 and 3 give you a small scaffold (the token maps, or the design and code token fixtures) and leave the resolution or comparison logic to you. Challenges 2 and 4 have no scaffolding: the whole program is yours. The two test-suite challenges turn it around: the Button codemod challenge gives you correct code and asks you to write the tests that prove it; the headless Dialog challenge gives you a correct test suite and asks you to fix broken code until it passes.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your Button codemod tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the Button codemod challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "The Museum Design System."** Expected time is 12–14 hours.

1. **Three-tier tokens** in DTCG-style JSON (`$value`, `$type`, `{alias}`) for color, space (s9 fluid steps), radius, type, and motion duration (s10), with light, dark, and high-contrast themes for two museum brands. Include a build script (your s11-e1 resolver) that emits layered CSS custom properties and **fails** on unresolved references, cycles, or any text/background pair below 4.5:1 (AAA 7:1 in high contrast). *(o1)*
2. **Headless Select and Dialog** (React + TypeScript) with compound components (`Select.Trigger`, `Select.Listbox`, `Select.Option`; `Dialog.Trigger`, `Dialog.Content`, `Dialog.Title`, `Dialog.Description`, `Dialog.Close`), `asChild` slots, a memoized context, unique ids, and the full s7 keyboard contracts. Style both for two brands with no behavior changes. *(o2)*
3. **Button** with typed props (the s11-ts1 union), the runtime contract (s11-e2) as a dev-mode check, loading and disabled states, and a **decision record** on props vs composition. *(o3)*
4. **Figma ↔ code sync:** export variables (Variables REST API if your plan allows, or a plugin that writes JSON), then run your s11-e3 drift checker in CI and post a PR comment. Document the source-of-truth rule. *(o4)*
5. **Versioned release:** publish `2.10.0` with `kind` deprecated (a dev warning), a **codemod** (s11-t1 logic wrapped with jscodeshift or ts-morph), and a **migration guide**. Then publish `3.0.0` removing `kind`, with a changelog and the version computed by your s11-e4 function in CI. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for the Museum Design System (100 points)
rows: Three tiers, three themes × two brands, and a validation build that fails on problems (including contrast).
Compound + slots, correct a11y contracts, unique ids, two brands with shared behavior.
Closed sets, typed rules, loading keeps focus, a clear rationale and escape hatch.
Normalized, all token types, useful PR output, agreed source of truth.
Correct semver, warning + codemod + guide, then a clean removal in the major.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 4 (scaffolded): a three-tier token resolver with themes

Implement `resolveTokens(tokens, theme)`, which returns a flat object mapping every **component** token to its final value for `theme`. References look like `{name}` and are looked up in the theme's semantic map, then the primitives, then the component tokens. Throw `Error('Unknown theme: <theme>')`, `Error('Unresolved token {<ref>} in <name>')`, or `Error('Token cycle: a -> b -> a')` when appropriate.

This is the same walk-with-a-visited-path idea Section 4 used for graph traversal, applied to token references instead of a DOM or dependency graph.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: The theme decides only which semantic map you consult first.
Resolution is a graph walk (s4). Keep the path to report cycles.
Memoize resolved names, since many tokens share the same semantic ones.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 4 (independent): a Button contract that resists prop explosion

Implement `buttonProps(input)` that validates and maps Button props to `{ className, attrs }`.

- `variant` ∈ primary/secondary/ghost/danger (default `primary`). `size` ∈ sm/md/lg (default `md`). Anything else throws `Unknown variant: x` or `Unknown size: x`.
- `iconOnly: true` requires `label`, else throw `Icon-only buttons need a label`. The label goes to `attrs['aria-label']`.
- `loading: true` adds class `is-loading` and sets `aria-busy` and `aria-disabled` to `'true'`. It does **not** set `disabled`.
- `disabled: true` sets `attrs.disabled = true`.
- Allowed pass-through props: `onClick`, `type` (default `'button'`), `id`, `className` (appended), and any `aria-*` or `data-*`. Any other prop throws `Unsupported prop "<name>": use a variant or compose`.
- `className` is `btn btn--<variant> btn--<size>`, then ` is-loading` if loading, then the consumer's `className` if given. `attrs` includes only keys that are set.

Note: `icon` and `iconStart` are consumed by the component to render the glyph; they never become attributes on the returned object.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Closed sets are arrays you check with `includes`.
Which pass-through props carry behavior or accessibility, and which only carry styling?
`disabled` removes focus. What does a *loading* button need instead?

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 4 (scaffolded): token drift between design and code

Implement `tokenDrift(design, code)`, where both are flat `name → value` maps. Return `{ onlyInDesign, onlyInCode, changed }`: names sorted alphabetically, and `changed` as `{ name, design, code }` sorted by name. Compare **normalized** values: trim and lowercase, expand 3-digit hex to 6 digits, and convert `Npx` to `N/16 rem` (`1rem`, not `1.0rem`). Check every token, not only colors.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

cases.name: boundary: equivalent units and cases are not drift

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Normalize both sides with the same function before comparing.
The union of both key sets, sorted, is your loop.
Durations and radii drift too. Don't filter by name prefix.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 4 (independent): semantic versioning for a design-system release

Implement `nextVersion(current, changes)`, where the most severe change wins. **Major:** `removed-component`, `removed-prop`, `renamed-prop`, `changed-prop-type`, `removed-token`. **Minor:** `added-component`, `added-prop`, `deprecated`, `added-token`, `token-value-change`. **Patch:** `bugfix`, `docs`. Throw `Error('Unknown change type: <x>')` for anything else, and return `current` for no changes.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Check major first, then minor, then patch.
Parse the parts as numbers, so that 9 + 1 = 10, not "9.1".
A deprecation adds something (a warning plus a new path) without removing anything, so it's minor.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working Button codemod, you write the tests

`migrateButtonProps(props)` migrates v2 Button props to v3: `kind` → `variant` (with `outline` → `secondary`), `size` `small`/`medium`/`large` → `sm`/`md`/`lg`, and `icon` (boolean) + `iconName` → `iconStart` (only when `icon` is true). Unknown props pass through unchanged. It returns `{ props, warnings }`, with one warning per migrated concept. It's correct. Write tests that would catch the three hidden wrong versions. Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **four** tests). Then confirm your suite catches each of the three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks the kind-to-variant rename with the outline-to-secondary mapping, the legacy size mapping (with an already-migrated size left alone), that icon plus iconName becomes iconStart only when icon is true (and produces nothing when icon is false), that unknown props pass through unchanged while each migrated concept gets exactly one warning, and that an empty input returns an empty result. Wrong version 1 drops every prop it does not explicitly recognize, so onClick and id silently disappear; wrong version 2 copies kind straight through without mapping outline to secondary; wrong version 3 maps iconName to iconStart even when icon is false. A suite that only checks the kind rename catches none of the other two.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests here pin down the exact migration contract, not just "it renames kind to variant."
hints: Test the outline special case separately from a plain kind rename: outline should become secondary, not just move to variant.
Write a case where icon is false but iconName is present, and check that iconStart is not produced.
Include a pass-through test (an unrelated prop like onClick survives) and an empty-input test (no props in, empty result out).

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken headless Dialog state, make the tests pass

`createDialogState()` is the headless core behind `Dialog.Root`. It hands out prop getters for the trigger, the dialog, and the title slot. It has three bugs: ids collide between two dialogs on the same page, ARIA state values are booleans instead of the strings the tests expect, and closing doesn't say where focus should return. Fix it.

codeExercise.solutionNote: a headless core's value is its **guarantees**. Two dialogs on the exhibition page must not share ids, or `aria-labelledby` points at the wrong title. ARIA state attributes are string tokens (`"true"`/`"false"`), and focus return (s7) is part of the contract, not an afterthought.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three bugs come from the same shortcut: treating a single shared id as good enough, and treating ARIA state and focus return as implementation details instead of part of the contract.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. Do two separate createDialogState() calls actually get two different ids?
What type does aria-expanded and aria-modal need to be: a boolean, or the literal string "true" or "false"?
What should close() return, and what is it supposed to tell the caller to do with focus?

interactionSequence.prompt: When your Museum Design System build is done, paste a link or summary and answer: which decision in your build would have been hardest to reverse later, a token name, a component's prop contract, or a version bump, and what would reversing it now cost a consumer?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong reports name a specific artifact (a token name, a Button prop, a major version) that at least one other part of the system, or an actual consumer app, now depends on, and reason concretely about what changing it later would require: a migration, a codemod, a deprecation cycle. Check your build against the rubric table above before you submit.

learningExperiences.title: In the Wild: Contribute to a Real Design System

contentBlocks.content: This exercise happens on a real design system, not inside the course engine. The 20 minutes here cover picking a system and a target; finding and making the actual contribution, or running the interview, takes longer. Nothing here is graded or gates your progress. It builds evidence you will reuse in the Section 13 portfolio.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: An open-source design system (Adobe Spectrum, Shopify Polaris, GitHub Primer, Radix, the GOV.UK Design System) or your company's own.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Read a real design system's contribution guide, token structure, and deprecation policy, then make or attempt a small, real contribution, or interview someone who uses the system daily.
instructions: Pick an open-source design system (Adobe Spectrum, Shopify Polaris, GitHub Primer, Radix, the GOV.UK Design System, or your company's). Read its contribution guide, token structure, and deprecation policy.
Find a small, real issue (a docs gap, an accessibility bug, a missing token or variant discussion) and contribute: a PR, a well-reasoned issue comment, or an RFC-style proposal.
**Alternative:** interview a designer who uses a design system daily for 30 minutes. Ask what makes them trust it or work around it, and write up three insights.
materialsOrPrerequisites: A GitHub account, if you plan to open a PR or issue on an open-source system.
Or: a designer or engineer willing to give 30 minutes for an interview.
A place to save the evidence (PR link, issue link, or interview notes) for Section 13.
reflectionPrompts: What did the contribution guide or the interview reveal about how this system's governance actually works, versus how you assumed it worked?
Where did the token structure or deprecation policy differ most from this section's three-tier model or deprecation path, and why might that difference exist?
What would make you trust, or not trust, this design system if you had to build a real product on top of it?

selfAssessmentCriteria: I read the contribution guide, token structure, and deprecation policy before choosing an issue or interview question.
I made a real, specific contribution or asked specific, prepared questions, not a generic drive-by comment.
I saved the PR, issue, or interview notes and a paragraph on what the system's governance taught me, for my Section 13 portfolio.

learningExperiences.title: Review: Retrieval, Transfer, and the Section 11 Quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Close the section in three moves

1. **Retrieve** without looking back: answer the cues below from memory.
2. **Transfer** the token, component-API, and versioning ideas to two systems with nothing to do with museums: a city government's forms and a game studio's in-game UI.
3. **Prove it** in the Section 11 quizzes and the cumulative mastery checks for design-system-architecture and accessible-component-engineering, which live here because this is the section that finishes teaching them.

contentBlocks.title: Everything this section reaches back to
contentBlocks.content: This section leans on Section 9's cascade layers and fluid scales (which become the tokens layer and its values here), Section 7's combobox and dialog contracts (which the headless core carries for every brand), Section 3's context and re-renders (which decide whether a compound component's options re-render on every keystroke), Section 1's discriminated unions (which rule out an invalid Button prop combination at compile time), and Section 8's CI and versioned releases (which decide how a deprecation actually ships). One retrieval item below brings each of those back.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before the quiz: which idea from this section would you least want to explain live in an interview, three-tier tokens and theming, headless compound components, props versus composition, design-code drift, or semantic versioning and deprecation? Name it and write one sentence on what feels shaky.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Naming the shaky part precisely is what makes the next review useful. Re-read that lecture's summary and its worked example before you open the quiz.
