retrievalPractice.prompt: Where do design tokens live in the CSS cascade, and why does that layer come early?
What is the AAA contrast ratio requirement for normal text, and which theme in this section must meet it?
Name the three token tiers and what each one is for. Which tier changes per theme?
What does a headless compound component split apart, and why?
Why does adding props rarely make a component more flexible? What do you use instead?
Describe a deprecation path from the first warning to removal, with the version numbers.

transferExercises.scenario: Twelve departments (parking, libraries, permits) each want their own look, but residents need consistent, accessible forms across every department.
transferExercises.task: Design the token tiers (what is shared centrally versus per department), the component API boundaries for a FormField family, and the governance and release rules that let departments upgrade independently. Decide where you would allow escape hatches.
successCriteria: Keeps primitives and a shared semantic base, accessible contrast, spacing rhythm, focus styles, common across all twelve departments, and lets only a narrow per-department layer of semantic aliases (brand color, logo) vary.

Designs FormField as a small, closed set of props or variants (label, error, help text, required) plus slots or composition for anything department-specific, rather than a prop per department's special case.

Gives each department an independently versioned release path, so one can stay on an older major while another upgrades, with a shared deprecation and codemod process rather than one all-or-nothing release.

Names a specific, narrow escape hatch (for example className for spacing and layout only), not an open color or style prop, and explains what governance rule stops departments from bypassing the shared accessibility guarantees.

transferExercises.context: A game studio's in-game UI kit
transferExercises.scenario: Menus, HUD, and inventory are shared across three titles on consoles and PC. Controllers drive focus instead of a mouse, and themes change per game and for colorblind modes.
transferExercises.task: Adapt the three-tier token model, including colorblind themes validated by contrast and distinguishability, and describe how you would detect drift between the art team's source files and the engine's style definitions.
successCriteria: Extends the semantic tier with per-game and per-accessibility-mode theme maps, including colorblind modes, while keeping primitives and component tokens unchanged across games and modes.
Specifies a validation the token build runs for every colorblind theme beyond standard contrast, such as checking that critical UI states stay distinguishable by more than color alone.

Describes a drift check between the art team's source files and the engine's token definitions that flattens, normalizes to the engine's units, and compares both sides, reporting onlyInArt, onlyInEngine, and changed the way this lecture's checker does for Figma versus code.

Adapts the component API for controller-driven focus (for example a focus-visible state distinct from hover) without a prop for every game's specific need, using composition or per-game skins the way brands do for the museum Select.

sections.title: Taste, Prototyping, and the Design Conversation
sections.description: Learn to see and name what makes an interface work: **type scale, measure, rhythm, proximity, alignment, and hierarchy**, and to build hierarchy mainly by *removing* emphasis rather than adding it. Structure critique as **observation → principle → outcome → change**, redesign a form-heavy screen for clarity, speed, and accessibility, choose a **prototype's fidelity** to match the actual question, ship a deployed prototype from a two-sentence brief in a day, and set a clear, checkable position on where **AI tools** help and what always gets verified before anything ships. Examples come from a school district's family portal: attendance, grades, lunch balances, event sign-ups, and messages from teachers, used by parents on phones in between everything else.

learningObjectives.description: Write three critiques of real screens covering type, spacing, hierarchy, and color, each with concrete changes and rationale
Ship a deployed prototype from a two-sentence brief in one day and justify the fidelity chosen
Redesign a form-heavy screen and present the before, the after, and the reasoning
Build a type specimen that sets scale, measure, and rhythm
Write a position on where AI tools help and where they aren't trusted in the learner's workflow

motivationHooks.prompt: A parent scans the family portal at 7:30 am, between everything else. When the attendance card, the absence form, or a teacher's message makes them guess at what matters, the cost isn't an abstract usability score, it's a missed deadline or a misread instruction on a day that already had no slack.

The attendance card has five equally loud accent-colored elements. A designer's first instinct is often to make the primary action even louder: an extra shade, a bigger badge. Guess: does that create more hierarchy, or does taking color and bold away from the other four? Lecture 12.1's Predict-the-Output P1 comes back to this with real numbers.

An AI assistant generates an events-widget component. It renders. Its own generated tests pass. A teammate says "ship it, it works." What's still missing, and why was "it runs" never the bar, even for code you wrote yourself?

This section reaches back to Section 9's fluid clamp() scales, Section 11's token tiers, Section 7's accessible forms and contrast rules, Section 10's motion-as-feedback and audit prioritization, and Section 5's pushback pattern, then reaches forward: Section 13's portfolio case studies lean on this section's critique structure and evidence-first presentation.

Taking emphasis away from the other four elements wins, and it's not close: it barely moves the primary's own share (from 19% to 24%), but it more than doubles its lead over the next-loudest element (24% vs 11%, compared to 26% vs 17% when you make the primary louder instead). Hierarchy is the gap between levels, not the loudness of the top one.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- Taste is trained, named perception (scale, measure, leading, rhythm, proximity, alignment, hierarchy), not an innate trait.
- Hierarchy comes from contrast between levels; removing emphasis from secondary elements usually beats adding it to the primary.
- A useful critique note has four parts, observation, principle, outcome, change, and the same lens goes both ways: engineering view into design critique, design view into engineering review.
- A form redesign removes what the system already knows, defaults and discloses progressively, groups into a single column, and puts errors inline with `aria-describedby`.
- Match a prototype's fidelity to the actual question, keep the code disposable, and gate AI-assisted work on running, tests, accessibility (automated and keyboard), tokens, states, and a named human reviewer.
keyTakeaways: Taste is trained, named perception, not an innate trait: name proximity, measure, alignment, and hierarchy and the perception follows.
Hierarchy is contrast between levels. Removing emphasis from secondary elements creates a bigger, more reliable gap than adding emphasis to the primary.
A critique note has four parts: observation, principle, outcome, change. Bring the engineering lens to design critique and the design lens to engineering review.
A form redesign removes known data, defaults and discloses progressively, groups into one column, and wires errors inline with aria-describedby.
Match a prototype's fidelity to the question you actually have, and treat prototype code as disposable: rebuild properly once a direction is chosen.

AI is strong at exploration (variations, drafts, scaffolding) and untrusted by default in production; a ship gate (runs, tests, accessibility, tokens, states, human review) applies to AI-touched code and hand-written code alike.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 12.1: Seeing Clearly: Type, Space, Hierarchy, Color

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Describe an interface using precise vocabulary: scale, measure, leading, rhythm, proximity, alignment, contrast, hierarchy. (objective o1, o4)
2. Create hierarchy mainly with size, weight, and space, using color sparingly. (objective o1)
3. Set a type system with a modular scale, a comfortable measure, and a vertical rhythm. (objective o4)

terms.definition: A set of sizes related by a ratio (1.2, 1.25, 1.333…) so sizes feel related rather than arbitrary.
Line length, in characters. About 45–75 characters per line is comfortable for body text, and about 66 is a common target.
The vertical distance between lines. Body text usually needs 1.4–1.6× its size, while large headings need less.
Spacing and line-heights that share a base unit (for example 4 or 8 px), so the page has a steady cadence.
Things placed close together are read as related. Space *between* groups should be larger than space *within* them.
Shared edges create order. Every element should line up with something.
The order in which the eye visits things. It's built with contrast in size, weight, space, and position, and only sparingly with color.
How strongly an element draws attention relative to everything around it.

contentBlocks.content:
### Taste is trained pattern recognition

"I just have an eye for it" is how skill feels from the inside. It isn't innate (misconception `visual-design-judgment.m1`). People who critique well have seen thousands of interfaces and can **name** what they see: "the label is closer to the field above than to its own input" (proximity), "four font sizes within 4 px of each other" (no scale), "the line runs to 110 characters" (measure). Naming comes first, and practice turns names into perception. This section gives you the names and the exercises to practice them.

### Hierarchy comes from contrast, used sparingly

On the attendance card, a parent needs to see, in order: *how many absences*, *what to do* (report an absence), then details. The first draft makes everything loud. The title is bold, the badge is bold and red, the calendar link is blue, and both buttons are bold and colored. When everything is emphasized, nothing is. More color and emphasis doesn't create hierarchy (misconception `visual-design-judgment.m3`). Contrast *between* levels does, and that means taking emphasis away from the things that aren't first.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s12-m1): Attendance card: shouting vs speaking. Left: the first draft, with five competing accents (red badge, blue link, two identical bold teal buttons, bold title). A grayscale squint-test version below shows no clear focal point. Right: the revision, with the title at step 2, the count in a large numeral, one accent-colored primary button ("Report an absence"), a quiet secondary button, and the link underlined in body color. Its squint test shows a clear path: title → count → primary action.

contentBlocks.content:
### Type systems: scale, measure, rhythm

- **Scale:** choose a base (18 px for a reading-heavy portal) and a ratio (1.25): 14.4, 18, 22.5, 28.13, 35.16, 43.95 px. Map the steps to roles (caption, body, h4…h1) and use nothing in between. With s9's `clamp()` it becomes fluid.
- **Measure:** cap text containers at about `66ch`. On a desktop, a teacher's message at full width becomes 140 characters per line, and readers lose their place returning to the next line.
- **Rhythm:** line-heights and spacing on a 4 px grid. Body 18 px × 1.5 = 27 px is off-grid, so 28 px is better. Headings 28.13 px get a line-height of 1.15 ≈ 32 px.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: a modular scale is generated by size = base x ratio^step, so the ratio alone decides how far apart the steps feel. Edit ratio (try 1.2 or 1.333) and predict how the caption-to-h1 spread changes before you run it.

contentBlocks.caption: Runnable Example R1: the modular scale from the worked example above (base 18, ratio 1.25), mapped to caption through h1. Predict each line before running.
Runnable Example R2: estimated characters per line at three container widths, plus the pixel cap for a ~66 character measure. Predict each verdict before running.
Runnable Example R3: which spacing values used on the Lunch balance screen are already on the 4/8/12/16/24/32/48/64 scale, and which are not. Predict the off-scale list before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: visual fundamentals
contentBlocks.content:
- **Many near-identical sizes** instead of a scale.
- **Full-width text blocks** on large screens.
- **Equal spacing everywhere**, so the groups disappear.
- **Adding color or bold to fix hierarchy**, which adds noise.
- **Color as the only signal.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 12.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Taste is named, trained perception. Learn the vocabulary and apply it deliberately.
- Hierarchy is contrast in size, weight, space, and position. Remove emphasis from secondary things.
- Type systems: a modular scale, a 45–75 character measure, and rhythm on a base unit.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Emphasize the primary, or quiet everything else?.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
make primary bigger: report 26% vs download 17%
quiet the others:    report 24% vs download 11%
```

**Why intuition fails.** The instinct is to make the important thing louder. That does raise its share, from 19% to 26%, but the competing button is still at 17%, and the whole card got louder. Quieting everything else barely changes the primary's share (24%), yet it **more than doubles its lead** over the competing button (24% vs 11%), and the card becomes calmer. Hierarchy is the *difference* between levels, not the loudness of the top one. This is misconception `visual-design-judgment.m3`: adding color and emphasis rarely creates hierarchy, and taking it away usually does.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The instinct is to make the important thing louder. That does raise its share, from 19% to 26%, but the competing button is still at 17%, and the whole card got louder. Quieting everything else barely changes the primary's share (24%), yet it **more than doubles its lead** over the competing button (24% vs 11%), and the card becomes calmer. Hierarchy is the *difference* between levels, not the loudness of the top one. This is misconception `visual-design-judgment.m3`: adding color and emphasis rarely creates hierarchy, and taking it away usually does.
hints: A salience score here is area x weight x color emphasis; making one thing louder raises the whole card's volume, including the thing it's competing with.
Compare not just each button's own share, but the GAP between the primary's share and the next-loudest element's share.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: **Which lines land on the 4 px grid?.** Write down the exact output, one line at a time, before you run the program. Commit to an answer even if you are unsure; the gap between your prediction and the real output is what you will learn from.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
body: 27px off grid
body (fixed): 28px on grid
h3: 33.76px off grid
h3 (fixed): 32px on grid
caption: 21.6px off grid
```

**Why intuition fails.** "1.5 line-height is the rule" sounds like it guarantees rhythm, but a ratio times an arbitrary size rarely lands on a grid, and each off-grid line compounds down the page. Choosing line-heights as **grid values** (28 px, 32 px, and 20 or 24 px for captions) and expressing them as unitless ratios where needed gives rhythm deliberately. It's a small, nameable rule, not a matter of innate taste (misconception `visual-design-judgment.m1`).

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: "1.5 line-height is the rule" sounds like it guarantees rhythm, but a ratio times an arbitrary size rarely lands on a grid, and each off-grid line compounds down the page. Choosing line-heights as **grid values** (28 px, 32 px, and 20 or 24 px for captions) and expressing them as unitless ratios where needed gives rhythm deliberately. It's a small, nameable rule, not a matter of innate taste (misconception `visual-design-judgment.m1`).
hints: A ratio like 1.5 times an arbitrary size rarely lands on a whole multiple of 4.
Check px % 4 === 0 for each line, not whether the ratio "looks like" a clean number.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: The attendance card's first draft makes the title bold, the badge bold and red, the calendar link blue, and both buttons bold and colored, so a parent sees five loud things at once. What actually fixes the hierarchy?
options: Add one more accent color so the primary action stands out from the other four
Keep every element's current styling, since the real problem is information density, not styling
Remove color and bold from everything except the primary action (and the heading), so there is a real gap between levels
Make the badge even more prominent, since absences are the most urgent information

optionFeedback.feedback: Adding a sixth loud element doesn't create a gap; it just adds to the noise.
The problem is squarely about styling: five equally loud elements have no visual order, no matter how much text is on the screen.
Right. Hierarchy is contrast between levels. Quieting everything but the primary (and the heading) creates the gap that loudness alone never does.
Adding weight to a second element just creates two competing focal points instead of one clear one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: More color and emphasis doesn't create hierarchy; taking emphasis away from everything but the first thing does. This is the "shouting vs speaking" example from the lecture.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The Lunch balance screen uses sizes of 15, 16, 17, 18, and 20 px. Why does the worked example call this out as a problem, even though every size is "in use" somewhere?
options: There are simply too many CSS declarations to maintain
The sizes are too close together to read as distinct levels; a modular scale with real gaps (like 14.4/18/22.5/28.13) lets the eye tell them apart
Five sizes is one more than a hard "four-size rule" in CSS
15 px and 17 px are not valid CSS pixel values

optionFeedback.feedback: The count of declarations isn't the issue; it's whether the sizes read as different levels at a glance.
Right. A scale needs steps far enough apart to be perceived as different levels; five near-identical sizes don't function as a scale at all.
There is no such CSS rule; the problem is perceptual, not syntactic.
All of those are perfectly valid pixel values; the problem is how close together they are, not their validity.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A type scale is a set of sizes related by a ratio, with real gaps between steps. Sizes within a few pixels of each other don't read as levels no matter how many of them exist.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teacher's message renders at full width on a desktop monitor and runs to about 140 characters per line. What's the fix, and why?
options: Increase the font size so fewer characters fit per line
Cap the message container's width, for example with max-inline-size: 66ch, so lines land in the comfortable 45-75 character range
Nothing; wider lines let readers scan more text per glance
Switch to a monospace font, since proportional fonts are the real problem

optionFeedback.feedback: This could work by accident, but it's an indirect fix for a measure problem, and it also changes the type scale's proportions for no real reason.
Right. Capping the measure directly targets the actual problem: too many characters per line, and readers losing their place on the return sweep.
Wider lines don't help scanning; past about 75 characters, readers lose their place going back to the start of the next line.
The font family isn't what determines measure; the container's width relative to the font size is.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: About 45-75 characters per line (around 66 as a common target) is comfortable for body text. max-inline-size: 66ch caps a container's width to roughly that measure regardless of font size.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A teammate says "I just don't have an eye for design, I'll leave the visual calls to you." Using this lecture's claim that taste is trained pattern recognition, not an innate trait, explain what's actually different between someone who "has an eye for it" and someone who doesn't, and name two vocabulary words from this lecture a beginner could start using today to close that gap.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The difference isn't an inborn sense; it's exposure plus naming. Someone who "has an eye for it" has seen thousands of interfaces and, critically, can name what they're seeing: "the label is closer to the field above than to its own input" (proximity), or "four sizes within 4 px of each other" (no scale). A beginner can start closing that gap immediately by learning to name proximity, measure, alignment, or hierarchy in a screen they're looking at right now, and practicing pointing at exactly what's wrong instead of saying it "feels off." Naming comes first; practiced perception follows.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Naming what's wrong with one screen
workedExamples.problem: The "Lunch balance" screen, described in the vocabulary:
steps: **Scale:** sizes of 15, 16, 17, 18, and 20 px are all in use. They're too close to read as levels. *Change:* use body 18 and label 14.4, with the amount at 35 px.
**Proximity:** the "Add funds" button sits 8 px below the balance and 8 px above the transaction list, so it's unclear which it belongs to. *Change:* 8 px from the balance, 32 px before the list.
**Alignment:** amounts are left-aligned in a table. *Change:* right-align them and use tabular numerals (`font-variant-numeric: tabular-nums`) so decimals line up.
**Color:** negative amounts are red only. *Change:* add a minus sign and a "charge" label, since color can't be the only signal (s7).
workedExamples.conclusion: Each point names a principle, points at something visible, and proposes a specific change. That's the shape every critique in this section takes.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What ratio and base does the lecture's worked type scale use, and what are the resulting caption and h1 sizes?
What's a comfortable measure for body text, in characters, and what CSS declaration gets you close to it?

Section 9 built a fluid clamp() scale from a rem-based minimum, preferred value, and maximum, and Section 11 organizes values into primitive, semantic, and component-tier tokens. This lecture's modular scale (base 18, ratio 1.25) is neither fluid nor tokenized yet. Which token tier would a value like --font-size-h1 belong to, and what does wrapping the scale in a clamp() add that a fixed px step from this lecture can't?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 12.2: Critique That Changes Things

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Structure a critique as observation → principle → user outcome → concrete change. (objective o1)
2. Contribute usefully to design critiques and engineering reviews without making it about preference. (objective o1, o3)
3. Receive critique of your own work productively. (objective o1)

terms.definition: Something anyone can see on the screen ("the two buttons have identical styling").
The named idea that explains why it matters (hierarchy, proximity, affordance…).
The effect on the user ("parents can't tell which action reports an absence").
A specific, testable proposal ("make 'Download report' a secondary button: body color, no fill").
Critique asks whether the design achieves its goals. Review asks whether the implementation is correct. You'll do both.

contentBlocks.content:
### Why "I don't like it" doesn't help

Useful critique isn't personal opinion (misconception `visual-design-judgment.m2`). Opinions are true, but nobody can act on them, and they invite a debate about taste. A four-part note is actionable and checkable:

> **Observation:** "Report an absence" and "Download report" are both bold, teal, filled buttons of the same size.
> **Principle:** hierarchy. The primary action should be the most salient interactive element.
> **Outcome:** parents in a hurry hesitate or tap the wrong one. The tap-analytics funnel shows 18% of "Download" taps followed by a Back.
> **Change:** make "Download report" a secondary (outline, body text color) button, and keep the teal fill only on "Report an absence."

### In design critique and in engineering review

- **In design critique**, bring the engineering view: "This hover-only affordance won't exist on touch." "This layout needs a container query at 22rem, so here's how it collapses."
- **In engineering review**, bring the design view: "This spacing is 13 px, and our scale is 12/16. Was that intended?" "This component adds a fourth accent color. Should it be a semantic token?"
- **Receiving critique:** restate the concern, ask which outcome worries them, separate what you'll change from what you'll test. The same constraint → cost → conditional pattern from s5 works here.

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Video (s12-m2): Two critiques of the same screen. Production brief: A 3-minute split-screen roleplay. Left: "It feels cluttered, I don't love the colors" — the designer gets defensive and nothing changes. Right: two four-part notes (hierarchy on the buttons, proximity on the form groups) — the designer asks a clarifying question, and a revised screen appears with the changes applied.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: critique
contentBlocks.content:
- **Opinion without observation** ("feels off").
- **Observation without outcome** (a pixel note nobody can prioritize).
- **A vague change** ("make it pop").
- **Critiquing the person**, not the work.
- **Defending instead of clarifying** when you receive critique.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 12.2 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Observation → principle → outcome → change.
- Bring the design lens to code reviews and the engineering lens to design critiques.

interactionSequence.prompt: A reviewer writes: "This screen feels cluttered, I don't love the colors." What's the most useful next move?
options: Accept it as valid feedback and start changing colors
Push back that it's "just an opinion" and ignore it entirely
Ask what specifically reads as cluttered (an observation), which principle it violates, and what outcome it causes, turning the opinion into an actionable note
Defer to whoever has the most design experience in the room

optionFeedback.feedback: Acting on a bare opinion means guessing at which colors and why; there's no observation or principle to act on yet.
Dismissing it loses whatever real problem is behind the reaction; the fix is to extract the structure, not discard the feedback.
Right. Every opinion has a real problem behind it; the four-part structure is how you find it and make it fixable.
Seniority doesn't turn an opinion into an observation, a principle, or a testable change.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Opinions are true but unactionable. Asking for the observation, principle, and outcome behind "cluttered" or "I don't love the colors" turns a debate about taste into a specific, checkable note.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In a design critique, an engineer stays quiet because "the visuals aren't my department." What's this lecture's guidance?
options: Stay quiet; critique is for designers, engineering review is for engineers
Bring the engineering view into the critique too, for example naming that a hover-only affordance won't exist on touch, or that a layout will need a container query at a given width
Wait until the engineering review to raise any engineering concerns
Only comment if asked directly by the designer running the critique

optionFeedback.feedback: That's exactly the split this lecture argues against: each side brings its own view into the other's room, not just its own.
Right. Design critique benefits from the engineering view (feasibility, states, touch vs hover), the same way engineering review benefits from the design view.
Raising it after the design is finalized costs more than raising it while the direction is still open.
Waiting to be invited misses the point: useful critique goes both ways, proactively.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Bring the engineering view to design critique (feasibility, states, input methods) and the design view to engineering review (spacing scale, tokens). Both venues benefit from both lenses.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: You receive a critique note you disagree with. What does this lecture recommend before you respond?
options: Explain immediately why the reviewer is wrong
Restate the concern back, ask which outcome worries them, and separate what you'll change from what you'll test
Say nothing and quietly ignore the note
Agree to every suggested change to keep the conversation short

optionFeedback.feedback: Jumping straight to defending your choice is the common error this lecture names: defending instead of clarifying.

Right. Restating the concern, asking about the outcome, and separating changes from things to test keeps the conversation productive, the same constraint-cost-conditional shape Section 5 uses for pushback.
Ignoring it doesn't resolve whether the concern is valid, and it burns trust with the reviewer.
Agreeing to everything skips the useful step of understanding which outcome the reviewer actually cares about.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Receiving critique well means restating the concern, asking which outcome worries the reviewer, and separating what you'll change now from what you'll test, before defending anything.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The redesigned absence form still has a "Download report" button styled identically to the primary "Send to school" button: same size, same teal fill, same weight. Write a complete four-part critique note (observation, principle, outcome, change) about this.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong note names exactly what's identical ("Download report" and "Send to school" are both bold, teal, filled buttons of the same size), names the principle (hierarchy: the primary action should be the most salient interactive element), states a plausible user outcome (parents in a hurry may tap the wrong one, or hesitate between the two), and proposes a specific, testable change (make "Download report" a secondary button: outline or body-color text, no fill, keeping the teal fill only on "Send to school").

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Turning opinions into critique
workedExamples.problem: Three quick opinions about the same screen, translated into checkable notes.
steps: **"It feels busy."** Observation: six accent-colored elements on one card. Principle: hierarchy/contrast. Outcome: no clear first action. Change: keep one accent (the primary); everything else uses body color.

**"The form is ugly."** Observation: labels sit 4 px from the field above and 12 px from their own field. Principle: proximity. Outcome: labels read as belonging to the wrong field. Change: label 4 px above its own field, 24 px between field groups.

**"Text is hard to read."** Observation: messages run about 120 characters per line on desktop. Principle: measure. Outcome: readers lose their line. Change: max-inline-size: 66ch on the message body.
workedExamples.conclusion: Every opinion had a real problem behind it. The structure finds it and makes it fixable.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What are the four parts of a useful critique note, in order?

Section 7 orders accessibility findings by severity then effort, never by how many pages a tool flagged, and Section 10 does the same for a motion inventory. Which part of this lecture's four-part critique note plays the role that "severity" plays in those two audits, and why does jumping straight to "change" without it produce the same bad prioritization problem?

Section 4's live talk track and Section 5's constraint-cost-conditional pattern for pushback both give you a structure to lean on under pressure. When you're receiving, not giving, critique of your own work, which step of this lecture's guidance plays the same role as Section 5's "cost," and why does skipping it lead straight to defending instead of clarifying?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 12.3: Redesigning a Form-Heavy Screen

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Redesign a form for clarity, speed, and accessibility, and show the before and after with reasoning. (objective o3)
2. Apply grouping, a single-column layout, input sizing, and error design. (objective o3)

terms.definition: One field per row in reading order. It's faster to complete and works at every width.
Related fields under a `<fieldset>`/`<legend>` or heading, with more space between groups than within them.
Field width that suggests the expected length (a 5-digit ZIP vs a street address).
Showing extra fields only when a previous answer requires them.
A pre-filled or pre-selected value that's right for most people (today's date for an absence).

contentBlocks.content:
### The "Report an absence" form, before

Eleven fields in two columns: student, date (three dropdowns), all day? (a checkbox), from time, to time, reason (a dropdown with 14 options), details, doctor's note (upload), parent name, parent phone, and "I confirm" (a checkbox). Errors appear only at the top, in red. It's usually done on a phone, at 7:30 am.

### After, and why

1. **Remove what the system knows:** the parent's name and phone come from the account. The student defaults to the only child, or to a choice if there are several.
2. **Smart defaults:** the date defaults to today, and a native date input replaces the three dropdowns.
3. **Progressive disclosure:** "Part of the day?" reveals the time fields only when needed.
4. **Reason:** 14 options become 5 radio buttons (the most common reasons plus "Other," which reveals a text field). Radios show every option at once, which makes them faster than a dropdown for few choices.
5. **Upload** appears only when the reason is "Medical" and the district requires a note.
6. **One column**, with groups ("Who and when," "Why") separated by 32 px, and labels 4 px above their fields.
7. **Errors:** inline, with `aria-describedby` and a summary on submit (s7), in plain language: "Choose a date on or after today."
8. **Primary action:** a single "Send to school" button, the only accent on the screen.

Result: 11 visible fields become 3–5, and a 2-column desktop layout that breaks on phones becomes a single column that works everywhere.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s12-m3): Before/after of the absence form. Two phone screenshots side by side. Before: cramped two-column fields, three date dropdowns, a 14-option select, a red error banner at the top. After: a single column with the student and today's date pre-filled, five reason radios, a revealed time range, an inline error under the date with an icon, and one teal "Send to school" button. Annotations number each change 1–8, matching the list.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: form redesigns
contentBlocks.content:
- **Asking for data the system already has.**
- **Multi-column layouts** for sequential input.
- **Dropdowns for fewer than about 6 options.**
- **Placeholders instead of labels.**
- **Errors only at the top, or only in red.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 12.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Remove, default, disclose, group, one column, inline errors, one primary action.
- Present each change with its principle and the outcome you'll measure.

interactionSequence.prompt: The redesigned absence form no longer asks for the parent's name and phone number. Why, and what happens if a redesign skips this kind of change?
options: Removing fields always makes a form better, regardless of what they ask for
The system already knows this from the account, so asking again wastes the parent's time; skipping this step leaves the form asking for data it already has
Parent name and phone aren't needed to report an absence at all
It's purely a visual simplification with no effect on completion time

optionFeedback.feedback: Fewer fields helps only when the removed fields were genuinely redundant; the reasoning matters, not just the count.
Right. Asking for data the system already knows is a named common error; removing it is a specific, justified change, not a generic simplification.
The district still needs to know who's reporting; the fix is pulling that from the account instead of asking again.
It directly affects completion time and error rate, which is exactly why the redesign measures both.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Asking for data the system already has is a named common error. Removing what's already known (and defaulting or disclosing the rest) is what takes 11 fields down to 3-5.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The "Reason" field had 14 dropdown options. The redesign replaces it with 5 radio buttons (the common reasons, plus "Other"). Why is this faster, not just prettier?
options: Radios are always faster than dropdowns, for any number of options
Dropdowns hide every option behind a tap; with roughly 6 or fewer choices, radios show them all at once, so there's no extra step to see what's available
Radio buttons take up less screen space than a dropdown
The reduction to 5 options is the only thing that matters; the control type is irrelevant

optionFeedback.feedback: Radios lose their advantage once the option count grows large; the "fewer than about 6" threshold is what this lecture names, not radios in general.
Right. For a small option count, showing everything at once beats hiding it behind a tap-to-open interaction.
Radios typically take up more vertical space than a closed dropdown; the win is speed and visibility, not screen area.
The control type matters specifically because dropdowns for fewer than about 6 options is a named common error.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Dropdowns for fewer than about 6 options is a named common error. Radios that show every option up front are faster to scan and select from than a control you have to open first.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The original form shows errors only in a red banner at the top of the page. What does the redesign do instead, and why does it matter for accessibility?
options: Nothing changes about error display; only the fields themselves were redesigned
Errors appear inline, wired to their field with aria-describedby, plus a summary on submit, and in plain language, so the error isn't communicated by color and position alone
Errors are removed entirely in favor of preventing all invalid input
The red banner is kept, just moved to the bottom of the page

optionFeedback.feedback: Error display is one of the eight numbered changes; it isn't left untouched.
Right. Inline errors tied to their field with aria-describedby, plus a summary and plain language, means the error is discoverable by more than color and position alone.
Some invalid input is unavoidable (a picked date in the past, for instance); the form still needs a way to communicate it.
Moving the same banner doesn't fix the underlying problem: it's still disconnected from the specific field and relies on being noticed and read.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Errors only at the top, or only in red, is a named common error. Inline errors wired to their field with aria-describedby, plus a submit summary and plain language, is this lecture's fix, and it directly reuses Section 7's accessible form-error wiring.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: You're presenting the absence-form redesign to a skeptical stakeholder who says "this just looks different, prove it's actually better." Using this lecture's three-part presentation structure, write the opening two sentences of your response.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong answer leads with evidence, not aesthetics: naming the actual problem with a number ("median completion time is 2 minutes 40 seconds on mobile, and 31% of submissions arrive with the reason 'Other' and no detail"), then naming what you'll measure to know whether the redesign worked (completion time, the error rate per field, the share of "Other," plus an accessibility check). The structure works because it never rests the argument on taste; it rests on a problem, a principled set of changes, and a plan to measure the outcome.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Presenting the redesign
workedExamples.problem: A three-slide structure (or a single page) for the design review:
steps: **The problem, with evidence:** "Median completion time is 2 min 40 s on mobile, and 31% of submissions arrive with the reason 'Other' and no detail." (Use real data if you have it, or say clearly that it's a hypothesis to test.)
**Before → after**, with the numbered changes and the principle behind each: proximity, defaults, disclosure, error recovery.

**What we'll measure:** completion time, the error rate per field, the share of "Other." Also a note on accessibility (keyboard order, labels, error announcements) and what's still open (a translation for Spanish-speaking families).
workedExamples.conclusion: The redesign is persuasive because each change maps to a principle *and* a measurable outcome.

retrievalPractice.prompt: List at least four of the eight kinds of change this lecture makes to the absence form, from removing known data to a single primary action.

Section 7 requires that a live region exist before its content changes, and that hints and errors reach a field through aria-describedby, which is additive, never a replacement for the field's name. When this lecture's "Part of the day?" toggle reveals new time fields through progressive disclosure, what does Section 7's guidance say you must do so a screen-reader user actually discovers the newly revealed fields, rather than tabbing past silence?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 12.4: Prototypes at the Right Fidelity

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Choose the fidelity that answers the question you actually have. (objective o2)
2. Plan and ship a deployed prototype from a two-sentence brief in one day. (objective o2)
3. Keep prototype code disposable, and know what it would take to productionize it. (objective o2)

terms.definition: How close a prototype is to the real thing in visuals, content, interaction, and data.
Low fidelity: structure and flow only.
Linked screens for testing findability and flow.
Real copy in a plain layout, for testing comprehension.
Final visuals, for testing trust, brand, and emotional response.
Real interactions on real devices, for testing feel (gestures, timing, performance).
Throwaway code to test technical feasibility.

contentBlocks.content:
### Match fidelity to the question

Higher fidelity isn't always better (misconception `prototyping-and-fidelity.m1`). Each step up costs time, and it attracts feedback on the wrong things ("I don't like that blue") when you wanted to learn whether parents can *find* the absence form.

| Question you have | Fidelity that answers it |
|---|---|
| Can parents find X / complete the flow? | clickable wireframes |
| Do they understand the wording? | content prototype (real copy, plain layout) |
| Do they trust this payment screen? | high-fidelity mockup |
| Does this swipe or timing feel right on a phone? | coded prototype on a real device |
| Can the lunch system's API support this? | throwaway spike |
| (you only have an hour or two) | paper sketches, unless the question is about feel |

### A one-day plan from a two-sentence brief

*Brief:* "Parents miss event sign-up deadlines. Let them see and sign up for upcoming events from the home screen."

| Time | Activity |
|---|---|
| 0:00–0:45 | Write the one question to answer ("Will parents notice and complete a sign-up from home?"), choose the fidelity (a coded clickable prototype, because the home screen's density and on-phone scanning matter), and write down the success signal. |
| 0:45–1:30 | Sketch three layouts on paper, pick one, and write real copy for three events. |
| 1:30–5:00 | Build with existing design-system components (s11) and fake data. Skip everything not needed for the question: no auth, no persistence. |
| 5:00–6:00 | Deploy a preview (s8). Run it on two real phones. |
| 6:00–7:30 | Test with 3–5 people (colleagues who are parents, or real parents if you can). Observe, don't guide. |
| 7:30–8:00 | Write up: what you learned, what you'd change, and what you **didn't** build. |

### Prototype code is disposable

Prototype code isn't production code, and it shouldn't try to be (misconception `prototyping-and-fidelity.m2`). It skips error states, accessibility hardening, tests, and edge cases *on purpose*, so you can learn fast. When a direction is chosen, rebuild it properly, reusing ideas and components but not the shortcuts. Label the prototype as a prototype in its UI and in the repository.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s12-m4): The fidelity ladder. Rungs from bottom to top: paper → wireframe → clickable wireframe → content prototype → high-fidelity mockup → coded prototype. Next to each rung, the question it answers best and its typical cost in hours. A red "overbuilt" zone marks using a high rung for a low-rung question, with the example of polishing visuals to test findability.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: prototyping
contentBlocks.content:
- **Building high fidelity by default.**
- **No written question before you start.**
- **Treating the prototype as the first version of production.**
- **Testing only with teammates who know the product.**
- **Letting a prototype linger** until someone ships it.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 12.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Name the question, then choose the lowest fidelity that answers it.
- A one-day prototype means scope ruthlessly, deploy, and test with real people.
- Prototype code is disposable. Productionizing means rebuilding with care.

interactionSequence.prompt: A team wants to know whether parents can find where to update emergency contacts. A designer proposes a polished, final-visuals mockup so "stakeholders can see the real thing." What's wrong with that choice?
options: Nothing; higher fidelity is always the safer choice
It answers the wrong question: findability needs clickable wireframes and a first-click test, and a polished mockup invites feedback on colors and branding instead
Mockups can't be made clickable, so they can't test findability at all
The team should skip prototyping and just ship the real feature

optionFeedback.feedback: Higher fidelity costs more time and, worse, pulls feedback toward the wrong thing: what looks polished, not what's findable.
Right. Match fidelity to the actual question. A findability question is answered by structure and flow, which clickable wireframes and a first-click test give you far more cheaply.
High-fidelity mockups can be made clickable; the problem isn't the mechanics, it's that visuals distract from what you actually wanted to learn.
Shipping the real feature is the most expensive, slowest way to learn something a lightweight prototype answers in hours.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Higher fidelity isn't always better. Each step up costs time and attracts feedback on the wrong things; the right fidelity is the lowest one that answers the actual question.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The one-day events-widget prototype tested well, and a manager says "great, just ship what you built." What's the correct response?
options: Ship it as-is; it already works and passed the user test
Refuse to reuse anything from it, and start the real version from a blank file

Explain that the prototype skipped error states, accessibility hardening, tests, and edge cases on purpose to learn fast, and rebuild it properly, reusing the validated decisions but not the shortcuts
Add a feature flag around the prototype code and ship it disabled by default

optionFeedback.feedback: Prototype code skips error states, accessibility hardening, tests, and edge cases on purpose; "it works" in a five-person test isn't the same bar as production.
The validated layout and interaction decisions are worth keeping; only the shortcuts need to go.
Right. The prototype's job was to learn fast, not to be production-ready. Productionizing means rebuilding with care, reusing ideas and components but not the shortcuts.
A flag controls exposure, not quality; the missing states and hardening are still missing whether the flag is on or off.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Prototype code isn't production code, and it shouldn't try to be. When a direction is chosen, rebuild it properly instead of shipping the disposable version.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A one-day prototype plan starts by sketching layouts on paper. What should have happened even before that, according to this lecture's timeline?
options: Nothing; sketching is always the right first step
Writing the one question the prototype needs to answer, choosing the fidelity that answers it, and writing down the success signal
Writing the production code's architecture
Scheduling the user test sessions

optionFeedback.feedback: Sketching without a stated question risks building toward no clear answer; the plan puts the question first for a reason.
Right. The first block of the day is naming the question, choosing the fidelity, and writing the success signal, before any sketching happens.
Prototype code is disposable; planning production architecture on day one contradicts the whole premise.
Scheduling matters, but it happens later, and it presupposes you already know what you're testing.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: No written question before you start is a named common error. The very first block of the one-day plan is naming the question, picking the fidelity, and writing the success signal.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rank these four rungs of the fidelity ladder from lowest fidelity to highest.
options: High-fidelity mockup
Paper sketch
Coded prototype
Clickable wireframe

optionFeedback.feedback: High-fidelity mockups come after clickable wireframes and before coded prototypes: real visuals, but not yet real interaction on a real device.
Paper sketches are the lowest rung: structure and flow only, for the smallest, cheapest questions.
Coded prototypes sit at the top: real interactions on real devices, for testing feel.
Clickable wireframes come right after paper: linked screens for testing findability and flow, still with no real visuals.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Paper, clickable wireframe, high-fidelity mockup, coded prototype, with content prototypes and spikes answering their own separate questions off to the side. Higher rungs cost more and answer narrower questions, so climb only as far as the question demands.
hints: Which rung needs nothing but a pen?
Which rung is the only one that requires a real device?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team wants to know whether the lunch top-up system's API can actually support a new "auto-reload when balance is low" feature before they design anything. Using this lecture's table of questions and fidelities, name the right fidelity, and explain in one sentence why building a clickable wireframe first would be the wrong order of operations here.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: This is a feasibility question, so the right fidelity is a throwaway spike: code written purely to test whether the API can do the thing, not to be kept. A clickable wireframe would be the wrong order of operations because it tests findability and flow for a feature whose underlying feasibility hasn't been confirmed yet; if the API can't support auto-reload, the wireframe's findability results are moot.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Choosing fidelity for three questions
workedExamples.problem: Choosing fidelity for three questions
steps: "Can parents find where to update their emergency contacts?" This is a findability question, so use **clickable wireframes** tested with a first-click test.
"Will parents trust entering card details for lunch top-ups?" This is about trust, so use a **high-fidelity mockup** with real branding, security cues, and copy.
"Is swipe-to-dismiss on notifications discoverable and comfortable?" This is about feel, so use a **coded prototype on a phone** (s10's gesture work).
workedExamples.conclusion: Three different questions need three different fidelities. None of them needs everything built.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name the six kinds of fidelity in this lecture's ladder, from lowest to highest, and the question each answers best.

Section 5's design docs and Section 11's decision records both write a decision down with its reasoning, so it doesn't get re-argued later. What's the equivalent artifact for a fidelity choice from this lecture, and what two things does it need to record before you can skip re-justifying "why not higher fidelity" the next time someone asks?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 12.5: AI Tools: Exploration vs What Ships

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Use AI tools where they speed up exploration: variations, copy drafts, scaffolding, test ideas. (objective o5)
2. Define what must be verified by a person before AI-produced work ships. (objective o5)
3. Write your own position statement. (objective o5)

terms.definition: Generating many options quickly to learn what's possible. Mistakes are cheap.
Work that real users depend on. Mistakes are expensive.
Checks a person (or a trusted automated gate) performs before shipping: behavior, accessibility, edge cases, and fit with the system.
Output that looks right and runs, but violates requirements you didn't state (accessibility, tokens, error states, security).

contentBlocks.content:
### Where AI helps

- **Divergence:** "Give me five layouts for an events widget on a phone home screen." Pick one and discard the rest.
- **Drafts:** plain-language copy for error messages (then check it with real parents), alt-text drafts, test case lists.
- **Scaffolding:** boilerplate for a prototype, or converting a sketch into rough JSX.
- **Review assistance:** "What edge cases am I missing in this form?"

### Where you don't trust it without checking

AI output isn't ready to ship just because it runs (misconception `prototyping-and-fidelity.m3`). Code that compiles and renders can still:

- use a `div` with a click handler instead of a button (s7),
- hard-code colors and spacing instead of tokens (s11),
- skip the empty, error, and loading states,
- animate layout properties (s10), or ignore reduced motion,
- mishandle privacy, like logging a student's name.

A **ship gate** makes this concrete: it runs, tests pass, there are no automated accessibility violations *and* a keyboard pass was done, it uses tokens and system components, the empty, error, and loading states exist, and a named person reviewed it. The same gate applies to code you wrote yourself. AI just makes it easier to skip.

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s12-m5): Explore wide, ship narrow. A funnel: on the left, many AI-generated variations and drafts (layouts, copy, scaffolds) fanning out. In the middle, human selection and user testing. On the right, a gate with checkboxes (runs, tests, a11y automated + keyboard, tokens, empty/error/loading states, named reviewer) before "Production." Red arrows show two shortcuts that skip the gate, labelled "it runs, ship it."

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: AI in the workflow
contentBlocks.content:
- **"It runs, ship it."**
- **Accepting generated markup** without an accessibility check.
- **Pasting sensitive data into unapproved tools.**
- **Letting generated variations replace user testing.**
- **Vague positions** ("I use it responsibly") instead of specific rules.

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 12.5 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Use AI to go wide: variations, drafts, scaffolding.
- Gate what ships: behavior, accessibility, tokens, states, tests, human review.
- Write a specific position and follow it.

interactionSequence.prompt: An AI assistant generates an events-widget component. It renders without errors and its own generated tests pass. Is it ready to ship?
options: Yes, if it runs and its tests pass, it's ready

Not necessarily: code that compiles and renders can still hard-code colors instead of tokens, skip empty/error/loading states, use a div instead of a button, or mishandle privacy, none of which "it runs" catches
Yes, because generated tests are inherently more thorough than hand-written ones
No code from an AI assistant should ever ship, regardless of review

optionFeedback.feedback: This is exactly the misconception this lecture names: "it runs" was never the bar, for AI-generated code or for code written by hand.
Right. Plausible-but-wrong output looks right and runs, but can still violate requirements that were never stated to the tool: tokens, states, accessibility, privacy.
Generated tests test whatever the same generation pass assumed was correct; they don't independently catch requirements the tool was never told about.
The lecture's position is calibrated trust with verification, not a blanket ban.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: AI output isn't ready to ship just because it runs. A ship gate exists precisely because plausible-but-wrong output passes the "does it run" bar while still failing real requirements.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Which of these is the strongest example of using AI the way this lecture recommends?
options: Asking for five layout variations for an events widget, picking one, and discarding the rest
Letting the AI's generated markup ship directly since it "looks complete"
Pasting a family's contact details into an unapproved tool to draft a personalized message
Treating every AI code-review suggestion as authoritative and applying it without reading it

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Divergence, generating many options quickly so a person can pick and discard, is exactly where this lecture says AI helps: exploration, where mistakes are cheap.
Shipping generated markup without checking is the "it runs, ship it" error this lecture names.
Pasting sensitive data into an unapproved tool is one of the named common errors, regardless of how useful the draft would be.
The lecture's position statement treats AI suggestions like a fast but new teammate's: often useful, never authoritative, which means reading and judging them, not auto-applying them.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: AI is strongest at divergence, drafts, scaffolding, and review assistance, generating options for a person to select from and verify, not at producing a final, unverified answer.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A generated component passes its tests and has no automated accessibility violations. Is it clear to ship?
options: Yes, tests and automated accessibility checks are the whole gate
Not yet: the gate also requires a manual keyboard pass, tokens instead of hard-coded styles, the empty/error/loading states, and a named human reviewer
Yes, as long as it also compiles
No, because AI-generated code can never pass a gate

optionFeedback.feedback: Automated accessibility checks alone are Section 7's "minority of what matters" problem all over again; a keyboard pass is still required.
Right. The ship gate is: runs, tests pass, no automated a11y violations and a keyboard pass, tokens and system components, the three states present, and a named reviewer.
Compiling is a subset of "it runs," which this lecture explicitly says is not the bar.
The gate applies equally to AI-generated and hand-written code; passing it is possible for either.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The ship gate is specific and complete: it runs, tests pass, no automated accessibility violations and a keyboard pass was done, it uses tokens and system components, the empty/error/loading states exist, and a named person reviewed it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In two or three sentences, write your own position on AI tools in your workflow, specific enough that a teammate could tell whether you followed it on a real PR: name one place you'd use it freely, one thing you'd never skip verifying before shipping AI-touched UI code, and one category of data you wouldn't paste into an unapproved tool.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong position is specific, not a vague "I use it responsibly." It names a concrete place AI helps (for example, generating layout variations or scaffolding a throwaway prototype), a concrete verification step that never gets skipped (for example, a keyboard accessibility pass, or replacing hard-coded values with tokens), and a concrete category of data that stays out of unapproved tools (for example, student or family information). A teammate reading it should be able to check, on an actual PR, whether you followed it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: A position statement (excerpt)
workedExamples.problem: An excerpt from a working position statement on AI tools, read as one paragraph and unpacked principle by principle.
steps: **Explore, don't decide.** "I use AI to explore, not to decide." AI generates layout variations, copy drafts, and throwaway prototype scaffolds; a person still picks and refines.

**A concrete gate before anything ships.** Generated UI code doesn't ship without an accessibility checklist pass (keyboard, names, contrast, focus, announcements), hard-coded values replaced with tokens, the missing states added, and tests written or reviewed.
**A hard line on data.** Student or family data never goes into a tool the district hasn't approved.
**A calibrated level of trust.** AI suggestions in code review are treated like a fast but new teammate's: often useful, never authoritative.
workedExamples.conclusion: A good position is specific about *where* the tool helps and *what* is verified before anything reaches users.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Name three things generated code can still get wrong even though it compiles and renders.
What are the six checks in this lecture's ship gate?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: The Family Portal Studio

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content: Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. Taste isn't executable. The engine exercises turn the **named principles** behind taste into checks you can run: type scales, measure, salience, a critique structure, fidelity choice, and a gate for AI output. The critiques, redesign, specimen, and prototype themselves are reviewed in the Practical Activity.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenge 1 (the critique linter) is entirely yours. Challenge 2 (salience and focus) gives you a fixture card and leaves the scoring and the focusing logic to you. Challenge 3 (choosing fidelity) has no scaffolding at all. Challenge 4 (the ship gate) is entirely yours. The two test-suite challenges turn it around: the typeScale challenge gives you correct code and asks you to write the tests that prove it; the measure-checker challenge gives you a correct test suite and asks you to fix broken code until it passes.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your typeScale tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the typeScale challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. All three wrong versions are wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on each.

## Practical activity

**Build: "The Family Portal Studio."** Expected time is 8–10 hours.

1. **Three written critiques** of real product screens (a school, public-service, or health portal you use): each with at least four four-part notes covering type, spacing, hierarchy, and color, run through your `lintCritique` before submitting, plus an annotated screenshot. *(o1)*
2. **A one-day prototype** from this two-sentence brief (or one you're given): *"Parents miss event sign-up deadlines. Let them see and sign up for upcoming events from the home screen."* Write the question first, choose the fidelity with `chooseFidelity` and justify it, build with design-system components, deploy a preview, test with 3–5 people, and write a one-page learning summary that includes what you deliberately didn't build. *(o2)*
3. **A form redesign:** the "Report an absence" form (or a real form-heavy screen), presented as before → after → reasoning, with the eight kinds of change from Lecture 12.3, s7's accessibility wiring, and the metrics you'd track. *(o3)*
4. **A type specimen page:** a scale from `typeScale` (a ratio you justify), fluid with s9's `clamp()`, line-heights on a 4 px grid (P2), a measure capped at about `66ch`, and real portal content (a teacher's message, a grade table, a lunch balance) set in each role. *(o4)*
5. **An AI position statement** (≤1 page) in the style of Lecture 12.5, with your concrete ship gate (s12-e4 as a PR checklist), where you use AI, where you don't, and one example where it saved time and one where it misled you. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for the Family Portal Studio (100 points)
rows: Every note has four parts, principles are named, and the changes are concrete and plausible.
Question-first, justified fidelity, deployed, tested with real people, and an honest scope note.
Clear before/after, principled changes, accessibility, and measurable outcomes.
A coherent scale, a comfortable measure, rhythm on a grid, real content.
Specific rules and a gate, with real examples of both success and failure.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 4 (independent): a critique linter Implement `lintCritique(note)` for notes shaped `{ observation, principle, outcome, change }`. It returns `{ valid, issues }` with issues in this order: 1. `missing ` for each empty field, in the order observation, principle, outcome, change. 2. `unknown principle:

` when the principle isn't in the list: hierarchy, proximity, alignment, contrast, repetition, consistency, rhythm, measure, white space, affordance, feedback, legibility, accessibility (case-insensitive). 3. `observation is an opinion` when the observation matches `/\b(i (don't |do not )?(like|love|hate)|ugly|pretty|feels (off|wrong|weird|busy)|looks (bad|off))\b/i`. 4. `change is not concrete` when the change contains no number and none of: move, align, group, increase, decrease, replace, remove, use, swap, add, reduce, limit. Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

args.observation: Both buttons are bold, teal and the same size
args.change: Use the secondary style for Download

args.observation: It feels busy and I don't like the colours
Labels are 12px from their own field

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Check the four fields in a fixed order, so the messages are predictable.
Compare the principle case-insensitively against the shared vocabulary.
A change is concrete if someone could implement it without asking what you meant.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 4 (scaffolded): build hierarchy by removing emphasis

Implement `salienceShares(elements)` (percent share per id, rounded, where score = (size/16)² × (bold ? 1.4 : 1) × (accent ? 1.5 : 1)) and `focusOn(elements, primaryId)`. `focusOn` returns **new** elements where the primary is bold and accent, every other element loses its accent, and only `role: 'heading'` elements keep their bold. Sizes don't change.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

codeExercise.solutionNote:
**The plausible wrong answer:**

```js
function focusOn(elements, primaryId) {
  return elements.map(e => (e.id === primaryId ? { ...e, size: 20, bold: true, accent: true } : e)); // louder primary; everything else still shouts
}
```

The starter's "make the primary 25% bigger" is **`visual-design-judgment.m3`**: more emphasis instead of more contrast. The competing button keeps its bold teal fill, so the primary never gets a 2× lead.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Hierarchy is the *gap* between levels. Which elements need to get quieter?
Return new objects with spread, and never assign to `e.accent` on the input.
Headings earn their weight. Most other things don't need bold.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 4 (independent): choose the fidelity

Implement `chooseFidelity({ question, hours })` returning `{ fidelity, disposable: true }`. The mapping is findability → `'clickable wireframes'`, comprehension → `'content prototype'`, trust → `'high-fidelity mockup'`, feel → `'coded prototype on device'`, feasibility → `'throwaway spike'`. If `hours < 2` and the question isn't `feel`, return `'paper sketches'`. Unknown questions throw `Error('Name the question first: <question>')`.

This one has no scaffolding: the whole function is yours.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Start from the question, not the tools.
Which question can only be answered by touching a real device?
`disposable: true` is a promise about what happens to the code afterwards.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 4 (independent): a ship gate for AI-assisted work

Implement `shipGate(review)` returning `{ ship, blockers }`, with the blockers in this order:

- `'does not run'` if `!runs`
- `'tests missing or failing'` if `!testsPass`
- `'accessibility violations: <n>'` if `a11yViolations > 0`
- `'keyboard not checked'` if `!keyboardChecked`
- `'hard-coded styles instead of tokens'` if `!usesTokens`
- `'missing <state> state'` for each of `empty`, `error`, `loading` not in `states`
- `'no human review'` if `!reviewedBy`

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Each field is one question in your position statement.
Missing states are listed individually, so the author knows exactly what to add.
An empty string isn't a reviewer.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working typeScale, you write the tests

`typeScale({ base, ratio, up, down, rootPx })` returns steps from `-down` to `up`, each `{ step, px, rem }`, with `px = base × ratio^step` rounded to 2 decimal places and `rem = px / rootPx` rounded to 3 decimal places. It's correct. Write tests that catch the three hidden wrong versions. Use the R1 values. Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **4** tests). Then confirm your suite catches each of the three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite checks four behaviors: the exact multiplicative scale from Runnable Example R1 (base 18, ratio 1.25), that steps below the base divide by the ratio rather than growing, the exact rem-relative-to-root relationship, and the single-step case when up and down are both zero. Wrong version 1 adds instead of multiplying, so it produces a linear scale, not a modular one. Wrong version 2 uses Math.abs on the step, so sizes below the base grow instead of shrink. Wrong version 3 computes rem against the base instead of the root size, so a custom rootPx is silently ignored. A suite that only checks the array's length catches none of the three.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests here pin down the exact numeric contract from Runnable Example R1, not just "it returns an array of the right length."
hints: Start with R1's own numbers: base 18, ratio 1.25, up 4, down 1 should produce exactly [14.4, 18, 22.5, 28.13, 35.16, 43.95] in px.
Write a second test with down greater than 0 and check that the px values below the base SHRINK, not grow.
Pass a rootPx other than 16 and check that rem actually changes, to make sure your suite would catch a version that computes rem against the base instead of the root.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken measure checker, make the tests pass

The type-specimen page warns when a text container's measure is uncomfortable. `measureCheck(widthPx, fontSizePx, charEm)` should estimate characters per line as `round(width / (fontSize × charEm))` (default `charEm` 0.5) and return `{ chars, verdict }`, with `45–75` inclusive being comfortable. It must throw for non-positive sizes. It has three bugs. Fix it.

codeExercise.solutionNote: dividing by the font size counts *ems*, not characters (a character is roughly half an em). The comfortable range is inclusive at both ends. A zero font size would divide by zero and report "too wide" when it should fail.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three bugs come from treating the measure estimate as an afterthought: dividing by the wrong quantity, an exclusive boundary, and no guard on non-positive sizes.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. Does dividing width by fontSize alone count characters, or something else?
Is 45 characters treated as comfortable, or does the current code require strictly more than 45?
What should happen when fontSizePx is 0? What does the current code do instead of throwing?

interactionSequence.prompt: When the Family Portal Studio is done, paste a link or summary and answer: which of your critique notes led to the biggest concrete change, and which fidelity choice in your one-day prototype are you most confident (or least confident) was the right one?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong reports name a specific critique note with all four parts, tie it to a specific before/after change, and explain the fidelity choice in terms of the actual question the prototype needed to answer, not just how much time was available. Check your work against the rubric table above before you submit.
