learningExperiences.title: In the Wild: Join a Real Critique

contentBlocks.content: This exercise happens in a real critique, not inside the course engine. The 20 minutes here cover planning and reflection; actually attending a crit, offering a design-eye session, or volunteering a redesign takes longer. Nothing here is graded or gates your progress. It builds evidence you will reuse in the Section 13 portfolio.

selfGuidedExercise.realWorldContext: A real design critique (at work, at a local meetup, or in a public online design-review community), or an engineer friend willing to spend 30 minutes reviewing a screen together.
selfGuidedExercise.objective: Contribute at least two real four-part critique notes to someone else's work, and practice the same vocabulary outside the course's own examples.
instructions: Attend a design critique: at work (ask to sit in on the design team's crit), at a local design meetup, or online in a public design-review community. Contribute at least two four-part notes, and write down how they were received.
Offer a 30-minute "design eye" session to an engineer friend or colleague: review one screen of their product together using this section's vocabulary.
**Stretch:** volunteer a small redesign for a local nonprofit, school, or community group's form (with their permission), and share the before/after and outcome.
materialsOrPrerequisites: Access to a design critique, meetup, or online design-review community, or a colleague willing to sit for a 30-minute review.
A real screen to critique: your own product, a colleague's, or (for the stretch goal) a local nonprofit or school's form.
A place to note down how your critique was received.
reflectionPrompts: Which of your notes landed as actionable, and which one needed a follow-up question before it was clear?
Did anyone push back on one of your notes, and did the four-part structure make that conversation easier or harder than an unstructured one would have been?
What did you notice about your own reaction when you received critique during the session, and did you catch yourself defending instead of clarifying?

selfAssessmentCriteria: I contributed at least two complete four-part notes (observation, principle, outcome, change), not opinions.
I wrote down how each note was received, not just that I gave it.
I saved my notes (and any before/after, if I did the stretch goal) for my Section 13 portfolio.

learningExperiences.title: Review: Retrieval, Transfer, and the Section 12 Quiz

contentBlocks.content:
## Close the section in three moves

1. **Retrieve** without looking back: answer the cues below from memory.
2. **Transfer** the critique, type, and fidelity ideas to two systems with nothing to do with a school: hospital discharge instructions and a bike-share unlock flow.
3. **Prove it** in the Section 12 quiz and the cumulative mastery checks for visual-design-judgment and prototyping-and-fidelity, which both live here because this is the section that teaches them.

contentBlocks.title: Everything this section reaches back to
contentBlocks.content: This section leans on Section 9's fluid clamp() scales (Lecture 12.1's type scale, made fluid), Section 11's token tiers (Lecture 12.1 and 12.4), Section 7's accessible forms and contrast rules (Lecture 12.3's redesign), Section 10's motion-audit prioritization (Lecture 12.2's critique structure), and Section 5's design docs and pushback pattern (Lecture 12.2 and 12.4). A retrieval item in each participating lecture brings the connection back explicitly.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before the quiz: which idea from this section would you least want to explain live in an interview, the vocabulary of type and hierarchy, structuring a critique, the form redesign, choosing fidelity, or the AI ship gate? Name it and write one sentence on what feels shaky.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Naming the shaky part precisely is what makes the next review useful. Re-read that lecture's summary and its worked example before you open the quiz.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

retrievalPractice.prompt: In one line, what's the difference between critique and review?
What are the four parts of a useful critique note?
Why does removing emphasis usually create more hierarchy than adding it?
What measure and rhythm rules would you apply to a teacher's message on desktop?
How do you choose a prototype's fidelity, and why is prototype code disposable?

transferExercises.scenario: Nurses hand patients a two-page discharge sheet, and many patients are older, anxious, or reading in a second language.
transferExercises.task: Nurses hand patients a two-page sheet, and many patients are older, anxious, or reading in a second language. Critique a typical sheet using the four-part structure (at least three notes covering hierarchy, measure, and proximity), then propose a type scale and layout for both print and phone.
successCriteria: Writes at least three complete four-part critique notes (observation, principle, outcome, change), covering hierarchy, measure, and proximity specifically, not vague "make it clearer" notes.
Proposes a type scale with a base and ratio suited to an anxious, possibly-older reader (larger base size, generous steps between levels), not just a smaller version of a marketing scale.
Caps measure for both the printed sheet and the phone version, recognizing the two need different concrete widths even though the same ~45-75 character target applies to both.

Uses hierarchy (size, weight, and space, not just color) so the single most important instruction (for example, a danger sign to watch for) is visually first, independent of whether the sheet is printed in black and white.

transferExercises.scenario: The team debates whether a new unlock animation "feels fast," and a teammate has already generated a first version of the unlock screen's code with an AI assistant.
transferExercises.task: The team debates whether the new unlock animation "feels fast." Choose the prototype fidelity to answer that question, plan a one-day test, and write the AI position you'd apply if a teammate generated the unlock screen's code with an assistant.
successCriteria: Chooses a coded prototype on a real phone as the fidelity, since "feels fast" is a question about timing and gesture feel that no wireframe or mockup can answer.

Plans a one-day structure that states the question first ("does the unlock animation feel fast enough on a real device?"), then scopes ruthlessly (no real bike-locking hardware, no auth) before building.

Writes an AI position specific to this scenario: what the assistant's generated code is trusted for (scaffolding the interaction, generating a few timing variations) and what still needs a human check (keyboard/reduced-motion behavior, real-device feel, token usage) before anything ships.
Names testing with real people on a real device, not just teammates who already know the product, as part of judging whether the animation actually feels fast.

sections.title: Capstone and Interview Readiness
sections.description: Ship a deployed capstone built around **one hard problem** — a document model, convergent merges, dense-data rendering, tree operations, or mixed-value editing — measured against performance and accessibility bars you write down before you build. Turn it into a **case study** structured around decisions, not features, curate it into a **portfolio** with three or four other deep pieces, prepare four **behavioral stories** in STAR+L with unmistakable individual ownership, and run two full **mock interview loops**, recorded and self-reviewed. Examples come from film production tooling: a shot-list editor, a call-sheet scheduling board, an editing timeline, and a dailies review app.

learningObjectives.description: Ship a deployed capstone (editor, page builder, collaborative canvas, dense data visualization, or inspector) that meets stated performance and accessibility bars
Write a case study covering decisions, tradeoffs, and what the learner would change
Publish a portfolio presenting the capstone plus three or four earlier builds, each with a "why it matters" note
Write four behavioral stories (a migration, an incident, a disagreement, mentoring) with a clear individual contribution
Complete two full mock loops (frontend engineer and design engineer) and write self-reviews

motivationHooks.prompt: A reviewer spends minutes on your portfolio and an interviewer spends 45 minutes per round. Both are fixed, scarce budgets. Everything in this section — one hard problem, decisions instead of features, curation instead of a gallery, "I" instead of "we" — is about spending someone else's limited attention on your strongest, clearest signal.

Two replicas of a storyboard card receive the exact same two edits, in a different order because of normal network jitter. If each replica just applies updates as they arrive ("last arrival wins"), do the two replicas end up agreeing on the card's final color? Keep your guess; the Runnable Example and P1 come back to it.

One candidate's portfolio has twenty projects. Another has five, each with a "why it matters" note. A reviewer spends the same six minutes on both. Which candidate's best work is more likely to actually get read?

This section is the course's culmination: the merge logic reuses Section 3-5's keyed identity, the capstone scoping reuses Section 3, 6, and 10's rendering-strategy judgment, the mock loops reuse Section 4's talk track and Section 5's pushback structure, and the case study and stories reuse Section 5, 11, and 12's evidence-based decision writing.

No — "last arrival wins" gives the two replicas *different* final colors, because they received the same edits in different orders, and they silently disagree forever unless something fixes it. Comparing a Lamport clock (a logical counter, tie-broken by client id) instead of arrival time makes the merge order-independent: both replicas compute the exact same winner regardless of which edit reached them first. If you guessed "yes, they'll agree," you've now met the trap R1 and P1 are built around.

sectionSummary.content:
## What you should now believe

- A capstone is judged on one hard problem, done well, measured against bars stated before you build — not on the number of features.
- A case study is a narrative of decisions: the choice, the alternatives considered, why, and the cost accepted, backed by measured evidence — not a feature tour.
- Reviewer attention is fixed. A curated portfolio (the capstone plus 3-4 deep pieces chosen for skill coverage, each with a two-sentence "why it matters" note) beats a gallery of everything you've built.
- Use "I" for your own actions — the longest part of a STAR+L story — and "we" only for genuine team context. Prepare four distinct stories: a migration, an incident, a disagreement, and mentoring.
- A convergent merge needs an order-independent reconciliation rule (a logical clock plus a deterministic tie-breaker), not "apply updates as they arrive" — the collaborative-editing version of "an update is more than just setting the new value."
- In a live round or a critique, narrate intent continuously and answer pushback with constraint → cost → conditional alternative; a follow-up after working code or a shipped decision usually means you've met the baseline, not that you've failed it.
keyTakeaways: A capstone centers on one hard problem, with performance and accessibility bars written down before building and verified at the end.
A case study records decisions (choice, alternatives, why, cost, evidence), never just features.
Reviewer attention is fixed — curate a few deep, coverage-chosen pieces instead of a gallery.
Use "I" for your own actions in STAR+L stories, and prepare four distinct core stories.
A convergent merge needs an order-independent reconciliation rule, not arrival order.
Narrate intent under time pressure, and answer pushback with constraint → cost → conditional alternative.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 13.1: Choosing and Shipping the Capstone

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Choose a capstone niche you can own, and identify its **one hard problem**. (objective o1)
2. Set explicit performance and accessibility bars before building, and verify them at the end. (objective o1)
3. Plan three weeks of milestones that end with a deployed, measured product. (objective o1)

terms.definition: A kind of interface you want to be known for (editors, canvases, data-dense tools, design tools).
The technical core that makes this capstone worth discussing: a document model, conflict resolution, rendering thousands of points, multi-selection editing.
Numeric performance targets and accessibility criteria, fixed before building.
A thin, end-to-end version of the product that works: data model → UI → deploy → measurement.
A feature deliberately left out and documented.

contentBlocks.content:
### Five options, each with its hard problem

| Capstone | The hard problem | Course sections it draws on |
|---|---|---|
| **Rich-text editor with a custom document model** (a screenplay editor: scene headings, action, dialogue) | the document model plus undoable operations, selection mapping, IME and paste | s1 types, s3 reconciliation, s5 editor walkthrough, s8 tests |
| **Drag-and-drop page builder** (a call-sheet builder) | tree operations, drop-target calculation, keyboard-accessible drag and drop | s4 trees, s7 widgets, s10 gestures |
| **Real-time collaborative canvas** (a storyboard wall) | convergent merges, presence, offline and reconnect | s5 client data, s3 query cache, s8 flags and observability |
| **Interactive data visualization with thousands of points** (a dailies review timeline with per-frame metrics) | rendering and decimation, interaction latency, accessible data alternatives | s2 pipeline, s6 INP, s7 alternatives, s9 layout |
| **Design-tool-style inspector** (a shot properties panel for multi-selection) | "mixed" values, batch edits, undo, token-aware controls | s11 tokens and components, s12 hierarchy, s5 normalized store |

Pick the one closest to the jobs you want, and make the hard problem the center of the case study.

### Bars first

Write them in the README before any code, for example:

- **Performance (lab, median of 5 runs, mid-range mobile profile):** LCP ≤ 2.5 s, INP ≤ 200 ms for the three core interactions, CLS ≤ 0.1. With 5,000 items (points, blocks, shapes), frames stay within budget during the core interaction (s2, s6).
- **Accessibility:** every feature is operable by keyboard. There are no axe violations. A screen-reader smoke test of the core flow passes (VoiceOver or NVDA). Reduced motion is respected (s10). Contrast passes in every theme (s11).
- **Quality:** unit tests on the hard problem, one E2E journey, CI with a preview deploy, error tracking (s8).

### Three weeks

| Week | Goal |
|---|---|
| 1 | The hard problem in isolation, with tests (the engine exercises below are starting points). A vertical slice deployed. |
| 2 | Core UI on the design system (s11), full keyboard and screen-reader support, and the performance budget checked early and often. |
| 3 | Polish, motion, measurement against the bars, the case study, and a recorded demo. Scope cuts written down. |

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s13-m1): Capstone map. Five capstone cards, each showing its hard problem in bold and lines to the course sections it draws on. Underneath, a three-week Gantt strip: "hard problem + slice" → "UI + a11y + budget" → "measure + case study + demo," with a milestone diamond for "bars verified."

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **a Lamport clock (lamport time, then client id) makes a merge order-independent, so both replicas agree regardless of who applies which edit first.** Change the director's clock below to `[7, "zzz"]` (a tie-breaking id that sorts after "ed") and predict both merge directions before running.

contentBlocks.caption: Lamport clocks make "who wins" deterministic: predict both merge directions before running, then compare with your edited playground above.
Why decimation keeps min and max, not just every Nth frame. Predict both max-y lines before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: capstones
contentBlocks.content:
- **A feature list instead of a hard problem.**
- **Setting bars after building** (or never).
- **Leaving accessibility to week 3.**
- **No deployment**, so there's nothing anyone can touch.
- **Scope creep without written cuts.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 13.1 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Choose a niche and its hard problem. State the bars first. Ship a slice in week 1.
- Measure against the bars at the end, and write down the cuts.

interactionSequence.prompt: Put these capstone-planning moves in the order they belong, first to last.
options: Week 3: polish, motion, measurement against the bars, the case study, and a recorded demo, with scope cuts written down
Write the performance and accessibility bars in the README, before any code
Week 1: the hard problem in isolation, with tests, and a vertical slice deployed
Choose the one niche and hard problem closest to the jobs you want
Week 2: core UI on the design system, full keyboard and screen-reader support, and the performance budget checked early and often

optionFeedback.feedback: Last: polish and the case study come once the hard problem is proven and the UI is built, not before.
Second: bars go in the README before any code, so every later decision is made against a number, not a feeling.
Third: the hard problem in isolation, deployed as a thin vertical slice, is week 1 — proof the core idea works before spending two more weeks on it.
First: you can't write a bar or plan a week around a hard problem you haven't chosen yet.
Fourth: UI, accessibility, and the performance budget are week 2, once the hard problem already works.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Niche and hard problem → bars in the README → Week 1 (hard problem + slice) → Week 2 (UI + a11y + budget) → Week 3 (polish, measurement, case study, demo). Each step is judged against what the step before it produced.
hints: What has to exist before you can write a testable bar?
Which week is explicitly about proving the hard problem works at all, before any UI is built on top of it?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this order?

interactionSequence.prompt: A capstone README lists ten features (drag and drop, dark mode, comments, real-time sync, export...) and no single hard problem. What's wrong, and what should replace it?
options: A feature list gives a reviewer nothing to discuss; name the one hard technical problem (a document model, conflict resolution, decimation, tree operations, mixed-value editing) and center the whole project on it
Nothing; more features show more effort and a wider skill set
The features should be reordered so the easiest one is first
The fix is to add a short demo video; the list itself is fine

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. "A feature list instead of a hard problem" is the first common error this lecture names — a reviewer can't evaluate ten shallow features the way they can one deep, well-solved one.
A feature list is exactly the error named in this lecture: it describes *what* exists, not the one hard problem worth discussing.
Reordering a feature list doesn't give it a hard problem; the list itself is the issue, not its order.
A demo video doesn't fix a project that has no hard problem at its center; it would just be a nicer tour of the same feature list.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Every one of the five capstone options has a named hard problem (a document model, convergent merges, decimation, tree operations, mixed-value editing). Choose the niche closest to the jobs you want, then make that hard problem the center of the build and the case study.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A team sets performance and accessibility bars only after the capstone is built, by running Lighthouse once and reading off the score. What's wrong with that approach?
options: Bars set after the fact are descriptions, not targets that shaped any decision, and a single lab Lighthouse score misses INP and real accessibility testing entirely
Nothing; a high Lighthouse score is proof the product performs and is accessible
Bars should be set after building, since you can't know what's achievable beforehand
Lighthouse alone is a complete accessibility check, so no further testing is needed

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Bars belong in the README before any code, as numbers that shape decisions, and a single Lighthouse run is not the same as INP measured on real interactions plus a keyboard and screen-reader pass.
A good Lighthouse score does not mean users have a good experience — it is a lab proxy that can miss real interaction latency (INP) and most accessibility issues entirely.
Setting bars after building means nothing was measured against them during development; that is exactly the "setting bars after building (or never)" error this lecture names.
Lighthouse does not replace a keyboard-only pass, a screen-reader smoke test, or an axe scan — the bars in this lecture name all three explicitly, on top of the lab metrics.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: State performance (LCP, INP, CLS, measured under load) and accessibility (keyboard operability, axe-clean, a screen-reader smoke test, reduced motion, contrast) bars in the README before building, then verify them at the end. A single Lighthouse number after the fact is neither a bar nor a full accessibility check.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 3 chose a rendering strategy (CSR, SSR, SSG, or a mix) to match a page's actual constraints, rather than defaulting to one strategy everywhere. How does that same "match the approach to the constraint, not a default" habit show up in choosing a capstone niche and its hard problem?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Just as Section 3 picked CSR, SSR, or SSG based on what a specific page actually needed (freshness, SEO, interactivity) rather than reaching for one default everywhere, choosing a capstone means picking the ONE hard problem whose real constraints (conflict resolution under concurrent, possibly offline edits; rendering thousands of points at a stable frame rate; multi-selection editing with mixed values) match the jobs you want to be hired for — not defaulting to 'add more features' or copying whichever capstone looks most impressive. The niche should be chosen because its hard problem is the one you want to be known for solving, the same way a rendering strategy is chosen because it fits the page, not out of habit.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Scoping the storyboard wall (collaborative canvas)
workedExamples.problem: Scoping the storyboard wall (collaborative canvas)
steps: **Hard problem:** two people move and recolor the same card at the same time, one of them offline, and every replica ends up identical. Approach: per-property last-writer-wins registers with Lamport clocks (Exercise s13-e1), and a CRDT library for text inside cards.

**Bars:** 500 cards, dragging at 60 fps on a mid-range laptop, INP ≤ 200 ms for "add card," keyboard move with the arrow keys plus an announced position ("Card 'Night exterior' moved to column 3, row 2").
**Cuts:** no comments, no image uploads (placeholder colors instead), no permissions beyond "anyone with the link." All documented.
**Week 1 slice:** two browser tabs syncing through a tiny WebSocket relay, with the convergence tests passing.
workedExamples.conclusion: The capstone is judged on the hard problem done well, measured against bars you stated in advance, not on the number of features.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What must a capstone center on?
What three properties must a convergent (LWW) merge have?
interleaved (s8) — Why build once in CI rather than trust a local build?

Section 3 matched old and new list items by key, Section 4's LRU cache was keyed by request, and Section 5 merged a refreshed feed head by id, not position. What plays the same "identity, not arrival order" role in the storyboard's Lamport-clock merge?

Section 3 chose a rendering strategy to fit a page's real constraints instead of using one default everywhere. How does that same discipline show up in choosing a capstone niche and its one hard problem?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 13.2: The Case Study

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Structure a case study around decisions and trade-offs, not features. (objective o2)
2. Show alternatives considered, evidence, and outcomes. (objective o2)
3. Write "what I'd change" honestly. (objective o2)

terms.definition: A narrative of a project that shows how you think: the problem, constraints, decisions, trade-offs, results, and reflection.
A choice, the alternatives, the reason, and the cost accepted (s11's ADR format).
Measurements, test results, user observations, and screenshots that support a claim.

contentBlocks.content:
### Decisions, not features

"It has drag and drop, dark mode, and real-time sync" describes *what*. Interviewers want *why* and *what you gave up*. A case study that describes features misses the point (misconception `senior-narrative-and-portfolio.m2`).

**Template (about 1,200–1,800 words, plus visuals):**

1. **Problem and audience:** who it's for, and what's hard about it (one paragraph).
2. **Constraints and bars:** the numbers from Lecture 13.1.
3. **Three to five decisions**, each with the choice, the alternatives considered, why, and the cost accepted.
4. **Trade-offs I'd revisit.**
5. **Outcome:** measured against the bars, with the evidence.
6. **What I'd change next time:** concrete and non-defensive.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s13-m4): A case-study page layout. A long-form page with a hero (one-sentence hard problem, a 20-second demo loop), a constraints box with the bars as numbers, three decision cards (choice, alternatives, why, cost, evidence), a trade-offs section, an outcome table measured against the bars, and a closing "What I'd change" section. Diagrams appear alongside each decision.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: case studies
contentBlocks.content:
- **A feature tour.**
- **Decisions with no alternatives.**
- **Outcomes with no numbers.**
- **A "what I'd change" section that's really a humble-brag.**
- **Walls of text with no diagrams or screenshots.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 13.2 summary
contentBlocks.content: - Problem → constraints → decisions (with alternatives, why, and cost) → trade-offs → measured outcome → what I'd change.

interactionSequence.prompt: A case study's "Decisions" section reads: "It has drag and drop, dark mode, and real-time sync." What's missing, and what should replace it?
options: That describes what exists, not why it was chosen or what was given up; replace it with 3-5 decisions, each stating the choice, the alternatives considered, the reason, and the cost accepted
Nothing; listing the features clearly is exactly what a case study should do
It should be expanded into a longer feature list with screenshots for each one
It should be shortened to just the single most impressive feature

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Interviewers want *why* and *what you gave up* — a feature tour answers neither.
A feature tour is the exact error this lecture names: it describes *what*, not *why* or *what you gave up*, which is what a reviewer is actually evaluating.
More features, more screenshots — this is still a feature tour, just a longer one; it still names no decision, no alternative, and no cost.
Trimming to one feature still describes *what*, not *why*; the fix is structural (decisions with alternatives and cost), not length.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A case study is a narrative of decisions: the choice made, the alternatives considered, why, and the cost accepted — not a list of what got built.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: A case study's "Outcome" section says: "It felt a lot faster and users seemed happier." What's the fix?
options: Replace it with measured evidence against the stated bars: numbers from tests, RUM, or user observations, like "pan INP went from 340ms to 90ms, tested across 3 replicas"
Nothing; a qualitative impression is honest and that is enough for an outcome section
Add more adjectives to make the improvement sound more convincing
Remove the outcome section entirely, since results can't really be proven

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. "Outcomes with no numbers" is one of the common errors this lecture names — evidence means measurements, test results, and observations tied to the bars set in Lecture 13.1.
"Felt faster" and "seemed happier" are exactly the un-evidenced outcome this lecture flags as a common error — there is nothing here a reviewer can verify or compare to the stated bars.
More adjectives make the claim sound stronger without making it any more true or verifiable; the fix is numbers, not enthusiasm.
An outcome section measured against the bars is one of the six required parts of the template — removing it removes the proof the decisions actually worked.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Evidence means measurements, test results, and user observations, tied back to the bars from Lecture 13.1 — "felt faster" is a claim; "pan INP dropped from 340ms to 90ms" is evidence.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 5's design docs justified each decision with evidence and a rejected alternative, and Section 11's ADRs recorded a decision, its alternatives, and its cost. What do those two formats share with the "choice, alternatives, why, cost, evidence" shape a case-study decision needs, and why does that shape make a decision defensible under pushback later, in Lecture 13.5?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: All three formats (a design-doc justification, an ADR, and a case-study decision) record the same underlying discipline: state the choice, name the alternatives that were seriously considered, give the reason, and be explicit about the cost accepted. That shape is what makes a decision defensible later, because when someone pushes back ("why not locking instead of merges?"), the alternative and its rejection reason are already written down — you're not inventing a justification on the spot, you're restating one you already worked out, which is exactly the constraint → cost → conditional structure Lecture 13.5 asks you to use live.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Write one sentence describing your own (or a planned) capstone's hard problem, followed by one decision in the case-study shape: choice, alternative rejected, why, and cost accepted.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong answers name a specific hard problem (not "make it fast" or "make it nice"), a real alternative that was seriously considered and rejected (not a strawman), a concrete reason tied to the project's actual constraints, and a cost that is honestly a downside — not a humble-brag disguised as a cost ("my code was too elegant" is not a cost).

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: One decision, written well
workedExamples.problem: Decision: per-property last-writer-wins with Lamport clocks for card layout; a text CRDT only inside card descriptions.
steps: **Alternatives considered:** (a) a full-document CRDT for everything, (b) server-authoritative locking ("someone is editing this card").

**Why:** layout conflicts are rare and low-stakes (the last move wins, which matches what users expect), and LWW registers are small and easy to reason about and test. Text needs character-level merging, so it gets a proven CRDT library. Locking felt heavy for a brainstorming tool and fails when a user goes offline.
**Cost accepted:** simultaneous moves of the same card resolve to one winner, and the other user sees their card jump — mitigated with a 300 ms highlight showing who moved it (presence).
**Evidence:** a property test with 10,000 random operation orderings across 3 replicas, all converged. The two-tab offline demo is in the video.
workedExamples.conclusion: One decision told this way shows system design, testing, UX judgment, and honesty, all in one paragraph.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What are the six parts of a case study, and why isn't a feature list enough?
What four things should each decision in a case study include?

Section 5's design docs and Section 11's ADRs both recorded a decision, its alternatives, and its cost. What's the case-study equivalent of that same shape, and why does having it written down help under live pushback?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 13.3: The Portfolio

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Curate the capstone plus three or four earlier builds for depth and coverage. (objective o3)
2. Write a "why it matters" note for each piece. (objective o3)
3. Apply s12's visual standards to the portfolio itself. (objective o3)

terms.definition: Choosing few, deep pieces that together cover the skills you want to be hired for.
Two or three sentences: the hard problem, your decision, and the result.
The set of competencies your chosen pieces demonstrate between them.

contentBlocks.content:
### Fewer, deeper

More projects don't make a stronger portfolio (misconception `senior-narrative-and-portfolio.m1`). A reviewer spends minutes, not hours. Five deep pieces, each with a clear hard problem, a decision, and evidence, beat twenty screenshots. Choose for **coverage**: the capstone, plus earlier builds that add *different* skills. For example: the s6 performance changelog (measurement), the s7 accessible widgets (a11y depth), the s10 spring sheet (motion craft), the s11 design system (systems thinking).

### The portfolio is itself a design artifact

Apply s12: a type scale, a comfortable measure, one accent color, clear hierarchy (project title → why it matters → link to the case study → demo), fast (s6), accessible (s7), and respectful of reduced motion (s10). A portfolio for a design-engineering role *is* part of the interview.

contentBlocks.altText: Image (s13-m2): Portfolio home page wireframe. Five project cards in a column (not a grid of 20 thumbnails): each has a title, a two-line "why it matters," tags for the skills shown, and links to "Case study" and "Live demo." The capstone card is first and larger. A side note lists the checks: Lighthouse and field-style metrics, a keyboard pass, and contrast.

contentBlocks.caption: Twenty projects or five? Predict both understood-percentage lines before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: portfolios
contentBlocks.content:
- **A gallery of everything you've ever built.**
- **Screenshots with no explanation.**
- **Broken demo links.**
- **A slow, inaccessible portfolio for a frontend role.**
- **No clear first piece.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 13.3 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Capstone first, then 3–4 deep pieces chosen for coverage, each with "why it matters."
- The portfolio itself shows your craft.

interactionSequence.prompt: **Twenty projects or five?.** Write down the exact output, line by line, before you run it. Commit to an answer even if you're unsure — the gap between your prediction and the real output is what teaches you something.

codeExercise.explanation:
**Actual output:**

```text
gallery: 2 of 20 pieces understood (10%)
curated: 2 of 5 pieces understood (40%)
```

**Why intuition fails.** It seems that more projects give the reviewer more reasons to say yes. Their attention is fixed, though: in both cases they understand about two pieces. With a gallery, *which* two is random, and your best work may be among the 90% never read. With curation, you choose the two that get seen, the capstone first, and each has a clear "why it matters." This is misconception `senior-narrative-and-portfolio.m1`. *(These are illustrative numbers. The point is the fixed attention budget.)*

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: It seems that more projects give the reviewer more reasons to say yes. Their attention is fixed, though: in both cases they understand about two pieces. With a gallery, *which* two is random, and your best work may be among the 90% never read. With curation, you choose the two that get seen, the capstone first, and each has a clear "why it matters." This is misconception `senior-narrative-and-portfolio.m1`. *(These are illustrative numbers. The point is the fixed attention budget.)*
hints: A reviewer's attention (in minutes) is fixed in both plans — what changes between the two plans is only how many pieces divide that fixed budget.
Whose choice is it, in the curated plan, WHICH two pieces the reviewer actually understands?

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your prediction?

interactionSequence.prompt: A portfolio shows all twenty projects from the course, each as a thumbnail with no explanation, "to show range." What's the actual effect?
options: A reviewer's attention is fixed at a few minutes; spreading it over twenty shallow pieces means most of them, possibly the best one, are never actually read
It works as intended — more projects always give a stronger impression of range and effort
It has no real effect either way, since reviewers eventually see everything
The fix is simply better thumbnail images, not fewer projects

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Reviewer attention is the scarce resource; a gallery just makes it more likely your best work is among the pieces that never get read.
This is the misconception this lecture names directly: reviewer attention is fixed, so more projects doesn't mean more gets understood — it means each one gets less.
Reviewers spend minutes, not hours; "they'll get to it eventually" assumes an amount of attention this lecture explicitly says doesn't exist.
A gallery of twenty pieces, however well photographed, still spreads a fixed attention budget over twenty shallow entries instead of a few deep, explained ones.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Curation is the signal of judgment. Choose the capstone plus 3-4 pieces for coverage — different skills, not just different projects — and put a two-to-three-sentence "why it matters" note in front of each one.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Which "why it matters" note is stronger, and why?
options: "Gesture-driven rest-timer sheet: velocity-based snapping with a spring integrator I wrote from scratch, keyboard and reduced-motion paths included. Shows I can make direct manipulation feel physical and stay accessible." — it names the hard problem, the decision, and why a reviewer should care
"A bottom sheet built with React and springs." — it is shorter, and shorter is always better in a portfolio
Neither; a portfolio card should have no text at all, only a screenshot
The weak version, because it avoids sounding boastful about the spring integrator

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. In two sentences it names the hard problem (physical-feeling gestures), the decision (a spring integrator written from scratch), and the payoff (physical *and* accessible) — everything a reviewer needs to decide whether to click through.
"Built with React and springs" is a stack list, not a note on why it matters — it tells a reviewer nothing about the hard problem or the decision behind it.
A card with no text forces a reviewer to guess the hard problem from a screenshot alone, which is strictly less information than two well-written sentences.
Naming a specific technical decision (writing the integrator from scratch) isn't boastful — it's exactly the evidence a reviewer needs; avoiding it removes the signal.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong "why it matters" note names the hard problem, your decision, and the result, in two or three sentences — the same "decision, not feature" discipline as the case study, compressed.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: The portfolio itself is a design artifact, not just a container for your work. Name one Section 12 visual-design principle this lecture reuses for the portfolio page, and explain what it would look like to violate it here.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Section 12's principles this lecture reuses include a clear type scale and comfortable measure, one accent color, and clear hierarchy (project title → why it matters → case-study link → demo). Violating hierarchy here would mean, for example, giving every project card the same visual weight with no clear "read this first" signal, or burying the capstone (which should be first and larger) among the other 3-4 pieces as just another equally-sized card — a reviewer with a few minutes would then have no cue for where to start.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Writing "why it matters"
workedExamples.problem: Writing "why it matters"
steps: **Weak:** "A bottom sheet built with React and springs."

**Strong:** "Gesture-driven rest-timer sheet: velocity-based snapping with a spring integrator I wrote from scratch, keyboard and reduced-motion paths included. Shows I can make direct manipulation feel physical *and* stay accessible."
workedExamples.conclusion: The strong note names the hard problem, the decision, and why a reviewer should care, in two sentences.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What's the portfolio rule for how many pieces to include, and chosen for what?
How does a "why it matters" note differ from a plain project description or a tech-stack list?

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 13.4: Behavioral Stories with Clear Ownership

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Write stories in STAR+L form: Situation, Task, Action, Result, Learning. (objective o4)
2. Make your individual contribution unmistakable. (objective o4)
3. Prepare four core stories: a migration, an incident, a disagreement, mentoring. (objective o4)

terms.definition: Situation (brief context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what *you* did, the bulk of the story), Result (measurable outcome), Learning (what you'd carry forward).
How far your impact reached: your code, your team, several teams, the organization.
What the interviewer is looking for in a story: ownership, judgment, collaboration, growth.

contentBlocks.content:
### "I," specifically

"We migrated to TypeScript" tells the interviewer that it happened, not what *you* did. Saying "we" throughout to sound collaborative hides the signal (misconception `senior-narrative-and-portfolio.m3`). Use "I" for your actions and "we" for team context: "I proposed the incremental plan, wrote the codemod, and paired with the two teams most affected. We then moved 40% of the codebase in a quarter." Collaboration shows through the *actions* you describe (aligning people, unblocking them, mentoring), not through the pronoun.

### The four stories

| Story | What it signals | Senior-level detail to include |
|---|---|---|
| **A migration you drove** (for example the shot-list app from class components to hooks and TS) | technical leadership, incremental risk management | how you sequenced it, measured progress, and kept shipping |
| **An incident you owned** (the dailies player crashing for one studio during a premiere) | ownership under pressure, systems thinking | detection, mitigation (kill switch, s8), root cause, the prevention you put in place |
| **A disagreement you resolved** (designers wanted a custom date picker, you wanted native) | influence without authority, judgment | how you found shared goals, the evidence (an accessibility test), and the outcome for both sides |
| **Someone you mentored** (a junior engineer on their first performance project) | multiplying others | what you did specifically, how they grew, and what you learned about teaching |

contentBlocks.altText: Diagram (s13-m5): STAR+L proportions. Two horizontal stacked bars for the same story. Weak version: Situation 50%, Task 10%, Action 20%, Result 15% (no numbers), Learning 5%, with "we" highlighted six times. Strong version: Situation 15%, Task 10%, Action 50% (with "I" highlighted), Result 15% (with numbers), Learning 10%.

contentBlocks.title: Try to break the claim
contentBlocks.content: The claim: **counting whole-word "I" versus "we" in the Action alone is a fast, useful proxy for whether a story hides individual ownership.** Edit the `after` story below to add two more "we" sentences and predict both counts before running.

contentBlocks.caption: "I" vs "we" in a story's Action, before and after a rewrite. Predict both lines before running.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: behavioral stories
contentBlocks.content:
- **"We" throughout.**
- **All situation, little action.**
- **Results with no measure.**
- **Blaming others in the disagreement or incident story.**
- **Stories that are really about the technology, not about you.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 13.4 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- STAR+L with the action as the longest part, "I" for your actions, and measurable results.
- Four core stories: migration, incident, disagreement, mentoring.

interactionSequence.prompt: A migration story says: "We migrated to TypeScript over a quarter. It went well." What signal is missing, and what should replace "we"?
options: It tells the interviewer the migration happened, not what the candidate specifically did; replace it with "I" for the candidate's own actions (proposing the plan, writing tooling, pairing with teams) and "we" only for genuine team outcomes
Nothing; "we" sounds collaborative and modest, which interviewers prefer
The fix is to add more detail about the technology, like which TypeScript version was used
The story should be rewritten entirely in the passive voice to sound more objective

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. "I" for your actions and "we" for team context is the rule; collaboration shows through the actions described (aligning people, unblocking them, mentoring), not through the pronoun chosen.
Saying "we" throughout to sound collaborative is the exact misconception this lecture names — it hides the individual signal an interviewer is listening for.
More technical detail doesn't fix a story that never says what the candidate personally did — the missing piece is ownership, not the TypeScript version.
The passive voice ("TypeScript was adopted") removes ownership even more completely than "we" does; it is a worse version of the same problem, not a fix.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Use "I" for your actions — the bulk of the story — and "we" for real team context and outcomes. Collaboration is shown through what you describe doing with others, not through avoiding "I".

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: In STAR+L, a candidate's story spends 50% on Situation, 10% on Task, 20% on Action, 15% on Result (no numbers), and 5% on Learning. What's wrong with these proportions?
options: Action should be the longest part — it's where individual contribution and judgment show — and the Result needs a measurable number, not a vague outcome
Nothing; a long, detailed Situation shows thorough context-setting, which interviewers value most
The proportions are fine, but the story should be told in reverse chronological order
The Learning section should be removed since it rarely matters to interviewers

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. This is the weak-version proportions this lecture's diagram calls out directly: heavy on setup, light on action, and no number in the result.
A long Situation at the expense of Action is exactly the "all situation, little action" error named in this lecture — Action is where the signal (ownership, judgment) actually lives.
Reordering the sections doesn't fix proportions that under-weight Action and give no measurable Result; the structure (S-T-A-R-L in order) isn't the problem here.
Learning is one of the five STAR+L parts and signals growth and transferable judgment; dropping it removes a required part of the story, not an optional one.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong STAR+L proportions run roughly Situation 15%, Task 10%, Action 50% (with "I"), Result 15% (with numbers), Learning 10% — Action carries the story because it is where your specific judgment and ownership are visible.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Rewrite this into a stronger Action sentence, keeping it to two sentences: "We had a lot of performance issues on the call-sheet page, so we decided to fix them. We added code splitting and it got much faster."

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A strong rewrite uses "I" for the candidate's specific, sequenced actions and defers "we" only to genuine team steps: for example, "I profiled real sessions with RUM attribution and found that toggling crew departments re-rendered 900 rows, so I colocated that state, virtualized the crew list, and moved a PDF-preview library behind a component-level split. I then wrote the changelog tying each fix to a metric and walked the team through it so they could keep the budget." The key changes: specific technical actions attributed to "I", the diagnosis step included (not just the fix), and a measurable trigger ("900 rows") instead of a vague "a lot of issues."

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Name the four core behavioral stories this lecture asks you to prepare, and for each, name the ONE signal it's meant to demonstrate.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: A migration you drove (technical leadership and incremental risk management), an incident you owned (ownership under pressure and systems thinking), a disagreement you resolved (influence without authority and judgment), and someone you mentored (multiplying others' impact). Each should be a genuinely different story, not variations on the same anecdote, since interviewers use different rounds to probe different signals.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Rewriting a "we" story
workedExamples.problem:
**Before:** "We had a lot of performance issues on the call-sheet page, so we decided to fix them. We added code splitting and it got much faster."

**After (STAR+L):**
steps: **S:** The call-sheet page was used by assistant directors on set, on old tablets. Field p75 INP was 480 ms.
**T:** I owned the page and was asked to get it under 200 ms before the next production started.

**A:** I profiled real sessions with RUM attribution and found the slow interaction (toggling crew departments) re-rendered 900 rows. I colocated the toggle state, virtualized the crew list, and moved a PDF-preview library behind a component-level split. I wrote the changelog tying each fix to a metric and walked the team through it so they could keep the budget.
**R:** p75 INP dropped to 150 ms. Support tickets about "frozen tablets" went from 12 a month to 1.
**L:** Measure the interaction users complain about, not the page load. And make the budget the team's, not mine.
workedExamples.conclusion: "I" appears for each action, the result is measured, and the learning is transferable.

retrievalPractice.prompt: Which part of a STAR+L story should be longest, and told with which pronoun?
Name the four core behavioral stories to prepare.

learningExperiences.title: Lecture 13.5: The Full Loop

contentBlocks.content:
## Learning objectives

By the end of this lecture you will be able to:

1. Run two complete mock loops: frontend engineer and design engineer. (objective o5)
2. Apply the talk track (s4), the design structure (s5), and your stories (Lecture 13.4) under time pressure. (objective o5)
3. Write a self-review that turns each loop into a practice plan. (objective o5)

terms.definition: A set of interviews for one role on one day (or several days).
Typically: a coding round (algorithms or a UI component), frontend system design, a JavaScript/browser deep dive, and behavioral.
Typically: a UI build or prototype round, a portfolio walkthrough with critique, a design-system or interaction discussion, and behavioral.
A structured reflection per round: what went well, what didn't, the evidence, and one practice action.

contentBlocks.content:
### Two loops to rehearse

| Round | Frontend engineer loop | Design engineer loop |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Coding (45 min): a timed problem with a follow-up (s4) | Build (60 min): implement a small interactive component from a spec, with a11y and motion (s7, s10) |
| 2 | Frontend system design (45 min, s5) | Portfolio walkthrough + critique (45 min, s12, this section) |
| 3 | JS/browser deep dive (45 min, s1–s3, s6) | Design system / interaction discussion (45 min, s11, s10) |
| 4 | Behavioral (45 min: your four stories) | Behavioral (45 min: your four stories) |

Remember the communication lessons from s4. Silence isn't efficient (`live-problem-solving-communication.m1`). The process is graded, not only the answer (`.m2`). A follow-up usually means you're doing well and they're probing for depth (`.m3`).

### Self-review format (per round)

| Dimension | Score 1–5 | Evidence from the recording | One practice action |
|---|---|---|---|

Turn the lowest two dimensions into your next week's parallel-track and practice plan.

contentBlocks.captionOrTranscript: Video (s13-m3): Anatomy of a strong portfolio walkthrough. Production brief: A 5-minute edited mock: the candidate opens with the capstone's hard problem in one sentence, shows the live demo for 60 seconds, walks through two decisions with alternatives and trade-offs, handles a critique question ("why not locking?") with constraint → cost → conditional (s5), and closes with what they'd change. Captions highlight each technique as it happens.

contentBlocks.title: Common errors: loops
contentBlocks.content:
- **Practicing rounds in isolation, never a full day.**
- **No recording, so the self-review has no evidence.**
- **Reusing one story for every behavioral prompt.**
- **Treating the portfolio walkthrough as a demo** instead of a decision narrative.
- **Self-reviews without a practice action.**

contentBlocks.title: Lecture 13.5 summary
contentBlocks.content:
- Rehearse both loops fully, record them, and self-review with evidence.
- Each loop produces a practice plan for the next week.

interactionSequence.prompt: Ten minutes into the coding round of the frontend engineer loop, a candidate goes silent while typing, then presents finished code. What's the risk, and what should happen instead?
options: An interviewer can't grade reasoning they never heard; narrate intent while coding ("now I restore the invariant by shrinking the active set") the way s4's talk track describes
There's no real risk, since silence while coding is the most efficient way to actually produce correct code
The candidate should narrate every keystroke and syntax choice instead, to fill the silence
Silence is fine as long as the final code passes all the tests

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. Silence isn't efficient from a grading standpoint — the interviewer can only credit reasoning they actually hear.
Silence while coding is exactly this section's callback to `live-problem-solving-communication.m1` — an interviewer can't grade reasoning they can't observe.
Narrating syntax ("now a for loop") isn't the fix either; the talk track calls for narrating *intent*, not mechanical narration of every character typed.
Rubrics in this section's loops score problem understanding, approach, testing, and communication separately from the final code — passing tests silently still loses the communication dimension.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Narrate intent, not syntax, continuously while coding. The process is graded alongside the result — silence forfeits credit for reasoning the interviewer never got to hear.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: Partway through a portfolio walkthrough, the interviewer asks: "Why didn't you use locking instead of merges?" The candidate has already presented working, deployed code. What does the question most likely mean?
options: They're probing the trade-off reasoning behind an already-working design, not signaling it's wrong; answer with the design's constraint, the cost of the question's alternative, and the conditional under which you'd switch
The design must actually be wrong, since a working interviewer wouldn't ask otherwise
It's time to abandon the current explanation and pivot to a different project entirely
Only the live demo matters at this point, so the best response is to show more features instead of answering

optionFeedback.feedback: Right. A follow-up after a working design is almost always a probe for depth, not a verdict — answer it with constraint → cost → conditional, the same structure Section 5 teaches for design-session pushback.
A follow-up question after you've already shown a working system usually means you've met the baseline and they're now probing for depth, not signaling failure.
Pivoting away from the question avoids engaging with the interviewer's reasoning entirely, which reads worse than a direct, structured answer.
The reasoning behind a design choice is exactly what's being graded here, not just the demo; dodging into more features answers a different question than the one asked.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Treat pushback as a probe, not a verdict. Restate the constraint that drove the decision, name the cost of the alternative being asked about, and state the conditional under which you'd actually choose it.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in this answer?

interactionSequence.prompt: After recording a full mock loop, fill out one self-review row: a dimension (clarifying, approach, code, testing, communication, or follow-ups), a 1-5 score, one piece of evidence from the recording (a timestamp or a quote, not a vague impression), and one specific, checkable practice action.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong self-reviews cite something concrete from the recording ("at 6:40 I started coding before restating the constraint on empty input") rather than a vague feeling ("I could communicate better"), and commit to one checkable action for next time ("I will say the invariant out loud before I write the first line" is checkable; "be more confident" is not). Turn your two lowest-scoring dimensions across both loops into next week's practice plan.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

interactionSequence.prompt: Section 4's talk track structured a 45-minute coding round (clarify, examples, approach, code, test, follow-ups) and Section 5 gave you constraint → cost → conditional for handling pushback in a design session. Which of those two do you draw on for the design engineer loop's portfolio-walkthrough-plus-critique round, and why does the same structure work there even though nothing is being coded live?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: The portfolio walkthrough and critique round draws on Section 5's pushback structure (constraint → cost → conditional), because a critique question about a shipped, already-built decision ("why not locking?") is functionally the same kind of probe as a design-session follow-up — it's asking you to defend a trade-off, not to solve a new problem live. It works without any live coding because the underlying skill isn't writing code under time pressure; it's making your past reasoning legible and defensible on demand, which is exactly what constraint → cost → conditional is built for.

confidencePrompt.prompt: How confident are you in your explanation?

workedExamples.title: Timing a coding round
workedExamples.problem: Problem: "Given clips on an edit timeline, return all pairs that overlap on the same track." (This is Exercise s13-e5.)
steps: **Minutes 0-4, clarify:** is end exclusive? Do touching clips overlap? Pairs across tracks? Sizes (n up to 10⁴)? Output order?
**Minutes 4-7, examples:** worked on the board, including touching clips and a clip overlapping two others.

**Minutes 7-10, approach:** brute force is O(n²). Sort each track by start and sweep with an active set, which is O(n log n + k). Invariant: "active holds the clips on this track that haven't ended before the current start."
**Minutes 10-28, code:** narrating intent while writing it.
**Minutes 28-36, test:** dry-runs the touching case and a triple overlap, and fixes a `<` vs `<=` bug calmly.
**Minutes 36-45, follow-up:** "What if clips stream in live from collaborators?" Discusses an interval tree, or a sorted structure per track with incremental updates.
workedExamples.conclusion: The candidate showed pattern recognition (intervals), invariants, testing, and follow-up reasoning, which is the full set of signals.

retrievalPractice.prompt: What are the four rounds of the frontend engineer loop, and of the design engineer loop?
What should a self-review of a mock round produce, per dimension?
interleaved (s5) — What's the answer structure for handling pushback, whether in a design session or a portfolio critique?

learningExperiences.title: Lab: Proving It

contentBlocks.title: How your code is checked
contentBlocks.content:
Exercises run in the course engine, which provides a Jest-compatible subset (describe/it/expect, common matchers, beforeEach/afterEach, jest.fn), not Jest itself. There is no module mocking, no snapshots and no fake timers, so wherever time matters, the code you write accepts a clock or scheduler you can control. The engine exercises here are the cores of the capstone options (a convergent merge, decimation, undoable operations), a timed mock-round problem, and checkers that hold your case study, stories, and portfolio to this section's standards.

JavaScript runs entirely in your browser and works offline.

## How this lab is sequenced

Challenges 1 and 5 give you fixtures (two editors, a timeline of clips) and leave the core algorithm to you. Challenges 2, 3, and 4 give you a starter that only checks the easy cases and leave the rest of the checker logic to you. Challenge 5 is also a **timed mock round**: do it cold, recorded, following the s4 talk track, before you look at the hints. The two test-suite challenges turn the direction around: first you write tests against decimation code that's already correct, then you fix a screenplay editor's undo logic against tests that are already written.

These five challenges are starting points for the capstone's hard problem, not the whole capstone. The actual build — deployed, measured against the bars from Lecture 13.1 — is the Practical Activity below, and it runs over about three weeks.

contentBlocks.title: Check that your minMaxDecimate tests can fail
contentBlocks.content: After the decimation test-writing challenge, paste your suite into each playground below. Each wrong version is wrong in a specific, plausible way, and a good suite fails on all three.

## Practical activity

**Build: "Proving It."** The capstone runs over about three weeks. The guided portion covers planning, the case study, the portfolio, stories, and loops.

1. **The capstone** (one of the five options), deployed, with the bars from Lecture 13.1 in the README and verified at the end: lab median-of-5 for LCP, INP, and CLS; a keyboard-only video of the core flow; screen-reader smoke-test notes; axe clean; reduced-motion behavior; tests on the hard problem (start from s13-e1, s13-t1, or s13-t2 as fits); CI with previews; and error tracking. Written scope cuts. *(o1)*
2. **Case study** (1,200–1,800 words plus diagrams) that passes `checkCaseStudy`: problem, constraints and bars, 3–5 decisions with alternatives, reasons, and costs, trade-offs, a measured outcome, and what you'd change. *(o2)*
3. **Portfolio site:** the capstone plus the 3–4 pieces chosen with `curatePortfolio` from your course builds. Each has a two-sentence "why it matters," a live demo, and a case-study link. The site itself meets s6, s7, and s12 standards. *(o3)*
4. **Four behavioral stories** (migration, incident, disagreement, mentoring) in STAR+L, each passing `checkStory`, and each rehearsed out loud in under 3 minutes. *(o4)*
5. **Two full mock loops**, recorded, with peers or a mentor as interviewers: frontend engineer (coding using s13-e5 or an unseen problem, system design, JS/browser deep dive, behavioral) and design engineer (UI build, portfolio walkthrough and critique, design system and interaction, behavioral). **Self-review per round** in the Lecture 13.5 format, and a two-week practice plan from the two weakest dimensions. *(o5)*

contentBlocks.caption: Rubric for "Proving It" (100 points)
rows: A real hard problem solved well, bars stated first and met (or misses explained), accessible, deployed, instrumented.
Decisions with alternatives and costs, a measured outcome, an honest reflection.
Curated, "why it matters" notes, fast and accessible, visually coherent.
STAR+L, clear "I," measurable results, the four themes covered.
Both loops completed and recorded, evidence-based self-reviews, a concrete practice plan.

contentBlocks.title: Get real eyes on it (after the capstone and portfolio are live)
contentBlocks.content:
1. Share your portfolio with three people outside the course: a senior frontend or design engineer, a designer, and a recruiter or hiring manager if you can reach one. Ask each: "What do you think I'm best at, and which piece convinced you?" Compare their answers with what you intended.
2. Present your capstone at a local meetup, a company demo day, or an online community showcase (a 10-minute talk built from your case study's decisions). Note the questions you got. They're your next interview follow-ups.
3. Schedule at least one real interview loop, or an informational conversation with a team you'd like to join, within four weeks of finishing.

Nothing here is graded or gates your progress. Keep the feedback notes, the talk slides or recording, and a one-page "what I'll change before the next loop" as your last piece of course evidence.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 1 of 5: convergent merge for a collaborative storyboard

Implement `setProp(state, clientId, lamport, shapeId, prop, value)` (immutable) and `merge(a, b)`. Every property is a last-writer-wins register `{ value, clock: [lamport, clientId] }`, and the higher Lamport time wins, with ties broken by the larger `clientId` string. `merge` must be commutative, associative, and idempotent.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Merge property by property. Two people can change different properties of the same card without conflict.
The winner must not depend on which replica you call "local."
Tie-breaking must be deterministic and the same everywhere. A string comparison of client ids works.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 2 of 5: behavioral story checker

Implement `checkStory(story)` for `{ situation, task, action, result, learning }`. Return `{ ok, issues, iCount, weCount }`, with issues in this order:

1. `missing <section>` for each empty section.
2. `action says "we" more than "I"` when the Action has more whole-word "we" (any case) than "I" (capital).
3. `result has no measurable outcome` when the Result contains no digit.
4. `action is shorter than the situation` when the Action has fewer words than the Situation.

`iCount` and `weCount` count words in the Action only.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: `\b` word boundaries stop "we" from matching "weekly" or "welcome."
"I" is always capitalized in English, so count it case-sensitively.
The Action should be the longest part of the story.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 3 of 5: case-study structure check

Implement `checkCaseStudy(cs)` for `{ problem, constraints, decisions, tradeoffs, outcome, nextTime, features }`. Return `{ ok, issues }`, with issues in this order:

1. `missing <field>` for each of problem, constraints, tradeoffs, outcome, nextTime that is empty.
2. `lists features, not decisions` when `decisions` is empty or missing (even if `features` has entries).
3. For each decision at index *i* (1-based), `decision <i> has no alternatives` if `alternatives` is empty, and `decision <i> has no reason` if `why` is empty.
4. `outcome has no evidence` if the outcome has no digit.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Features describe *what*. Decisions record *why* and *instead of what*.
Number the decisions from 1 in messages, since that's how readers count.
"Evidence" here means at least one number: a metric, a count, a time.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 4 of 5: curate the portfolio

Implement `curatePortfolio(projects, maxPieces)` (default 5), returning ids. The capstone (`isCapstone`) comes first if it exists. Then projects are chosen **greedily by the number of new skills each adds**, with ties broken by newer `updated`, then `id`. Only projects that are `deep`, `deployed`, **and** `hasCaseStudy` are eligible. Stop at `maxPieces`, or when no eligible project adds a new skill.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Keep a set of covered skills. Each pick adds to it.
Recompute each candidate's gain after every pick, because gains shrink as coverage grows.
Eligibility is a filter *before* ranking, not a tiebreaker.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge 5 of 5 (timed round): overlapping clips on the timeline

Implement `findOverlaps(clips)`, where each clip is `{ id, track, start, end }` with `end` exclusive. Return all pairs `[a, b]` of clips on the **same track** whose time ranges overlap. Touching clips don't overlap. Within a pair, the clip that starts first comes first (ties by id). Pairs are sorted by first id, then second id. Target O(n log n + k).

*Do this one as a timed round: 45 minutes, recorded, following the s4 talk track. Score yourself with the rubric in s4's Practical Activity.*

**Do this one as a timed round: 45 minutes, recorded, following the s4 talk track.** Score yourself with the rubric from s4's Practical Activity, and compare your own timing against the coding-round worked example in Lecture 13.5.

Run **Check** as often as you like; each run shows which cases pass.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Compare your version with the reference, then read the note on the plausible wrong answer: it names the belief this exercise is built to expose.
hints: Which pattern from s4's map has "overlapping ranges" as its signal?
Sorted by start, a clip can only overlap clips that started earlier and haven't ended yet.
`end > start` (strict) is what makes touching clips *not* overlap.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: working min/max decimation for the dailies chart, you write the tests

**Brief:** `minMaxDecimate(points, buckets)` reduces a sorted series (`{ x, y }` by x) to at most `2 × buckets` points by keeping, for each equal-sized bucket, its minimum and maximum `y`, in **x order**. Inputs already at or below `2 × buckets` points are returned as a copy. It's correct. Write tests that catch the three hidden wrong versions. Think about spikes, order, the last bucket, and small inputs. Check runs your suite against the correct code (it must pass, with at least **four** tests). Then confirm your suite catches all three wrong versions in the playgrounds below.

codeExercise.solutionNote: The reference suite pins down four separate behaviors, one per hidden wrong version: keeping a spike a stride sample would skip (wrong version 1 samples every Nth point and can walk right past a one-frame exposure spike); the correct x order of the output (wrong version 2 always pushes min then max regardless of which comes first by x, so a bucket where the max occurs before the min comes out of order); the extreme surviving in the LAST bucket specifically (wrong version 3 drops the final bucket with an off-by-one on the loop bound); and small or empty input returned unchanged. A suite that only checks one typical bucket catches none of these — you need a case that isolates a spike, a case that checks x-ordering within a bucket, a case that checks the last bucket specifically, and the small/empty boundary.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Good tests here pin down what decimation must preserve (spikes, order, the last bucket), not just that it returns roughly the right number of points.
hints: Build a series with one obvious spike (like the frame-612 exposure spike in R2) and check the decimated output still contains it.
Check that the x values in the output are non-decreasing — a bug that pushes max before min by mistake still returns the right VALUES, just in the wrong order.
Check the LAST bucket specifically, and check that input already at or under 2 × buckets comes back unchanged.

interactionSequence.prompt:
### Challenge: broken undoable operations for the screenplay editor, make the tests pass

**Brief:** The screenplay editor's document model applies text operations and records their inverses for undo. `applyOp(doc, op)` returns `{ doc, inverse }`, and `applyAll(doc, ops)` returns `{ doc, undo }`, where applying `undo` in order restores the original. It has four bugs. Fix them.

codeExercise.solutionNote: a delete's inverse must *remember what was deleted* (the operation must be invertible). Undo replays inverses in **reverse** order (a stack, s4). Positions and lengths must be clamped, so the inverse describes what actually happened. Unknown operations must fail loudly. This is the core of the editor capstone's document model, and it's also exactly the kind of thing to put in its case study.

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Every bug here comes from an inverse that doesn't fully remember what happened, or an undo order that doesn't reverse the original sequence.
hints: Run the tests and read the first failure. Does the delete's inverse (an `insert`) actually remember the text that was removed?
`applyAll`'s `undo` array: should later operations be undone before or after earlier ones? What order does `push` give you, and is that the order you want?
What should happen when `pos` or `length` go past the end of the document, and what should happen for a completely unknown op type?

interactionSequence.prompt: When your capstone, case study, portfolio, stories, and two mock loops are all done, answer: which single piece of feedback (from a checker, a mock-round self-review, or someone outside the course) changed something you actually shipped, and what did you change?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Strong reports name a specific piece of feedback (not "the checker helped"), the exact change it produced (a rewritten decision, a restructured story, a dropped project from the portfolio, a fixed undo bug), and, where relevant, the misconception it traces back to. Check your five deliverables against the rubric table above before you consider the section done.

contentBlocks.content:
## Close the course in three moves

1. **Retrieve** without looking back: answer the four cues below from memory.
2. **Transfer** the curation, case-study, and story tools to two audiences with nothing to do with film production: a hospital scheduling team and an internal promotion packet.
3. **Prove it** in the Section 13 quiz and the four cumulative mastery checks that live here: `live-problem-solving-communication`, `frontend-system-design`, `client-data-management`, and `senior-narrative-and-portfolio` — the most of any section, because this is where the whole course closes.

contentBlocks.title: Everything this section reaches back to
contentBlocks.content: This is the last section, and it draws on nearly all of them by name: keyed identity from Sections 3-5 (now a Lamport-clock merge), rendering-strategy judgment from Sections 3, 6, and 10 (now capstone scoping), the talk track and pushback structure from Sections 4, 5, and 12 (now the full mock loop), and evidence-based decision writing from Sections 5, 11, and 12 (now the case study and stories). One retrieval item below is marked interleaved for each of these, on top of the ones already placed inside Lectures 13.1, 13.2, and 13.5.

interactionSequence.prompt: Before the quiz: which of this section's five deliverables (capstone, case study, portfolio, stories, or mock loops) would you least want to be reviewed cold right now, and why?

feedback.elaborativeFeedback: Naming the shaky deliverable precisely is what makes the last review useful. Re-read that lecture's summary and worked example, and if it's the mock-loop skill, re-watch the portfolio-walkthrough video before you open the quiz.

transferExercises.context: Switching fields: a hospital's clinical-scheduling team
transferExercises.scenario: You're interviewing for a senior frontend role building scheduling tools for nurses.
transferExercises.task: Choose which of your portfolio pieces to lead with and rewrite their "why it matters" notes for this audience. Then adapt one behavioral story (the incident) to show judgment in a safety-critical setting.
successCriteria: Re-curates rather than reuses the same lead piece unchanged — picks whichever pieces show skills this audience cares about most (data-dense, accessible, reliable UI), the same coverage logic as `curatePortfolio`, applied to a new audience.
Rewrites at least one "why it matters" note to name the hard problem, the decision, and the result in this audience's terms, not just swapping a few nouns.
Adapts the incident story with the same STAR+L shape and a clear individual "I", but reframes the stakes and the result around safety and trust rather than the original studio context.
Keeps every fact honest — adapting emphasis and framing for the audience, not inventing new events or exaggerating the original story's scope.

transferExercises.context: A promotion packet at your current company
transferExercises.scenario: Your manager asks for a promotion case to senior design engineer.
transferExercises.task: Reuse this section's tools: pick three projects (curation), write one decision-focused case study, and turn one "we" story from your last quarter into an "I" story with measured results. Say what you'd leave out, and why.
successCriteria: Applies the same eligibility and coverage logic as `curatePortfolio` (deep, deployed, documented work chosen for skill coverage) to internal work, not just course projects.
Writes one case-study decision in the full shape: choice, alternatives considered, why, cost accepted, and evidence — not a feature or a technology list.
Rewrites the "we" story with "I" for the candidate's own actions as the longest part, a measurable Result, and a transferable Learning.
Names at least one piece of real work explicitly left out, with a reason tied to coverage or depth, not just recency.
